A public GitHub repository is readable by anyone, indexed by search engines, and scanned continuously by automated tools that look for credentials and addresses. Secrets committed to one are often found and tried within minutes.

So prevention is the only real remedy, and the cheap time to catch a leak is before the commit. See Chapter 23 and Chapter 1.

docs.title: What should I record next to every benchmark result so it can be reproduced?
docs.text:
Write the pin down on day one. Next to every result you keep, record:

  • the exact model tag,
  • the model file's checksum,
  • the inference server version, and
  • the date.

A table of scores with no version beside each one cannot be reproduced and cannot be fairly compared. With a local deployment you can pin completely, because the weights file does not change unless you change it. With a cloud service you can request a specific version only while the provider offers it, and you cannot keep it past its deprecation, so a result recorded against a retired model can never be repeated.

The same habit extends to the rest of the stack. Chapter 8 pins the Python version and exports the environment, Chapter 12 verifies file checksums on download, and Chapter 19 turns "same harness, same prompts" into lines in a record that say what the value was and how you know. Pinning is a precondition of a fair benchmark, because a result is only meaningful for the version that produced it. See Chapter 4.

docs.title: What habits keep a remote-access setup from becoming a liability?
docs.text:
Chapter 7 calls them host hygiene, and five habits are enough:

  1. Keep private keys private. Never copy id_ed25519 to another machine, a chat, or a repository.
  2. Use one key per purpose. A separate key for the DGX project can be revoked without affecting anything else.
  3. Remove what you added. When the project ends, delete your public key from the server's authorized_keys and ask the administrator to remove the account.
  4. Tell the owner. Installing a key on a machine you do not own is a change to their security, and they are entitled to know.
  5. Read the output before saving it. A pasted SSH session contains hostnames and addresses, and Chapter 23 builds the review that catches them.

The first and fifth bear directly on this book's public repository. Git history is permanent, so a private key committed once is exposed for good, and a pasted terminal session can carry a hostname or an address into a chapter without anyone noticing. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Why take a read-only inventory first, and how do I do it?
docs.text:
A five-minute read-only look tells you whether a plan is possible before you install anything: the architecture, the free space, whether Docker answers. Finding out after a two-hour download that the disk is full is a much worse way to learn it. It is also the right first step on a machine that belongs to someone else, because it needs no permission to install or change anything.

A small set of standard Linux inventory commands covers the questions, and each prints a few lines and writes nothing:

Question Command Which operating system? grep PRETTY_NAME /etc/os-release Which kernel and architecture? uname -srm Which processor? lscpu How much memory? free -h How much disk? df -h / Which GPU and driver? nvidia-smi Are containers available? docker --version Which groups am I in? id -nG

To run a whole script without copying it to the machine, pipe it over SSH: ssh <user>@<dgx-host> 'bash -s' < inventory.sh > inventory.txt. The remote shell reads the script from standard input, so nothing is written to the DGX's disk.

Read the output before you save or share it. An inventory describes a specific machine, and some files, such as the DGX release file, contain a serial number. See Chapter 9.

docs.title: How do I stop a model from padding a section to reach its word target?
docs.text:
Treat the target as a guideline, not a quota. A model that sees "500 words" will often manufacture 500 words by restating itself. The remedy is to read a short section against its target and ask what is missing. If the answer is "nothing", the section is finished, and adding words only lowers quality.

The book's anti-padding rules state this as four instructions:

  1. Quality over quantity. A dense, correct section beats a padded one that reaches the number.
  2. Expand by showing, not telling. If a section is thin, add a worked example, another simulation, or more technical detail, and never restate earlier paragraphs.
  3. No formulaic templates. Avoid boilerplate such as "Let's talk about X" and weave concepts into flowing narrative.
  4. Examples over prose. Prefer a short commented example or a MicroSim to a long description of abstract logic.

Put these rules in a file the agent can re-read, as this book does in its content generation guide. A rule that lives only in a prompt is lost when the context fills up, while a rule in a file can be read again, and the same file makes two runs comparable. See Chapter 2.

docs.title: How should I read a model card?
docs.text:
Read it like a marketing page with facts in it. A model card is the document a publisher releases with a model, describing its purpose, training, benchmark results, limits, and license. It is the fastest way to learn the size, the context window, and the license, so read those fields first and trust them.

Treat everything else as the publisher's own claim, to be tested. Benchmark scores and statements of strength describe what the publisher optimized for. They do not describe the conditions under which the property fails, and your workload may be one of them. Never carry a card's score into your report as a measured result.

Apply three license questions to every model. Is commercial use allowed? Are there size or revenue exceptions? And is the license actually stated by the publisher, or only reported by a third party? This evaluation records a license that was reported without independent verification as "reported", not as confirmed. See Chapter 3 and Chapter 12.

docs.title: Which assumptions in a cost model deserve the most attention?
docs.text:
Find out by running a sensitivity analysis: change one assumption at a time, record how the output moves, restore it, and then change the next. Varying two together means you cannot say which one moved the answer. The cost analysis ran it on the reference case:

Change Cost per book Price at 20% margin Reference case $53 $66 Operations labor of 8 hours a month $81 $101 No operations labor $25 $32 Hardware at $9,000 $57 $72 Hardware at the launch price of $3,999 $47 $58 The three stages are 5% of the book $106 $132

The result is a ranking of what to worry about. Labor, and the share of the whole book that the benchmark's three stages represent, move the answer by as much as a factor of two. The hardware price moves it by about ten percent. A planner who spent a week negotiating the hardware price and an hour on the labor estimate had the effort the wrong way round.

Treat the cost model's output as a model, not a measurement, and respond to a surprising number by inspecting an assumption. See Chapter 6.

docs.title: How do I prove that my environment specification actually rebuilds?
docs.text:
A specification you have never rebuilt from is an unverified claim, and the rebuild is the test. Create a throwaway environment from the file, check that it works, compare its package list with the original's, and delete it:

conda env create -n dgx-test -f environment.yml
conda run -n dgx-test tailscale version
diff <(conda list -n dgx --export) <(conda list -n dgx-test --export)
conda env remove -n dgx-test

An empty diff means the rebuild matches. A few differing lines are the packages that were not pinned and resolved to a newer release, and they are exactly what to pin next.

Watch how you export. A full conda env export records exact builds that are specific to one platform. Taken on a Mac with an Arm laptop chip, it lists builds that do not exist for a Linux aarch64 DGX, and the rebuild fails with a list of packages that cannot be found. conda env export --from-history records only the packages you asked for and crosses platforms, at the price of letting each dependency resolve to whatever is current unless you pin it yourself.

Remember what a specification does not cover: the operating system, the GPU driver, system CUDA libraries, and model weights. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: What rules should every probe script follow?
docs.text:
A good probe script follows four rules, and each one prevents a specific failure:

Rule Failure it prevents Read only, never write A probe that changes the machine it is measuring Standard library only A probe that cannot run on a fresh machine without an install Bounded run time A probe that hangs forever when a tool misbehaves Report unknown as null, never guess A report that looks complete and hides a failed measurement

The last rule is the one people skip. A probe that returns zero when it cannot read a value turns a failed measurement into a machine with no memory. Return null for anything you could not read, and a reader can tell a missing measurement from a measured zero. Not Supported and [N/A] from nvidia-smi should become None, not 0.

The base of every probe is a helper that runs a command and returns its text, or None if the command is missing, fails, or takes longer than a timeout. A missing nvidia-smi on a machine without a GPU then produces an empty answer instead of a crash.

Standard library only is a deliberate cost. Without psutil, you read memory from /proc/meminfo and parse nvidia-smi text, but the probe runs on a machine that has nothing installed. See Chapter 10.

docs.title: What should I log during a long run, and how often?
docs.text:
Start vitals logging before any long run. Record a few measurements at a fixed interval, 30 seconds works well, so that a machine that fails leaves its last readings behind. Three are enough: available memory, GPU temperature, and GPU power draw.

import json, os, time

with open("vitals.txt", "a") as out:
    while True:
        gpu = probe_gpu()["gpus"]
        row = {"t": int(time.time()),
               "mem_available_gib": probe_ram()["available_gib"],
               "gpu_temp_c": gpu[0]["temperature_c"] if gpu else None,
               "gpu_power_w": gpu[0]["power_w"] if gpu else None}
        out.write(json.dumps(row) + "\n")
        out.flush()
        os.fsync(out.fileno())
        time.sleep(30)

The flush and fsync calls matter. They ask the operating system to put each line on the disk now, because a machine that freezes does not get to finish its buffers.

A machine that overheats or freezes cannot tell you what happened afterward, so the last line the log wrote becomes your evidence. This is the idea behind the project's log_vitals.sh script, which was added after a unit stopped responding and left no record of why. Pair the log with a watchdog that acts on the same readings, as Chapter 18 describes. See also Chapter 10.

docs.title: How do I decide which models are worth testing?
docs.text:
Start from the workload, not from a leaderboard. For this course's workload, which is running a long skill through an agent harness, four criteria cover it, and each can be checked before downloading:

Criterion Why the workload needs it Supports tool calling A harness acts only through tool calls Context window of at least 64,000 tokens The harness prompt alone takes about 19,000 tokens Fits with headroom A model that fits tightly can freeze a unified-memory machine Identifiable publisher and checkable terms A result cannot be recommended if readers cannot check the license

Read each candidate's model repository on the Hugging Face Hub, the main public site for sharing models, as the primary source: who published it, the license file, the model card, the file list, and the history.

Use leaderboards and public benchmark scores to build a long list, not to decide. They answer a question that is rarely yours, since a general-knowledge or coding score says little about whether a model follows a thousand-line skill or keeps a blank line before every list.

Read publisher claims as hypotheses. This evaluation's candidate page states each claim and then what testing found, for example a model "built for long agent tasks" that produced the cleanest learning graph and was by far the slowest. Neither tool-calling reliability nor writing quality can be read from a model's name; both are measured, in Chapter 19 and Chapter 20. See Chapter 12.

docs.title: Who should reach my inference endpoint, and how do I share it?
docs.text:
Start closed and open deliberately. An Ollama endpoint has no login of its own, so anyone who can send it a request can use the machine's GPU and tie up its memory. localhost binding keeps it private: the server listens only on 127.0.0.1, and a request from any other machine, even one on the same network, is refused before it reaches the server.

Confirm everything works there, and then choose how to share it with exactly the people who need it:

Method Who can reach the endpoint Changes on the DGX SSH port forward Only you, for as long as the forward runs None Tailscale Serve Tailnet members the access rules allow Needs the client and a command on the DGX Bind to all interfaces (0.0.0.0) Anyone who can reach the port A server setting

This evaluation used the SSH forward, because it costs nothing on the DGX and exposes nothing. Tailscale Serve publishes the loopback port to the tailnet over HTTPS while the server stays bound to loopback, and the access control list still applies. Check tailscale serve --help, because flags have changed across versions.

Binding to every interface to make a tutorial command work is a decision you cannot easily see later. After you open anything, test from a second machine that the endpoint is refused where you expect it to be. See Chapter 13.

docs.title: Which setting should I change first to speed up a run?
docs.text:
The one aimed at your bottleneck, and only one at a time. Performance optimization is changing a single setting and measuring the result against a fixed baseline. A comparison between two runs that differ in three settings tells you nothing about which one mattered.

First find where the time goes with a time breakdown: loading, reading, writing, and tool time. Then match the setting to the cause:

Setting What it moves What it costs Quantization to fewer bits Generation speed up, memory down Some quality Context length down Memory down, room for the system up Smaller conversations Keep-alive up Fewer reloads Memory held while idle Prompt caching working Prompt processing time down per turn Nothing, when it works Batching and concurrency up Throughput up Latency per request Sampling parameters The output, not the speed Different results

The last row is the trap. Temperature, top-p, and top-k change the output and have little effect on speed, so a reader looking for speed will not find it there, and a benchmark must fix and record them or its runs are not comparable. Quantization is the one dial that changes both speed and quality, so whether the loss matters is a measurement.

Batching helps a service that handles many sessions at once. For one benchmark session at a time, it is a lever left unused. See Chapter 15.

docs.title: How do I confirm a model works in the harness before a long run?
docs.text:
Run the three-minute test before the three-hour one. A model that fails the short skill will fail the long one more slowly. The check this project uses is a short run of the course-description analyzer skill, whose output can be inspected quickly. Skill execution verification passes when four things are true:

  • The report was written. The skill's output file exists.
  • A score was given. The report contains the quality score the skill is meant to assign.
  • The project files were updated. The frontmatter and the site navigation reflect the skill's work.
  • The site builds. A strict mkdocs build finishes with no errors.

A script applies exactly these four checks, so the verdict does not depend on someone reading the output. Put the analyzer run, with its scripted checks, in front of every model you intend to benchmark, and discard the ones that fail for reasons you can name.

A harness compatibility test runs the same short skill against several harness and model combinations, to find which pairs work at all. Failures at this stage are cheap and informative. In this evaluation it showed a model that wrote its first tool call as plain text and a model that lost the task after a few turns, both within minutes, and neither would have been found by a first-prompt smoke test, which tests only the server. See Chapter 17.

docs.title: How do I write a good evaluation question and choose metrics?
docs.text:
A good question names what is being compared, on what task, under what conditions, and what would count as an answer. The test is whether you can imagine two different outcomes. If you cannot, it is not a question for an experiment.

Poor question Why it fails Better question Which model is best? Best at what, for whom? Which candidate completes stages 1 to 3 on Algebra I with the fewest structural faults on one DGX unit? Is local cheaper than cloud? Mixes cost and price, and ignores quality What is the cost per textbook at the measured speed, and what would a service charge at a 20% margin? Does the DGX work? Nothing could ever answer "no" Does a local model produce a learning graph that passes structural checks within a 150-minute limit?

Then do metric selection, and do it before you see the data. A useful metric answers the question, can be computed the same way for every run, and was decided in advance. The evaluation groups them as completion (stage finished, files present, build succeeds), efficiency (wall-clock time, tool calls, failed tool calls, tokens, peak memory), and quality (structural checks, reading level, human review). Completion and efficiency are computed by a program and are repeatable. Quality matters most and is hardest to measure.

If you look at the data and then choose the measure that favors your favorite model, you have not run an experiment. Write the metrics and how each is computed into the record first, and add new ones afterward only as clearly labeled extras. See Chapter 19.

docs.title: What should I record about each run so the result can be checked later?
docs.text:
Logging is recording what happened during a run in enough detail to reconstruct it, because the log is the difference between a measurement and a memory, and a surprising result can only be investigated later if the record exists. This evaluation keeps six records for each run:

Record What it holds Answers The event stream Every message, tool call, and result What did the agent actually do? The final result Turns, token counts, timings How much did it use? The status file Exit code and wall-clock seconds Did it finish, and how long? The server log Loads, memory, request timings Why was it slow? The vitals log Memory, temperature, power every 30 seconds What did the machine look like? The configuration Versions, settings, dates Can this be repeated?

Then state your explicit assumptions and label every number as measured or assumed, the distinction the book calls measured versus assumed values. A measured value came from an observation in this evaluation, and an assumed one came from a rule, a published figure, or a guess. The cost analysis does this: six of its ten speeds are assumed, and it tests its own rule against the one case it can check. The rule predicted 34 tokens a second for one model, and the measured figure was 26. Reporting the miss is what makes the other assumptions credible.

Finally, keep a design decision record: what was chosen, what else was considered, and why, along with who decided. Attribution matters because a choice made by a person with a goal and a choice made by an assistant filling a gap deserve different scrutiny. See Chapter 19 and the Design Choices appendix.

docs.title: Why test a model on its own before testing it in the harness?
docs.text:
Because failures are cheap and diagnosable when the layers are separated. Two-layer testing runs a model-only test first, sending short, fixed tasks directly through the server with no harness, and then a harness smoke test.

Layer Time per model What a failure means Model-only test Minutes The model cannot follow a rule on its own, such as a blank line before a list Harness smoke test About three minutes The model cannot work through a skill with tools Full stage Tens of minutes to hours The model fails at scale, or is too slow

A model that fails the first layer fails in seconds and for a reason you can name. A model that passes it and fails the second fails for a reason that involves the harness. Going straight to the full pipeline makes every failure slow and mixes the causes. The project's model-only test has five tasks: Markdown writing, p5.js code, schema-constrained JSON, a tool call, and a 30,000-token prompt.

The 30,000-token task is a long-context recall test: a value is placed in a long block of text and the model is asked to return it. It found something the other tasks did not. One model returned the wrong value in two of its model-only runs and again in a third.

When a result traces to a faulty check or a faulty skill example, that is the evaluation working. Correct the defect, retest the models it touched, and note which conclusions changed. See Chapter 19.

docs.title: How do I calibrate a check before trusting it?
docs.text:
Test the checks themselves, on inputs whose answers you know, before you trust them on real output. Scoring check calibration matters because a check can be wrong in two directions: it can pass a bad result, or it can fail a good one. The second is easy to miss because it looks like a model failure.

This evaluation met it. The first versions of three model-only checks were too strict and failed output that was correct. Each was fixed and the saved output was scored again. Without that step, a model would have been marked down for a defect in the test.

A calibration set for a check is small:

  1. A known-good input that must pass.
  2. A known-bad input that must fail, for the reason it should.
  3. An edge case at the threshold. For a 32-character label limit, test a label of exactly 32 characters and one of 33.

Run the set whenever you change a check, and save raw output so you can rescore it without rerunning the model. The same idea at the level of the whole experiment is the retest after a fix: when a result traces to a faulty check, correct the defect, rescore or rerun what it touched, and note which conclusions changed. See Chapter 20 and Chapter 19.

docs.title: How should I report provisional, negative, and limited results?
docs.text:
Label them as what they are, with the same care as a success.

Provisional results are real observations that are not yet established, because they rest on too few runs, an unvalidated check, or an incomplete review. Every result from a first round is provisional. Use them to decide what to test next, not to write a recommendation.

Negative results are findings. A model that lost the task after a few steps, one that wrote its first tool call as plain text so the run ended after one turn, and one that could not fit a usable context all tell a reader choosing a model for their own machine more than the successes do. Report the failure, the evidence, and your best account of the cause, with your confidence stated, since several causes in this evaluation were never identified.

A limitations statement says what the result does not show. This evaluation's carries concrete items: each model was run once, so rankings are not supported; one course, one machine type, one harness, and one skills version; structural checks only, with no completed human review; no cloud baseline; six of ten speeds in the cost analysis assumed; and reasoning mode not held constant.

Then write a design critique before someone else does, pairing each flaw with its effect and its repair, such as "one run per model" with "rankings could be noise" and "three to five runs each". See Chapter 20.

docs.title: Why does the benchmark runner copy the starting directory for every run?
docs.text:
So that a run can never change its own input. The template is never the working copy: a run works on a copy, and the original stays byte for byte what it was. That is the whole mechanism by which a failed run, a killed run, or a run that wrote garbage cannot reach the next one. If a run changes its own starting point, you can never again say what it started from.

The benchmark runner does five things in order:

  1. Copies the starting directory to a fresh run directory.
  2. Starts the harness container with that directory mounted and the model's tag set.
  3. Feeds the prompt file in and captures every event.
  4. Stops the run at its time limit if the limit is reached.
  5. Records the exit code and the wall-clock seconds.

For stage 1 the starting directory is the benchmark workspace template, which holds the unchanged course description and the site configuration. For each later stage it is the previous stage's run directory, which is how work accumulates through stage chaining.

The time limits are 150 minutes for stage 1, 2 hours for stage 2, and 90 minutes for each chapter in stage 3. A run stopped by its limit exits with code 124 and keeps what it wrote, so a timeout is a result and not a lost run. See Chapter 21.

docs.title: When is it fair to leave a model off the shortlist?
docs.text:
When you can state the criterion that excluded it, and you have confirmed the cause. A model shortlist is the written list of candidates you will test, each with its reasons, and the exclusion rationale is the reason a model was left off. The second matters as much as the first, because a reader who sees a famous model missing will wonder whether you missed it. One line each, tied to a criterion, answers them. For example, this evaluation left out a 122-billion-parameter model because at 81 GB it was a very large download and gpt-oss:120b already covered the large tier.

The harder case is excluding a model for a fault. This evaluation set aside its fastest model partly for broken navigation files, and the fault turned out to be a faulty example in the skill that the model had copied. The model was set aside before it was retested against the corrected skill. It was retested afterward and passed the short skill test, which is the order to avoid. An exclusion based on a symptom needs the cause confirmed, and an exclusion that has not been retested should say so in its rationale.

So before you write that a model "cannot" do something, check whether the failure is in the model or in the setup around it: the skill, the harness configuration, or the prompt. Chapter 22 returns to this with a quick test, and Chapter 14 reminds you that one run is an observation, not a ranking. See Chapter 12.

docs.title: How many times should I repeat a run before trusting a result?
docs.text:
More than once, and the number depends on what you want to claim. A language model samples its output, and a long agent session takes a path that depends on small differences early on, so two runs of the same configuration are not the same run. Run variance is how much the results differ among repeated runs, and sample size is the number of runs behind a conclusion.

Runs per configuration What you can say 1 What happened; which things failed outright 3 Whether the result is stable, roughly 5 or more A typical value and a range, with caution

Here is why. Suppose a model finishes a stage in 20 minutes on one run and 45 on another, because in the second it made a wrong turn and recovered. A second model finishes in 30 minutes on its one run. Ranking the second ahead of the first from those numbers is a coin flip. With five runs of each, the spread is visible and the comparison can be stated with its uncertainty.

Nearly every result in this evaluation so far is one run, which is enough to find what fails and not enough to rank. Say so when you report it.

Add a control run: repeat a run that should give the same answer, to check the apparatus and not the subject. If the control differs from the original by more than the expected variation, something changed between them, such as memory pressure, a thermal state, or a server setting. A control is the first thing to do when a surprising number appears. See Chapter 19.

docs.title: How can I tell whether a cloud baseline is a fair comparison?
docs.text:
Ask three questions of any baseline:

  1. Did it use the same inputs?
  2. Is its configuration recorded?
  3. Was it scored by the same method as the thing you are comparing it to?

A baseline that fails any of the three is a reference point, and the comparison should call it that. A baseline comparison judges a result against a reference produced under the same rules, and a fair comparison is one in which the only meaningful difference between the two sides is the thing being compared.

This evaluation applies the test to itself, honestly. It has a reference for scale and not yet a baseline. The published Algebra I book was made with cloud models and has 200 concepts and 13 chapters of about 55,000 words, but:

Requirement for a fair comparison Satisfied by the published book? Same course description Yes Same skill versions No, earlier versions Same prompts Not recorded Timings and token counts recorded No Same scoring applied Not yet

The book shows how large a finished book is. It cannot say how long a cloud model takes or how good its output is under these exact conditions. The cloud baseline remains to be run, and until it is, the comparison should say "reference for scale". See Chapter 19 and Chapter 4.

docs.title: Should I use a language model to judge the generated chapters?
docs.text:
Only as an instrument you have calibrated, and with its costs in view. LLM-as-judge is fast, cheap, and scales to thousands of outputs, and it is also the largest source of bias in this kind of evaluation. Bias in evaluation is a systematic tilt toward some results for reasons unrelated to quality. Unlike noise, it does not average out over many runs: it points the same way every time.

Weakness What it does to a score Mitigation Self-preference Rates output like its own higher Use a different model family as judge Verbosity Rewards length Control for length, or score against a rubric Position Prefers the first candidate Randomize order and score twice Confidence Rewards fluent errors Require evidence for each rubric score Data exposure Sends generated text to a service Use a local judge, or do not use one

The last row has nothing to do with accuracy. Sending a local model's output to a cloud model to be scored sends the text to the cloud, which undoes the reason for generating it locally. This evaluation recorded that as the reason it did not use an LLM judge as its scoring method.

Treat a judge as another model under test. Calibrate it against human scores on a sample before you trust it on the rest. If its scores disagree with the people's on the cases you checked, it has told you something about itself, not about the outputs.

The right test of quality is blind human review: a person scores output against the rubric without knowing which model produced it, in randomized order. It is slow and costs money, so use two reviewers on a sample and record their disagreement, which measures how much the rubric leaves to taste. See Chapter 20.

docs.title: How do I run a queue of ten models so it survives disconnects and freezes?
docs.text:
A benchmark of ten models is a queue, and a queue needs more than the runner. This project's batch script works through the models one at a time, in phases: download and model-only test, harness smoke test, then stages 1, 2, and 3. Three practices make it survivable:

  • Run it in tmux. The queue runs in a session named bench, with the watchdog in a session named watchdog, so a dropped connection stops neither.
  • Choose each model's context on purpose. The script restarts the server for each model with a context chosen from a memory estimate that keeps about 45 GiB free, not one value for all models.
  • Fetch as you go. Each model's results come back as it finishes, so a unit that freezes does not take unfetched results with it.

Two small mechanisms help. A run that already has a status file is skipped, so a stopped queue restarts where it left off. And an empty file named skip-<model> in the runs directory makes a running queue pass over that model.

Also stop early when it is pointless. A stage 3 queue stops after two time-outs in a row, because a model that cannot finish two chapters in 90 minutes each will not finish twelve, and the remaining runs would only occupy the machine. The runs not made are recorded as "not run", with the reason, in a status table with a "last updated" line. See Chapter 21 and Evaluation Status.

docs.title: What safeguards keep device details out of the repository?
docs.text:
Use several layers, because each catches a different kind of slip:

Layer What it does What it misses Raw output isolation Keeps unsanitized output outside the repository, so nothing has to be removed because it never entered it A file someone copies in by hand Gitignore rules Refuse patterns such as *.log, *.jsonl, .env, id_*, *.pem Files already tracked, and an explicit git add -f Hosts via environment variable Real addresses live in the shell of the person running the script, never in a file A value typed into a document A narrow publishing script Copies only a model's learning graph, chapter text, and the course description, and leaves out any file with an address, a host name, or a home-directory path Nothing it does not copy, which is the point: it fails closed Secret scanning (gitleaks) Finds strings with the shape of a credential, in the tree, staged changes, or history An IP address in a paragraph or a hostname in a caption Pre-commit scan Refuses a commit whose added lines match address, tailnet, key, token, home-path, or serial patterns Anything that does not match a pattern Publication safety review A person reads everything against the catalog Nothing a person reads carefully, but it is slow

Make the scan part of the publish command. A check you must remember to run will be skipped on the tired evening that matters most, so put it in the same script as git commit and the site deploy.

A pre-commit hit is a prompt to read the line, not proof of a leak: a version number can match the address pattern. Check your own diff before every commit as well. See Chapter 23.

docs.title: How do I find break-even volume, and why check capacity?
docs.text:
The break-even volume is the amount of production at which two options cost the same. For a local machine against a per-book price, it is the fixed cost divided by the saving on each book:

N* = F ÷ (P − v)

Here F is the local fixed cost for the year, P is the alternative's price per book, and v is the local variable cost per book. With F = $8,275 and v = $0.58, and using illustrative prices rather than quotes from any provider:

Alternative price per book Break-even books per year Reachable by one unit at 156 books a year? $100 83 Yes $50 167 No $20 426 No

The last column is the part most often missed. A break-even above what the machine can produce is not a target to grow into. It means that against that alternative, one unit does not break even at any volume it can reach. Compute the machine's capacity as generating hours divided by hours per book, and compare. The formula also has no answer when P is less than or equal to v, because the alternative is then cheaper at every volume.

See Chapter 6, and the Local Versus Cloud Break-Even Explorer MicroSim there.

docs.title: What did the first round show that no name, size, or leaderboard predicted?
docs.text:
Four results contradicted the obvious expectation, and none could have been read from a model's name, size, or published score:

  • The model built for long agent tasks was the cleanest and the slowest. qwen3.8:27b produced a learning graph with exactly 200 concepts, no cycles, and no duplicate labels, and it took 102 minutes where the five others that finished took 6 to 22. In the chapter-writing stage it could not finish a chapter inside 90 minutes.
  • The fastest model wrote a flawed graph. gemma4:26b ran at 86 to 130 tokens per second and finished in under six minutes, with 40 duplicate concept labels out of 200.
  • The largest dense model did not fit with a usable context. mistral-medium-3.5:128b ran at 3 tokens per second and used 88 GiB at a 32,000-token context, so no context of 64,000 tokens or more would fit.
  • A model built to drive software-engineering agents did no work in the harness. devstral-small-2:24b wrote its first tool call as plain text both times, so the harness saw no tool call and the run ended after one turn. A second model, gpt-oss:120b, printed a tool call as plain text in one of its runs.

The caution that goes with the table matters as much as the table. Every figure is a single attempt, and a model that failed once may succeed on a second try, as one candidate did after its skill was corrected. Treat the first round as a way to decide what to test further, and repeat a run before you write a sentence that begins "model X cannot". See Chapter 14.

docs.title: What are the weaknesses in this evaluation's own design?
docs.text:
The book states them, which is what makes the results credible. An uncontrolled variable is something that could affect the result and that the design did not hold fixed. The honest response is to record it and say which direction it might push. This evaluation had at least three:

  • Reasoning mode. The model-only tests ran with reasoning turned off to bound their time, while the harness runs used each model's own default. One model spent nineteen minutes on a single turn, and predictions from the model-only test did not match.
  • Context length. It was chosen for each model from a memory estimate, so the models did not all run at the same setting.
  • Server behavior. One model's server re-read the conversation on every turn and the cause was not identified, so a speed difference could belong to the server and not to the model.

There are structural limits too:

  • Single runs. Nearly every result is one attempt per model per stage, enough to find what fails and not enough to rank.
  • No cloud baseline yet. The published Algebra I book is a reference for scale, not a baseline under the same rules.
  • Assumed speeds. Six of the ten speeds in the cost analysis are assumed to equal a measured model.
  • One hardware configuration. All ten candidates ran on DGX units of the same type, so the timings and fit verdicts do not transfer to a different DGX without re-running the probes.

An experimental design critique applies these standards to your own evaluation, in writing, before someone else does. Work down the same list: the question, what varies, what is held fixed, what is recorded, how many runs, and what the comparison is against. See Chapter 19 and Chapter 20.

docs.title: What is quality-adjusted cost, and why include human review?
docs.text:
Quality-adjusted cost corrects the generation cost for the quality of what came out: how much of it is usable, and what it costs a person to review it. A book generated for $53 of which only 10 of 13 chapters are written has not cost $53 for a book. One way to express the first part is the cost per usable chapter: the cost divided by the chapters that met the completion criterion.

Case Cost to generate Usable chapters Cost per usable chapter All 13 chapters complete $52.92 13 $4.07 10 of 13 complete $52.92 10 $5.29 6 of 13 complete $52.92 6 $8.82

A model that writes only 6 of 13 chapters therefore costs $8.82 per usable chapter, more than twice the $4.07 of a complete book, however fast it is.

Human review cost is the price of the person who judges quality. It is not in the generation cost, and it can be much larger. Ten hours of subject-expert review at $90 an hour is $900, seventeen times the $53 generation cost. A quality-adjusted comparison that leaves it out has priced the book as though nobody had to read it.

The service price calculation is a separate step: the price a service would have to charge to keep a margin is the cost divided by one minus the margin, so $52.92 at a 20% margin becomes $66.15. That price covers generation only, and review is a separate and larger cost, so a comparison that stops at the generation price leaves out the biggest line. See Chapter 22.

docs.title: How do I decide whether a DGX is sufficient for textbook generation?
docs.text:
Write the thresholds down before you see the data. A machine is sufficient for a purpose, and the purpose has to say how fast, how good, and at what cost. If you decide what counts as enough after seeing what the machine can do, the answer is always yes.

A DGX sufficiency judgment is a judgment, not a calculation, and the criteria this evaluation can state are concrete:

  1. Does at least one model complete all three stages without a fault that makes the output unusable?
  2. Does it do so within a time and cost the user can accept?
  3. Does the quality, once reviewed, meet the standard the course sets?

The honest answer at any given moment can be that the first is established, the second is estimated, and the third is not yet known, and a report says which. On the evidence the book has, this evaluation has no cloud baseline textbook yet and no completed human review, so it can state costs and structural results and cannot state a quality gap.

When you do your own, use the probes' report for the hardware facts, the fit calculation for memory, the run reports for time, and the cost model for cost. Keep what you measured separate from what you assumed, and carry the same caveats into the recommendation. See Chapter 22 and Evaluation Status.

docs.title: How do I write a local, cloud, or hybrid recommendation I can defend?
docs.text:
Structure the report in five parts, in this order, so that a reader can judge the conclusion for themselves:

Part What it states The question a reader asks of it Question What was being evaluated, for whom Is this my question? Method The design: variables, inputs, runs, metrics Could I repeat it, and was it fair? Results What was measured, with the assumed marked What actually happened? Limitations What the results do not show How far can I trust this? Recommendation Local, cloud, or hybrid, and the conditions What should I do?

Then state the recommendation as rules, because a reader can apply rules to their own circumstances and cannot apply a verdict:

If the evidence shows Then the recommendation leans A local model completes every stage, at a cost per book below the service price, and review finds the quality acceptable Local No local model completes a stage the skills need Cloud for that stage Local completes the high-volume or sensitive stages and fails a hard one Hybrid, routed by stage Quality is acceptable and the cost depends on utilization the user cannot reach Cloud, or a shared unit

An illustrative reading from this evaluation's provisional first round: several models completed the learning-graph and chapter-structure stages, and chapter text exposed the capability differences. That pattern would point to a hybrid with the structural stages local and a stronger model for the hard prose, until a local model's prose is reviewed. If the evidence is mixed, say so and state what would change your mind. See Chapter 22.

docs.title: What would a complete capstone evaluation of my own DGX involve?
docs.text:
The capstone evaluation is a complete, objective evaluation of a DGX system, published. It uses every chapter, and sanitization is a graded step and not an afterthought. The steps follow the order of the book:

  1. Reach the machine. Join the tailnet, prove the connection at three layers, and log in without a password (Chapter 7 and Chapter 9).
  2. Probe the hardware. Run the probe suite and produce a report with identifying fields left out by default (Chapter 5 and Chapter 10).
  3. Choose and install a model. Compute the fit, select and download a model, and put it behind a local endpoint that only you can reach (Chapter 11 to Chapter 13).
  4. Connect and contain the harness. Install the skills, point a harness at the endpoint, run it in a container, and start the watchdog and the vitals log (Chapter 16 to Chapter 18).
  5. Design the experiment. State the question, the variable, the controls, and the metrics before running anything (Chapter 19).
  6. Run and score. Run each stage from a fixed template, apply the checks, and calibrate them (Chapter 20 and Chapter 21).
  7. Diagnose, cost, and decide. Explain each failure, compute cost per textbook, compare with a baseline, and write the report (Chapter 22).
  8. Sanitize and publish. Redact, scan, review, and publish only what passes (Chapter 23).

The capstone is finished when the report is public and the review has found nothing in it that makes the machine easier to find, reach, or log in to.

docs.title: 4-Bit Quantization
docs.text:
A level that stores each weight in about 4 bits, roughly a quarter of the 16-bit size, at a larger loss of accuracy than 8-bit.

Example: The same 30 billion parameters take about 15 GB.

See also: 8-Bit Quantization, Quantization Tradeoffs, Quantized File Overhead

docs.title: 8-Bit Quantization
docs.text:
A level that stores each weight in 8 bits, one byte, which halves the memory of a 16-bit model with usually small loss of accuracy.

Example: A 30-billion-parameter model at 8 bits needs about 30 GB for weights.

See also: 4-Bit Quantization, Quantization Level

docs.title: aarch64 Architecture
docs.text:
The 64-bit Arm instruction set, reported by Linux as aarch64. Some DGX systems use Arm processors, so downloads for them are the aarch64 builds.

Example: A DGX Spark reports aarch64, so a server release archive has to be the Arm build.

See also: x86_64 Architecture, DGX Spark, Architecture-Specific Wheels

docs.title: Access Configuration
docs.text:
The description of how a machine can be reached: the access control policy, the open ports, the firewall rules, and the SSH server's settings. It shows an attacker what is allowed.

Example: A copy of the tailnet's policy file pasted into a chapter.

See also: Access Control List, Device-Identifying Details

docs.title: Access Control List
docs.text:
A policy that states which users and devices may connect to which others, and on which ports. In Tailscale it is a policy file applied across the whole tailnet.

See also: Tailscale SSH, Access Configuration, Tailnet

docs.title: Access Token Handling
docs.text:
The practice of keeping a hub access token, a credential that identifies an account, out of scripts, logs, and published files.

Example: Passing the token through an environment variable and showing <token> in every shared example.

See also: Keys and Tokens, Gated Model Access, Hosts via Environment Variable

docs.title: Active Parameters
docs.text:
In a mixture-of-experts model, the number of parameters used to produce each token, which is smaller than the total held in memory.

Example: A model with 117 billion parameters in total and about 5 billion active needs memory for all of it but computes each token with only the small part.

See also: Mixture of Experts, Parameter Count

docs.title: Administration Time
docs.text:
The hours a person spends setting up, maintaining, and troubleshooting a system, valued at a labor rate. It is a real part of owning a machine even though no invoice arrives for it.

Example: Forty hours spent connecting, inventorying, installing, and testing candidate models.

See also: Setup Labor, Operations Labor, Total Cost of Ownership

docs.title: Administrator Privileges
docs.text:
The right to change system-wide settings: install software for all users, change the driver, open network ports, and manage accounts. On Linux this means root access, usually through sudo.

Example: Packet capture needs it because reading raw packets is a privileged operation.

See also: System Administrator, User-Space Installation, Docker Group Membership

docs.title: Agent Loop
docs.text:
The repeating cycle in which a harness sends the conversation to the model, receives either a reply or a tool request, runs the tool, appends the result, and sends again until the task is done.

See also: Agent Turn, AI Agent Harness, Tool Calling

docs.title: Agent Skill
docs.text:
A folder of instructions, and sometimes helper files, that teaches a harness how to carry out one kind of task: the steps, the order, the checks, and the formats of the files to produce. It adds no capability the model lacks.

See also: SKILL.md Format, Skill Loading, ibook-skills Skill Chain

docs.title: Agent Turn
docs.text:
One pass of the agent loop: the harness sends the conversation, the model replies or requests a tool, and the harness runs the tool and records the result.

Example: A single chapter run is many turns of reading, writing, and checking.

See also: Agent Loop, Turn Overhead

docs.title: Agentic Framework
docs.text:
A software system that wraps a language model in a loop of planning, tool use, and checking so it can carry out multi-step tasks with little supervision.

See also: AI Agent Harness, Agent Loop, Devin

docs.title: AGENTS.md File
docs.text:
A plain Markdown file at a project's root that gives any coding agent the project's standing instructions: how to build, which rules apply, and where things live. It is the cross-harness counterpart of a harness-specific file.

Example: This book's CLAUDE.md contains only a pointer to AGENTS.md, so different agents read the same rules.

See also: Content Generation Guide, AI Agent Harness

docs.title: AI Agent Harness
docs.text:
The program that turns a model's single replies into a working sequence: it sends the prompt, executes the tool calls the model requests, returns the results, and repeats until the task ends.

See also: Agent Loop, Tool Definition, Claude Code

docs.title: Algebra I Benchmark
docs.text:
This evaluation's instance of the textbook benchmark: the input is a high school Algebra I course description, and the task is to produce its learning graph, chapter structure, and chapter content.

Example: Each model receives the same description and the same stage prompts.

See also: Textbook Benchmark, Reference Book for Scale

docs.title: Anthropic Claude
docs.text:
A family of cloud language models from the company Anthropic, together with the coding agent built on them. The course uses it as a cloud comparison baseline.

See also: Cloud Baseline, Claude Code

docs.title: Anthropic-Compatible API
docs.text:
An interface that copies the shape of Anthropic's messages API, which Ollama also offers and which Claude Code is built to speak.

Example: Pointing Claude Code at the local server uses this interface instead of the vendor's.

See also: OpenAI-Compatible API, Claude Code, Local Endpoint Connection

docs.title: Anti-Padding Rules
docs.text:
Instructions that keep a generator from reaching a word target by inflating text. They address the tendency of models to repeat and pad, which yields prose that is repetitive and sometimes wrong.

Example: A rule telling the generator to stop at a concept's own content when the target is not met, instead of adding filler.

See also: Word-Count Targets, Content Generation Guide

docs.title: Apache 2.0 License
docs.text:
A permissive open-source license that allows use, modification, redistribution, and commercial use, with an express patent grant from contributors. It requires keeping notices and stating changes.

Example: The Granite family is published under it, which makes the license check straightforward.

See also: Open-Source License, Commercial Use Terms, Granite Family

docs.title: Architecture-Specific Wheels
docs.text:
Prebuilt Python packages compiled for one CPU instruction set and operating system, which pip selects by matching the machine's platform tags and falls back to building from source when none match.

Example: A package that ships only x86_64 wheels fails to install, or compiles from source, on an aarch64 DGX.

See also: CPU Architecture, aarch64 Architecture, pip

docs.title: Automated Quality Score
docs.text:
A single number a program computes from the checks so outputs can be ranked at a glance. One number hides the profile, and a weighting that favors easy checks quietly defines quality.

Example: A weighted sum of structural check results.

See also: Human Quality Score, Structural Checks, Scoring Rubric

docs.title: Background Service
docs.text:
A program managed by the operating system that starts at boot and is restarted if it fails, running without a logged-in terminal.

See also: tmux Session, Runtime Installation

docs.title: Baseline Comparison
docs.text:
Judging a result against a reference produced under the same rules, since a number alone has no meaning without something to compare it with.

Example: A local learning graph with 200 concepts is judged against a cloud-generated graph for the same course.

See also: Cloud Baseline, Fair Comparison

docs.title: Baseline Textbook
docs.text:
The cloud-generated version of the same book, made from the same inputs as the local runs and used as the reference against which local books are scored.

Example: Local chapters are scored with the same rubric as the cloud-generated Algebra I book.

See also: Cloud Baseline, Baseline Comparison, Reference Book for Scale

docs.title: Batch Size
docs.text:
How many tokens, or requests, the server processes together in one step. A larger batch uses the GPU more fully because the same weights are read once and applied to many tokens.

Example: Processing 512 prompt tokens in one batch is faster than 512 separate steps.

See also: Batched Serving, Concurrency, Throughput

docs.title: Batched Serving
docs.text:
A server design that combines concurrent requests into batches so that several users share one pass over the model's weights.

See also: Batch Size, Concurrency, vLLM

docs.title: BatchMode
docs.text:
An SSH client option that tells it to refuse every prompt for a password or passphrase and to fail at once if a prompt would be required.

Example: ssh -o BatchMode=yes <user>@<dgx-host> true fails fast when key login is not set up.

See also: Unattended SSH Login, ssh-copy-id

docs.title: Benchmark Runner
docs.text:
A Python program that executes the pipeline stages for a model, copies a fresh workspace, applies the stage prompts and time limits, and logs metrics for each stage.

Example: It starts stage 1 for a model and writes the event stream to a run directory.

See also: Pipeline Stage, Stage Chaining, Run Event Stream

docs.title: Benchmark Workspace Template
docs.text:
The starting directory for stage 1: a minimal book project holding the unchanged course description and the site configuration, copied fresh for every run.

Example: No run sees another run's output.

See also: Fixed Inputs, Pipeline Stage

docs.title: Bias in Evaluation
docs.text:
A systematic tilt in scoring that favors some results over others for reasons unrelated to quality. Unlike noise, it does not average out over many runs.

Example: A model judge that prefers longer answers rates a padded chapter above a tight one.

See also: LLM-as-Judge, Blind Human Review

docs.title: Bits per Parameter
docs.text:
The count of bits used to store each model weight, such as 16, 8, or 4. Dividing it by 8 gives the bytes per weight that multiply the parameter count in a memory estimate.

Example: A file described as 4-bit uses about 4 bits for each parameter, though file overhead raises the average slightly.

See also: Numeric Precision, Bytes per Weight, Quantized File Overhead

docs.title: Blackwell Architecture
docs.text:
NVIDIA's name for one generation of GPU design, the one used by the GB10's GPU. The generation determines which instructions and numeric precisions the GPU supports.

See also: NVIDIA GB10, Compute Capability

docs.title: Blind Human Review
docs.text:
A person scoring output against a rubric without knowing which model produced it, with the order randomized. It is the most trustworthy test of quality and is slow and costly.

Example: A reviewer reads chapters labeled A through J with no model names attached.

See also: Human Review Cost, Scoring Rubric, Human Quality Score

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy
docs.text:
A classification of learning objectives by the kind of thinking they require. The 2001 revision names six levels, from simplest to most demanding: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create.

Example: "List the DGX components that determine inference capacity" is a remember-level objective, while "Judge whether a configuration is sufficient" is evaluate-level.

See also: Learning Outcomes, Quiz

docs.title: Books per Year
docs.text:
The number of complete textbooks a machine can produce in a year, found by dividing the generating hours available in a year by the hours one book takes.

Example: A machine generating for half of 8,760 hours and needing 28 hours per book yields about 156 books.

See also: Utilization Rate, Whole-Book Time Estimate, Break-Even Volume

docs.title: Break-Even Volume
docs.text:
The amount of production at which two options cost the same. Below it the option with the lower fixed expense wins, and above it the option with the lower per-unit expense wins.

Example: Dividing a local machine's fixed expense by its saving on each book gives the number of books at which it pays for itself.

See also: Fixed Costs, Variable Costs, Cost per Textbook

docs.title: Build Success
docs.text:
Whether a strict site build of the generated book finishes with exit code zero. Defining it in advance settles whether a build with warnings counts.

Example: mkdocs build --strict returning 0.

See also: Strict Site Build, Per-Stage Metrics

docs.title: Bytes per Weight
docs.text:
The storage each model weight takes, equal to bits per parameter divided by 8. It is the figure that multiplies the parameter count in a memory estimate.

Example: A 4-bit weight takes half a byte, so 30 billion parameters need about 15 GB for weights.

See also: Bits per Parameter, Memory for Weights, Parameter Count

docs.title: Capital Cost
docs.text:
The up-front outlay to buy hardware and its accessories, treated as a single amount that is then spread over the machine's useful life.

See also: Depreciation, Hardware Lifespan, Fixed Costs

docs.title: Capstone Evaluation
docs.text:
The course's final project: a complete, objective evaluation of a DGX system, published, which uses every chapter and treats sanitization as a graded step.

See also: Evaluation Report, Sanitization

docs.title: Chapter Completion Criterion
docs.text:
The rule that a chapter counts as written when its placeholder text is gone and it has at least 1,000 words, since a model's claim to be finished is not evidence.

Example: A chapter file that still contains its placeholder text fails the rule.

See also: Per-Chapter Generation Run, Premature Turn Termination

docs.title: Chapter Content
docs.text:
The prose, tables, and worked examples written for each chapter of a textbook after the learning graph and chapter structure exist. It also includes a specification for every MicroSim.

Example: A chapter built from about 20 concepts has an explanation, an example, and a check for each concept.

See also: Elaboration Budget, MicroSim, Per-Chapter Generation Run

docs.title: Chapter Dependency Check
docs.text:
A step in the chapter-content skill that verifies that each chapter's concepts depend only on concepts in earlier chapters, stopping and reporting if it finds a violation.

Example: A chapter that uses a concept first defined in a later chapter fails the check.

See also: Concept Dependency, Chapter Content

docs.title: Chat Completions Endpoint
docs.text:
The main route of an OpenAI-compatible API, at /v1/chat/completions, which accepts a list of messages and returns the model's reply.

See also: OpenAI-Compatible API, curl Request

docs.title: Checksum Verification
docs.text:
Comparing a downloaded file's computed hash with the hash the publisher lists, to confirm that the file is complete and unaltered.

Example: Running sha256sum on a GGUF file and comparing the result with the value on the model page.

See also: Model Download, Publisher Provenance

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Anthropic's command-line coding agent, and the harness this evaluation uses. It was chosen because the comparison books were generated with it, so the model is the only thing that changes.

Example: It is pointed at the local server through the Anthropic-compatible interface.

See also: AI Agent Harness, Anthropic-Compatible API, Harness Prompt Overhead

docs.title: Cloud Baseline
docs.text:
A reference result produced by a cloud model on the same inputs and under the same rules as a local run, used as the point of comparison. Without one, a local result has no yardstick.

Example: A cloud-generated Algebra I book scored with the same checks as each local model's book.

See also: Baseline Comparison, Baseline Textbook, Fair Comparison

docs.title: Cloud LLM Service
docs.text:
A language model run by a provider and reached over the internet, with usage billed by the provider. The user rents the capability and does not hold the weights.

See also: Local Model Deployment, Per-Token Pricing, Anthropic Claude

docs.title: Code Generation
docs.text:
A model's ability to write programs, scripts, and configuration in a programming language. The benchmark uses it for the shell and Python scripts an agent writes and for the JavaScript of MicroSims.

Example: A generated p5.js sketch either runs in a browser or throws an error on its first frame.

See also: MicroSim Code Correctness, p5.js

docs.title: Codex CLI
docs.text:
OpenAI's command-line coding agent, an agent harness that implements the same skill format as the other harnesses, so a skill written for one can be tried in another.

See also: OpenCode, Goose, SKILL.md Format

docs.title: Command Line Basics
docs.text:
The skills of navigating directories, running programs, and editing files by typing text commands into a shell instead of using a graphical interface. Every setup step in the course is issued this way.

Example: Running cd docs and ls to look around a book's folder, then cat to read one of its files.

See also: Python Scripting Basics, SSH, Git Version Control

docs.title: Commercial Use Terms
docs.text:
The part of a model's license that states whether the model, or what it writes, may be used to make money, and under what conditions.

See also: Model License Terms, License Review

docs.title: Compute Capability
docs.text:
A version number NVIDIA assigns to each GPU generation that indicates which CUDA features and instructions the hardware supports, and therefore which prebuilt libraries can run on it.

See also: CUDA, Blackwell Architecture, CUDA Version Probe

docs.title: Concept Dependency
docs.text:
A statement that one concept is a prerequisite of another, meaning a learner who lacks the first will struggle with the second. It describes the subject itself, not the order of any particular chapter list.

Example: "Percent depends on decimals" becomes an edge from decimals to percent in an arithmetic course's graph.

See also: Learning Graph, Directed Acyclic Graph

docs.title: Concept Impact Score
docs.text:
A number measuring how much of a learning graph rests on a concept, defined recursively as 1 for the concept itself plus the scores of every concept that depends on it directly.

Example: A concept with three direct dependents, none of which has dependents of its own, scores 1 plus 3, which is 4.

See also: Elaboration Budget, Concept Dependency, Word-Count Targets

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
A classification that assigns every concept in a learning graph to exactly one named category, each with a short identifier such as FOUND or HW. It lets an author see the graph by theme and spot neglected areas.

Example: Counting concepts per category reveals one category that holds only two concepts.

See also: Learning Graph, Foundational Concepts

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
The number of separate requests an inference server is handling at the same time, such as two harness sessions running together, which determines how much batching the server can apply.

Example: Two harness sessions running at once make a concurrency of two.

See also: Batched Serving, Throughput

docs.title: Conda
docs.text:
A package and environment manager that installs software, including Python itself and non-Python libraries, into named, isolated environments that can be created, listed, exported, and deleted from the command line.

See also: pip, Conda Versus pip, Python Environment

docs.title: Conda Activate Command
docs.text:
The subcommand conda activate, which makes a named environment the current one, so its Python and packages are used by the commands that follow in that shell.

Example: Running conda activate mkdocs before mkdocs build --strict.

See also: Conda Create Command, Conda List and Export

docs.title: Conda Create Command
docs.text:
The subcommand conda create, which builds a new named environment, optionally with a pinned Python version and an initial set of packages.

Example: conda create -n dgx python=3.11 builds an environment named dgx.

See also: Conda Activate Command, Python Version Pinning

docs.title: Conda List and Export
docs.text:
Two subcommands for recording an environment: conda list prints the installed packages and their versions, and conda env export writes them to a specification file.

Example: Exporting to environment.yml captures exactly what was installed.

See also: environment.yml, Environment Rebuild, Reproducibility

docs.title: Conda Remove Command
docs.text:
The subcommand conda remove, which uninstalls named packages from an environment and, when given the name of an environment and the --all flag, deletes that whole environment and everything installed in it.

Example: Deleting an environment and recreating it from its specification confirms that the specification works.

See also: Environment Rebuild, Conda Create Command

docs.title: Conda Versus pip
docs.text:
The distinction between two installers: conda manages Python itself and non-Python dependencies across platforms, while pip installs Python packages only. Mixing them in one environment needs care.

Example: Install the GPU libraries with conda, add a pure-Python helper with pip, and record both in the specification.

See also: Conda, pip

docs.title: Connectivity Test
docs.text:
A check that one machine can actually reach another over the network, confirming a path, a name, and a response before later steps depend on them.

See also: Tailscale Ping, Remote Access

docs.title: Container Sandbox
docs.text:
The boundary a container creates: inside it the agent may run any command, and the only paths it can write to are the ones deliberately mounted in.

Example: An errant delete command inside the container cannot reach host files that were not mounted.

See also: Harness Container, Network Sandbox Gap, Network Boundary

docs.title: Content Generation Guide
docs.text:
The file CONTENT-GENERATION-GUIDE.md at the repository root that gathers every writing rule in one place, including concept-depth targets, anti-padding rules, and MicroSim expectations, so an agent can be told to read it first.

Example: A task prompt tells the agent to read the guide before writing any chapter.

See also: AGENTS.md File, Anti-Padding Rules

docs.title: Context Compaction
docs.text:
Asking the model to summarize the earlier conversation into a short note and replacing the old content with it. It keeps the thread and loses detail, and it costs a model call.

See also: Context Truncation, Context Management

docs.title: Context Length Memory
docs.text:
The memory the KV cache needs at a given context length, which grows in proportion to it. It is reserved for the configured window whether or not a conversation fills it.

Example: Raising the setting from 32,000 to 64,000 tokens roughly doubles this part of the estimate.

See also: KV Cache, Context Length Setting, Memory Estimation Formula

docs.title: Context Length Setting
docs.text:
The window size a server is configured with. It reserves memory for the KV cache and bounds how large a conversation can grow before the harness has to shrink it, and it can be set below the model's own maximum.

Example: A larger setting leaves room for long conversations but takes memory that could hold other things.

See also: Context Window, KV Cache, Context Length Memory

docs.title: Context Management
docs.text:
How a harness keeps a growing conversation within the model's window by dropping or summarizing earlier content, since the window is a fixed limit and the conversation only gets longer.

See also: Context Compaction, Context Truncation, Peak Context Size

docs.title: Context Overflow
docs.text:
The conversation exceeding the model's window, so earlier content is dropped or the request is rejected. Its signature is a run that does well for a while and then behaves as if it forgot the task.

Example: A peak context size close to the window size.

See also: Peak Context Size, Context Truncation, Context Window

docs.title: Context Truncation
docs.text:
Dropping the oldest content to shrink a conversation that is approaching the window. It is crude because the start of the conversation holds the task.

Example: A run that loses track of its task after a long session may have had its first messages truncated.

See also: Context Compaction, Context Overflow

docs.title: Context Window
docs.text:
The largest number of tokens a model can take into account at once, covering the prompt, earlier conversation, tool results, and the reply being generated. It is a property of the model, distinct from the length a server is configured to use.

Example: A harness that adds about 19,000 tokens of its own instructions leaves less of the window for the actual task.

See also: Context Length Setting, KV Cache, Context Overflow

docs.title: Control Run
docs.text:
A repeat of a run that is expected to give the same answer, done to check the apparatus rather than the subject.

See also: Repeated Runs, Scoring Check Calibration

docs.title: Controlled Variables
docs.text:
Everything else that could affect the result and that the design holds fixed on purpose, so a difference can be blamed on the independent variable.

Example: The same course description, prompts, harness, and time limit for every model.

See also: Independent Variable, Fixed Inputs, Uncontrolled Variable

docs.title: Coordination Plane
docs.text:
The part of Tailscale that handles identity, key distribution, and policy through the vendor's servers. It exchanges metadata and does not carry the traffic between devices.

See also: Data Plane, Tailscale Authentication

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
What an owner pays to own and operate hardware: the purchase, the electricity, and the labor of setting it up and running it, as opposed to what a provider charges for a service.

Example: A DGX's yearly share of its purchase, plus its electricity and administrator hours, is its cost, while a cloud bill is a price.

See also: Total Cost of Ownership, Capital Cost

Contrast with: Price

docs.title: Cost Model
docs.text:
A written set of assumptions and formulas that turns inputs, such as hours and power draw, into an expense figure. It makes the assumptions explicit so a reader can see which one to dispute.

Example: Changing the assumed share of hours the machine works from half to a quarter shows how the per-book figure moves.

See also: Sensitivity Analysis, Explicit Assumptions, Utilization Rate

docs.title: Cost per Chapter
docs.text:
The expense of generating one textbook divided by the number of chapters it contains, giving a unit figure that can be compared with a provider's per-chapter or per-book charge.

Example: A 13-chapter book that costs 52 USD to generate works out to 4 USD per chapter.

See also: Cost per Textbook, Books per Year

docs.title: Cost per Textbook
docs.text:
The expense of generating one complete book: the hours it takes multiplied by the expense of one generating hour. It is the local figure set against a provider's charge for the same book.

Example: A 28-hour run on a machine with a known hourly expense yields one number to set against a cloud service's charge.

See also: Cost per Chapter, Whole-Book Time Estimate, Service Price Calculation

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
A short document, written by a person, that states a course's audience, prerequisites, topics, exclusions, and learning outcomes. Every downstream part of the textbook inherits its scope from this document.

Example: The Algebra I benchmark starts each run from a published course description copied unchanged into the workspace.

See also: Course Description Quality Score, Learning Graph, Learning Outcomes

docs.title: Course Description Quality Score
docs.text:
A number from 0 to 100 that rates how completely a course description supplies the elements the generators need: a title, an audience, prerequisites, topics, and outcomes written at the Bloom levels.

See also: Course Description, Learning Outcomes

docs.title: CPU Architecture
docs.text:
The instruction set a processor executes, which decides which compiled programs and package builds run on the machine. DGX systems in this course use either x86_64 or aarch64.

Example: uname -m prints the architecture, which decides which installer archive to download.

See also: x86_64 Architecture, aarch64 Architecture, Architecture-Specific Wheels

docs.title: CPU Core Count
docs.text:
The number of processing cores a CPU provides, which bounds how many host tasks, such as builds and tool calls, can run in parallel.

See also: CPU Probe, CPU Architecture

docs.title: CPU Probe
docs.text:
A probe that reports the processor's model name, its core count, and its instruction-set architecture, which together tell later steps which software builds apply and how much parallel work the host can take.

Example: On a DGX Spark it reports aarch64 and the number of Arm cores.

See also: CPU Architecture, CPU Core Count, psutil

docs.title: CSV-JSON Agreement
docs.text:
Whether the two files that hold the same learning graph, one as CSV and one as JSON, describe exactly the same concepts and the same dependencies.

See also: Required Output Files, Structural Validity

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
NVIDIA's platform and programming interface for running general computation on its GPUs. Libraries such as PyTorch and inference servers use it to run models on the GPU.

Example: A CUDA-enabled PyTorch build can use the GPU, while a CPU-only build cannot.

See also: NVIDIA Driver, CUDA-Enabled PyTorch, Compute Capability

docs.title: CUDA Cores
docs.text:
The small parallel arithmetic units inside an NVIDIA GPU that execute CUDA work. Their number describes parallel capacity but, taken alone, says little about generation speed.

See also: GPU, Memory Bandwidth

docs.title: CUDA Version Probe
docs.text:
A probe that reports the CUDA version the driver supports or the toolkit provides. The two can differ, so the figure's meaning depends on where it was read.

Example: A PyTorch build for a newer CUDA than the driver supports fails when it tries to use the GPU.

See also: CUDA, Driver Version Probe, PyTorch CUDA Check

docs.title: CUDA-Enabled PyTorch
docs.text:
A PyTorch build compiled with CUDA support so it can run on an NVIDIA GPU, in contrast to a CPU-only build that installs without error but cannot use the GPU.

Example: A default install can pull the CPU-only build, which is why the CUDA check exists.

See also: PyTorch CUDA Check, CUDA, Architecture-Specific Wheels

docs.title: curl Request
docs.text:
A single curl command that sends one request to the endpoint. It removes every layer between the user and the server, so a failure points to the server or the model and not to a program.

Example: Posting a one-word prompt to the chat completions route and reading the JSON reply.

See also: Chat Completions Endpoint, Python Client, First-Prompt Smoke Test

docs.title: Data Egress Trace
docs.text:
An accounting of every place a system's data goes when it leaves. It is built component by component, recording the destination, what is sent, and how often, so the result is a table that can be checked against reality.

Example: A table listing inference traffic to the local machine, Tailscale coordination metadata, package downloads, and the orchestrator's reads.

See also: Supervision Data Exposure, Packet Capture Verification, Network Boundary

docs.title: Data Plane
docs.text:
The part of Tailscale that carries the actual traffic directly between devices over encrypted WireGuard tunnels, bypassing the coordination servers wherever a direct path exists.

See also: Coordination Plane, Peer-to-Peer Connection, DERP Relay

docs.title: Data Sovereignty
docs.text:
The principle that data is subject to the laws and control of the country or organization where it is stored and processed. Local deployment keeps data in a place its owner chooses.

See also: Privacy, Local Model Deployment

docs.title: Data-Driven MicroSim
docs.text:
A MicroSim that keeps its content in a separate data file, usually JSON, and reads it at load time instead of writing the facts into the program. This separates the logic from the facts.

Example: Correcting a model's listed download size means editing one row of the data file, not changing the JavaScript.

See also: MicroSim, Learning Graph Viewer

docs.title: Decision Attribution
docs.text:
Recording who made each design decision, since a choice by a person with a goal and a choice by an assistant filling a gap deserve different scrutiny.

See also: Design Decision Record, Role Separation

docs.title: Dedicated GPU Memory
docs.text:
Memory physically attached to the GPU and separate from system RAM. The model's weights and cache are held in it, so its size caps what can be loaded.

Example: A GPU with 24 GB of its own memory cannot load a 40 GB model, whatever the system RAM holds.

See also: Unified Memory, Memory for Weights, GPU Memory Total and Free

docs.title: Dedicated Tool Environment
docs.text:
An environment that exists for one tool or job and holds nothing else. In this evaluation the tools for reaching the DGX live in one named dgx, separate from the environment that builds this book.

Example: A package conflict in the book-building environment cannot break the Tailscale client.

See also: Environment Isolation, Python Environment

docs.title: Dense Model
docs.text:
A model in which every parameter takes part in producing each token, so both memory use and per-token computation scale with its full size.

Example: gemma4:31b is dense, so all 30.7 billion of its parameters work on every token.

See also: Mixture of Experts, Active Parameters

docs.title: Dependency Cycle Check
docs.text:
A check that a graph is acyclic by repeatedly removing the concepts that have no remaining prerequisites; if all can be removed, there is no cycle.

Example: When A depends on B, B on C, and C on A, three concepts remain that cannot be removed.
