docs.title: Diagram: Command Output Predictor
docs.text:
Run Command Output Predictor Fullscreen

Command Output Predictor

Type: microsim sim-id: command-output-predictor Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-linux/tree/main/docs/sims/command-syntax Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: execute Learning Objective: The learner will execute five shell commands against a given directory tree by predicting the output and the resulting working directory after each, with at least 4 of 5 correct.

Prerequisites: terminal, shell, working directory, path, absolute path, relative path, command, argument (all defined in the section "Command Line Basics" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner selects one predicted output per command before the sim shows the real output. A selection is correct when it equals the option marked correct in Content. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct. Reading the directory tree and reading the feedback are exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) ls lists everything below the working directory, including the contents of subfolders. (2) cd prints the new path. (3) .. names the current folder rather than the parent folder. (4) Each command starts fresh instead of continuing from the working directory the previous command left.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level execution needs the learner to carry state from one command to the next, so the five commands run in a fixed order and each prediction depends on the working directory the earlier commands produced. Committing to an answer before it is revealed turns watching a terminal into producing a result.

Content:

The sim shows this practice directory, labeled "synthetic example". The shell starts in /home/student/lab.

Path Kind Contents /home/student/lab/notes.txt file Three lines: model: unset, context: 4096, status: draft /home/student/lab/readme.md file One line: Probe results go in results. /home/student/lab/probes folder Contains cpu.py and gpu.py /home/student/lab/results folder Empty

The five commands, in this order, each with exactly four options shown in the order listed:

# Command typed Option A Option B Option C Option D Correct Why (shown as feedback) 1 pwd /home/student /home/student/lab lab notes.txt probes readme.md results B pwd prints the full absolute path of the working directory, not just its last folder name. 2 ls probes results notes.txt readme.md notes.txt probes readme.md results cpu.py gpu.py C ls lists both files and folders in the working directory, and does not list what is inside the folders. 3 cd probes Prints cpu.py gpu.py Prints /home/student/lab/probes Prints nothing; the working directory becomes /home/student/lab/probes Prints probes: Is a directory C cd changes state silently. Its only evidence is the working directory that later commands see. 4 ls notes.txt probes readme.md results cpu.py gpu.py cpu.py gpu.py notes.txt Prints nothing B After cd probes the working directory is probes, so ls lists that folder's two files. 5 cat ../notes.txt cat: ../notes.txt: No such file or directory notes.txt cpu.py gpu.py The three lines model: unset, context: 4096, status: draft D .. names the parent folder, so the path reaches /home/student/lab/notes.txt, and cat prints the file's contents.

Provenance: The directory and its file contents are synthetic and invented for this exercise; the sim labels them "synthetic example". The behavior of pwd, ls, cd, cat and .. is the behavior stated in the chapter section "Command Line Basics".

Rules: The commands run in the fixed order 1 to 5 and state carries over: the working directory after command 3 is /home/student/lab/probes and stays so through commands 4 and 5. Option order is fixed as listed. There is no randomness and no numeric tolerance. Each command allows exactly one selection, and it is final.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the directory table and the first command, pwd, with its four options.
  2. The learner selects one option. The sim immediately shows the real output, marks the selection correct or incorrect, shows the correct option, and shows the Why text.
  3. The learner moves to the next command. The sim shows the working directory that the earlier commands left, so the learner can see the state change after command 3.
  4. After command 5 the sim shows the score and lists the Misconceptions that correspond to any commands answered incorrectly.

Feedback: Five commands, fixed order, one selection each, and the selection is final. The real output, the correct option, and the Why text are shown immediately after the selection. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the Why text. The final score reads "n of 5 correct".

Starting State: Command 1 is shown with no option selected, the working directory is /home/student/lab, and the question on screen is "What does the shell print?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that pwd prints the absolute path, ls lists files and folders without descending into folders, cd prints nothing on success, cat prints a file's contents, and .. names the parent folder.

docs.title: Python Scripting Basics
docs.text:
A Python script is a text file of Python statements that the Python interpreter runs from top to bottom. Python is the language of the hardware probes, the model-fit calculator, and the benchmark runner in this course, so you will read far more scripts than you write. The standard library is the set of modules that ship with Python itself. A script that uses only the standard library runs on any machine with Python and needs nothing installed.

Before the example, here is what its parts do. The import statement makes a module available. The platform module reports facts about the machine and the interpreter, and the os module reports facts about the operating system, including the number of CPU cores. The print function writes a line to the terminal.

import platform
import os

print("system:", platform.system())
print("machine:", platform.machine())
print("python:", platform.python_version())
print("cpu cores:", os.cpu_count())

Saved as machine_report.py and run with python3 machine_report.py, the script prints four lines. The values below are illustrative; yours depend on the machine.

system: Linux
machine: aarch64
python: 3.11.9
cpu cores: 20

The machine line is the one to watch in this course. DGX systems are built on either x86_64 or aarch64 processors, and that difference decides which software packages install. This six-line script is the seed of the hardware probes in Chapter 10, which grow it into a full report.

A second script shows the other half of the skill, which is reading data. The json module turns a JSON file into Python lists and dictionaries, open gives access to the file, and len counts the items in a list. The script below counts the concepts and dependencies in this book's own learning graph.

import json

with open("docs/learning-graph/learning-graph.json") as f:
    graph = json.load(f)

print("concepts:", len(graph["nodes"]))
print("dependencies:", len(graph["edges"]))

Run from the root of this book's repository, it prints concepts: 506 and dependencies: 824. Reading structured data and checking it with a few lines of Python is exactly what the benchmark's structural checks do, so this is the pattern to recognize.

To do this Run this Run a script python3 machine_report.py Check the interpreter version python3 --version Run one statement without a file python3 -c "print(2 + 2)"

docs.title: Git Version Control
docs.text:
Git is a version control system: it records the history of a folder of files as a series of snapshots called commits, each with a message that says why the files changed. You can compare any two snapshots, return to an earlier one, and see who changed what. For a project made of text files, which includes every textbook in this course, Git is how work stays recoverable.

The daily cycle has three steps. You inspect what changed, you stage the files you want recorded, and you commit them with a message. A fourth step, git push, sends the commits to a remote copy.

$ git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
        modified:   docs/index.md
$ git add docs/index.md
$ git commit -m "Reword the home page summary"
$ git push

The git add step exists because a commit is a deliberate selection. You may have edited five files and want only one recorded, and git add is how you say which. Writing the message in terms of why the change was made, not what file it touched, pays off months later when you read the history.

docs.title: GitHub Repository
docs.text:
A GitHub repository is a remote, hosted copy of a Git project, along with the pages and tools GitHub builds around it. Pushing to it gives you a backup, a shared copy collaborators can pull, and, for this book, a place that can publish the finished site. This book's source lives in a repository, and its site is served from the same one.

Two properties of a repository matter for this course. A repository can be public or private, and a public one can be read by anyone on the internet. Git also keeps the complete history, so a file that was committed once remains reachable in older commits even after a later commit deletes it.

A Public Repository Remembers Everything

This book's repository is public, and Git history is permanent, so a login, address, or token committed even once is exposed for good. Look at git diff before every commit, never commit raw command output, and if something sensitive does get committed, stop and fix it using the history steps in Chapter 23 instead of simply deleting it in the next commit.

docs.title: Markdown Source Files
docs.text:
Markdown is a plain-text format in which a few punctuation conventions mark structure: a leading # makes a heading, a leading - makes a list item, and pipes make a table. A Markdown source file is a text file in that format, usually with the extension .md. Because it is plain text, Git can diff it, a model can generate it, and a build tool can turn it into a web page.

Many Markdown files in this course also begin with a short block of settings between two --- lines. That block is called frontmatter, and it carries metadata such as the page title. The file below shows the whole set of pieces you will meet most often.

---
title: "Practice Chapter"
---

# Practice Chapter

A paragraph of ordinary prose.

- first list item
- second list item

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| shell | The program that interprets typed commands |

The table shows what each piece becomes on the rendered page.

Source Rendered result # Practice Chapter A top-level page heading A line of plain text A paragraph Lines starting with - A bulleted list Rows of text between pipes A table Text between two --- lines at the top Page metadata; not displayed as text

Blank Line Before Every List

MkDocs does not start a list unless a blank line comes before it, so a list typed straight after a sentence collapses into one run-on paragraph. The page still builds with no error, which is why it goes unnoticed. Always leave one empty line before the first bullet or number, and the same goes for tables.

docs.title: What Makes a Textbook Intelligent
docs.text:
An intelligent textbook is a textbook whose content is structured so that software can read it, check it, and respond to the reader. Two properties define it. The first is explicit structure: the concepts, their dependencies, and the learning outcomes are stored as data, not only implied by the prose. The second is interactivity: the book contains elements the reader operates and that report back what the reader did.

Explicit structure is easier to grasp from a small example. The fragment below stores two concepts and one dependency between them, in the JSON format this book's learning graph uses. The edge points from the dependent concept to the concept it depends on, so it reads "a MicroSim depends on the intelligent-textbook idea".

{
  "nodes": [
    {"id": 6, "label": "Intelligent Textbook"},
    {"id": 14, "label": "MicroSim"}
  ],
  "edges": [
    {"from": 14, "to": 6}
  ]
}

A worked comparison shows the difference. Suppose the concept is "quantization", which a later chapter covers. In a static textbook the treatment is a paragraph and a table of numbers. In an intelligent textbook the same concept has a stated place in a dependency graph, so the book knows which concepts must come first. It also carries an interactive simulation in which the reader moves a precision control and watches the memory estimate change, and a short quiz that records which options the reader chose.

Aspect Static textbook Intelligent textbook Concept order Implied by chapter order Stored as dependencies between concepts Explanation Prose and fixed figures Prose plus interactive elements Reader feedback None Quizzes and simulations that respond Revision Edit the page by hand Regenerate or revise from the same structured sources

Why This Book Can Be Generated

An intelligent textbook is a set of plain text files plus a build, so a model can write it and a program can check it. That is the property that makes textbook generation a benchmark you can measure at all: the output is machine-readable, so "did it work?" has an answer other than a reader's opinion.

docs.title: Levels of Intelligent Textbooks
docs.text:
The levels of intelligent textbooks are a five-step scale for how much intelligence a book has. Each level adds a capability the previous one lacks, and the higher levels are progressively more aspirational.

Level Name What the reader gets 1 Static content Fixed text and images; no navigation aids or interactivity 2 Interactive content Hyperlinks, quizzes, MicroSims, and a searchable glossary 3 Adaptive content Material that changes with the reader's demonstrated progress 4 Chatbot integration A conversational tutor that answers the reader's questions in real time 5 Autonomous AI Fully customized lessons generated in real time for each reader

This book targets Level 2 and above, so it contains MicroSims and quizzes. The books the benchmark generates are Level 2 books as well: Markdown prose, interactive elements, quizzes, and a glossary. The Book Levels MicroSim below lets you compare the five levels directly.

docs.title: Diagram: Book Levels MicroSim
docs.text:
Run the Book Levels MicroSim fullscreen

Book Levels MicroSim (reused MicroSim)

Type: microsim sim-id: book-levels Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/ibook-skills/sims/book-levels/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/ibook-skills/tree/main/docs/sims/book-levels Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare the five levels of intelligent textbooks by the capability each level adds over the one below it.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.7579).

docs.title: MicroSim
docs.text:
A MicroSim is a small, self-contained interactive simulation, embedded in a textbook page, that demonstrates exactly one idea. The scope is the point: a MicroSim has one learning objective, a few controls, and a result the reader can see change. A slider that redraws a chart as the reader changes a value is the typical shape.

Each MicroSim in this book lives in its own folder under docs/sims/, named by a short lowercase identifier. The folder holds a main.html page that runs the simulation and an index.md lesson page that describes it. That layout lets the same simulation be embedded in a chapter, opened fullscreen, or reused in another book.

Two examples already exist in this repository. The Parameters That Fit in Memory MicroSim lets you move a memory slider and see the largest model whose weights fit, and the Testing Architecture MicroSim lets you step through how the evaluation machines connect. Both follow the folder layout above.

Because a MicroSim is a small program, it has a build status as it moves from a plan to a finished sim. This book marks each MicroSim as scaffold (a specification exists, but no implementation), built (implemented and awaiting the Primary Author's review), or approved (tested and cleared for learners).

docs.title: Iframe Embedding
docs.text:
Iframe embedding places one web page inside another by using the HTML iframe element. It is how a MicroSim's main.html appears inside a chapter page without being copied into it. The iframe element takes the address of the page to show, plus a height and width.

<iframe src="../../sims/example-sim/main.html" width="100%" height="500px" scrolling="no"></iframe>

The address in src is relative to the page that contains the iframe. A chapter's index.md renders two folders deep, so it reaches the sims folder with ../../. A wrong relative path produces a blank box, with no build error to point at it.

docs.title: MkDocs Material
docs.text:
MkDocs is a static site generator: it reads a folder of Markdown files and a configuration file and produces a website. MkDocs Material is a widely used theme for it that adds search, navigation, callout boxes called admonitions, code highlighting, and a responsive layout. This book is built with it, and so are the books the benchmark generates.

The configuration file is mkdocs.yml. It names the site, selects the theme, and lists the pages. A minimal one is only a few lines.

site_name: Practice Book
theme:
  name: material
nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Chapters:
      - Introduction: chapters/01-introduction/index.md

Each page you write is a Markdown file under the docs folder. The configuration decides which of them appears on the site and in what order.

One extension you will see in every chapter is the admonition, a callout box that sets a note apart from the body text. It is written as !!!, a type, an optional title in quotes, and a body indented by four spaces. The mascot's messages in this book are admonitions with a custom type.

!!! note "A Short Title"
    The body of the callout is indented four spaces.

docs.title: MkDocs Navigation
docs.text:
MkDocs navigation is the sidebar tree, and it is defined by the nav: block in mkdocs.yml. Each entry is a label followed by the path of a Markdown file relative to docs. Entries can nest, which is how a chapter's sub-pages sit under the chapter.

A page that exists on disk but is missing from nav: is built, yet no reader can find it from the sidebar. Adding a page is therefore always two steps: create the file, then list it. In the example above, adding chapters/02-setup/index.md means adding one line under Chapters:, at the same indentation as the entry above it.

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Chapters:
      - Introduction: chapters/01-introduction/index.md
      - Setup: chapters/02-setup/index.md

docs.title: Static Site Build
docs.text:
A static site build is the step that converts the Markdown files and configuration into finished web files. Running mkdocs build writes a site folder of plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Nothing in that folder needs a database or a server-side program, so any file host can serve it, and GitHub Pages is the usual choice here.

For the practice project above, the site folder holds one HTML file per page, plus shared assets.

site/
  index.html
  chapters/01-introduction/index.html
  assets/

Static output has a useful consequence for this course. A built site can be inspected and checked as a set of files, with no running service to configure. It also means a local model never has to operate a server to produce a textbook; it only has to write files that build.

docs.title: Strict Site Build
docs.text:
A strict site build is a build that treats every warning as an error. You run it with mkdocs build --strict. An ordinary build prints a warning about a broken link and then finishes anyway; a strict build stops.

$ mkdocs build --strict
WARNING -  Doc file 'index.md' contains a link 'chapters/02-setup/index.md',
           but the target is not found among documentation files.
Aborted with 1 warnings in strict mode!

The wording above is abbreviated and illustrative. The behavior is the point: a defect that would have shipped as a dead link becomes a failed build you must fix.

Run Strict Before You Commit

Run mkdocs build --strict before every commit. It catches broken links and unlisted files while the change is still small, and later in the book the same check becomes one of the objective measurements of whether a model's output is any good.

docs.title: Describing What a Course Must Teach
Bloom's Taxonomy
docs.text:
Bloom's Taxonomy is a classification of learning objectives by the kind of thinking they require. The 2001 revision names six levels, from simplest to most demanding: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create. Each level has characteristic verbs, and the verb in an objective tells you what the learner must do to show it.

The value for this course is that the verb makes an objective checkable. "Understand Tailscale" cannot be tested, because there is no action to observe. "Describe how Tailscale builds an encrypted mesh between devices" can be tested, since you can read the description and judge it. The table shows each level with a real outcome from this course's description.

Level Typical verbs Outcome from this course Remember list, define, recall List common quantization levels and model file formats Understand explain, summarize, interpret Explain why an isolated conda environment makes an evaluation reproducible Apply use, execute, calculate Create a conda environment with a pinned Python version Analyze compare, distinguish, deconstruct Compare candidate open-weight models by license, size, and context window Evaluate judge, critique, justify Judge whether a DGX configuration is sufficient for end-to-end generation Create design, construct, compose Build a model-fit calculator that returns a fit verdict with headroom

A Verb Is a Measurement

Swapping a vague word like "understand" for an observable verb turns a hope into something you can measure. The evaluation in this book runs on the same instinct: a claim about a model counts only when it comes with a number you can check.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: Learning outcomes are statements of what a learner will be able to do after finishing a course, written as observable actions. Each begins with a verb from the Bloom's Taxonomy list, so each can be checked by watching the learner do it. A good set of outcomes does double duty: it tells the learner what to aim for and tells the author what to teach and what to test.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
A course description is a structured document that states what a course covers, who it is for, what it excludes, and what learners can do afterward. In this workflow it is the seed document. Every later artifact inherits its scope from it, so a gap or a vague statement in the course description becomes a gap or an invented topic everywhere downstream.

This book's own course description, the one you can read in full, is a good worked example. The table shows each part, what it tells a generator, and what this book put there.

Section What it tells the generators In this book Target audience The reading level and tone Professional development and adult continuing education: AI engineers, instructional technologists, technical authors, IT leads Prerequisites What may be assumed, and so not explained Command line, basic Python, Git and GitHub, and experience with an AI assistant Course overview The question the course answers Can one DGX running a small model generate a textbook with no cloud tokens? Main topics covered The concepts to enumerate Sixteen numbered topics, from intelligent textbooks to sanitizing artifacts Topics not covered The boundary that stops invented content Ten exclusions, such as training, fine-tuning, and cluster-scale infrastructure Learning outcomes What each concept must support Outcomes at all six Bloom levels, ending in a capstone evaluation

Specificity in the topics section also drives how many concepts a generator can extract. The pair below describes the same topic at two levels of detail.

Version Statement What a generator can do with it Vague "Covers AI hardware." Invent a generic list of components Specific "CPU architecture (x86_64 and aarch64), system RAM, GPU configuration, dedicated versus unified memory, storage, power, and thermals." Enumerate each named concept and relate them

The "Topics not covered" section deserves attention because it is the one authors skip. A model asked to write about a DGX will happily write about training and fine-tuning unless the course description rules it out. An explicit exclusion costs one line and prevents a chapter nobody wanted.

The course description is also the first of a chain of artifacts. Before looking at the chain, four terms need a definition. A learning graph is a graph of the course's concepts in which each connection records that one concept depends on another; Chapter 2 builds one. A skill is a packaged set of instructions that an AI agent follows to do one job, covered in Chapter 17. A glossary defines each concept in a sentence, and an FAQ answers questions a reader is likely to ask. A quiz is a set of questions that test a chapter's content.

With those terms in hand, the pipeline has eight artifacts: the course description and seven that the skills generate from it. The first four are tiers 1 to 4 of the diagram that opened this chapter, and the other four together make up tier 5. The diagram below lets you explore what each one contains and then test whether you can say what each one is built from.

docs.title: Diagram: Textbook Generation Pipeline Explorer
docs.text:
Run Textbook Generation Pipeline Explorer Fullscreen

Textbook Generation Pipeline Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: textbook-pipeline-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/signal-processing/tree/main/docs/sims/book-gen-workflow Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify, for each of the seven generated artifacts of the textbook pipeline, which of the other seven artifacts it is built from, with at least 6 of 7 exactly correct.

Prerequisites: course description, learning graph, skill, glossary, FAQ, quiz, MicroSim (all defined in the sections "Course Description" and "MicroSim" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each generated artifact, the learner checks every other artifact it is built from, then submits. A submission is correct only when the checked set equals the set in the "Built from" column of Content exactly. Mastery is 6 of 7 correct. Reading the "Contains" and "Location" text is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The chapters are written directly from the course description without a learning graph. (2) The glossary is written from the chapters rather than from the concept list. (3) A MicroSim is built from the course description rather than from a specification inside a chapter.

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level mastery of a chain is the ability to say what comes from what, so the check asks for the set of inputs of each artifact. Letting the learner read each artifact's contents first makes the dependencies something they have seen before they are asked to recall them.

Content:

Eight artifacts. The learner can open any of them and read its row. The sim labels the "Built from" column as the answer key and hides it until the learner has submitted.

# Artifact Built from Contains Location 1 Course Description none (written by the author) audience, prerequisites, overview, topics, exclusions, outcomes docs/course-description.md 2 Learning Graph Course Description concepts and dependency edges, as a CSV file and a JSON file docs/learning-graph/learning-graph.json 3 Chapter Structure Course Description, Learning Graph chapter folders with titles, summaries, and assigned concept lists docs/chapters/NN-slug/index.md 4 Chapter Content Course Description, Learning Graph, Chapter Structure prose, tables, and specifications for interactive elements docs/chapters/NN-slug/index.md 5 MicroSims Chapter Content one main.html and one index.md per simulation docs/sims/<sim-id>/ 6 Glossary Learning Graph one definition for each concept in the concept list docs/glossary.md 7 FAQ Chapter Content, Learning Graph, Glossary questions and answers drawn from the book docs/faq.md 8 Quizzes Chapter Content, Learning Graph questions for each chapter docs/chapters/NN-slug/quiz.md

Why each answer is correct, shown as feedback after the learner submits:

Artifact Why (shown as feedback) Learning Graph The concepts are enumerated from the topics and outcomes the course description states. Chapter Structure Chapters group the graph's concepts under the course description's scope, with prerequisites in the same or an earlier chapter. Chapter Content Each chapter is written from its outline and concept list, within the course description's audience and scope, and the graph's impact scores set how much space each concept gets. MicroSims A MicroSim is built from the specification block written inside a chapter. Glossary One definition is written for each concept in the graph's concept list. FAQ Questions come from what the chapters teach, the concepts in the graph, and the terms the glossary defines. Quizzes Questions test what a chapter teaches and are aligned to the graph's concepts.

Provenance: The artifact names, inputs, and locations come from this chapter's section "Course Description" and from the skill descriptions in the ibook-skills library (learning-graph-generator, book-chapter-generator, chapter-content-generator, glossary-generator, faq-generator, quiz-generator, microsim-generator). No value is synthetic.

Rules: The seven check items run in the fixed order 2 to 8. Each item offers all seven other artifacts as checkboxes, including artifacts that come later in the pipeline. An item is correct only when the checked set equals the "Built from" set exactly: a missing artifact and an extra artifact are both incorrect. The Course Description has no inputs, so it is never a check item.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner opens each of the eight artifacts in any order and reads its Contains and Location text. The learner should notice that Chapter Structure and Chapter Content share a file.
  2. The learner starts the check. The sim shows artifact 2, Learning Graph, with seven checkboxes for the other artifacts.
  3. The learner checks every artifact they think it is built from and submits. The sim shows the correct set, marks the item correct or incorrect, and shows the Why text.
  4. The learner repeats for artifacts 3 to 8 in order. The sim then shows the first-attempt score and, for each missed item, the misconception it corresponds to.

Feedback: Seven items, fixed order, one submission per item, and the submission is final. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite. It is built from: " followed by the Why text. The correct set is revealed immediately after each submission. The final score reads "n of 7 correct".

Starting State: All eight artifacts are shown in pipeline order with the course description first, nothing selected, and the question on screen is "What is each artifact built from?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the pipeline has eight artifacts: the course description and seven generated ones. It states that the course description is the seed document and that the learning graph is generated from it.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Score
docs.text: The course description quality score is a number, from 0 to 100, that rates how completely a course description supplies the elements the generators need: a title, an audience, prerequisites, topics, and learning outcomes written at the Bloom levels. A low score points at a specific missing element. This book's course description carries a score of 100 in its frontmatter, which is why the rest of the pipeline could start from it without guesswork.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
A lesson plan is a structured teaching outline for one session. It lists the objectives, the activities, and the time each takes. A chapter plus its MicroSims is the raw material, and a lesson plan arranges it into an hour a group of learners can follow. The sketch below is illustrative, for a 60-minute session on this chapter.

Minutes Activity Material 10 Predict command output, then compare answers Command Output Predictor 15 Check an assistant's command in a scratch directory The ls and head example 10 Break a link, then run a strict build The strict build example 15 Read this book's course description and find the exclusions Course Description table 10 Discuss: which pipeline step is hardest for a small model? Pipeline Explorer

docs.title: What the Benchmark Workload Produces
docs.text:
Everything above exists to make the benchmark workload legible, so it is time to state it. The workload is the ibook-skills skill chain, run by a local model on the DGX against the course description for Algebra I. This evaluation deliberately runs three of the pipeline's stages and no more. They are tiers 2, 3, and 4 of the five-tier diagram.

  1. Learning graph. The model runs the learning-graph skill on the Algebra I course description. The stage is done when the run ends on its own and leaves the graph as both a CSV file and a JSON file.
  2. Book structure. The model runs the chapter-design skill to organize its own learning graph into chapters.
  3. Chapters generated. The model runs the chapter-content skill once per chapter. A chapter counts as written when its placeholder is gone and it has at least 1,000 words.

The scale comes from a reference book. The published Algebra I book, made with cloud models, has 200 concepts, 13 chapters, and about 55,000 words of chapter text. A local model that finishes the three stages has therefore produced a structured data file with hundreds of connections, a chapter outline, and tens of thousands of words of Markdown.

Baseline Algebra I Textbook Metrics

The baseline metrics for the published Algebra I book are stored on that book's Book Metrics page. The page counts the book's concepts, chapters, MicroSims, quizzes, glossary terms, FAQ entries, and words. A program regenerates it, so its numbers can move as that book is revised. Its word count for chapters is higher than the figure used in this chapter, because it also includes each chapter's quiz and reference list.

docs.title: Why It Is a Demanding Test for a Local Model
docs.text:
The workload is hard in a specific way: it is not one hard task but a sequence of different ones, and a failure in any link breaks the next. Each demand below uses something this chapter introduced.

Demand What the model must do Concept from this chapter Structured output Write a learning graph as CSV and JSON that agree, with no cycles and no duplicate labels Course Description, Markdown Source Files Long-form writing Produce about 55,000 words of chapter prose that stays on topic and at the right level Learning Outcomes, Bloom's Taxonomy Command-line tool use Run shell commands, edit files, and run scripts through an agent harness Command Line Basics, Python Scripting Basics Format precision Follow Markdown rules such as the blank line before a list, and keep navigation entries valid Markdown Source Files, MkDocs Navigation A build that must pass Leave a site that survives a strict build Strict Site Build, Static Site Build Many turns of focus Stay on task across roughly 280 model turns, by this book's cost model Generative AI Assistant Use

A model that writes beautiful prose but breaks the JSON fails the first stage. A model that writes valid files but loses the thread after the fortieth tool call fails the third. That is why this benchmark reports per-stage results instead of one score, and why the course spends its early chapters on measuring the machine before it measures the model.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
You started from the question this book asks and a five-tier picture of how a textbook is generated, and you ended with a description of the benchmark that answers it. In between came the skills, the vocabulary, the toolchain, and the planning documents. The skills were a way of working with a generative AI assistant, the command line, Python scripts, Git and GitHub, and Markdown. The vocabulary was the intelligent textbook, its five levels, and the MicroSims inside it. The toolchain was MkDocs Material with its navigation and its static and strict builds, and the planning documents were Bloom's Taxonomy, learning outcomes, the course description and its quality score, and the lesson plan.

Groundwork Laid

You can now predict what a shell command will print, read a Python script, trace a change through Git and GitHub, read an mkdocs.yml, and say what the benchmark produces and why it is hard for a small model. That is the whole prerequisite stack, and Chapter 2 builds the learning graph on top of it.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
docs.text: Test your understanding of the working skills, the intelligent-textbook model, the MkDocs toolchain, and the course description with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which two properties define an intelligent textbook?
docs.text:
1. Cloud hosting and a conversational tutor on every page
  2. Explicit structure stored as data, and interactive elements
  3. A searchable glossary and a strict build that passes
  4. Adaptive lessons and chapters generated for each reader
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An intelligent textbook is defined by explicit structure and interactivity. Its concepts, dependencies, and learning outcomes are stored as data that software can read and check, and it contains elements the reader operates and that report back what the reader did. A conversational tutor and per-reader lessons belong to Levels 4 and 5 of the five-level scale; they are higher levels, not the defining properties.

Concept Tested: Intelligent Textbook

See: What Makes a Textbook Intelligent

docs.title: 2. What is a MicroSim?
docs.text:
1. A static figure that summarizes one chapter's main ideas
  2. A full-chapter simulation covering several related topics
  3. A build script that checks a chapter for broken links
  4. A small interactive simulation that demonstrates one idea
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A MicroSim is a small, self-contained interactive simulation, embedded in a textbook page, that demonstrates exactly one idea. The narrow scope is the point: it has one learning objective, a few controls, and a result the reader can see change, such as a slider that redraws a chart. A simulation spanning several topics breaks that rule, and a static figure gives the reader nothing to operate.

Concept Tested: MicroSim

See: MicroSim

docs.title: 3. What does mkdocs build --strict do that an ordinary build does not?
docs.text:
1. It treats every warning as an error and stops the build
  2. It publishes the finished site straight to GitHub Pages
  3. It adds every page on disk to the navigation sidebar
  4. It rewrites broken links so the build can still finish
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A strict site build treats every warning as an error. An ordinary build prints a warning about a broken link and finishes anyway, so the defect ships as a dead link. With --strict the build aborts, and the defect becomes a failed build you must fix. It does not repair links or edit the navigation for you; it only refuses to finish while warnings remain.

Concept Tested: Strict Site Build

See: Strict Site Build

docs.title: 4. What is true of a Python script that uses only the standard library?
docs.text:
1. It must be compiled to a binary before the interpreter can run it
  2. It runs on any machine with Python, with nothing installed
  3. It can run only on the aarch64 processor architecture
  4. It needs a conda environment to locate its modules
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The standard library is the set of modules that ship with Python itself, such as platform, os, and json. A script that imports only those modules needs no extra packages, so it runs on any machine that has Python. That portability is why the chapter's short machine report works unchanged on different systems. The interpreter runs a script from top to bottom; there is no separate compile step to perform first.

Concept Tested: Python Scripting Basics

See: Python Scripting Basics

docs.title: 5. Why does the typical failure of a generative AI assistant call for a habit of verification?
docs.text:
1. The answer is plausible and fluent but slightly wrong
  2. The answer is usually nonsense that will not run at all
  3. The assistant refuses requests that lack enough context
  4. The assistant returns a different command on every request
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The typical failure is not nonsense. It is an answer that is plausible, fluent, and slightly wrong, which makes it easy to accept without checking. The chapter's example command for listing the five largest files is a good answer, yet it would still list a large subdirectory among the files. Obvious nonsense is easy to catch; a nearly right answer is the dangerous one, so you run it on a scratch copy where you know the right result.

Concept Tested: Generative AI Assistant Use

See: Generative AI Assistant Use

docs.title: 6. Why does an explicit "Topics not covered" section matter in a course description?
docs.text:
1. It raises the quality score above its 100-point maximum value
  2. It lists the prerequisites the generators may assume
  3. It sets the boundary that stops a model inventing content
  4. It tells the generators which reading level and tone to write at
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The course description is the seed document, and every later artifact inherits its scope from it. A model asked to write about a DGX will happily write about training and fine-tuning unless the description rules those topics out, so an exclusion costs one line and prevents a chapter nobody wanted. Prerequisites and reading level are set by other sections: the prerequisites list and the target audience.

Concept Tested: Course Description

See: Course Description

docs.title: 7. Why can "Describe how Tailscale builds an encrypted mesh" be tested when "Understand Tailscale" cannot?
docs.text:
1. The verb names an action that an observer can check
  2. The longer wording covers more of the course content
  3. The first objective sits at a higher Bloom level
  4. The second objective lacks a clearly named learning outcome
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Bloom's Taxonomy classifies objectives by the kind of thinking they require, and each level has characteristic verbs. The verb tells you what the learner must do to show the objective was met. "Understand" gives no action to observe, while "describe" produces a description you can read and judge. The gain comes from observability, not from the length of the statement or from moving to a higher level of the taxonomy.

Concept Tested: Bloom's Taxonomy

See: Bloom's Taxonomy

docs.title: 8. Why is plain text a useful property of a Markdown source file in this workflow?
docs.text:
1. It lets a browser display the file directly without any build step
  2. It keeps a chapter's metadata hidden from the site's build tool
  3. It prevents formatting mistakes such as a collapsed list
  4. It lets Git diff it, a model write it, and a tool build it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Markdown marks structure with a few punctuation conventions in an ordinary text file. Because the file is plain text, Git can diff it, a model can generate it, and a build tool can turn it into a web page. That combination is what lets a model write a textbook and a program check it. Plain text does not prevent mistakes: a list with no blank line before it still collapses into one paragraph.

Concept Tested: Markdown Source Files

See: Markdown Source Files

docs.title: 9. You type cd docs and the shell prints nothing. Which command confirms where you are now?
docs.text:
1. cat docs, which prints the folder's contents as text
  2. pwd, which prints the working directory's absolute path
  3. grep -n docs, which prints the matching folder name
  4. cd docs again, which prints the new path on the second attempt
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Silence from a shell command usually means success, and cd prints nothing when it works. The only evidence is the state that later commands see. pwd prints the absolute path of the working directory, so it shows directly that you are now inside docs; a different listing from ls would show it as well. cat prints the contents of a file, not a folder, and grep searches a file for a pattern.

Concept Tested: Command Line Basics

See: Command Line Basics

docs.title: 10. A new chapter file exists under docs and the site builds, yet no reader can find the page in the sidebar. What is the most likely cause?
docs.text:
1. The file's frontmatter block has no title entry
  2. The iframe src in the page uses a wrong relative path
  3. The page was never listed in nav: in mkdocs.yml
  4. The site was built on a machine without GitHub Pages
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. MkDocs navigation is the sidebar tree defined by the nav: block in mkdocs.yml. A page that exists on disk but is missing from nav: is still built, yet no reader can reach it from the sidebar. Adding a page is therefore two steps: create the file, then list it. A wrong iframe path causes a different symptom, a blank box inside a page that readers can already open.

Concept Tested: MkDocs Navigation

See: MkDocs Navigation

docs.title: References: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
docs.text:
1. Git - Wikipedia - Describes Git's history, distributed design, data structures, commands, and merge strategies. Explains the version control tool behind this chapter's Git and GitHub skills, where every revision of a textbook is committed to a repository.

  2. Markdown - Wikipedia - Traces Markdown from its original syntax through CommonMark standardization and variants such as GitHub Flavored Markdown. Clarifies the plain-text source format in which every chapter and generated page of this textbook is written.

  3. Hallucination (artificial intelligence) - Wikipedia - Defines AI hallucination, its causes in language generation, and mitigation methods. Supports this chapter's warning that assistant answers can be fluent and slightly wrong, so every result must be checked before it is trusted.

  4. A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives (Complete Edition) - Lorin W. Anderson and David R. Krathwohl (editors) - Addison Wesley Longman - Replaced Bloom's single list of nouns with action verbs and a two-dimensional table crossing six cognitive processes with four knowledge types. That grid is how learning outcomes and quiz questions are labeled.

  5. Understanding by Design (Expanded 2nd Edition) - Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe - ASCD - Names and systematizes backward design: decide the desired results first, then the acceptable evidence, then the lessons. This is the logic behind writing a course description and learning outcomes before any chapter.

  6. Material for MkDocs - Material for MkDocs Documentation - Official documentation for the theme that turns Markdown files into a searchable static site, with getting started, setup, plugin, and reference sections. Shows how this book's navigation, admonitions, and build are configured.

  7. The Missing Semester of Your CS Education - MIT - Lecture series on the shell, command-line environment, development tools, and version control with Git. Practices the command-line skills this chapter assumes and that every later benchmark step relies on.

  8. The Python Tutorial - Python Documentation - Official tutorial covering the interpreter, control flow, data structures, modules, input and output, and virtual environments. Prepares you to read and run the short Python scripts the evaluation uses throughout.

  9. Prompting best practices - Anthropic Documentation - Vendor guide to writing effective prompts, including being clear and direct, adding context, and using examples. Backs this chapter's habits of stating context and asking for reasoning when working with a generative AI assistant.

  10. The Return of Intelligent Textbooks - AI Magazine - Brusilovsky, Sosnovsky, and Thaker trace intelligent textbooks across four generations, from hand-built domain models to interaction data mining. Gives research context for the intelligent-textbook model this chapter defines.

docs.title: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the data structures and rules behind generated content. Students learn how concept dependencies form a learning graph, how taxonomies and impact scores organize it, and how MicroSims, glossaries, FAQs, and quizzes are produced from it. They finish able to read the content-generation guide and predict what each pipeline stage asks of a model.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 19 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Concept Dependency 36 Directed Acyclic Graph 32 p5.js 2 vis-network 2 Foundational Concepts 1 MicroSim Status Levels 1 Learning Graph 30 Data-Driven MicroSim 1 Chapter Content 20 Concept Impact Score 2 Concept Taxonomy 1 Glossary 1 Learning Graph Viewer 1 Word-Count Targets 4 FAQ 1 Quiz 1 Content Generation Guide 1 Elaboration Budget 1 Anti-Padding Rules 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook

Where the Book's Structure Comes From

This chapter shows you the data structure behind every intelligent textbook, and the rules that decide how much each concept gets written about. When you finish, you will be able to read a learning graph, compute how important a concept is, and tell a padded chapter from a dense one. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 1 defined the intelligent textbook and the MicroSim. This chapter looks underneath them. It first explains the learning graph, the structured list of concepts and dependencies from which every chapter, glossary entry, and quiz is derived. It then explains the content generation rules, the budget and style constraints that tell an author, human or model, how much to write about each concept. A short closing section returns to MicroSims to cover the libraries and conventions you will meet when you read one.

The ideas in the first half feed directly into the second. The rules for how long a concept's section should be depend on a score computed from the learning graph, so the graph has to come first.

docs.title: Concept Dependency
docs.text:
A concept dependency is a statement that one concept must be understood before another. "Percent depends on decimals" means a learner who does not know decimals will struggle with percent. Dependencies are a property of the subject, not of a chapter order: they say what a learner needs, whatever order a book happens to present things in.

The direction matters, and this book fixes a convention. A dependency is written as an edge that points from the dependent concept to its prerequisite. The edge Percent → Decimals reads "Percent needs Decimals". The table below shows three real dependencies from this book's own learning graph, so you can see the convention at work.

Dependent concept Prerequisite it needs Why Intelligent Textbook Generative AI Assistant Use The idea of generated, structured content builds on having used a generative assistant MicroSim Intelligent Textbook A MicroSim is a part of an intelligent textbook Concept Dependency Intelligent Textbook Dependencies are stored as structure in an intelligent textbook

Check the Edge Direction

If you read an edge backwards, every prerequisite becomes a follow-on topic and the whole ordering silently inverts. Before you trust any graph, list the concepts with no prerequisites: they should be simple, introductory terms. If an advanced term shows up there, the direction is wrong.

docs.title: Foundational Concepts
docs.text:
A foundational concept is a concept with no prerequisites inside the graph. Learning can start at any of them. This book's graph has twelve of them, and they are all plain, introductory terms:

  • Command Line Basics
  • Python Scripting Basics
  • Git Version Control
  • Generative AI Assistant Use
  • Markdown Source Files
  • Bloom's Taxonomy
  • Open-Source License
  • Privacy
  • CPU Architecture
  • System RAM
  • GPU
  • Storage Capacity

The check from the warning above is exactly this list. A graph built with reversed edges would put terms like "Evaluation Report" here, and the mismatch is easy to spot once you know to look.

docs.title: Directed Acyclic Graph
docs.text:
A directed acyclic graph, abbreviated DAG, is a graph whose edges have a direction and which contains no cycle. A cycle is a path that starts at a concept and, by following dependencies, returns to it. Learning graphs must be DAGs, because a cycle would make teaching order impossible: if A needs B, B needs C, and C needs A, there is no concept you can learn first.

A valid graph always has at least one valid teaching order, called a topological order, in which every concept comes after all of its prerequisites. To find one, repeatedly take a concept whose prerequisites have all been taken already. Here is a small example with four concepts, written one dependency per line.

Percent    needs  Decimals
Decimals   needs  Fractions
Ratios     needs  Fractions

Start with the concept that needs nothing: Fractions. Then both Decimals and Ratios are available, so either can come next. Percent comes after Decimals. One valid order is Fractions, Decimals, Ratios, Percent, and another is Fractions, Ratios, Decimals, Percent. Having more than one valid order is normal.

Now add a single line, Fractions needs Percent. Fractions can no longer be learned first, because it needs Percent, which needs Decimals, which needs Fractions. The graph has a cycle and no valid order exists. The exercise below gives you six small graphs to judge.

docs.title: Diagram: DAG Cycle Spotter
docs.text:
Run DAG Cycle Spotter Fullscreen

DAG Cycle Spotter

Type: microsim sim-id: dag-cycle-spotter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/graph-algorithms/tree/main/docs/sims/dag-viewer Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish prerequisite graphs that contain a cycle from graphs that do not, in 6 small graphs, with at least 5 of 6 classified correctly.

Prerequisites: concept dependency, edge direction, directed acyclic graph, cycle, topological order (all defined in the sections "Concept Dependency" and "Directed Acyclic Graph" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each graph the learner commits to one label, "Valid (no cycle)" or "Has a cycle", before the sim reveals the answer. For a graph labeled "Has a cycle", the learner also selects the concepts that lie on the cycle. A graph is correct when the label matches the answer column and, for cycle graphs, the selected set equals the cycle set exactly. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Looking at the graph is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Two concepts that share a prerequisite form a cycle. (2) A graph with two disconnected parts is invalid. (3) A concept that depends on itself is not a cycle. (4) A longer chain of dependencies is more likely to contain a cycle.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level distinguishing needs the learner to inspect structure and decide, so each graph is small enough to trace by eye but constructed so that surface features (a shared prerequisite, a long chain, two components) do not predict the answer. Committing a label before reveal turns tracing into evidence.

Content:

Each graph is a list of dependencies in the form "dependent needs prerequisite". Concepts are Fractions, Decimals, Percent, Ratios, Proportions, and Equations. The sim labels all graphs "synthetic example".

# Dependencies Answer Cycle set Why (shown as feedback) 1 Percent needs Decimals; Decimals needs Fractions; Ratios needs Fractions; Proportions needs Ratios Valid (no cycle) none Every path ends at Fractions, which needs nothing, so a teaching order exists. 2 Percent needs Decimals; Decimals needs Fractions; Fractions needs Percent Has a cycle Percent, Decimals, Fractions Starting at Percent and following needs returns to Percent, so none of the three can be learned first. 3 Equations needs Proportions; Equations needs Percent; Proportions needs Fractions; Percent needs Fractions Valid (no cycle) none Two concepts sharing one prerequisite is normal; there is no path that returns to its start. 4 Equations needs Proportions; Proportions needs Ratios; Ratios needs Equations; Ratios needs Fractions Has a cycle Equations, Proportions, Ratios Equations, Proportions, and Ratios each need the next; the dependency on Fractions is fine but does not break the cycle. 5 Decimals needs Fractions; Percent needs Ratios Valid (no cycle) none Two separate chains are allowed; a graph does not have to be connected. 6 Percent needs Percent; Percent needs Fractions Has a cycle Percent A concept that needs itself is a cycle of length one, so it can never be learned first.

Provenance: The graphs are synthetic, constructed for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The definition of a cycle and a valid graph is the one stated in the chapter section "Directed Acyclic Graph".

Rules: Graphs are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6, and each is a list of edges plus the set of concept names. A graph is "Has a cycle" if and only if some concept can reach itself by following needs, including by a single edge to itself. Disconnected graphs are valid. Each graph allows exactly one label commitment, and for cycle graphs one selection of cycle members, and both are final.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees graph 1 as a list of dependencies and its concept names.
  2. The learner chooses "Valid (no cycle)" or "Has a cycle".
  3. If the learner chose "Has a cycle", the sim asks them to select the concepts on the cycle, then the learner confirms.
  4. The sim shows the correct label, the cycle set if there is one, and the Why text, and marks the graph correct or incorrect.
  5. The learner repeats for graphs 2 to 6. The sim then shows the score and the misconception behind each missed graph.

Feedback: Six graphs, fixed order, one committed answer each, and the answer is final. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct label, the cycle set, and the Why text. The correct answer is revealed immediately after the learner confirms. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: Graph 1 is shown with no label chosen, and the question on screen is "Can these concepts be taught in some order?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a learning graph must be a DAG, that a cycle makes teaching order impossible, that having several valid orders is normal, and that a graph may have shared prerequisites and disconnected parts.

docs.title: The Learning Graph
docs.text:
A learning graph is a directed acyclic graph of a course's concepts in which each edge is a concept dependency. In practice it is two things stored together: a list of concepts, each with an identifier, a label, and a category, and a list of dependency edges that connect them. This book keeps the graph in both a CSV file and a JSON file, and the two must agree.

The graph is the source of truth for the book's structure. The chapters of this book are a partition of its concepts, no concept appears before its prerequisites, and every glossary entry and quiz traces back to a node. The table below summarizes this book's graph. These are real values from its quality report.

Measure Value Concepts 506 Dependency edges 824 Foundational concepts (no prerequisites) 12 Terminal concepts (nothing depends on them) 193 Orphans (no edges at all) 0 Average dependencies per concept 1.67 Longest dependency chain 16 concepts Cycles 0

An Order Is Derived, Not Authored

A learning graph does not store a chapter order; it stores what depends on what, and any order that respects it is valid. That is why the same graph can be regrouped into a different number of chapters without breaking a single prerequisite.

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
A concept taxonomy assigns every concept to exactly one named category. Categories give the author a way to see the whole graph by theme and to check that no area is neglected. In this book each category has a short identifier, such as FOUND or HW, and that identifier is stored on every concept.

The graph holds 14 categories. The counts are real, and the largest two have 50 concepts each.

Category ID Concepts Environments and Hardware Probes ENV 50 Benchmark and Reporting BENCH 50 Inference Servers and Performance INFER 48 Evaluation Methodology EVAL 44 Agent Harnesses and Containment AGENT 43 Foundations and Intelligent Textbooks FOUND 39 Secure Remote Access NET 39 Model Selection and Candidates MSEL 35 Cost, Price, and Quality COST 30 Small Language Models SLM 28 DGX Hardware Architecture HW 28 Model Sizing and Fit FIT 26 Sanitization and Publication Safety SAN 25 Local Versus Cloud Services LVC 21

A category is a grouping for the author, not a teaching order. This book's chapters deliberately cut across categories when a dependency demands it, as Chapter 6 does when it reaches into the secure-access category for two concepts about administration.

docs.title: Concept Impact Score
docs.text:
The concept impact score, abbreviated CIS, measures how much of a graph rests on a concept. It is defined recursively. A concept's score is 1, counting itself, plus the scores of all concepts that depend on it directly:

\[ \mathrm{CIS}(x) = 1 + \sum_{d \in \mathrm{dependents}(x)} \mathrm{CIS}(d) \]

Recursion Is Easier Backwards

A formula defined in terms of itself looks circular, and most people need two passes at it. Start at the concepts nothing depends on, which score exactly 1, and work backwards toward the foundations; every score you need is already computed.

A concept that nothing depends on scores 1. A concept with dependents scores more, and the score accumulates through chains, so a concept deep in the foundations can score very high even if only one or two concepts depend on it directly. Consider a six-concept graph with these dependencies, where "B needs A" means B depends on A.

B needs A
C needs A
D needs B
D needs C
E needs D
F needs C

Work from the end of the graph. E and F have no dependents, so each scores 1. D has one dependent, E, so D scores 1 + 1 = 2. C has dependents D and F, so C scores 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. B has dependent D, so B scores 1 + 2 = 3. A has dependents B and C, so A scores 1 + 3 + 4 = 8.

Concept Direct dependents Calculation CIS E none 1 1 F none 1 1 D E 1 + 1 2 C D, F 1 + 2 + 1 4 B D 1 + 2 3 A B, C 1 + 3 + 4 8

The result is intuitive: A is the most foundational concept and scores highest. The formula adds a shared descendant once for every route that reaches it, which is how the scores grow quickly in a large graph. In this book, Generative AI Assistant Use scores 2,518 and Generative AI Model scores 2,364, while 193 of the 506 concepts score 1. Most of the book is narrow detail resting on a small foundation.

docs.title: Diagram: CIS Calculator
docs.text:
Run CIS Calculator Fullscreen

CIS Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: cis-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/concept-dependencies Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the concept impact score of each of 6 concepts in a small dependency graph, working from the concepts nothing depends on, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: concept dependency, dependents, concept impact score and its formula (all defined in the section "Concept Impact Score" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner enters one whole number for each concept, in the order the sim presents them, before the sim reveals the correct value. An entry is correct when it equals the CIS column in Content exactly. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Inspecting the graph before answering is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A concept's score counts only its direct dependents' count, not their scores. (2) A concept's score excludes itself. (3) The concept with the most direct dependents always has the highest score.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation requires the learner to carry a procedure through a structure, and CIS can only be computed in an order where each dependent's score is already known. Presenting concepts in that order makes the order itself visible, and revealing a value after each entry corrects a misconception before it propagates.

Content:

The graph is shown with six concepts, A to F, and these six dependencies in the form "dependent needs prerequisite". The sim labels the graph "synthetic example".

Dependent Needs B A C A D B D C E D F C

Concepts are presented in this order, which is a valid order for computing the scores. The learner enters a whole number from 1 to 20.

Step Concept Direct dependents CIS Why (shown as feedback) 1 E none 1 Nothing depends on E, so only E itself counts: 1. 2 F none 1 Nothing depends on F, so only F itself counts: 1. 3 D E 2 D counts itself plus E's score: 1 + 1 = 2. 4 C D, F 4 C counts itself plus D's score and F's score: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. 5 B D 3 B counts itself plus D's score: 1 + 2 = 3. 6 A B, C 8 A counts itself plus B's score and C's score: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8.

Provenance: The graph is synthetic, constructed for this exercise, and the sim labels it "synthetic example". The formula is the one stated in the chapter section "Concept Impact Score".

Rules: CIS(x) = 1 + the sum of CIS(d) for every concept d that needs x directly. A concept with no dependents scores 1. The accepted entry is a whole number from 1 to 20 with step 1, and the default entry is empty. The expected values are in the CIS column, and correctness is an exact match.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the graph and the first concept, E, with an empty entry.
  2. The learner enters a whole number and confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct value, marks the entry correct or incorrect, and shows the Why text, then adds the confirmed value beside that concept in the graph.
  4. The learner continues through steps 2 to 6. Each Why text uses the values already shown for the concepts that depend on it.
  5. After step 6 the sim shows the score and, for any missed step, the misconception it corresponds to.

Feedback: Six steps, fixed order, one entry each, and the entry is final. The correct value and the Why text are shown immediately after the learner confirms. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct value and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: The graph is shown with no values, E is the first concept, and the question on screen is "How much of this graph rests on E?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the formula CIS(x) = 1 + the sum of the scores of x's direct dependents, that a concept with no dependents scores 1, and that in the worked example A scores 8, C scores 4, B scores 3, D scores 2, and E and F each score 1.

docs.title: vis-network
docs.text: vis-network is a JavaScript library that draws nodes and edges in a web page and lets the reader drag, zoom, and click them. It expects data in a simple shape: a list of nodes, each with an id and a label, and a list of edges, each with a from and a to. This book's learning graph is stored in exactly that shape, which is why the same file can both describe the course and be drawn directly.

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text: The learning graph viewer is a MicroSim that draws a learning graph with vis-network. It colors nodes by category, lets you search for a concept, and lets you click a node to see its prerequisites and dependents. Viewing the whole graph is the fastest way to find a surprising dependency or a neglected area. The viewer below opens this book's own graph.

docs.title: Diagram: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text:
Run the Learning Graph Viewer fullscreen

Learning Graph Viewer (reused MicroSim)

Type: graph-model sim-id: graph-viewer Library: vis-network Status: Reused Source: sims/graph-viewer/index.md in this book Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/dgx-eval/tree/main/docs/sims/graph-viewer Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine this book's learning graph to find the concepts a chosen concept depends on and the concepts that depend on it.

Reused from this book's own MicroSims, which already exists locally, so no new specification is needed.

Search for the Hub First

Search the viewer for "Generative AI Model" and follow its edges outward. A concept with a CIS in the thousands touches a big share of the graph, which makes it the quickest way to see how the book hangs together.

docs.title: Chapter Content
docs.text:
Chapter content is the body of a chapter: the prose, tables, worked examples, and specifications for interactive elements that teach the chapter's concepts. It is written into the chapter's index.md file, below a fixed header that already lists the title, summary, concepts, and prerequisites.

The chapter file you are reading has this anatomy, abbreviated.

---
title: "..."
description: "..."
---

# Chapter Title
## Summary
## Concepts Covered      <- table of concept and impact score
## Prerequisites
---
(chapter content: prose, tables, worked examples, MicroSim specifications)

A generator is given the header and asked to fill in everything below the final rule. The header is also the checklist the output is judged against: every concept in the table should be taught, so a missing concept is a defect that a program can find.

docs.title: Word-Count Targets
docs.text:
Word-count targets are guidelines for how many words a section of chapter content should have. This book does not use a single number per chapter. Instead each concept gets its own target, driven by its impact score, because a concept many others rest on deserves more careful explanation than a leaf.

The calculation has two steps. First normalize the concept's CIS against the largest CIS in the whole book, using a logarithm, because CIS is heavy-tailed and a straight proportion would crush the large majority of concepts to nearly zero. Call the result the elaboration score, E:

\[ E(c) = \frac{\ln(\mathrm{CIS}(c) + 1)}{\ln(\mathrm{CIS}_{\max} + 1)} \]

Second, map E to a tier. In this book \( \mathrm{CIS}_{\max} \) is 2,518.

Tier E range Target words Required elements A 0.5 or more 500 to 750 A worked example and a diagram, chart, table, or MicroSim B 0.2 up to 0.5 250 to 400 A worked example C under 0.2 120 to 200 A clear definition

Here are three real concepts worked through. Generative AI Assistant Use has CIS 2,518, so E is \( \ln 2519 / \ln 2519 = 1.00 \), which is tier A. Concept Dependency has CIS 36, so E is \( \ln 37 / \ln 2519 \approx 0.46 \), which is tier B and just below the tier A line. Anti-Padding Rules has CIS 1, so E is \( \ln 2 / \ln 2519 \approx 0.09 \), which is tier C.

docs.title: Elaboration Budget
docs.text:
An elaboration budget is the table of every concept in a chapter with its elaboration score, tier, and target words, together with their sum. It is computed before any prose is written, and the chapter's length follows from it instead of being chosen separately.

This chapter's budget is a worked example. It has 5 tier B concepts, at 250 to 400 words each, and 14 tier C concepts, at 120 to 200 words each. The sum is 2,930 to 4,800 words. A chapter with several tier A concepts, such as Chapter 3, runs longer for the same reason, and that variation is intentional.

docs.title: Anti-Padding Rules
docs.text:
Anti-padding rules are the instructions that stop a generator from reaching a word target by inflating text. Models are prone to this, and padded text is repetitive and sometimes wrong. This book gives four.

  1. Quality over quantity. A target is a guideline; a dense, correct section beats a padded one that reaches the number.
  2. Expand by showing, not telling. If a section is thin, add a worked example, another simulation, or more technical detail, and never restate earlier paragraphs.
  3. No formulaic templates. Avoid boilerplate like "Let's talk about X" and weave concepts into flowing narrative.
  4. Examples over prose. Prefer a short commented example or a MicroSim to a long description of abstract logic.

A Target Is Not a Quota

A model that sees "500 words" will often manufacture 500 words, restating itself to get there. The remedy is to read a short section against its target and ask what is missing; if the answer is "nothing", the section is finished, and adding words only lowers the quality.

docs.title: Content Generation Guide
docs.text:
The content generation guide is the file, CONTENT-GENERATION-GUIDE.md at the root of this repository, that gathers every writing rule in one place so that an agent can be told to read it first. It holds the concept-depth and word-count targets, the anti-padding rules, the MicroSim expectations, the Markdown formatting rules, and the learning mascot's identity and placement rules. The repository's agent instructions require it to be read before any student-facing content is written.

Putting the rules in a file matters for small models in particular. A rule that lives only in a prompt is lost when the context fills up; a rule in a file can be re-read. The same file is also what makes two runs comparable, because both started from the same instructions.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: A glossary defines each concept in the course in one precise, concise, non-circular sentence, usually followed by a short example. It is generated from the learning graph's concept list, so every concept in the graph gets exactly one entry and the book uses the same wording everywhere. A good definition names the category of the thing and what distinguishes it, without using the term itself.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: An FAQ is a set of questions readers are likely to ask, each with a short answer drawn from the book. It is generated from the chapter content, the learning graph, and the glossary, typically at least thirty questions, so it is written after those exist. Its value is that it answers in the reader's own words what the chapters answer in the author's.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
A quiz is a set of questions, one set per chapter, that tests what the chapter taught. Questions are multiple choice and are spread across the Bloom's Taxonomy levels from Chapter 1, so a quiz tests more than recall. Each question is tied to a concept in the learning graph, which lets a reader's wrong answers point back to the exact concept to review.

The Graph Drives Everything Downstream

The graph does not only order the chapters. Its scores size every section, its concept list generates the glossary, and its edges let a quiz point a wrong answer at a prerequisite. One careful structure feeds five outputs, which is exactly why a flaw in it is so costly.

docs.title: p5.js
docs.text:
p5.js is a JavaScript library for drawing shapes and responding to the mouse and keyboard. Most MicroSims in this book are p5.js programs. A p5.js sketch has two main functions: setup() runs once at the start and creates the canvas and any controls, and draw() runs repeatedly and redraws the picture.

This book requires that controls be p5.js's own built-in ones, such as createSlider and createButton, never hand-drawn shapes made to look like controls. Built-in controls get keyboard support and consistent behavior for free.

let slider;

function setup() {
  createCanvas(300, 100);
  slider = createSlider(10, 90, 40);
}

function draw() {
  background(255);
  circle(150, 50, slider.value());
}

In this sketch setup() creates a canvas 300 pixels wide and 100 tall and one slider that ranges from 10 to 90, starting at 40. Each time draw() runs it clears the canvas and draws a circle whose diameter is the slider's current value, so dragging the slider changes the circle immediately.

docs.title: Data-Driven MicroSim
docs.text:
A data-driven MicroSim keeps its content in a separate data file, usually JSON, instead of writing it into the program. The program reads the file and draws what it finds. This separates the logic from the facts, so correcting a number or adding a model means editing a data file, not the code.

This book's Parameters That Fit in Memory MicroSim works this way: its ten candidate models live in a model-data.json file next to its main.html. The program is the same whatever the file holds.

docs.title: MicroSim Status Levels
docs.text:
MicroSim status levels record how far a MicroSim has progressed. The status is stored in the frontmatter of its index.md page and shown as a colored dot in the navigation sidebar.

Status Dot Meaning scaffold Red A specification exists, but there is no implementation yet built Orange Implemented, awaiting the Primary Author's review approved Green Tested by the Primary Author and approved for learners

The site configuration also recognizes implemented and instrumented, used by other books in this series. Only a human reviewer moves a MicroSim to approved; a generator may reach built, and no further.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
You started with the dependency between two concepts and ended with the rules that size a chapter. A concept dependency is an edge from a dependent to its prerequisite. A learning graph is a DAG of concepts and their dependencies, grouped by a taxonomy and scored by CIS. Those scores set a word-count target per concept, summed into an elaboration budget and constrained by anti-padding rules written in the content generation guide. The glossary, FAQ, and quizzes follow from the same graph, and MicroSims built with p5.js or vis-network make it interactive.

The Structure Is Yours Now

You can now check a graph's edge direction, compute a concept impact score by hand, and read an elaboration tier off it. That is the machinery that decides how every later chapter is shaped, and Chapter 3 turns to the models whose output it will judge.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
docs.text: Test your understanding of learning graphs, concept impact scores, and the rules for generated content with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. In this book's convention, which way does a concept dependency edge point?
docs.text:
1. From the prerequisite to the concept that depends on it
  2. From the dependent concept to its prerequisite
  3. From an earlier chapter to a later chapter
  4. From a taxonomy category to each concept inside it
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A concept dependency states that one concept must be understood before another, and this book writes it as an edge from the dependent concept to its prerequisite.
