The edge Percent → Decimals reads "Percent needs Decimals". Reading an edge the other way turns every prerequisite into a follow-on topic and silently inverts the whole ordering. Dependencies are a property of the subject, so they do not point from chapter to chapter.

Concept Tested: Concept Dependency

See: Concept Dependency

docs.title: 2. What is a directed acyclic graph?
docs.text:
1. A graph in which every concept has exactly one prerequisite
  2. A graph whose concepts are all connected in a single chain
  3. A graph with undirected edges and at most one cycle
  4. A graph whose edges have a direction and form no cycle
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, has edges with a direction and contains no cycle, where a cycle is a path that follows dependencies back to its starting concept. A learning graph must be a DAG because a cycle leaves no concept that can be learned first. A DAG does not have to be a single chain, and a concept in it may have several prerequisites or share one with another concept.

Concept Tested: Directed Acyclic Graph

See: Directed Acyclic Graph

docs.title: 3. What serves as the checklist that generated chapter content is judged against?
docs.text:
1. The word count of the previous chapter in the book
  2. The chapter header, whose concept table must all be taught
  3. The FAQ entries that were generated for the chapter
  4. The navigation sidebar entry that points to the chapter
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Chapter content is written into the chapter's index.md below a fixed header that lists the title, summary, concepts, and prerequisites. A generator is given that header and asked to fill in everything below the final rule. The header doubles as the checklist: every concept in its table should be taught, so a missing concept is a defect a program can find. The FAQ is generated afterward from the chapters, so it cannot be the standard.

Concept Tested: Chapter Content

See: Chapter Content

docs.title: 4. Who may move a MicroSim from built to approved?
docs.text:
1. The generator, once the site passes a strict build
  2. Any agent that has read the content generation guide
  3. Only a human reviewer who has tested the MicroSim
  4. The site build, when the sidebar dot turns green
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. MicroSim status levels record how far a sim has progressed: scaffold means only a specification exists, built means it is implemented and awaiting review, and approved means it was tested and approved for learners. Only a human reviewer moves a MicroSim to approved; a generator may reach built and no further. The colored dot in the sidebar displays the status stored in the page's frontmatter. It does not set it.

Concept Tested: MicroSim Status Levels

See: MicroSim Status Levels

docs.title: 5. Why can the same learning graph be regrouped into a different number of chapters without breaking a prerequisite?
docs.text:
1. Each taxonomy category maps to exactly one chapter
  2. The graph stores a fixed chapter number on every concept
  3. It stores dependencies, not an authored chapter order
  4. Orphan concepts can be moved freely between any two chapters
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A learning graph is a DAG of concepts whose edges are dependencies. It does not store a chapter order; it stores what depends on what, and any order that respects those dependencies is valid. Chapters are a partition of the concepts in which no concept appears before its prerequisites. Taxonomy categories are a grouping for the author, not a teaching order, and this book's chapters deliberately cut across them.

Concept Tested: Learning Graph

See: The Learning Graph

docs.title: 6. Why does the elaboration score normalize CIS with a logarithm instead of a straight proportion?
docs.text:
1. Impact scores can be negative for the graph's terminal concepts
  2. A logarithm places every concept in the top tier
  3. Word counts must stay under a fixed chapter limit
  4. CIS is heavy-tailed, so a plain ratio crushes most scores
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A concept's word-count target comes from its elaboration score, which divides the logarithm of its CIS plus one by the logarithm of the largest CIS plus one. The logarithm is needed because CIS is heavy-tailed: a few foundational concepts score in the thousands while 193 of the 506 concepts score 1. A straight proportion would crush the large majority to nearly zero. With the logarithm, a concept with a CIS of 36 scores about 0.46 and lands in tier B.

Concept Tested: Word-Count Targets

See: Word-Count Targets

docs.title: 7. Why does keeping the writing rules in a file matter for small models in particular?
docs.text:
1. A rule in a file can be re-read after the context fills up
  2. A rule in a file is enforced automatically by the build
  3. A file lets the model skip any rules that it finds irrelevant
  4. A file is always shorter than the same rules written in a prompt
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The content generation guide gathers every writing rule in one file so an agent can be told to read it first. That matters for small models because a rule that lives only in a prompt is lost when the context fills up, while a rule in a file can be re-read. The same file also makes two runs comparable, since both started from the same instructions. The build does not enforce the writing rules for the model.

Concept Tested: Content Generation Guide

See: Content Generation Guide

docs.title: 8. Why does the book treat a word-count target as a guideline and not a quota?
docs.text:
1. The tier boundaries change from one chapter to the next
  2. Short sections always score higher when they are reviewed
  3. Padding to reach a number adds repetition and errors
  4. A generator has no means of counting the words it wrote
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Anti-padding rules stop a generator from reaching a word target by inflating text. A model that sees "500 words" will often manufacture 500 words by restating itself, and padded text is repetitive and sometimes wrong. A target is therefore a guideline: a dense, correct section beats a padded one that reaches the number. If a section is thin, the remedy is a worked example or more technical detail, never a restatement of earlier paragraphs.

Concept Tested: Anti-Padding Rules

See: Anti-Padding Rules

docs.title: 9. In a small graph, Q needs P, R needs P, and S needs R. Nothing depends on Q or S. What is the concept impact score of P?
docs.text:
1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 3
  4. 4
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A concept's impact score is 1 for itself plus the scores of every concept that depends on it directly. Work from the ends: Q and S have no dependents, so each scores 1. R has one dependent, S, so R scores 1 + 1 = 2. P has dependents Q and R, so P scores 1 + 1 + 2 = 4. An answer of 2 counts only the number of direct dependents, and an answer of 3 leaves out P itself.

Concept Tested: Concept Impact Score

See: Concept Impact Score

docs.title: 10. In a generated learning graph, the concepts with no prerequisites are advanced terms such as "Evaluation Report", and no introductory term appears among them. What does this pattern indicate?
docs.text:
1. The dependency edges were written in the reversed direction
  2. The graph contains a cycle among its advanced concepts
  3. The advanced concepts were put in the wrong taxonomy category
  4. The impact scores were normalized without a logarithm
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A foundational concept has no prerequisites inside the graph, so learning can start there. In a correct graph these are plain, introductory terms such as Command Line Basics. If advanced terms such as "Evaluation Report" show up there instead, the edges were written backwards, which turns every prerequisite into a follow-on topic. Listing the concepts with no prerequisites is the check to run before trusting any graph. A cycle gives a different symptom: no valid teaching order exists at all.

Concept Tested: Foundational Concepts

See: Foundational Concepts

docs.title: References: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
docs.text:
1. Directed acyclic graph - Wikipedia - Defines DAGs and covers their mathematical properties, computational problems, and applications. Explains the structure of a learning graph, in which no concept may depend on itself through any chain of prerequisites.

  2. Topological sorting - Wikipedia - Describes ordering a DAG's vertices so every edge points forward, with Kahn's algorithm and depth-first search. Shows why any valid chapter order is derived from dependencies rather than authored.

  3. Knowledge space - Wikipedia - Summarizes the mathematical model in which a prerequisite partial order defines states of knowledge and the fringe of what a learner is ready to study next. Gives theoretical grounding for storing concept dependencies as data.

  4. Introduction to Algorithms (3rd Edition) - Thomas H. Cormen, Charles E. Leiserson, Ronald L. Rivest, and Clifford Stein - MIT Press - Teaches topological sort through the recurring example of Professor Bumstead putting on his clothes in a valid order, a dependency example many courses reuse. It makes prerequisite ordering and cycle detection concrete.

  5. On Writing Well (30th Anniversary Edition) - William Zinsser - HarperCollins - Widely praised for its Simplicity and Clutter chapters, which show how cutting words that do no work strengthens prose. It is the human discipline behind the anti-padding rules, which prefer dense sections to word-target inflation.

  6. Directed Acyclic Graphs - NetworkX Documentation - Reference for Python functions that test whether a graph is a DAG and compute topological order, ancestors, and descendants. Shows how a script can check a learning graph for cycles and trace which concepts depend on a given concept.

  7. The Theory Underlying Concept Maps and How to Construct and Use Them - IHMC - Novak and Cañas explain concept maps, in which concepts joined by labeled linking phrases form propositions organized around a focus question. Gives the educational background for representing a course's concepts and their relationships as a graph.

  8. vis-network documentation - vis.js - Documents the canvas-based Network library, including nodes, edges, layout, physics, interaction options, and events. Describes the library that draws this book's interactive learning graph viewer from a list of nodes and edges.

  9. createSlider() - p5.js Reference - Reference entry for the built-in slider control, with its minimum, maximum, value, and step parameters. Shows the kind of built-in control that this book requires in MicroSims instead of hand-drawn widgets.

  10. Creating Exams - Carnegie Mellon University Eberly Center - Advice on writing multiple-choice items, including one best answer, plausible distractors drawn from common student errors, and matching item types to learning objectives. Applies to the quiz rules that tie each question to a concept.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter defines small language models and what separates them from frontier models. It explains tokens, parameters, context windows, open weights, and licenses, and names the capabilities that textbook generation demands: long-form writing, structured output, tool calling, and code generation. Students finish able to state precisely what a small language model is and what it must do to be a viable generator.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 23 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Open-Source License 12 Generative AI Model 2364 Large Language Model 1035 Parameter Count 591 Inference 556 Token 101 Open-Weight Model 62 Model Family 18 Small Language Model 386 Structured Output 214 Context Window 68 Frontier Model 19 Model Card 10 Model License Terms 9 Long-Form Writing 3 Code Generation 3 Tokenizer 2 Instruction Following 2 Multimodal Model 2 Reasoning Mode 1 Tool Calling 205 Image Input 1 Tokens per Word 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook

Meet the Thing Being Measured

Everything in this course is measured against a language model, so this chapter makes sure you know exactly what one is. By the end you will be able to define a small language model, estimate whether a document fits in its memory of a conversation, and name the five abilities that textbook generation demands. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 1 gave you the textbook and Chapter 2 gave you its data structure. This chapter turns to the machine that has to write it. It begins with the vocabulary of language models: what they are, how they read text in tokens, and what the numbers attached to them, such as parameter count and context window, actually mean. It then separates a small language model from a frontier model, explains what open weights and licenses allow, and ends with the capabilities that the benchmark workload exercises.

Several of these ideas are quantitative, and they come back repeatedly. Parameter count reappears in Chapter 11 when it is converted into gigabytes, and the context window decides what a harness can load in Chapter 16. Learning them precisely here costs less than re-deriving them later.

docs.title: Language Models From the Ground Up
Generative AI Model
docs.text:
A generative AI model is a trained program that produces new content, such as text, images, code, or audio, in response to an input. It learned statistical patterns from a large body of training data, and it generates by applying those patterns to produce output that is plausible given the input. This course concerns only models that generate text.

The contrast with a classifier makes the definition concrete. A classifier maps an input to one label from a fixed set. A generative model produces open-ended output, so there is no fixed list of possible answers. Consider the same email handled both ways.

Classifier Generative model Input The text of an email The text of an email and an instruction Output One label: spam or not spam Any text: a summary, a reply, a rewrite Possible outputs Two Effectively unlimited Failure mode Wrong label Fluent text that is wrong or off-task

The last row is the important one for this course. A classifier's mistakes are bounded: there are only two labels to get wrong. A generative model's mistakes are not, which is why measuring one needs the careful design that Chapters 19 and 20 teach.

docs.title: Large Language Model
docs.text:
A large language model, abbreviated LLM, is a generative AI model trained on very large amounts of text to predict what text comes next. It is a neural network, a program built from many layers of simple numeric operations, whose behavior is determined by a very large set of learned numbers. The word "large" refers to the number of those numbers and the amount of text used in training.

The core mechanism is one repeated step. Given the text so far, the model assigns a probability to every possible next piece of text. A piece is chosen, appended to the text, and the process repeats until a stop condition is met. The table shows one step of that process for the input "The capital of France is". The probabilities are illustrative.

Candidate next piece Illustrative probability Paris 0.92 a 0.02 the 0.01 located 0.01 all other candidates combined 0.04

If the model always takes the highest-probability piece, its output is repeatable; if it samples in proportion to the probabilities, the output varies from run to run. Chapter 15 covers the settings that control this. What matters here is the mechanism: a language model writes one piece at a time, and every piece depends on everything before it.

One consequence is easy to miss. Everything a model knows was fixed when training ended, and during use it sees only the text it is given. It cannot look at your files, your machine, or yesterday's news unless that text is placed in its input. This is why the tools and harnesses of Chapters 16 and 17 exist: they are how a model gets to see, and act on, anything outside its prompt.

Everything Else Is Built on This Loop

A language model that writes a chapter, fills a JSON file, or calls a tool is doing the same thing at each step: choosing the next piece of text. That explains both its fluency and its failures, because a mistake early in the output is never revisited, only built upon.

docs.title: Token
docs.text:
A token is the unit of text a language model reads and writes. A token is usually a whole common word, a piece of a longer or rarer word, a number, or a punctuation mark. Models do not see letters or whole sentences; they see a sequence of tokens, each identified by a number.

Rare words split into several tokens, so a sentence's token count is not its word count. The split below is illustrative, because the exact pieces depend on the model.

Sentence:  Quantization shrinks models.
Tokens:    Quant | ization |  shr | inks |  models | .
Count:     6 tokens for 3 words

The same text can have a different token count under a different model, because each model has its own vocabulary of pieces. Counting tokens is therefore always relative to a particular model. That component is the next concept.

docs.title: Tokenizer
docs.text:
A tokenizer is the component that converts text into tokens before the model reads it, and converts tokens back into text afterwards. It uses a fixed vocabulary learned alongside the model, and it is not interchangeable between models: text tokenized for one model must be decoded with the same tokenizer. The tokenizer also decides how efficiently a model handles different kinds of text.

Count With the Model's Own Tokenizer

A words-to-tokens ratio is a good planning estimate, but the budget that matters is the one the model's own tokenizer reports. Run the real text through it before you commit to a context size; the gap grows for code, numbers, and non-English text.

docs.title: Tokens per Word
docs.text:
Tokens per word is the average number of tokens produced per word of ordinary English prose. A common planning figure is about 1.33 tokens per word, which is the same as saying about three-quarters of a word per token. This book's cost model uses 1.33, so a 55,000-word book is about 73,000 tokens.

The figure is an estimate with a known direction of error. Text full of code, identifiers, numbers, or technical terms produces more tokens per word, so the 1.33 figure understates it. Use it for planning, and use the real tokenizer for decisions.

docs.title: Context Window
docs.text:
The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can consider at one time, counting both the text it is given and the text it generates. When a conversation grows past the window, something has to be dropped or the request fails. The window is a hard limit, and it is measured in tokens, not words. In a multi-turn session it is also a running total: each new turn adds the earlier conversation, every file the model has read, and every result a tool returned, so a long agent session fills the window faster than a single prompt would suggest.

A worked example shows the arithmetic. Suppose a model has an 8,000-token window and you give it a 5,000-word document to summarize and expect a reply of up to 2,000 tokens. The document is about 5,000 × 1.33 = 6,650 tokens. Add the reply's room and you need about 8,650 tokens, which is more than 8,000. The document fits by itself, and the task does not.

The following table lists the context windows of five of this evaluation's candidate models, as their publishers report them. They span nearly an order of magnitude.

Model Context window (tokens) devstral-small-2:24b 384,000 nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 1,000,000 qwen3.8:27b 256,000 gemma4:26b 128,000 gpt-oss:120b 128,000

A larger window is not free. Chapter 11 shows that a longer context takes memory from the same pool as the model's weights, so the largest advertised window is often not the largest usable one. The exercise below drills the arithmetic you just saw.

docs.title: Diagram: Words to Tokens Estimator
docs.text:
Run Words to Tokens Estimator Fullscreen

Words to Tokens Estimator

Type: microsim sim-id: words-to-tokens-estimator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/Digital-Transformation-with-AI-Spring-2026/tree/main/docs/sims/tokenization-process Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the estimated token count of a document from its word count and decide whether the document and a 2,000-token reply fit in a given context window, correct on at least 5 of 6 items.

Prerequisites: token, tokens per word, context window (all defined in the sections "Token", "Tokens per Word", and "Context Window" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each item the learner enters an estimated token count and then chooses "Fits" or "Does not fit" before the sim reveals the answer. An item is correct when the entry is within 1% of the value in the Estimated tokens column and the choice equals the Answer column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Reading the reference formula is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A token is a word, so the token count equals the word count. (2) The context window holds only the document, and the reply does not count against it. (3) A document that fits by itself also fits with the reply. (4) A model with a larger window can always use all of it.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs a procedure carried to a decision, so the learner converts words to tokens and then compares to a limit. Items are ordered so that item 2 fits before the reply is added and does not fit after, which makes the second misconception visible.

Content:

The formula shown to the learner is: estimated tokens = words × 1.33. The reserved reply is always 2,000 tokens. An item fits when estimated tokens + 2,000 is less than or equal to the window. The sim labels all numbers "illustrative".

# Document (words) Window (tokens) Estimated tokens Estimated tokens + 2,000 Answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 1,000 8,000 1,330 3,330 Fits 3,330 is below 8,000, so there is room to spare. 2 5,000 8,000 6,650 8,650 Does not fit The document alone is 6,650 tokens, but with the 2,000-token reply the total is 8,650, which is over 8,000. 3 4,000 8,000 5,320 7,320 Fits 7,320 is below 8,000, so the reply also fits. 4 55,000 128,000 73,150 75,150 Fits 75,150 is below 128,000, so a whole book of this size fits. 5 95,000 128,000 126,350 128,350 Does not fit The document alone is under the window, but 128,350 is over 128,000 by 350 tokens. 6 95,000 256,000 126,350 128,350 Fits The same document fits easily in a 256,000-token window.

Provenance: The tokens-per-word figure of 1.33 and the 55,000-word book size are the values used in this book's cost model (cost analysis page). The documents, windows, and reply size are illustrative and invented for this exercise.

Rules: Estimated tokens = words × 1.33, so 1,000 words is 1,330 tokens. The word count entry is fixed per item and not adjustable. The learner's token entry is a whole number from 0 to 300,000 with step 1, and the default is empty. The entry is correct when it is within 1% of the Estimated tokens value. Fit rule: Estimated tokens + 2,000 <= window.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees item 1: a document's word count and a window size.
  2. The learner enters an estimated token count and chooses "Fits" or "Does not fit", then confirms.
  3. The sim reveals the model value, the total with the reply, the correct choice, and the Why text, and marks the item correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for items 2 to 6. After item 6 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each missed item.

Feedback: Six items, fixed order, one confirmed answer each, and the answer is final. An item is correct only when both the entry and the choice are correct. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the model value, the correct choice, and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: Item 1 is shown with an empty entry and no choice, and the question on screen is "How many tokens is this, and does it fit?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that tokens per word is about 1.33, that the context window counts both the text given and the text generated, that a 5,000-word document in an 8,000-token window with a 2,000-token reply needs about 8,650 tokens and does not fit, and that a 55,000-word book is about 73,000 tokens.

docs.title: Parameter Count
docs.text:
A parameter is one of the learned numbers inside a model, and the parameter count is how many there are. It is the usual measure of a model's size. A model described as 27B has 27 billion parameters, which is 27,000,000,000 separate numbers that were adjusted during training and are fixed at the time you use it.

Parameter count is the main driver of two practical quantities. The first is memory: every parameter must be held in memory to run the model, so more parameters means more memory, a conversion Chapter 11 performs exactly. The second is the work per token: a model with more parameters generally does more arithmetic for each token it produces and so, other things equal, generates more slowly.

The five models below show the range this evaluation covers. Parameter counts are as the publishers report them.

Model Parameters Relative to the smallest devstral-small-2:24b 24 billion 1.0 times qwen3.8:27b 27 billion 1.1 times gemma4:31b 30.7 billion 1.3 times gpt-oss:120b 117 billion 4.9 times mistral-medium-3.5:128b 128 billion 5.3 times

Size Is a Cost, Not a Score

Parameter count tells you what a model costs to hold and run. It does not tell you how well it writes or follows a skill, and a smaller model can outperform a larger one on a given task. Treat the number as an input to the memory calculation and let a measurement decide quality.

Some models report two counts, a total and a smaller number that is active for each token. The distinction between dense and mixture-of-experts models is part of Chapter 11, and it explains why gpt-oss:120b in the table can run fast despite its size.

docs.title: Inference
docs.text:
Inference is the act of running a trained model to produce output. It is distinct from training, which is the process that created the model's parameters from data. A model is trained once, at great expense, and then used for inference many times. This course evaluates inference only; training and fine-tuning are out of scope.

Inference happens in two phases. First the model reads the whole prompt, which can be processed in parallel. Then it generates the reply one token at a time, and each new token requires another pass through the network. Output length therefore dominates the time a long generation takes. As an illustration, generating 1,000 tokens at 20 tokens per second takes 50 seconds, and a 10,000-token chapter takes 500 seconds at the same rate. The rate here is invented to show the arithmetic; Chapter 15 measures real ones.

Training Inference What it does Creates the parameters from data Uses fixed parameters to produce output How often Once per model version Every time the model is used Hardware demand Very large clusters One machine can be enough In this course Out of scope The whole subject

docs.title: Small Language Model
docs.text:
A small language model, abbreviated SLM, is a language model small enough to run on a single machine you control. There is no universal parameter threshold, and the boundary moves as hardware improves. This course uses a working definition tied to the machine under test: a model that fits in the memory of one DGX system and can be served from it.

Under that definition the candidates in this evaluation range from 24 billion to 128 billion parameters, large by the standard of older "small" models and small next to the largest frontier systems. What makes a model an SLM in this course is not an absolute size but a circumstance: you can download it, run it on hardware you own, and keep every token on that machine.

The working definition has two parts, and a model can pass one and fail the other. Consider two candidates from this evaluation's first round on one DGX unit with 128 GB of memory. Each can be downloaded and loaded, so each meets the first test of being open-weight and local.

Model Download Result on one unit Usable as an SLM here? qwen3.8:27b 17 GB Completed the first benchmark stage Yes mistral-medium-3.5:128b 80 GB Loaded and ran at 3 tokens per second; no context of 64,000 tokens or more fit No

The second model is a language model you can own, and on this machine it is not a small one in the sense that matters. The definition is relative to the hardware, so the answer for the same model could change on a larger system.

docs.title: Frontier Model
docs.text:
A frontier model is one of the most capable models available at a given time, typically operated by a leading AI lab and offered as a cloud service. Its weights are usually not released and its size is often not disclosed. "Frontier" is a moving target: a model leaves the frontier when a newer one surpasses it.

The comparison below is the one this course returns to throughout. It is a summary of definitions already given, not a verdict on quality.

Small language model Frontier model Where it runs On hardware you own On the provider's servers Weights available Yes, downloadable Typically no Size Known Often undisclosed Typical access Local endpoint Cloud API or subscription Who controls the version You The provider

Chapter 4 treats the practical consequences of each row, including the capability gap that the table does not state.

docs.title: Open-Weight Model
docs.text:
An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run. Having the weights lets you run the model locally and inspect or fine-tune it. It does not necessarily mean that the training data, the training code, or the right to do anything you like with the weights are also public.

A typical open-weight release is a folder of files rather than a service. It holds the weights, usually as one or more large files; the tokenizer files; a small configuration file that describes the model's shape; and a model card with the license, which a later section covers. The weights dominate the size, so a 27-billion-parameter model is a download of tens of gigabytes.

The term is often confused with "open source", so the distinction deserves its own comparison.

Closed model Open-weight model Open-source model Weights downloadable No Yes Yes Training data and code published No Usually not Yes Runs on your hardware No Yes Yes Use is governed by Provider terms of service A model license An open-source license

Open Weights Are Not a Blank Check

Being able to download a model does not mean you may use it for any purpose. Each model ships with a license that can limit commercial use, and a model's own page sometimes states none at all. Read the license before you build a workflow on a model, and record what it says.

docs.title: Open-Source License
docs.text: An open-source license is a license that grants anyone the right to use, modify, and redistribute software, subject to stated conditions. Permissive licenses, such as Apache 2.0 and MIT, impose few conditions; others require that changes be shared. The defining feature is that the rights granted are broad and the conditions are published and uniform.

docs.title: Model License Terms
docs.text:
Model license terms are the conditions attached to a specific model's weights. They may be a standard open-source license, or they may be a custom or modified one that restricts use. One candidate in this evaluation is released under a modified MIT license that allows commercial use but carves out an exception for companies with large revenue. Another candidate's page does not state a license at all.

Three questions apply to every model. Is commercial use allowed? Are there size or revenue exceptions? And is the license actually stated by the publisher or only reported by a third party? In this evaluation, a license that a publisher's page reports without independent verification is recorded as "reported", not as confirmed.

docs.title: Model Family
docs.text: A model family is a group of related models from one publisher that share a design and training lineage and differ in size or specialization. The two gemma4 models in this evaluation, gemma4:26b and gemma4:31b, belong to one family. Families matter because the behavior you measured in one member is a reasonable, though not certain, guide to the others. Chapter 14 surveys the families behind this evaluation's candidates.

docs.title: Model Card
docs.text:
A model card is the document a publisher releases with a model, describing what it is for, how it was trained, how it performed on benchmarks, and what its limits and license are. It is the primary source for the facts in this section, and also the source of claims the publisher makes about its own model.

Read the Card Like a Marketing Page With Facts In It

A model card is the fastest way to learn size, window, and license, so read those fields first and trust them. Treat the benchmark scores and strength claims as the publisher's own, to be tested, and never carry them into your report as measured results.

docs.title: What Textbook Generation Demands
docs.text: The benchmark workload exercises a short list of abilities. Each is defined here, because Chapters 12 through 22 ask a model to demonstrate them and score the result.

docs.title: Instruction Following
docs.text: Instruction following is a model's ability to do what a prompt or a document of instructions says, including the constraints, in the order given. A skill file that runs past a thousand lines is a long instruction, and a model that drifts from it produces a book that violates the rules it was handed.

docs.title: Long-Form Writing
docs.text: Long-form writing is sustained, coherent prose across many paragraphs, with consistent terminology and a stable argument. A chapter of several thousand words tests whether a model stays on topic and avoids repeating itself, which is a different skill from answering a question.

docs.title: Structured Output
docs.text:
Structured output is output that conforms to a required format, such as a JSON object with named fields of given types. A downstream program reads it, so a single missing field or stray character can break the whole step. A learning graph in this workload must be a valid JSON file and a CSV file that agree, with no duplicate labels.

A short example shows what "valid" means. The required format is a JSON object with an integer id, a string label, a string group, and an array of integers depends_on. This reply is valid:

{"id": 7, "label": "Token", "group": "SLM", "depends_on": [40]}

This one is not, because id is a string instead of an integer:

{"id": "7", "label": "Token", "group": "SLM", "depends_on": [40]}

Both look right at a glance, which is the problem. Judging output against a schema takes a precise eye, so the exercise below trains it.

docs.title: Diagram: Structured Output Judge
docs.text:
Run Structured Output Judge Fullscreen

Structured Output Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: structured-output-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of 6 model replies is valid JSON that matches a given required format, naming the defect in each invalid reply, with at least 5 of 6 judged correctly.

Prerequisites: structured output, JSON object, field, integer, string, array (the format is defined in the section "Structured Output" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each reply the learner chooses "Valid" or "Invalid" and, when "Invalid", chooses the defect from the four defect types listed in Content. A judgment is correct when the choice equals the Answer column and, for invalid replies, the defect equals the Defect column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Reading the required format is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A reply that looks right is valid. (2) A reply containing valid JSON inside explanatory text is valid. (3) A trailing comma is harmless. (4) An empty array is a missing field.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level judging needs criteria applied to evidence, so the required format is fixed and visible and the replies differ from it in one precise way each. Requiring the learner to name the defect shows whether they can justify the judgment, not only guess it.

Content:

The required format, shown on screen for every reply: a JSON object with exactly these four fields. id is an integer. label is a string. group is a string. depends_on is an array of integers, and it may be empty. The only text in the reply must be the JSON object itself. The four defect types the learner can choose from are: "Wrong type", "Missing field", "Extra text around the JSON", and "Invalid JSON syntax".

# Reply shown to the learner Answer Defect Why (shown as feedback) 1 {"id": 7, "label": "Token", "group": "SLM", "depends_on": [40]} Valid none All four fields are present with the right types and there is no other text. 2 {"id": "7", "label": "Token", "group": "SLM", "depends_on": [40]} Invalid Wrong type id is the string "7", but the format requires an integer. 3 {"id": 7, "label": "Token", "group": "SLM"} Invalid Missing field depends_on is required and is absent. 4 Here is the record: {"id": 7, "label": "Token", "group": "SLM", "depends_on": [40]} Invalid Extra text around the JSON The JSON is correct, but the sentence before it means a program cannot parse the reply as JSON. 5 {"id": 7, "label": "Token", "group": "SLM", "depends_on": [40],} Invalid Invalid JSON syntax JSON does not allow a trailing comma after the last field. 6 {"id": 7, "label": "Token", "group": "SLM", "depends_on": []} Valid none An empty array is valid; it means the concept has no prerequisites.

Provenance: The required format and the six replies are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The meaning of valid follows the chapter section "Structured Output" and the JSON syntax rules.

Rules: Replies are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6, with the required format visible throughout. A reply is Invalid if any field is missing, any field has the wrong type, any text appears outside the JSON object, or the JSON syntax is invalid. Each reply allows one Valid or Invalid choice and, when Invalid, one defect choice, and both are final.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the required format and reply 1.
  2. The learner chooses "Valid" or "Invalid". If "Invalid", the learner chooses one of the four defect types, then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct judgment, the defect if any, and the Why text, and marks the reply correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for replies 2 to 6. After reply 6 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each missed reply.

Feedback: Six replies, fixed order, one confirmed judgment each, and the judgment is final. A reply is correct only when both the validity choice and, where needed, the defect choice are correct. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct judgment, the defect, and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: The required format and reply 1 are shown with no choice made, and the question on screen is "Would a program accept this reply?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the required format as an integer id, a string label, a string group, and an array of integers depends_on, and that {"id": "7", ...} is invalid because id is a string.

docs.title: Tool Calling
docs.text:
Tool calling is a model's ability to ask a program to do something on its behalf by emitting a structured request, and then to use the result. The model does not run commands itself. It writes a request naming a tool and its arguments, a surrounding program called the harness executes it, and the result is returned to the model as new text. Tool calling is what turns a text generator into something that can read files and run scripts.

Here is one round of that exchange, with the user's question and a tool for running shell commands. The tool name and fields are illustrative.

Step Who What happens 1 User Asks "How many lines are in notes.txt?" 2 Model Emits a tool call: {"name": "run_shell", "arguments": {"command": "wc -l notes.txt"}} 3 Harness Runs wc -l notes.txt and returns the output 3 notes.txt 4 Model Reads the result and answers "It has 3 lines."

Tool calling depends directly on structured output, because step 2 must be valid JSON for the harness to execute it. A malformed call is one of the failure types Chapter 22 teaches you to diagnose, and a call that the model writes as ordinary prose instead of as a structured request is another.

The Model Asks, the Harness Acts

A language model never touches your machine. It only produces text, and one kind of text is a request that a separate program chooses to carry out. Keeping that boundary in mind explains both what agents can do and where the safety limits sit.

docs.title: Code Generation
docs.text: Code generation is a model's ability to write programs, scripts, and configuration in a programming language. The benchmark uses it in two places: shell and Python scripts that an agent writes to do its work, and the JavaScript for MicroSims. Code has a property prose lacks, which is that it can be run, so a model's code can be checked by executing it.

docs.title: Reasoning Mode
docs.text: Reasoning mode is a setting or behavior in which a model produces intermediate reasoning, extra tokens that work through a problem, before it gives its final answer. It can improve results on multi-step problems. It also uses more tokens, which costs time and fills the context window, so it is a trade-off to measure, not to assume.

docs.title: Multimodal Model
docs.text: A multimodal model is a model that accepts or produces more than one kind of content, such as text together with images. Most language models in this course are text-only for generation. The multimodal capability exists on some candidates, and the benchmark does not use it.

docs.title: Image Input
docs.text: Image input is the ability of a multimodal model to accept an image as part of its prompt and answer questions about it. It is a distinct capability from generating images, which is out of scope for this course.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
You started with a definition of a generative model and ended with the abilities a benchmark exercises. A language model predicts the next token, one at a time, using parameters it learned in training, and it works within a context window measured in tokens. Inference runs it. A small language model is one you can run on your own hardware, in contrast with a frontier model, and an open-weight model's license decides what you may do with it. Instruction following, long-form writing, structured output, tool calling, and code generation are what textbook generation asks of it.

Vocabulary Locked In

You can now convert words to tokens, test whether a document fits a context window, tell an open-weight model from an open-source one, and name the five abilities this benchmark scores. Chapter 4 puts those terms to work in the case for and against running them locally.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Small Language Models
docs.text: Test your understanding of tokens, parameters, context windows, open weights, and the abilities textbook generation demands with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a token?
docs.text:
1. One of the learned numbers stored inside a model
  2. A single letter or character in the model's input
  3. A complete sentence that the model handles as one unit
  4. The unit of text that a model reads and writes
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A token is the unit of text a language model reads and writes: usually a whole common word, a piece of a longer or rarer word, a number, or a punctuation mark. Models do not see letters or whole sentences; they see a sequence of tokens, each identified by a number. Because rare words split into several tokens, a sentence's token count is not its word count. The learned numbers inside a model are parameters, a different idea.

Concept Tested: Token

See: Token

docs.title: 2. What does it mean when a model is described as 27B?
docs.text:
1. Its weights take 27 gigabytes of memory to hold
  2. Its context window holds 27 billion tokens
  3. It has 27 billion learned numbers, called parameters
  4. It was trained on 27 billion words of text
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A parameter is one of the learned numbers inside a model, and the parameter count is how many there are. A 27B model has 27 billion parameters that were adjusted during training and are fixed when you use it. The count is the main driver of memory and of the work per token, but it is not a size in gigabytes, and it does not tell you how well the model writes or follows a skill.

Concept Tested: Parameter Count

See: Parameter Count

docs.title: 3. What is inference?
docs.text:
1. Creating a model's parameters from training data
  2. Running a trained model to produce output
  3. Converting text into tokens before the model reads it
  4. Adjusting a released model's weights for a new task
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Inference is the act of running a trained model to produce output. It is distinct from training, which creates the parameters from data once, at great expense. Inference then happens every time the model is used, and one machine can be enough for it. This course evaluates inference only; training and fine-tuning are out of scope. Converting text into tokens is the tokenizer's job, a step that comes before the model reads anything.

Concept Tested: Inference

See: Inference

docs.title: 4. What is structured output?
docs.text:
1. Prose that is organized into headings, lists, and tables
  2. Reasoning tokens produced before a final answer
  3. Output that conforms to a required format such as JSON
  4. A reply that combines text with an attached image
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Structured output is output that conforms to a required format, such as a JSON object with named fields of given types. A downstream program reads it, so a single missing field or stray character can break the whole step. In this workload the learning graph must be a valid JSON file and a CSV file that agree, with no duplicate labels. Intermediate reasoning tokens belong to reasoning mode, and image handling belongs to multimodal models.

Concept Tested: Structured Output

See: Structured Output

docs.title: 5. Why is a mistake early in a large language model's output never revisited?
docs.text:
1. It writes one piece at a time, each built on all text before it
  2. It drafts the whole reply first and then is unable to edit the draft
  3. Its tokenizer discards earlier tokens to save context space
  4. Its parameters are updated after every token it generates
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A large language model repeats one step: given the text so far, it assigns a probability to every possible next piece, one piece is chosen and appended, and the process repeats. Every piece depends on everything before it, so an early mistake is never revisited, only built upon. That mechanism explains both the fluency and the failures. The parameters do not change during use; they were fixed when training ended.

Concept Tested: Large Language Model

See: Large Language Model

docs.title: 6. How does an open-weight model differ from an open-source model?
docs.text:
1. An open-weight model cannot be run on hardware you own
  2. An open-weight model is always free for commercial use
  3. Its weights are public, but its training data and code usually are not
  4. Its weights stay private while its training code and data are published
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An open-weight model publishes its trained parameters so anyone can download and run them. That does not mean the training data, the training code, or unrestricted rights are also public. In an open-source model the data and code are published and use is governed by an open-source license. An open-weight model's use is governed by a model license that can limit commercial use, so being able to download a model is not permission to use it for any purpose.

Concept Tested: Open-Weight Model

See: Open-Weight Model

docs.title: 7. In tool calling, what does the model itself do?
docs.text:
1. It emits a structured request that the harness then executes
  2. It runs the shell command and returns the output as text
  3. It edits files on the machine through its tokenizer
  4. It asks the user to run the command and then paste the result back
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Tool calling is a model's ability to ask a program to act on its behalf. The model does not run commands itself. It writes a structured request naming a tool and its arguments, a surrounding program called the harness executes it, and the result returns to the model as new text. A language model only ever produces text, and that boundary explains both what agents can do and where the safety limits sit.

Concept Tested: Tool Calling

See: Tool Calling

docs.title: 8. Why are a generative AI model's mistakes harder to bound than a classifier's?
docs.text:
1. A generative model is trained on far less data
  2. A classifier checks every label it assigns against a JSON schema
  3. A generative model cannot be given instructions
  4. A generative model's output has no fixed set of answers
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A generative AI model produces open-ended output, so there is no fixed list of possible answers. A classifier maps an input to one label from a fixed set, which bounds its mistakes: with two labels there are only two ways to be wrong. A generative model can instead fail by producing fluent text that is wrong or off-task. That unbounded failure mode is why measuring one needs the careful evaluation design taught later in the book.

Concept Tested: Generative AI Model

See: Generative AI Model

docs.title: 9. A model has a 16,000-token context window. You give it a 10,000-word document and expect a reply of up to 3,000 tokens. Using 1.33 tokens per word, does the task fit?
docs.text:
1. Yes, because 10,000 words is well under the 16,000-token window
  2. No, because about 13,300 plus 3,000 tokens exceeds 16,000
  3. Yes, because the reply does not count against the context window
  4. No, because the document alone is about 16,300 tokens
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The context window counts both the text a model is given and the text it generates, and it is measured in tokens, not words. The document is about 10,000 × 1.33 = 13,300 tokens, which fits alone. Adding room for a 3,000-token reply brings the need to about 16,300 tokens, which is over 16,000. The document fits by itself and the task does not. Comparing words to tokens directly, or ignoring the reply, gives the wrong answer.

Concept Tested: Context Window

See: Context Window

docs.title: 10. On one DGX unit with 128 GB of memory, mistral-medium-3.5:128b downloaded and loaded, yet it was not counted as a usable small language model there. Why?
docs.text:
1. It ran at 3 tokens per second and no large context fit
  2. Its weights could not be downloaded to the unit at all
  3. Its license did not permit running it on local hardware
  4. Its parameter count exceeded a fixed limit for small models
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The course's working definition has two parts, and a model can pass one and fail the other. This model is open-weight and could be downloaded and loaded, so it met the first test. On that unit it ran at 3 tokens per second and no context of 64,000 tokens or more fit, so it could not be served usefully. The definition is relative to the hardware, not to a parameter threshold, so the answer could change on a larger system.

Concept Tested: Small Language Model

See: Small Language Model

docs.title: References: Small Language Models
docs.text:
1. Large language model - Wikipedia - Surveys how LLMs are trained, how they generate text one token at a time, and their architecture, inference, evaluation, and limitations. Supplies background for this chapter's definitions of parameter count, context window, and inference.

  2. Open weights - Wikipedia - Distinguishes open-weight releases from open-source AI, comparing what each publishes, and covers model cards and benefits and concerns. Clarifies the chapter's open-weight model, model card, and license distinctions.

  3. Byte-pair encoding - Wikipedia - Explains how repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of symbols builds a subword vocabulary, with worked examples and a byte-level variant. Shows where a tokenizer's pieces, and so a model's token counts, come from.

  4. Hands-On Large Language Models (1st Edition) - Jay Alammar and Maarten Grootendorst - O'Reilly Media - Carries Alammar's illustrated style, known from his Illustrated Transformer blog post, into a book of diagrams showing how text becomes tokens and flows through a model. It makes tokens and context windows visible.

  5. Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) - Sebastian Raschka - Manning Publications - Widely praised for building a GPT-style model in code step by step, from tokenizing text through pretraining to instruction fine-tuning. Seeing the pieces assembled makes parameter count, tokens, and context length concrete.

  6. Tokenization algorithms - Hugging Face Transformers Documentation - Compares word, character, and subword tokenization, working BPE, Unigram, WordPiece, and SentencePiece through small examples. Explains why a tokenizer fixes a model's vocabulary and why token counts differ between models.

  7. The Open Source AI Definition 1.0 - Open Source Initiative - States four freedoms and requires data information, code, and parameters to be available under OSI-approved terms. Gives the standard against which this chapter judges open-weight releases and model license terms.

  8. Context length - Ollama Documentation - Explains that context length is the maximum number of tokens a model holds in memory, how defaults scale with available VRAM, and how to change it. Ties the context window concept to the memory cost examined later.

  9. Structured outputs - Ollama Documentation - Shows how to constrain a model's reply to a JSON schema, using Pydantic or Zod to generate and validate it. Demonstrates the structured output ability this chapter says textbook generation requires.

  10. Tool calling - Ollama Documentation - Covers single, parallel, and multi-turn tool calls, in which the model requests a function and the calling program returns the result. Illustrates the chapter's model-asks, harness-acts loop in a local runtime.

docs.title: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
Summary
docs.text: This chapter makes the case for and against running a model locally. It compares a local deployment with cloud LLM services and agentic frameworks on privacy, data sovereignty, rate limits, availability, lock-in, and operational burden. Students finish able to list the reasons to prefer each option and describe a hybrid workflow.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 19 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Privacy 66 Cloud LLM Service 226 Local Model Deployment 384 Cloud Baseline 17 Anthropic Claude 2 Model Deprecation 2 OpenAI ChatGPT 1 Data Sovereignty 1 Rate Limits 1 Service Availability 1 Vendor Lock-In 1 Frontier Model Capability Gap 1 Agentic Framework 3 Hybrid Workflow 2 Version Pinning 1 Operational Burden 1 Offline Operation 1 Google Antigravity 1 Devin 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models

Two Ways to Get the Same Tokens

A model can sit on a server you rent or on a machine you own, and the choice changes what you pay, what you control, and what can go wrong. By the end of this chapter you will be able to list the reasons for each side and recommend a local, cloud, or hybrid workflow for a stated situation. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
The whole course asks whether a local model can do what a cloud model does. Before measuring that, you need the strongest honest case for each side, because an evaluation that starts from a conclusion measures nothing. This chapter lays out what a cloud service offers and costs you, what a local deployment offers and costs you, how the quality difference between them is framed, and how agentic frameworks and hybrid workflows blur the line.

The chapter keeps three terms apart, a habit that Chapter 6 formalizes. Cost is what you pay to own and operate hardware. Price is what a provider charges for a service. Quality is how good the output is. A statement that mixes them, such as "the cloud is cheaper", is usually unanswerable until you say which of the three you mean.

docs.title: Cloud LLM Service
docs.text:
A cloud LLM service is a language model that a provider runs on its own servers and that you reach over the internet. You send a prompt, the provider's hardware runs inference, and the reply comes back. You never hold the model's weights and you do not operate the machine that runs it.

Providers offer access in a few forms, and the form decides how you are billed.

Form of access How you use it Typical billing API Your program sends requests to an endpoint Per token, input and output Chat subscription You type into the provider's application A fixed amount per month Agentic or coding tool A tool runs multi-step tasks with the model behind it Subscription or per-seat, often with usage limits

Following one request shows where the boundary sits. The steps below are the same whichever form of access you use.

Step What happens Where it happens 1 Your text, and any files you attached, are sent over the network Your machine, then the network 2 The provider authenticates you and applies your plan's limits Provider 3 The model reads the prompt and generates the reply Provider hardware 4 The reply is returned and the usage is recorded for billing Network, then your machine

The convenience is real. You need no hardware, no installation, and no model management, and you get access to the strongest models available, which are often not released any other way. The costs are the subjects of the next five concepts.

docs.title: Anthropic Claude
docs.text: Anthropic Claude is a family of language models and assistants from Anthropic, available through an API, through chat applications, and through coding tools. In this evaluation it appears twice: the orchestrating session that starts and scores runs uses a Claude cloud model, and the harness that runs the skills is Claude Code, pointed at a local endpoint. Chapter 18 returns to the first use.

docs.title: OpenAI ChatGPT
docs.text: OpenAI ChatGPT is OpenAI's assistant product, built on its family of language models, and available as a chat application and, through the company's API, as a service for programs. It is the best-known example of a chat subscription and is used here as a representative cloud comparison point.

docs.title: Rate Limits
docs.text: Rate limits are caps a provider places on how many requests or tokens you may use in a period. They exist to protect shared capacity, and they vary with the plan. A job that must generate dozens of chapters in sequence can hit a limit and stall, or be slowed to the pace the provider allows, regardless of how much you are willing to pay.

docs.title: Service Availability
docs.text: Service availability is the fraction of time a provider's service is up and responsive. A cloud service has outages and degraded periods that you cannot fix and often cannot predict. A local deployment has outages too, but you can see and repair them. The difference is who holds the controls, not whether failures happen.

docs.title: Model Deprecation
docs.text: Model deprecation is a provider's retirement of a model version, after which requests to it fail or are redirected to a newer one. A workflow built on a specific model can change behavior or break on the provider's schedule, not yours. A benchmark result recorded against a deprecated model can no longer be reproduced.

docs.title: Vendor Lock-In
docs.text:
Vendor lock-in is the cost of switching away from a provider once your workflow depends on its specific models, formats, or features. The more your prompts, tooling, and evaluation habits are tuned to one provider's behavior, the more a move costs. Lock-in is not automatically bad, but it should be a conscious trade-off and not a surprise.

A Cloud Service Is a Dependency You Do Not Control

Rate limits, outages, deprecations, and lock-in are four views of one fact: the model lives on someone else's schedule. None of them is a reason to avoid a cloud service, only a reason to know which of them your workflow can tolerate.

docs.title: Local Model Deployment
docs.text:
A local model deployment is a language model that you run on hardware you control, serving requests from software on that machine. The weights are on your disk, inference runs on your GPU, and the requests are handled by a server on your own network. In this evaluation the hardware is an NVIDIA DGX system.

A deployment has four parts, and each one is a chapter of this course. The table shows how they stack.

Part What it does Chapter Hardware The CPU, memory, GPU, and storage that hold and run the model 5 and 10 Model weights The downloaded, open-weight model 11 and 12 Inference server Loads the weights and exposes a local endpoint 13 Harness Runs the agent loop and executes skills against the endpoint 16 to 18

This evaluation's own deployment is the worked example. A DGX unit holds an open-weight model on its disk, an inference server loads it into memory and answers on the machine's own loopback interface, and the harness runs in a container on the same machine and talks to that server. In the later runs a generation job kept going with the laptop disconnected, because nothing in the loop depended on a connection to anywhere else.

The trade is the mirror of the cloud's. You gain control, because you choose the model, the version, and where every token goes. You take on the work of acquiring, configuring, and maintaining all four parts, and you are limited to models that are open-weight and that fit your hardware.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
Privacy, in this context, is control over who can see the data you send to and receive from a model. A prompt can carry anything: unpublished drafts, internal documents, names, credentials pasted by mistake. When the model runs elsewhere, that text leaves your machine.

A worked comparison shows exactly what moves in each arrangement. The data items are the ones a textbook-generation run produces.

Data Cloud service Local deployment Your prompt, including attached files Sent to the provider Stays on your network The generated reply Returned from the provider Produced on your hardware Usage metadata (account, token counts) Recorded by the provider None The model's weights Never sent to you Downloaded once from a model registry

The last row shows that "local" is not "nothing ever crosses a network". Weights and software are downloaded, and the request for them is visible to whoever hosts them. What changes is that your content, which is the sensitive part, no longer has to leave.

Local Generation Is Not Local Everything

Running the model on your own machine keeps its prompts and tokens there, but anything else that reads the output, such as a supervising cloud assistant or a log uploaded for review, can still send it away. Trace every place the generated text goes, not just where the model runs, and Chapter 18 shows how.

docs.title: Data Sovereignty
docs.text: Data sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to the laws of the country or jurisdiction where it is stored or processed. If a provider processes your prompts in another country, that country's rules may apply to them. A local deployment lets you choose and know the jurisdiction, because the data never leaves your site. For regulated or contractual data this can decide the question before cost enters at all.

docs.title: Offline Operation
docs.text: Offline operation is running a model with no network connection once it is installed. A local deployment can do this, because the weights and the server are on your machine; a cloud service cannot. It matters for air-gapped sites and for work in places without reliable connectivity. The setup still needs a network to download the model and tools, so offline operation describes the steady state, not the installation.

docs.title: Version Pinning
docs.text:
Version pinning is fixing the exact model version and software used, so that results can be reproduced. With a local deployment you pin by keeping the weights file and recording its name and checksum; the model cannot change unless you change it. With a cloud service you can request a specific version while it is offered, but you cannot keep it past its deprecation. Pinning is a precondition of a fair benchmark, because a result is only meaningful for the version that produced it.

Write the Pin Down on Day One

Record the exact model tag, its file checksum, the server version, and the date next to every result you keep. A table of scores with no version beside each one cannot be reproduced and cannot be fairly compared.

docs.title: Operational Burden
docs.text: Operational burden is the work you take on by running your own deployment: installing and updating the driver and server, watching memory and temperature, handling failures, and managing storage. It is staff time, and it is a cost even when no money changes hands. In this evaluation, a unit froze during long runs, and a memory watchdog now runs before any model does. A cloud service has none of that work for you, and most of its price pays for the people who do it.

docs.title: Frontier Model Capability Gap
docs.text:
The frontier model capability gap is the difference in quality between the best cloud models and the best model you can run locally on a given task. It is not one number. On a hard multi-step task the gap may be large, and on a narrow, well-specified one it may be negligible. Chapter 3 defined the two kinds of model; the gap is what you measure between them.

The gap is also what this whole evaluation exists to measure for one task, textbook generation. It cannot be settled by reputation or by a publisher's benchmark chart. It has to be measured on the same inputs, against a reference, which is the next concept.

docs.title: Cloud Baseline
docs.text:
A cloud baseline is a reference result produced by a cloud model on the same inputs and under the same rules as a local run, used as the point of comparison. Without one, a local result has no yardstick: a learning graph with 200 concepts is either good or poor only relative to something.

Here is a real instance from this evaluation. The benchmark course is Algebra I, and a published Algebra I book was made with cloud models. It has 200 concepts, 13 chapters, and about 55,000 words of chapter text. That book is the baseline for scale, and every local run is compared against it.

A baseline is only fair if it was produced under comparable conditions. Three questions test it. Did it use the same course description and the same skills? Is its model version recorded? Was it produced by a human-reviewed process the local run did not get? A baseline that fails any of these is a reference, not a control, and the comparison should say so.

docs.title: Agentic Framework
docs.text:
An agentic framework is software that wraps a language model with tools, memory, and a planning loop so it can carry out multi-step tasks, such as reading files, running commands, and revising its own work. The model supplies the language ability, and the framework supplies the structure that lets it act. Chapter 3's tool calling is the mechanism, and Chapter 16 builds the loop.

Frameworks matter to this comparison because many are tied to a particular provider's models and are sold with them. When a task is run through such a framework, the quality you observe is the quality of the model and the framework together. Two of the best known are covered next.

docs.title: Google Antigravity
docs.text: Google Antigravity is an agent-oriented development environment from Google in which AI agents plan and carry out coding tasks. It is an example of an agentic framework from a cloud provider, where the model work happens on the provider's servers and you interact with the results.

docs.title: Devin
docs.text: Devin is an AI software-engineering agent from Cognition, offered as a cloud service that takes a task, works through it in its own environment, and returns code. Like Antigravity, it is a self-contained agentic framework: you buy the outcome of a whole loop, and you generally do not choose its underlying model.

docs.title: Hybrid Workflow
docs.text:
A hybrid workflow uses a local model for some steps and a cloud service for others. The split can follow data sensitivity, where confidential content stays local and non-sensitive drafting goes to the cloud. It can follow stage, where a cheap local model produces first drafts and a frontier model polishes the result. It can also follow volume, where steady high-volume work runs locally and rare peak demand overflows to the cloud.

A hybrid is routing, not compromise. Each step goes where its own requirements are best met, which means you have to know each step's requirements, and that is the skill the exercise below builds.

Decide Per Step, Not Per Project

The question "local or cloud?" usually has no single answer for a whole project, because the steps differ in sensitivity, volume, and quality demands. Break the work into steps first, and the answer often becomes obvious, and often becomes different for different steps.

docs.title: Diagram: Local, Cloud, or Hybrid Chooser
docs.text:
Run Local, Cloud, or Hybrid Chooser Fullscreen

Local, Cloud, or Hybrid Chooser

Type: microsim sim-id: local-cloud-hybrid-chooser Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend local, cloud, or hybrid deployment for each of 6 scenarios and identify the constraint that decides it, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: cloud LLM service, local model deployment, privacy, data sovereignty, offline operation, rate limits, operational burden, hybrid workflow (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each scenario the learner chooses one deployment ("Local", "Cloud", or "Hybrid") and one deciding constraint from the five listed in Content, before the sim reveals the answer. A scenario is correct when both choices equal the Answer and Deciding constraint columns. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Reading the scenario text is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Local is always cheaper. (2) Cloud always gives the best result for the task. (3) Hybrid is always the safest answer. (4) A privacy requirement can always be met by a cloud provider's contract.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level recommending needs the learner to apply criteria to a case and justify the result, so each scenario states its constraints plainly and is built so that exactly one deployment is best given them. Asking for the deciding constraint, not only the choice, separates a reasoned recommendation from a guess.

Content:

The five deciding constraints the learner can choose from are: "Data must not leave the site", "No outbound network", "High steady volume on owned hardware", "No hardware or staff to operate", and "Sensitive and non-sensitive steps mixed".

# Scenario shown to the learner Answer Deciding constraint Why (shown as feedback) 1 A clinic must generate summaries of patient intake transcripts. The transcripts may not leave the building under any circumstance. Volume is 50 documents a week and modest quality is acceptable. Local Data must not leave the site An absolute rule that data may not leave the site rules out any service that receives the prompt. 2 A research lab works in a secure room with no outbound network connection. It needs a model to draft internal reports from local notes. Local No outbound network A cloud service cannot be reached from the room, so only a model installed on site can run. 3 A publisher generates 300 chapters a month from public-domain source material. It owns GPU servers, has tested a model that meets its rubric, and wants a predictable monthly cost. Local High steady volume on owned hardware Steady high volume on hardware it already owns, with a model already shown to be good enough, makes a fixed local cost more predictable than per-token billing. 4 A small team has a two-week project, no GPU hardware, no one to administer a server, and non-confidential material under an acceptable provider contract. Cloud No hardware or staff to operate Buying and operating hardware would cost more in time than the project lasts, so a service is the practical choice. 5 A consultancy drafts client proposals. Client names and figures must stay on its own machines, but it wants frontier-quality polish on the final wording, which contains no client data. Hybrid Sensitive and non-sensitive steps mixed The sensitive step must stay local and the polish step benefits from a frontier model, so each step is routed to the place that suits it. 6 A newsroom drafts articles from public wire stories, has no GPU hardware, and no one to run a server. It wants the strongest writing quality available for each piece and has no confidentiality concerns. Cloud No hardware or staff to operate With no sensitive data and no capacity to operate hardware, a cloud service gives the best quality for the least effort.

Provenance: The scenarios are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The meanings of the three deployments and the five constraints come from the sections of this chapter above.

Rules: Scenarios are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6. A scenario allows exactly one deployment choice and one constraint choice, both final. A scenario is correct only when both match. The answer for each scenario follows from the constraint named in its Deciding constraint column; if two constraints appear to apply, the one that makes a deployment impossible decides over the ones that only make it costly.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads scenario 1.
  2. The learner chooses "Local", "Cloud", or "Hybrid", then chooses the one constraint that decides it, then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct deployment, the deciding constraint, and the Why text, and marks the scenario correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for scenarios 2 to 6. After scenario 6 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each missed scenario.

Feedback: Six scenarios, fixed order, one confirmed pair of choices each, and the choices are final. A scenario is correct only when both choices are correct. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct deployment, the deciding constraint, and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: Scenario 1 is shown with no choice made, and the question on screen is "Where should this work run, and what decides it?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that cost, price, and quality are three different things, that a local deployment keeps prompts on the owner's network, that a cloud service can be limited by rate limits and outages, and that a hybrid workflow routes each step to the place that best meets its requirements.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
You started with a question that sounds like a single choice and ended with the observation that it is usually several. A cloud LLM service offers the strongest models and no operational work, at the price of rate limits, availability you do not control, deprecations, and lock-in. A local deployment offers privacy, data sovereignty, offline operation, and version pinning, at the cost of the operational burden of running four layers yourself. The frontier model capability gap is what a cloud baseline lets you measure, and agentic frameworks such as Claude Code, Antigravity, and Devin, plus hybrid workflows, let you mix the two.

Both Cases Made Honestly

You can now state the reasons for and against a local model, keep cost, price, and quality separate, and recommend local, cloud, or hybrid for a stated situation. Chapter 5 starts building the local side, with the hardware a deployment stands on.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
docs.text: Test your understanding of the case for and against local deployment, cloud services, baselines, and hybrid workflows with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a cloud LLM service?
docs.text:
1. A model whose weights you download and then run on your own GPU
  2. A model registry from which open-weight files are downloaded
  3. A local server that forwards requests when demand peaks
  4. A model a provider runs on its servers and you reach online
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A cloud LLM service is a language model that a provider runs on its own servers and that you reach over the internet. You send a prompt, the provider's hardware runs inference, and the reply comes back. You never hold the model's weights and you do not operate the machine that runs it. Downloading weights and running them on your own GPU is the opposite arrangement, a local model deployment.

Concept Tested: Cloud LLM Service

See: Cloud LLM Service

docs.title: 2. Which four parts make up a local model deployment?
docs.text:
1. Prompt, tokenizer, context window, and reply
  2. API, chat subscription, agentic tool, and billing
  3. Hardware, model weights, inference server, and harness
  4. Privacy, sovereignty, offline operation, and pinning
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A local model deployment is a model you run on hardware you control, and it has four parts that stack: the hardware that holds and runs the model, the downloaded open-weight model weights, the inference server that loads the weights and exposes a local endpoint, and the harness that runs the agent loop against that endpoint. You gain control over the model, the version, and where every token goes, and you take on maintaining all four parts.

Concept Tested: Local Model Deployment

See: Local Model Deployment

docs.title: 3. Why is a local deployment not the same as "nothing ever crosses a network"?
docs.text:
1. A provider still records the token counts for each local request
  2. Weights and software are still downloaded from an outside host
  3. The inference server checks its license online at every single start
  4. Prompts are copied to a registry whenever a model is loaded
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Privacy here is control over who can see the data you send to and receive from a model.
