In a local deployment the prompt and the reply stay on your network, but the weights and software are downloaded once from a model registry, and that request is visible to whoever hosts them. What changes is that your content, the sensitive part, no longer has to leave. No provider records usage metadata for local requests.

Concept Tested: Privacy

See: Privacy

docs.title: 4. Why is version pinning a precondition of a fair benchmark?
docs.text:
1. A pinned model generates its tokens faster than an unpinned one does
  2. A pinned model is exempt from a provider's rate limits
  3. Pinning removes the need to keep the weights file on disk
  4. A result is meaningful only for the version that produced it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Version pinning fixes the exact model version and software used so that results can be reproduced. Locally you pin by keeping the weights file and recording its name and checksum, so the model cannot change unless you change it. A cloud version can be requested only while it is offered. Pinning is a precondition of a fair benchmark because a result is only meaningful for the version that produced it. It has nothing to do with speed.

Concept Tested: Version Pinning

See: Version Pinning

docs.title: 5. How does service availability differ between a cloud service and a local deployment?
docs.text:
1. Both fail at times; locally you can see and repair the fault
  2. Only a cloud service has outages and degraded periods
  3. A local deployment never stops once its model is loaded
  4. Cloud outages are shorter because all usage is billed per token
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Service availability is the fraction of time a service is up and responsive. A cloud service has outages and degraded periods that you cannot fix and often cannot predict. A local deployment has outages too, but you can see and repair them. The difference is who holds the controls, not whether failures happen. Claiming that local systems never fail ignores the operational burden, which in this evaluation included a unit that froze during long runs.

Concept Tested: Service Availability

See: Service Availability

docs.title: 6. A school district drafts material from student records that must stay on its own machines, then wants frontier-quality polish on a final summary that contains no student data. Which arrangement fits?
docs.text:
1. Cloud for both steps, under a contract covering the records
  2. Hybrid: the records step local, the polish step in the cloud
  3. Local for both steps, because one step uses sensitive data
  4. Hybrid: the records step in the cloud, the polish step local
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A hybrid workflow uses a local model for some steps and a cloud service for others, and one way to split is by data sensitivity: confidential content stays local and non-sensitive work goes to the cloud. Here the records step must stay on the district's machines, while the polish step carries no student data and benefits from a frontier model. A hybrid is routing, not compromise: each step goes where its own requirements are best met.

Concept Tested: Hybrid Workflow

See: Hybrid Workflow

docs.title: 7. You want to use a cloud-made book as the baseline for a local run. Which check helps establish that it is a control and not merely a reference?
docs.text:
1. That it used the same course description and the same skills
  2. That it was generated more recently than the local run
  3. That it contains more concepts than the local run produced
  4. That it was produced on the provider's most expensive plan
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A cloud baseline is a reference result produced by a cloud model on the same inputs and under the same rules as the local run. Three questions test whether it is fair: did it use the same course description and the same skills, is its model version recorded, and did it get a human-reviewed process the local run did not? A baseline that fails any of these is a reference, not a control, and the comparison should say so.

Concept Tested: Cloud Baseline

See: Cloud Baseline

docs.title: 8. A team plans to run a model at a site with no network connection and assumes no network is needed at any point. Which correction applies to the plan?
docs.text:
1. A cloud service can also run offline once a session is open
  2. The model must reconnect each day to refresh its weights
  3. Offline operation is impossible for a model that uses a GPU
  4. Setup still needs a network to download the model and tools
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Offline operation is running a model with no network connection once it is installed. A local deployment can do this because the weights and the server are on the machine; a cloud service cannot. The setup still needs a network to download the model and tools, so offline operation describes the steady state, not the installation. The team must plan how the weights and software reach the machine before it goes offline.

Concept Tested: Offline Operation

See: Offline Operation

docs.title: 9. A benchmark result recorded against a specific cloud model can no longer be reproduced, and requests to that model are now answered by a newer one. What is the cause?
docs.text:
1. The account reached a rate limit that capped its tokens for the day
  2. The provider deprecated that model version on its schedule
  3. The service had an outage during the original benchmark run
  4. The workflow became locked in to the provider's formats
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Model deprecation is a provider's retirement of a model version, after which requests to it fail or are redirected to a newer one. A workflow built on that model changes behavior or breaks on the provider's schedule, not yours, and a benchmark result recorded against it can no longer be reproduced. A rate limit or an outage would stall or interrupt a run, but neither one replaces the model that answers.

Concept Tested: Model Deprecation

See: Model Deprecation

docs.title: 10. A team runs a task through a cloud provider's agentic framework and credits the result entirely to the provider's model. What does that attribution overlook?
docs.text:
1. A framework's output cannot be scored against a rubric
  2. A framework always lowers the quality of its model
  3. The observed quality reflects the model and framework together
  4. A local model cannot be wrapped with tools, memory, or a planning loop
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An agentic framework wraps a language model with tools, memory, and a planning loop so it can carry out multi-step tasks. The model supplies the language ability, and the framework supplies the structure that lets it act. Many frameworks are tied to a provider's models and sold with them, so the quality you observe is the quality of the model and the framework together. Crediting everything to the model ignores half of what produced the result.

Concept Tested: Agentic Framework

See: Agentic Framework

docs.title: References: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
docs.text:
1. Cloud computing - Wikipedia - Covers cloud computing's characteristics, service and deployment models, value proposition, and challenges and limitations. Places a cloud LLM service among the service models and frames the trade-offs this chapter weighs against local deployment.

  2. Vendor lock-in - Wikipedia - Explains how switching costs trap customers in one provider's technology, with types of lock-in and examples that include cloud computing. Frames this chapter's concern that prompts and tooling become tuned to a single provider.

  3. Data sovereignty - Wikipedia - Describes the principle that data falls under the laws of the jurisdiction where it is stored, including national measures and extraterritorial data access laws. Underpins the argument that local deployment lets you know the jurisdiction.

  4. Privacy in Context: Technology, Policy, and the Integrity of Social Life - Helen Nissenbaum - Stanford University Press - Introduces contextual integrity, which judges a privacy violation by whether information flows match the norms of the context where it was shared, not by a public-private split. It offers a sharper test for which prompts may leave your machine.

  5. Information Rules: A Strategic Guide to the Network Economy - Carl Shapiro and Hal R. Varian - Harvard Business School Press - Devotes separate chapters to recognizing and managing lock-in, classifying the sources of switching costs and how to weigh them. It gives vocabulary for judging how costly leaving a cloud provider would be.

  6. The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing - NIST - Mell and Grance define cloud computing by five essential characteristics, three service models (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS), and four deployment models. Supplies standard terms for what a cloud LLM service is and who operates what.

  7. Model deprecations - Anthropic Documentation - Defines the model lifecycle states active, legacy, deprecated, and retired, and lists retirement dates, replacements, and the minimum notice given. A concrete case of this chapter's model deprecation risk and the case for version pinning.

  8. Rate limits - OpenAI API Documentation - Explains limits in requests and tokens per minute, usage tiers, 429 errors, and retrying with exponential backoff and jitter. Shows how a long generation job can be throttled however much you are willing to pay.

  9. Building Effective AI Agents - Anthropic - Distinguishes workflows from agents and describes patterns such as prompt chaining, routing, and orchestrator-workers. Clarifies what an agentic framework adds around a model, which this chapter weighs when comparing providers.

  10. Ollama FAQ - Ollama Documentation - Covers data privacy, network exposure, model storage, and context size for a local server, and states that Ollama does not see your prompts or data on local runs. Evidence for this chapter's privacy and operational burden points.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the NVIDIA DGX family without assuming a specific model. It covers CPU architecture, system RAM, GPU configuration, dedicated versus unified memory, storage, power, thermals, DGX OS, the driver, and CUDA. Students finish able to explain how each hardware variation changes the setup steps that follow.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

Know the Machine Before You Ask It for Anything

Every later chapter branches on what this hardware actually has, so a few minutes spent here saves hours of confusing failures. By the end you will be able to read a machine's specification and say which setup steps it changes. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
A DGX is not one machine. The name covers a desktop box that holds one chip and a rack-mounted server that holds eight GPUs, and the two need different setup steps, different packages, and different ways of asking whether a model fits. This course therefore treats the hardware as a set of questions to answer before anything is installed.

The chapter takes the questions in the order a setup follows. It starts with the product family, then the processor, memory, GPU, storage, power and cooling, and finally the three software layers that sit directly on the hardware: the operating system, the driver, and CUDA. Every section ends on the same point, which setup step changes depending on the answer.

One machine runs through the chapter as the worked example. It is the DGX Spark-class unit used in this evaluation, and its measured values appear next to the general rule each time. Chapter 10 turns every question here into a Python probe that measures it.

docs.title: NVIDIA DGX
docs.text:
NVIDIA DGX is NVIDIA's line of systems built for AI work, sold as complete machines with the hardware, the operating system, and the GPU software already matched to each other. A buyer receives a computer on which the driver, the compute libraries, and a container runtime are installed and known to work together, which removes the most common source of setup trouble on a self-assembled GPU server.

The line spans a wide range, and the range is the reason this course does not assume one model.

Kind of system Typical shape CPU architecture GPU memory arrangement Desktop personal system Small box on a desk aarch64 One chip, memory shared with the CPU Desktop workstation Tower with a large coherent memory pool aarch64 Memory shared with the CPU Rack server Eight GPUs in one chassis x86_64 Each GPU has its own dedicated memory

The MicroSim below draws the same three kinds of system side by side, with each device in the first row. Select a column to read what that kind of system changes in a setup, then choose Quiz Me to check that you can tell the three apart.

docs.title: Diagram: Three Kinds of DGX System
docs.text:
Run Three Kinds of DGX System Fullscreen

Three Kinds of DGX System

Type: infographic sim-id: dgx-system-comparison Library: Infographic overlay (grid-diagram.js) Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare the three kinds of DGX system by shape, CPU architecture, and GPU memory arrangement, and select the kind that matches each of 6 descriptions, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: The table of three kinds of system above this block. CPU architecture, unified memory, and dedicated GPU memory are defined later in this chapter, and the sim uses them only as labels.

Evidence of Mastery: In Quiz Me mode the learner selects the column that matches each of the 6 descriptions listed in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 selected correctly on the first attempt. Opening a column in Explore mode is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every DGX is a rack server. (2) Every DGX has the same processor architecture. (3) Every DGX GPU has its own memory.

Instructional Rationale: A comparison at the Understand level needs the three systems visible at once, with the same attribute in the same row, so the learner reads across a row to see what differs. The drawing in the first row ties each column to a physical shape. The image stays still and the overlay adds detail only when the learner asks for it, which suits a comparison better than animation does.

Content:

The image is a grid of three columns and four rows. The first row is a drawing of the device, and the other three rows repeat the table above.

Row Desktop personal system Desktop workstation Rack server Device A small box on a desk, next to a mug A tower standing on the floor A rack chassis with eight GPU modules showing Typical shape Small box on a desk Tower with a large coherent memory pool Eight GPUs in one chassis CPU architecture aarch64 aarch64 x86_64 GPU memory One chip, memory shared with the CPU Memory shared with the CPU Each GPU has its own dedicated memory

Each column is one overlay zone. Selecting a zone in Explore mode shows an example product and what that kind of system changes in a setup: which package build to download and what a model is sized against.

The six descriptions in Quiz Me mode are these.

# Description shown to the learner Correct column 1 uname -m prints x86_64. Which kind of system are you logged in to? Rack server 2 Which kind of system is the DGX Spark, the machine this evaluation used? Desktop personal system 3 A model's weights take 100 GB. On which kind of system must the model be split across GPUs before it can load? Rack server 4 Which kind of system puts the CPU and the GPU on one chip? Desktop personal system 5 Which kind of system is a tower whose CPU and GPU use one large coherent memory pool? Desktop workstation 6 Which of the two desktop systems has the larger memory pool? Desktop workstation

Provenance: The shape, architecture, and memory rows repeat the table above. The 128 GB figure comes from the Unified Memory section, and the DGX H100 figures come from the Dedicated GPU Memory section. The drawings are schematic and are not to scale.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads across each row to find what differs between the three kinds.
  2. The learner selects each column in turn and reads its example and its setup consequences.
  3. The learner chooses Quiz Me and selects the column that matches each description.

Feedback: A correct selection shows "Correct!" and moves to the next description after the learner confirms. An incorrect selection names the column that was selected and lets the learner try again. The final line reads "You correctly identified n of 6".

Starting State: Explore mode, with no column selected and the prompt "Click on any column to learn about it."

A DGX product family is the set of DGX models that share a design generation and a purpose. Models within a family differ in memory size and price, and families differ in nearly everything else. The practical lesson is that "I have a DGX" does not tell you how much memory a model may use, which processor architecture your downloads must match, or whether the GPUs can be treated as one device.

docs.title: DGX Spark, NVIDIA GB10, and the Blackwell Architecture
docs.text:
DGX Spark is the small desktop member of the family and the machine this evaluation used. It is built around a single chip, the NVIDIA GB10, which combines an Arm processor and a GPU in one package and connects them to one pool of memory. The GB10's GPU belongs to the Blackwell architecture, which is NVIDIA's name for one generation of GPU design. A generation name matters because software is compiled for a generation, and a library built for an older one may not run, or may run slowly, on a newer one.

Following one real inventory shows what these names turn into. The two units in this evaluation reported the same configuration.

Component Reported value System DGX Spark-class desktop, aarch64 CPU 20 Arm cores, 10 Cortex-X925 and 10 Cortex-A725 Memory 128 GB unified, shared by the CPU and the GPU Storage 1 TB NVMe SSD GPU NVIDIA GB10, Blackwell architecture, 6,144 CUDA cores Operating system DGX OS 7.4 on Ubuntu 24.04 Driver and compute NVIDIA driver 580, CUDA 13.0

Each row of this table is one of the sections below. The first thing to notice is that the table contains no mention of a separate GPU memory figure. That absence is the most important fact about this machine, and the memory section explains why.

docs.title: CPU Architecture
docs.text:
CPU architecture is the instruction set a processor executes. Two matter here. x86_64 is the architecture of nearly all desktop, laptop, and server processors from Intel and AMD, and it is what most downloadable software is built for. aarch64 is the 64-bit Arm architecture, used in phones, in recent laptops, and in the GB10 chip. The two are not compatible: a program compiled for one cannot run on the other without translation.

The reason this affects your work is packaging. Compiled Python packages are distributed as wheels built for one architecture and one operating system, and a download site chooses the right wheel by asking the machine what it is. On an aarch64 system a package without an aarch64 build either fails to install or compiles from source, which is slow and sometimes impossible. Chapter 8 covers wheels in detail.

The check takes one command, and its answer is the first branch of every setup.

uname -m

On the unit in this evaluation it prints aarch64. The same command on a typical rack DGX prints x86_64. A reader who copies an install command from a tutorial written for x86_64 will hit an architecture mismatch here, and the fix is to find the aarch64 build, not to retry.

The Download Page Assumes Your Architecture

Many install pages offer an x86_64 file first, and a download that completes on an aarch64 machine will still fail when you run it. Run uname -m before downloading, and pick the file whose name says arm64 or aarch64.

docs.title: CPU Core Count
docs.text:
CPU core count is the number of independent processing units on the processor, and it sets how many tasks the CPU can run truly at once. The unit in this evaluation has 20 cores. For model inference the GPU does most of the arithmetic, so the core count matters less than for other workloads. It still decides how fast the CPU-side work runs: tokenizing a prompt, running the harness, executing the tools a model calls, and building the site with MkDocs.

A worked example makes the point. A book build that runs on one core takes the same time on 4 cores or 20, so a build is bounded by single-core speed. A benchmark that runs two model servers and two harness containers at once has four busy processes, and 20 cores keep them from competing. Read the count with nproc, and treat anything above 8 as comfortable for this workload.

docs.title: System RAM
docs.text:
System RAM is the main memory of the computer, the fast storage where running programs keep their data. Everything the machine does at once shares it: the operating system, the model server, the harness, and any other process. A program that needs more than is free either slows down by swapping to disk or is stopped by the operating system.

On a conventional server, system RAM and GPU memory are separate pools. The model weights live in GPU memory, and system RAM holds everything else. Whether that separation exists on your machine is the single largest fact about it, and it is defined by the next two concepts.

docs.title: Dedicated GPU Memory
docs.text:
Dedicated GPU memory is memory that belongs to the GPU alone, mounted on the GPU's own board and connected to it by a very fast link. A model loaded onto such a GPU must fit entirely in that memory, because the GPU cannot use the system's RAM at full speed. A rack DGX with eight GPUs has eight separate pools, each of a fixed size, and each pool is a hard limit for the part of the model placed on it.

A worked example from a published configuration: a DGX H100 holds eight H100 GPUs with 80 GB each, 640 GB in total. A model whose weights take 100 GB cannot be placed on one of these GPUs, however much system RAM the server has. It must be split across at least two GPUs, and the software that does the splitting is a setup step of its own.

docs.title: Unified Memory
docs.text:
Unified memory is a single pool of memory shared by the CPU and the GPU, so that both read and write the same physical chips. The GB10 uses it, and its 128 GB is the whole of the machine's memory, with nothing set aside for the GPU. The GPU has no memory of its own.

The consequences run in both directions, and they are the reason the model-fit chapters in this course exist.

  • A larger model can fit. The limit is the whole pool, not a slice of it. A 65 GB model that would not fit on a single 24 GB gaming GPU loads on this machine.
  • Everything competes. The weights, the conversation context, the operating system, and every other program take memory from the same 128 GB. A model that fits on paper can still starve the system.
  • A memory exhaustion can freeze the whole machine. On a discrete-GPU system, running out of GPU memory stops one process. On unified memory, the pool is also what the operating system runs on, and this evaluation had a unit stop responding during a long run. The cause was not confirmed, and memory exhaustion is the leading suspect.

The GPU Does Not Have Its Own Memory Here

On a unified-memory machine, "GPU memory" and "system memory" are two names for one pool. Every calculation you learned for a discrete GPU changes: the weights, the context, and the operating system all draw on the same number, and the headroom you leave is the only thing between a slow run and a frozen machine.

The tools reflect this. On the unit in this evaluation, nvidia-smi reports the GPU's memory as Not Supported, because there is no separate figure to report. Memory use has to be read from the system side, with free -h. Chapter 10 builds that fallback into the memory probe.

docs.title: Memory Bandwidth
docs.text:
Memory bandwidth is how many bytes per second the memory can deliver to the processor. Generating one token requires reading the model's active weights from memory, so bandwidth, not arithmetic, usually limits how fast a model generates. This is why two models of different size run at very different speeds on the same machine.

This evaluation measured the effect directly. A mixture-of-experts model that reads about 4 billion parameters for each token ran at 86 to 130 tokens per second. A dense model of about 31 billion parameters on the same unit ran at 28 to 40. The dense model reads roughly eight times as many weights per token and runs about three times slower, so the speed does not fall in strict proportion. Bandwidth sets the ceiling, and other costs fill in the rest. Chapter 11 defines dense and mixture-of-experts models.

docs.title: GPU
docs.text:
A GPU, or graphics processing unit, is a processor built to run many simple operations at once. It started as hardware for drawing images, and its design turned out to suit the matrix arithmetic that neural networks consist of. A language model generating text is almost entirely matrix arithmetic, and a GPU does it far faster than a CPU can. Without one, the models in this course would take minutes per sentence.

Two properties of a GPU matter for choosing and running a model: how much memory it can use, and which software it supports. The memory property was the previous section. The software property is its compute capability, a version number NVIDIA assigns to each GPU generation that tells the software which GPU features exist. A library compiled with support for compute capability 8.0 will run on an A100, whose capability is 8.0, and may refuse to run on a GPU with a capability it was not built for. The H100's capability is 9.0, and the GB10's is published as 12.1.

A CUDA core is one of the small arithmetic units inside an NVIDIA GPU. The GB10 has 6,144 of them. The count is a rough indicator of raw arithmetic capacity and a poor indicator of model speed, because speed depends as much on memory bandwidth and on how well the software uses the cores. Compare machines on memory and measured tokens per second, not on core count.

A GPU configuration is how many GPUs a system has and how they are connected, and a multi-GPU system is one that has more than one. Two or more GPUs let a model larger than any single GPU's memory run, by splitting its layers or its experts across them, at the price of splitting software and a loss of speed to the traffic between GPUs. The unit in this evaluation has one GPU, so none of this applies to it, and the course notes only where a multi-GPU system would change a step.

The next table gathers the three memory arrangements and what each one changes, now that each is defined.

Arrangement Where weights live What limits model size Example Unified memory The one shared pool The whole pool, minus the system's own use DGX Spark One GPU, dedicated memory That GPU's memory One GPU's capacity A workstation with one discrete GPU Several GPUs, dedicated memory Split across the GPUs The sum of the GPUs, minus splitting overhead DGX H100, eight GPUs of 80 GB

docs.title: Storage Capacity
docs.text:
Storage capacity is the amount of data the disk can hold. A model is a file, often many gigabytes, and a benchmark of several models stores all of them on disk at once, plus their downloads in different formats. Capacity is the first limit you meet, ahead of memory, when you collect candidates.

A worked example uses this evaluation's own numbers. The unit has a 1 TB drive with about 780 GB free after the operating system. The ten candidate models took about 397 GB together, because two of them were on disk in two formats, which doubled their size. That leaves roughly 380 GB, enough for the book output and the container image, and not enough for a second large model family. Check free space with df -h / before starting a pull, because a download that fills the disk fails partway through.

docs.title: NVMe Storage and Storage Read Speed
docs.text:
NVMe storage is solid-state storage that connects directly to the processor over a fast bus, instead of through the older interface used by hard drives. It is the storage type in current DGX systems. Storage read speed is how many bytes per second the drive delivers when you read from it, and for a model it sets the model load time, the delay between asking for a model and being able to use it.

The relation is simple division, and it is worth doing once. A 20 GB model file read at 2 GB per second takes 10 seconds to load. The same file from a hard drive at 0.15 GB per second takes over two minutes. A server that unloads an idle model and reloads it on the next request pays this cost each time, so a fast drive makes a differently configured server practical. Chapter 10 measures read speed with a simple timed read.

docs.title: Power Draw
docs.text:
Power draw is the electrical power the system consumes, measured in watts. It matters for three reasons: it sets the running cost, it sets the heat that has to leave the box, and it bounds what circuit and uninterruptible power supply the machine needs. A GPU-heavy machine draws far more under load than at rest, so a single number misleads, and a measurement needs the workload that produced it.

One worked example ties this chapter to the cost chapter. A published review measured 60 to 90 W for many model workloads on this class of machine, and just under 200 W at the most. This evaluation's own logging read 69 W from the GPU, with the GPU at 92% utilization, during one run. The cost analysis uses a deliberately high 150 W while generating and 40 W idle, which comes to about 832 kWh a year at 50% utilization and under $120 in electricity. Chapter 6 builds that calculation, and the point to carry from here is that electricity is a small part of the cost of owning this machine.

docs.title: Thermal Design Power and Thermals
docs.text:
The thermal design power, or TDP, is the amount of heat a cooling system is designed to remove from a chip under sustained load. It is a cooling specification, not a measurement of draw: a chip can draw less than its TDP most of the time, and brief bursts can exceed it. It is useful for one purpose, which is judging whether the machine's cooling is sized for the load you plan to put on it.

Thermals is the general term for the temperatures a system reaches and how it manages them. As a chip heats up, it reduces its own speed to stay within safe limits, which is called thermal throttling and which Chapter 15 measures. A long benchmark is the situation where this shows, because short tests finish before the chassis reaches its steady temperature.

In this evaluation the memory-and-temperature watchdog used a ceiling of 95 degrees Celsius for the GPU, and logged the temperature every 30 seconds. One reading, taken 43 seconds into a heavy run, was 72 degrees. A single early reading proves little. A reading that climbs steadily over an hour and approaches the ceiling is the sign to improve airflow or to shorten runs.

Log Temperature Before You Need It

A machine that overheats or freezes cannot tell you what happened afterward. Start a script that writes temperature, power, and memory to a file every 30 seconds before any long run, and the last line it wrote becomes your evidence.

docs.title: The Software Directly on the Hardware
DGX OS
docs.text:
DGX OS is NVIDIA's operating system for DGX systems: a customized Linux distribution, based on Ubuntu, with the NVIDIA driver, CUDA, the container runtime, and system tuning installed and tested together. The unit in this evaluation runs DGX OS 7.4 on Ubuntu 24.04. The practical meaning is that ordinary Ubuntu instructions work, and that NVIDIA's own components are already present and compatible.

Two commands identify the system, and both are safe to run. The first prints the Ubuntu release, and the second prints the kernel and architecture.

grep -E '^(NAME|VERSION)=' /etc/os-release
uname -srm

Some system files contain identifiers

On DGX OS, /etc/dgx-release includes the unit's serial number. Read it with grep -v SERIAL /etc/dgx-release, and never paste its raw contents into a file you plan to publish. Chapter 23 treats this class of file as a source of leaks.

DGX OS also determines who may do what. The account used in this evaluation belongs to a user the machine's administrator created, with no administrator rights, so installing system packages is not possible and everything was installed into the home directory. Chapter 6 treats administrator privileges as a cost and a dependency.

docs.title: NVIDIA Driver
docs.text:
The NVIDIA driver is the software that lets the operating system and programs talk to the GPU. Nothing uses a GPU without it, and every GPU program is limited by what the installed driver supports. The version is a single number, and it decides which CUDA versions can run. The unit in this evaluation has driver 580.

The first line of nvidia-smi output holds both versions that matter. The block below is sanitized and abbreviated: the serial number, the GPU's unique identifier, and the bus address that a full listing carries have been removed, and the version numbers are shown with their last digits replaced.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------+
| NVIDIA-SMI 580.xx.xx    Driver Version: 580.xx.xx   CUDA Version: 13.0 |
|-----------------------------+------------------+----------------|
| GPU  Name        Persistence-M | Temp  Perf  Pwr:Usage/Cap | Memory-Usage |
|   0  NVIDIA GB10          On  | 44C   P8    4W / N/A      | Not Supported |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------+

Reading it from left to right, 580.xx.xx is the driver release. CUDA Version: 13.0 is the highest CUDA runtime that driver can support, not the version of any toolkit installed on the machine. The GPU is idle in this listing, which is why the performance state is P8 and the power is a few watts. Not Supported in the memory column is the unified-memory signature described above.

Driver trouble has a recognizable shape. A program reports that it found no CUDA device, or that the driver is too old for the CUDA runtime it was built with. The first diagnostic step is always the same: run nvidia-smi. If it lists the GPU and a driver version, the driver works, and the problem is in what is built on top of it.

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
CUDA is NVIDIA's platform for running general computation on its GPUs, and it is the layer that frameworks and inference servers use to reach the GPU. It has two parts that are easy to confuse. The CUDA runtime is the set of libraries a program is built against, and it ships inside the programs that use it. The CUDA version the driver reports is the newest runtime the driver can support.

The rule that follows from this is that the driver sets a ceiling and a program must be at or below it. This machine's driver supports CUDA 13.0, so a framework built for CUDA 12.8 runs and one built for CUDA 13.2 does not. Updating a driver needs administrator rights, so on a machine you do not administer the practical fix is to pick a framework build at or below the driver's version.

Putting the stack in order shows why a failure in one layer looks like a failure in all of them.

Layer What it is How to check it The failure it causes Hardware GPU, memory, storage nvidia-smi, free -h, df -h No device, or not enough memory DGX OS Linux with NVIDIA components cat /etc/os-release Wrong package source NVIDIA driver Lets software use the GPU nvidia-smi "No CUDA device" or "driver too old" CUDA The compute platform nvidia-smi, framework check A library built for a newer CUDA fails Inference server Loads and runs the model Its own log Model does not load or fit

docs.title: Diagram: Hardware Finding to Setup Branch Matcher
docs.text:
Run Hardware Finding to Setup Branch Matcher Fullscreen

Hardware Finding to Setup Branch Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: hardware-branch-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the hardware-to-setup rules of this chapter to 6 findings by choosing the setup branch each finding triggers, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: CPU architecture, x86_64, aarch64, dedicated GPU memory, unified memory, multi-GPU system, NVIDIA driver, CUDA (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 findings the learner commits one branch from the six listed in Content before the sim reveals the answer. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct branch column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the finding text is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every DGX has dedicated GPU memory. (2) A download that completes will run on any DGX. (3) nvidia-smi always reports how much GPU memory there is. (4) A newer CUDA build is always better.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to use a rule on a new case, so each finding is a realistic probe result that triggers exactly one branch. Committing before the reveal separates a reasoned choice from recognition.

Content:

The six setup branches the learner chooses from are: "Use aarch64 packages", "Use x86_64 packages", "Size models against one shared memory pool", "Size models against one GPU's dedicated memory", "Plan to split the model across several GPUs", and "Choose a CUDA build at or below the driver's version".

# Finding shown to the learner Correct branch Why (shown as feedback) 1 uname -m prints aarch64. Use aarch64 packages The processor is Arm, so only builds for aarch64 will run. 2 uname -m prints x86_64. Use x86_64 packages The processor is Intel or AMD, so builds for x86_64 are the ones that run. 3 nvidia-smi lists one GPU with memory reported as Not Supported; free -h shows about 120 GiB of memory. Size models against one shared memory pool The GPU has no memory of its own, so the system's memory is the limit. 4 nvidia-smi lists one GPU with 80 GB of memory; free -h shows 512 GiB. Size models against one GPU's dedicated memory The weights must fit in the GPU's own 80 GB, however much system RAM there is. 5 nvidia-smi lists eight GPUs of 80 GB each. Plan to split the model across several GPUs A model larger than 80 GB can run only if it is divided across the GPUs. 6 The driver reports CUDA 13.0; the framework build you downloaded needs CUDA 13.2. Choose a CUDA build at or below the driver's version The driver sets a ceiling, and a runtime above it will not start.

Provenance: The findings are synthetic examples written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The meanings of the branches come from the sections of this chapter above.

Rules: Findings are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6. Each finding allows exactly one branch choice, and the choice is final. A finding is correct only when the chosen branch equals the Correct branch. Each finding triggers exactly one branch of the six.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads finding 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the six branches and confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct branch and the Why text, and marks the finding correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for findings 2 to 6. After finding 6 the sim shows the score and, for each miss, the misconception behind it.

Feedback: Six findings, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct branch and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: Finding 1 is shown with no branch chosen, and the question on screen is "Which setup branch does this finding trigger?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that aarch64 and x86_64 builds are not interchangeable, that on unified memory the GPU has no memory of its own and nvidia-smi reports it as Not Supported, that a model larger than one GPU's dedicated memory must be split across GPUs, and that the driver sets a ceiling on the CUDA version.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
The hardware answers six questions before any software is installed. The processor's architecture, x86_64 or aarch64, decides which downloads run. The memory arrangement, unified or dedicated, decides how a model's size is judged and what a memory shortage does to the machine. The GPU's compute capability and the driver's CUDA ceiling decide which libraries start. Storage capacity and read speed decide how many models you can keep and how long a load takes, and power draw and thermals decide the running cost and whether a long run is safe.

The DGX Spark-class unit in this evaluation answers them as follows: aarch64, 20 cores, one GPU with no memory of its own, 128 GB of unified memory, 1 TB of NVMe storage, a draw well under 200 W, DGX OS 7.4, driver 580, and CUDA 13.0.

The Machine Is No Longer a Black Box

You can now read a DGX's specification and say which packages it needs, how a model's size is judged on it, and which layer to check when something fails. Chapter 6 puts a price on all of it.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
docs.text: Test your understanding of the DGX family, memory arrangements, storage, power, and the software layers on the hardware with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does a buyer of an NVIDIA DGX system receive?
docs.text:
1. A GPU card that the buyer installs in an existing server chassis
  2. A cloud subscription that rents GPUs by the hour
  3. A set of drivers to download for any Linux computer
  4. A complete machine with hardware, OS, and GPU software matched
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. NVIDIA DGX is NVIDIA's line of systems built for AI work, sold as complete machines with the hardware, the operating system, and the GPU software already matched to each other. The driver, the compute libraries, and a container runtime arrive installed and known to work together, which removes the most common source of setup trouble on a self-assembled GPU server. The line ranges from a desktop box to an eight-GPU rack server.

Concept Tested: NVIDIA DGX

See: NVIDIA DGX

docs.title: 2. What is unified memory?
docs.text:
1. Memory mounted on the GPU's own board for its sole use
  2. Disk space the system uses when its RAM runs out
  3. A single memory pool shared by the CPU and the GPU
  4. The combined memory of several GPUs in a single chassis
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Unified memory is a single pool of memory shared by the CPU and the GPU, so both read and write the same physical chips. The GB10 uses it: its 128 GB is the whole of the machine's memory, and the GPU has no memory of its own. Memory mounted on the GPU's own board is dedicated GPU memory, the arrangement on a rack DGX, where each GPU's pool is a separate hard limit.

Concept Tested: Unified Memory

See: Unified Memory

docs.title: 3. What is DGX OS?
docs.text:
1. An Ubuntu-based Linux with NVIDIA's components pre-installed
  2. A firmware layer that runs beneath the Linux kernel
  3. A container image that holds only an inference server
  4. A Windows-based system tuned for GPU workstations
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. DGX OS is NVIDIA's operating system for DGX systems: a customized Linux distribution, based on Ubuntu, with the NVIDIA driver, CUDA, the container runtime, and system tuning installed and tested together. The unit in this evaluation runs DGX OS 7.4 on Ubuntu 24.04. The practical meaning is that ordinary Ubuntu instructions work, and that NVIDIA's own components are already present and compatible with each other.

Concept Tested: DGX OS

See: DGX OS

docs.title: 4. Why does a GPU suit language-model inference?
docs.text:
1. It stores model weights far more compactly than system RAM is able to
  2. It executes x86_64 and aarch64 programs equally well
  3. It reads model files from disk faster than a CPU can
  4. It runs many simple operations at once, suiting matrix arithmetic
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A GPU is a processor built to run many simple operations at once. It began as hardware for drawing images, and its design turned out to suit the matrix arithmetic that neural networks consist of. A language model generating text is almost entirely matrix arithmetic, so a GPU does it far faster than a CPU can. Storage and compactness are not the reason. Without a GPU, the models in this course would take minutes per sentence.

Concept Tested: GPU

See: GPU

docs.title: 5. Why does a single power-draw number mislead for a GPU-heavy machine?
docs.text:
1. Draw under load far exceeds draw at rest, so workload matters
  2. Power draw is fixed by the chip's thermal design power
  3. Electricity is the largest cost of owning the machine
  4. The GPU reports power only when its memory is dedicated
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Power draw is the electrical power the system consumes, in watts. A GPU-heavy machine draws far more under load than at rest, so a single number misleads, and a measurement needs the workload that produced it. Thermal design power is a cooling specification, not a measurement of draw. Electricity is also a small part of the cost of owning this machine: under $120 a year in the book's estimate.

Concept Tested: Power Draw

See: Power Draw

docs.title: 6. What does the CUDA Version shown in the first line of nvidia-smi output mean?
docs.text:
1. The version of the CUDA toolkit installed on the machine
  2. The newest CUDA runtime the installed driver can support
  3. The compute capability assigned to the GPU generation
  4. The oldest CUDA runtime that programs are allowed to use
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. CUDA has two parts that are easy to confuse. The CUDA runtime is the set of libraries a program is built against, and it ships inside the programs that use it. The CUDA version in the nvidia-smi header is the newest runtime the installed driver can support, not the version of any toolkit on the machine. The driver therefore sets a ceiling: a framework built at or below that version runs, and one built above it does not.

Concept Tested: CUDA

See: CUDA

docs.title: 7. You copy an install command from a tutorial. The download completes on your unit but the file fails when you run it, and uname -m prints aarch64. What should you do?
docs.text:
1. Find the build whose name says arm64 or aarch64
  2. Retry the same download until the file runs correctly
  3. Update the NVIDIA driver to a newer release first
  4. Free some disk space and run the downloaded file again
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. CPU architecture is the instruction set a processor executes, and x86_64 and aarch64 are not compatible: a program compiled for one cannot run on the other without translation. Many install pages offer an x86_64 file first, and a download that completes on an aarch64 machine still fails when you run it. The fix is to find the aarch64 build, whose name says arm64 or aarch64, not to retry the same file.

Concept Tested: CPU Architecture

See: CPU Architecture

docs.title: 8. A model's weights take 120 GB. A server has four GPUs with 80 GB of dedicated memory each and plenty of system RAM. How must the model be placed?
docs.text:
1. On one GPU, with the overflow held in system RAM
  2. Split across at least two of the GPUs
  3. In system RAM, with the GPUs doing the arithmetic
  4. On one GPU, after the driver has been updated
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Dedicated GPU memory belongs to one GPU alone, and a model placed on that GPU must fit entirely in it, because the GPU cannot use system RAM at full speed. Each 80 GB pool is a hard limit. A 120 GB model cannot go on one of these GPUs however much system RAM the server has, so it must be split across at least two, and the software that does the splitting is a setup step of its own.

Concept Tested: Dedicated GPU Memory

See: Dedicated GPU Memory

docs.title: 9. A 30 GB model file is read from an NVMe drive at 2 GB per second. About how long does the model take to load?
docs.text:
1. About 2 seconds
  2. About 7 seconds
  3. About 10 seconds
  4. About 15 seconds
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Storage read speed is how many bytes per second the drive delivers, and for a model it sets the load time, the delay between asking for a model and being able to use it. The relation is simple division: 30 GB read at 2 GB per second takes 15 seconds. A server that unloads an idle model and reloads it on the next request pays this cost each time, which is why a fast drive matters.

Concept Tested: Storage Read Speed

See: NVMe Storage and Storage Read Speed

docs.title: 10. A program reports that it found no CUDA device, yet nvidia-smi lists the GPU and a driver version. Where does the problem most likely lie?
docs.text:
1. In the GPU hardware, which has failed and must be replaced
  2. In the driver, which must be reinstalled before anything else can run
  3. In a layer above the driver, such as the framework's CUDA build
  4. In the storage layer, which cannot hold the model file
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The NVIDIA driver is the software that lets the operating system and programs talk to the GPU. The first diagnostic step for a "no CUDA device" report is always to run nvidia-smi. If it lists the GPU and a driver version, the driver works, and the problem is in what is built on top of it, such as a framework built for a CUDA runtime above the driver's ceiling. Reinstalling the driver would repair a layer that is not broken.

Concept Tested: NVIDIA Driver

See: NVIDIA Driver

docs.title: References: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
docs.text:
1. Nvidia DGX - Wikipedia - Surveys the DGX line by GPU generation, from DGX-1 through Blackwell-era systems such as DGX Spark, with specification tables for accelerators, memory, and power. Maps the family variation that this chapter says changes setup steps.

  2. CUDA - Wikipedia - Covers NVIDIA's parallel computing platform, its programming model, supported GPUs, and the features of each compute capability version. Explains the CUDA layer and the compute capability that decides which software runs on a given GPU.

  3. ARM architecture family - Wikipedia - Details the Arm instruction set family, including its 64-bit architecture, cores, licensing, and operating system support. Explains the aarch64 side of this chapter's aarch64 versus x86_64 split that changes package choices.

  4. Programming Massively Parallel Processors: A Hands-on Approach (4th Edition) - Wen-mei W. Hwu, David B. Kirk, and Izzat El Hajj - Morgan Kaufmann - Widely used GPU programming text that teaches CUDA through a running matrix multiplication example, optimized with tiling to cut global memory traffic. It shows why memory, not arithmetic, often limits GPU performance.

  5. Computer Organization and Design ARM Edition: The Hardware Software Interface - David A. Patterson and John L. Hennessy - Morgan Kaufmann - Organizes the field around Eight Great Ideas, including hierarchy of memories and performance via parallelism, and teaches with the 64-bit ARMv8-A instruction set. It frames why memory placement and Arm CPUs matter on DGX Spark.

  6. Hardware Overview - DGX Spark User Guide - Lists the GB10 system's 20 Arm cores, 128 GB of unified LPDDR5x memory, 273 GB/s bandwidth, NVMe storage options, and power budget. Provides the authoritative figures behind this chapter's worked example hardware.

  7. NVIDIA DGX OS 7 User Guide - NVIDIA Documentation - Documents DGX OS 7 as a customized Ubuntu 24.04 with kernels for x86_64 and ARM64 systems, GPU driver branches, and CUDA toolkits. Explains the operating system layer this chapter places directly on the hardware.

  8. CUDA Programming Guide - NVIDIA Documentation - Official guide to the CUDA programming model, with sections on unified and system memory, Unified Memory, and a compute capabilities appendix. Clarifies the compute capability and unified memory concepts used in this chapter.

  9. NVIDIA Driver Installation Guide - NVIDIA Documentation - Gives instructions and best practices for installing GPU drivers on Linux, including verifying module loading and aligning driver versions with CUDA releases. Backs this chapter's rule that the driver sets the ceiling for CUDA versions.

  10. nvidia-smi: NVIDIA System Management Interface - NVIDIA Documentation - Documents the command-line tool that reports GPU temperature, power draw, memory use, and utilization as text, CSV, or XML. This is the tool the chapter uses to read the driver version, CUDA version, power, and thermals.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter keeps three terms separate: cost is what owning hardware takes, price is what a provider charges, and quality is how good the output is. It builds fixed and variable costs, depreciation, total cost of ownership, utilization, and break-even volume into a cost model. Students finish able to frame a local-versus-cloud comparison without mixing the three terms.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 2: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 4: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
  • Chapter 5: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture

Three Words That Get Mixed Up

"Is the local machine cheaper?" sounds like one question, and it is at least three. By the end of this chapter you will be able to build a cost model for a DGX and say what it does and does not tell you. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 4 introduced a rule that the rest of the course depends on: cost, price, and quality are three different things, and a sentence that blurs them cannot be answered. This chapter turns the rule into a calculation. It defines each term, lists what goes into a cost, and builds a model that turns a purchase price and a list of assumptions into a number per textbook.

The numbers come from the project's own cost analysis, and each calculation here uses the same figures so that the two pages agree. They are estimates built on assumptions, and the chapter says which is which. Chapter 22 reuses the model to produce a cost per textbook from measured run times.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Cost is what you pay to own and operate something: the money, time, and effort that go out of your organization to produce a result. It belongs to whoever bears it. When you generate a book on your own hardware, the cost is the share of the hardware, setup labor, electricity, and administration that the book uses up.

Cost is built by adding parts, so the first step in any cost question is to list the parts. The reference case from the cost analysis shows what the parts are for one DGX Spark-class unit used for textbook generation over a year.

Part Calculation Per year Hardware ($6,950 + $250) spread over 3 years $2,400 Setup labor 40 hours × $90, spread over 3 years $1,200 Electricity 832 kWh × $0.1385 $115 Operations labor 4 hours a month × 12 months × $90 $4,320 Network and space $20 × 12 months $240 Total $8,275

Two things are worth noticing before the next definitions. First, the largest items are people's time, which together are two thirds of the total, and the smallest is electricity, at about one percent. Second, every row is an assumption except the date of the hardware's list price, so the total is a model's output, not a measurement.

docs.title: Price
docs.text:
Price is what a provider charges you for a service. It is set by the provider, and it covers the provider's own costs and a profit. You pay a price whether or not you ever learn what it cost the provider to deliver, and a price can rise or fall for reasons unrelated to cost, such as competition or demand.

A cloud model's price is the number you compare against your own cost. The comparison is fair only when both sides cover the same work, which is why Chapter 4's cloud baseline exists. A cost of $53 per book on your own machine and a price of $20 per book from a service are not directly comparable unless the service produces the same book to the same standard.

docs.title: Quality
docs.text:
Quality is how good the output is. It is neither a cost nor a price, and it is the term most often left out of a comparison. A local model that costs half as much and writes a learning graph with 40 duplicate labels has not saved half. It has produced something that must be redone or reviewed at further cost.

This course measures quality directly. Chapter 20 builds the scoring methods, and Chapter 22 combines quality with cost into a quality-adjusted figure. In this chapter the point is only that a cost model without a quality statement is incomplete.

Ask Which of the Three It Is

When a claim says something is cheap, expensive, or good, put it through one test: is this what someone pays to own it, what someone charges for it, or how well it works? Most comparisons that look contradictory are two people answering different questions.

docs.title: Diagram: Cost, Price, and Quality Sorter
docs.text:
Run Cost, Price, and Quality Sorter Fullscreen

Cost, Price, and Quality Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: cost-price-quality-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/cost-quality-pareto-frontier Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of 10 statements about generating a textbook as describing a cost, a price, or a quality, with at least 9 of 10 correct.

Prerequisites: cost, price, quality (defined in the section above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 10 statements the learner commits one label, "Cost", "Price", or "Quality", before the sim reveals the answer. A label is correct when it equals the Correct label column. Mastery is 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading a statement is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A number in dollars must be a price. (2) A service's charge tells you what delivering the service costs it. (3) A generated text that builds without errors is good.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying a statement shows the learner has constructed the distinction, and mixed items in dollars and in non-money terms prevent a shortcut based on the unit of the number. Committing before the reveal separates understanding from recognition.

Content:

# Statement shown to the learner Correct label Why (shown as feedback) 1 The unit used about 832 kWh of electricity in a year. Cost It is what the owner spends to operate the machine. 2 A provider charges a fixed fee for each million tokens generated. Price It is what a provider asks of a customer for a service. 3 The generated learning graph has 200 concepts and no dependency cycles. Quality It describes how good the output is. 4 Setting up the machine took 40 hours of labor at $90 an hour. Cost It is effort the owner spends to put the machine into use. 5 A subscription lets one user generate chapters for a flat monthly amount. Price It is the provider's charge for access to a service. 6 A reviewer found every worked example in the chapter correct. Quality It describes how good the output is. 7 The hardware loses its value evenly over three years. Cost Depreciation is what owning the asset uses up. 8 A service adds a 20% margin to what it costs the service to generate a book. Price The margin is part of what the provider charges. 9 Chapter prose stays at the stated reading level across 10,000 words. Quality It describes how good the output is. 10 An uninterruptible power supply and cabling add $250 to the purchase. Cost It is spent by the owner to run the machine.

Provenance: The statements are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". Numeric values match the cost analysis page and the sections of this chapter.

Rules: Statements are shown in the fixed order 1 to 10. Each statement allows exactly one label, and the label is final. A statement is correct when its label equals the Correct label column.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads statement 1.
  2. The learner chooses "Cost", "Price", or "Quality" and confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct label and the Why text, and marks the statement correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for statements 2 to 10. After statement 10 the sim shows the score and, for each miss, the misconception behind it.

Feedback: Ten statements, fixed order, one confirmed label each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct label and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 10 correct".

Starting State: Statement 1 is shown with no label chosen, and the question on screen is "Is this a cost, a price, or a quality?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that cost is what you pay to own and operate, price is what a provider charges, and quality is how good the output is, and that these are three different things.

docs.title: Per-Token Pricing
docs.text: Per-token pricing charges for each unit of text the model reads or writes, usually quoted per million tokens, with separate rates for input and output. It makes the price proportional to use, so a small job costs little and a large one costs a lot. For textbook generation the bill follows the length of the conversation, because a harness resends a growing context on every turn.

docs.title: Subscription Pricing
docs.text: Subscription pricing charges a flat amount for each period, usually a month, for access up to a usage limit. The user pays the same whether the month was busy or quiet, and the provider decides what happens at the limit. It suits steady individual use, and it makes a heavy job depend on the plan's cap.

docs.title: Per-Seat Pricing
docs.text:
Per-seat pricing charges for each person who has access, commonly for a team or an organization. The price grows with the number of users and not with the amount of text. It suits tools used by many people lightly, and it is a poor match for one automated pipeline that does a great deal of work through a single seat.

The table below sets the three side by side, using the question that matters most for a planner: what makes the bill rise?

Model The bill rises with Predictable? Fits best Per-token Tokens read and written Only if you can estimate tokens Variable, automated work Subscription Time Yes, up to the cap One user, steady use Per-seat People with access Yes Many users, light use each

docs.title: Capital Cost and Hardware Lifespan
docs.text: Capital cost is the one-time money spent to acquire an asset that lasts, as opposed to money spent on running it. For this evaluation it is the hardware plus its accessories: $6,950 for the unit and $250 for a power supply and cabling, or $7,200. Hardware lifespan is how long you expect the asset to be useful, and it decides how widely the capital cost is spread. The cost analysis assumes three years and no resale value.

docs.title: Depreciation
docs.text:
Depreciation is the allocation of an asset's capital cost across the years of its useful life. The simplest method divides evenly, which is what the cost analysis does: $7,200 over 3 years is $2,400 a year. The method is a convention and not a measurement, because a machine does not actually lose a third of its value each year. It is useful because it lets an annual cost model include the purchase without a lump of $7,200 in year one.

The lifespan assumption moves the answer. Stretching the same unit's life to five years drops the depreciation of the hardware and setup together, and the cost per book falls from $53 to $44 in the cost analysis. A shorter life, because a newer model makes the unit obsolete sooner, raises it.

docs.title: Setup Labor and Operations Labor
docs.text:
Setup labor is the effort to get the system running: connecting it, taking the inventory, installing the server, building the container, and testing candidate models. The cost analysis assumes 40 hours. Operations labor is the continuing effort afterward: updates, new models, restarting runs that failed. It assumes 4 hours a month. The labor rate is $90 an hour, assumed as a full cost for a technical employee.

Setup labor is a one-time cost, so it joins the capital cost and is spread over the lifespan. Operations labor recurs, so it is an annual cost on its own. The distinction matters because the two respond to different decisions: a better install script reduces setup labor, and a more stable server reduces operations labor.

docs.title: Administration Time
docs.text: Administration time is the labor of someone who keeps the system running for others, such as granting access, applying updates, and restarting a machine that stopped responding. In this evaluation that person was not the person doing the benchmark. It is a cost to whoever bears it, even when no invoice is sent. A unit that freezes and needs a restart by its administrator has a real cost that appears in nobody's budget, and a cost model should name it.

docs.title: Electricity Cost
docs.text:
Electricity cost is the energy the system consumes times the price of that energy. The cost analysis uses 150 W while generating, 40 W while idle, and $0.1385 per kWh, the U.S. commercial average for the year to July 2026. Idle power draw is the electricity used while the machine is on and doing no work. It matters because a machine used half the time idles the other half, so its yearly energy has two terms.

The arithmetic is short enough to do by hand, and doing it once is worthwhile.

generating hours per year = 8,760 × 0.50 = 4,380
idle hours per year       = 4,380

energy = (4,380 h × 150 W + 4,380 h × 40 W) ÷ 1,000
       = (657,000 + 175,200) ÷ 1,000
       = 832 kWh

cost   = 832 kWh × $0.1385 per kWh = $115

Do the Electricity Sum Early

Teams often worry about the power bill of a GPU machine and then find it is about a hundred dollars a year. Work it out before the meeting. The real cost drivers are almost always the labor and the hours the machine sits unused.

docs.title: System Administrator
docs.text:
A system administrator is the person responsible for a machine's configuration, security, and availability. They decide who gets an account, which software is installed system-wide, when the machine is updated, and what happens when it stops responding. On a machine that is not yours, that person is a dependency of your project, and their time is a cost.

The two DGX units in this evaluation belong to the Administrator, who created the account that the Primary Author uses and who restarted a unit each time it stopped responding. A cost model for this project that counts only the Primary Author's hours understates the work. This is why the administration time above is listed as its own row, even when the person doing it sends no invoice.

docs.title: Administrator Privileges
docs.text:
Administrator privileges are the right to change system-wide settings: installing software for all users, changing the driver, opening network ports, and managing accounts. On Linux this means root access, usually through the sudo command. A standard account has none of it.

The effect on the evaluation was large and specific. The benchmark account had no administrator privileges, so every tool was installed into a home directory from a release archive, and nothing was changed system-wide. When the account needed to run containers, it required membership in the docker group, which is equivalent to administrator access on that machine and therefore a decision only the Administrator could make. Each such step is a request, and each request has a delay.

Action Needs administrator privileges? What this evaluation did Install a model server for one user No Unpacked a release archive into the home directory Install a system package Yes Avoided it, or asked the Administrator Use Docker Yes, via group membership The Administrator added the account to the group Change the NVIDIA driver Yes Never attempted Restart a frozen machine Yes, or physical access The Administrator did it

docs.title: Fixed Costs
docs.text:
Fixed costs are costs that stay the same regardless of how much you produce. The unit's depreciation, the setup labor, and the monthly operations labor are the same in a year with 10 books and a year with 150. A machine that sits idle costs what a busy machine costs.

In the reference case, the fixed costs are nearly the whole bill: about $8,160 of the $8,275 a year. This is the single most important structural fact about local generation. The cost of one more book is close to zero, and the cost of owning the machine is large and unavoidable.

docs.title: Variable Costs
docs.text:
Variable costs change in proportion to how much you produce. For local generation the one variable cost is the electricity used while generating. A whole book takes about 28 hours of generation in the reference case, which at 150 W is 4.2 kWh, or about $0.58 at $0.1385 per kWh. A cloud service has the opposite structure: its price is almost entirely variable, because you pay per token or per seat and nothing when you do not use it.

The contrast gives the two options their different risks, and it is worth setting out side by side.

Local generation Per-token cloud service Fixed cost per year High, about $8,275 None Variable cost per book Very low, about $0.58 The price per book Cost if you make no books Still $8,275 $0 Cost per book as volume rises Falls Stays constant

docs.title: Utilization Rate
docs.text:
Utilization rate is the share of available time that the machine spends doing useful work. It is the lever that fixed costs ride on: the same $8,275 spread over more books gives a lower cost per book. The cost analysis assumes the unit generates 50% of the hours in a year, which allows for waiting for orders, failed and repeated runs, and maintenance.

The figures from the analysis show how strongly utilization moves the result.

Utilization Books per year Cost per book 75% 235 $35 50% (reference) 156 $53 25% 78 $105 10% 31 $263

At 10%, the machine is a bad purchase for this job. The cost does not rise because the machine got worse. It rises because the same fixed cost is shared among a fifth as many books.

docs.title: Cost Model
docs.text:
A cost model is a written set of assumptions and formulas that turns inputs into a cost figure. Its value is that the assumptions are explicit, so a reader can see which one to dispute. A model is not a measurement, and the right response to a surprising output is to inspect an assumption, not to trust the number more.

The function below is the reference case as a program. The parameters are, in order: the hardware price, the accessories, the hours of setup labor, the hourly labor rate, the lifespan in years, the hours of operations labor each month, the monthly network and space cost, the energy used in a year, and the electricity price.

def annual_cost(hardware, accessories, setup_hours, rate, life_years,
                ops_hours_per_month, network_per_month, kwh, price_per_kwh):
    depreciation = (hardware + accessories) / life_years
    setup = setup_hours * rate / life_years
    operations = ops_hours_per_month * 12 * rate
    network = network_per_month * 12
    electricity = kwh * price_per_kwh
    return depreciation + setup + operations + network + electricity

print(round(annual_cost(6950, 250, 40, 90, 3, 4, 20, 832, 0.1385)))   # 8275

A worked per-book figure follows from it. At 50% utilization the unit generates for 4,380 hours a year, so each generating hour costs $8,275 ÷ 4,380, or $1.89. A whole book that takes 28 hours of generation then costs 28 × $1.89, or about $53.

docs.title: Total Cost of Ownership
docs.text:
Total cost of ownership, or TCO, is every cost of acquiring and running an asset over its whole life. It differs from the yearly cost in that it includes the one-time costs at full size, so it answers "what do I commit to?" and not "what does a year cost?". For the reference case over three years:

purchase and accessories      $7,200
setup labor (40 h × $90)      $3,600
3 years of running            3 × $4,675  = $14,025
                              -----------
total cost of ownership       about $24,825

The three-year TCO equals three times the annual figure of $8,275, which is what spreading the one-time costs over the lifespan means.

docs.title: Break-Even Volume
docs.text:
Break-even volume is the amount of production at which two options cost the same. Below it the option with the lower fixed cost wins, and above it the option with the lower variable cost wins. For a local machine against a per-book price, it is the fixed cost divided by the saving on each book:

\[ N^* = \frac{F}{P - v} \]

where \( N^* \) is the break-even number of books a year, \( F \) is the local fixed cost for the year, \( P \) is the price per book of the alternative, and \( v \) is the local variable cost per book. The formula has no answer when \( P \le v \), because the alternative is then cheaper at every volume.

A worked example uses illustrative prices, not quotes from any provider. With \( F = \$8{,}275 \) and \( v = \$0.58 \):

Alternative price per book Break-even books per year Reachable by one unit at 156 books a year? $100 83 Yes $50 167 No $20 426 No

The last column is the point most often missed. A break-even volume above what the machine can produce is not a target to grow into. It means that against that alternative, one unit does not break even at any volume it can reach.

Break-Even Has a Ceiling Too

A break-even formula can return a volume the hardware cannot produce, and the spreadsheet will not warn you. Always compare the result with the machine's capacity in books per year, which is the generating hours divided by the hours per book.

docs.title: Diagram: Local Versus Cloud Break-Even Explorer
docs.text:
Run Local Versus Cloud Break-Even Explorer Fullscreen

Local Versus Cloud Break-Even Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: local-break-even-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the break-even volume of a local machine against a per-book price to within 1 book for 3 challenges, and state whether one unit can reach it.

Prerequisites: fixed costs, variable costs, break-even volume, utilization rate (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 3 challenges the learner types a break-even volume in books per year and chooses "Reachable" or "Not reachable" before the sim reveals the answer. A challenge is correct when the typed value is within 1 of the model value and the reachability choice matches. Mastery is 3 of 3. Changing the sliders in exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Local generation is always cheaper than a service. (2) A break-even volume can always be reached by producing more. (3) A machine that is idle costs nothing.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs the learner to commit a number from a stated formula before seeing the answer, and the reachability question confronts the misconception that a computed volume is always attainable. Free exploration after the challenges lets the learner see how each input moves the result.

Content:

The learner can change four quantities:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Yearly fixed cost F 2,000 20,000 25 8,275 dollars a year Price per book of the alternative P 5 300 5 100 dollars per book Local variable cost per book v 0 5 0.01 0.58 dollars per book Local capacity 20 400 1 156 books a year

The three challenges, in this order:

# F P v Capacity Model break-even Reachable Feedback when wrong 1 8,275 100 0.58 156 83.2 Yes N = 8,275 ÷ (100 − 0.58) = 83.2, which is below the capacity of 156. 2 8,275 50 0.58 156 167.4 No N = 8,275 ÷ (50 − 0.58) = 167.4, which is above the capacity of 156, so one unit cannot reach it. 3 4,000 40 0.58 156 101.5 Yes N = 4,000 ÷ (40 − 0.58) = 101.5, which is below the capacity of 156.

Provenance: F, v, and capacity in challenges 1 and 2 are the reference-case values from the cost analysis page. The prices P are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative, not a provider quote". Challenge 3 uses an illustrative F, labeled the same way.

Rules: Break-even N = F ÷ (P − v) when P > v, shown to one decimal. When P ≤ v, the sim shows "no break-even: the alternative is cheaper at every volume". Reachable when N ≤ capacity. The annual local cost at volume V is F + v × V, and the annual alternative cost is P × V. For V above capacity the sim shows "needs another unit" in place of a local cost.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 (F, P, v, and capacity are shown) and types a break-even volume.
  2. The learner chooses "Reachable" or "Not reachable" and presses Check.
  3. The sim reveals the model value and the Feedback text, and marks the challenge correct or missed.
  4. After all three challenges the free-exploration mode unlocks, where the learner changes each of the four quantities and watches the break-even and the two annual cost lines update.
  5. In exploration the learner should notice that lowering F moves break-even down, and that lowering capacity can turn "Reachable" into "Not reachable" without changing the break-even.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: break-even is books a year." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge. After the second wrong attempt the model value and the worked calculation are shown, and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with an empty answer box and the four values at their defaults. The question on screen is "At what volume does the local machine cost the same as the alternative?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses F = $8,275, v = $0.58, and capacity 156 books a year, and states break-evens of 83, 167, and 426 books a year at prices of $100, $50, and $20.

docs.title: Profit Margin
docs.text: Profit margin is the share of a price that is profit: the price minus the cost, divided by the price. A provider that wants a 20% margin on a book that costs it $53 must charge enough that 20% of the price is profit, so the price is the cost divided by 0.80, which is $66.

docs.title: Margin Versus Markup
docs.text:
Markup is the same gap measured against the cost instead of the price: the price minus the cost, divided by the cost. The two sound interchangeable and give different prices, and the difference is large enough to matter in a business case.

Method Calculation Price Resulting margin 20% margin $52.92 ÷ (1 − 0.20) $66.15 20% 20% markup $52.92 × 1.20 $63.50 16.7%

A seller who intends a 20% margin and applies a 20% markup earns 16.7%. On a thousand books that is a difference of about $2,650.

docs.title: Sensitivity Analysis
docs.text:
Sensitivity analysis is changing one assumption at a time and recording how the output moves, so you learn which assumptions the answer depends on. It is the right response to an estimate built on guesses: instead of arguing about each guess, find the ones that matter.

The cost analysis page ran it on the reference case. Each row changes one assumption and holds the others.
