Change Cost per book Price at 20% margin Reference case $53 $66 Operations labor of 8 hours a month $81 $101 No operations labor $25 $32 Hardware at $9,000 $57 $72 Hardware at the launch price of $3,999 $47 $58 The three stages are 5% of the book $106 $132

The result is a ranking of what to worry about. Labor and the share of the book that the benchmark's three stages represent move the answer by as much as a factor of two. The hardware's price moves it by about ten percent. A planner who spent a week negotiating hardware price and an hour on the labor estimate had their effort the wrong way round.

Change One Thing at a Time

When you vary two assumptions together, you cannot say which one moved the answer. Vary one, record the result, restore it, then vary the next, and the table you end with tells you where to spend your attention.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Cost is what owning and operating costs you, price is what a provider charges, and quality is how good the output is, and a comparison needs all three stated. A cost model adds capital cost spread by depreciation, setup and operations labor, administration time, and electricity, and it separates fixed costs, which are nearly the whole bill for a local machine, from variable costs, which are nearly the whole bill for a per-token service. Utilization decides how far the fixed cost is spread. Break-even volume compares the two structures, and it must be checked against what one machine can produce. Margin and markup give different prices, and sensitivity analysis shows which assumptions deserve your attention.

You Can Price the Machine Honestly

You can now separate cost from price from quality, build an annual cost model from a purchase price, and find where a local unit breaks even against a service. Chapter 7 starts the hands-on work by reaching the machine securely.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Cost, Price, and Quality
docs.text: Test your understanding of cost, price, and quality, the parts of a cost model, break-even volume, and sensitivity analysis with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. In this book's terms, what is cost?
docs.text:
1. What a provider charges a customer for a service
  2. What you pay to own and operate something
  3. How good the output of a model turns out to be
  4. What a seller adds to a book's price as profit
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Cost is what you pay to own and operate something: the money, time, and effort that go out of your organization to produce a result. It belongs to whoever bears it. For a book generated on your own hardware, it is the share of hardware, setup labor, electricity, and administration that the book uses up. What a provider charges is a price, and how good the output is is quality. A comparison needs all three kept apart.

Concept Tested: Cost

See: Cost

docs.title: 2. Which statement describes fixed costs?
docs.text:
1. They rise in proportion to the number of books produced
  2. They are charged by a provider for each million tokens
  3. They stay the same regardless of how much you produce
  4. They are incurred only in the year hardware is purchased
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Fixed costs stay the same regardless of how much you produce. The unit's depreciation, the setup labor, and the monthly operations labor are the same in a year with 10 books and a year with 150, so a machine that sits idle costs what a busy machine costs. In the reference case they are about $8,160 of the $8,275 a year. Costs that rise with production, such as electricity used while generating, are variable costs.

Concept Tested: Fixed Costs

See: Fixed Costs

docs.title: 3. Why is a cost model without a quality statement incomplete?
docs.text:
1. Quality determines the electricity that a run consumes
  2. Quality sets the price a provider charges per token
  3. Poor output must be redone or reviewed at further cost
  4. Quality is fixed by the purchase price of the hardware
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Quality is how good the output is. It is neither a cost nor a price, and it is the term most often left out of a comparison. A local model that costs half as much and writes a learning graph with 40 duplicate labels has not saved half. It has produced something that must be redone or reviewed at further cost. That is why a cost figure needs a quality statement beside it before it supports a decision.

Concept Tested: Quality

See: Quality

docs.title: 4. Why does the cost per book rise from $53 to $263 when utilization falls from 50% to 10%?
docs.text:
1. The machine draws more idle power at low utilization
  2. The hardware depreciates faster when it sits unused
  3. Operations labor grows as fewer books are generated
  4. The same fixed cost is shared among far fewer books
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Utilization rate is the share of available time the machine spends doing useful work, and it is the lever that fixed costs ride on. At 50% the unit produces 156 books a year at $53 each; at 10% it produces 31 at $263 each. The cost does not rise because the machine got worse. It rises because the same fixed cost, about $8,275 a year, is shared among a fifth as many books.

Concept Tested: Utilization Rate

See: Utilization Rate

docs.title: 5. Why was every tool in this evaluation installed into a home directory from a release archive?
docs.text:
1. The account had no administrator privileges for system installs
  2. Release archives run faster than system-wide packages do
  3. DGX OS forbids installing software outside home directories
  4. The Administrator required all tools to run inside Docker
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Administrator privileges are the right to change system-wide settings: installing software for all users, changing the driver, opening network ports, and managing accounts. The benchmark account had none, so every tool was installed into a home directory from a release archive and nothing was changed system-wide. Steps that did need those rights, such as joining the docker group, were requests to the Administrator, and each request has a delay.

Concept Tested: Administrator Privileges

See: Administrator Privileges

docs.title: 6. A unit's annual cost is $8,275 and it generates for 4,380 hours a year, so each generating hour costs about $1.89. What does a book that needs 40 hours of generation cost?
docs.text:
1. About $47
  2. About $53
  3. About $76
  4. About $207
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A cost model is a written set of assumptions and formulas that turns inputs into a cost figure. Here the annual cost of $8,275 divided by 4,380 generating hours gives $1.89 per generating hour, and 40 hours × $1.89 is about $76. The $53 figure belongs to the reference book, which takes 28 hours. Dividing the annual cost by 40 confuses hours per book with books per year and gives a meaningless $207.

Concept Tested: Cost Model

See: Cost Model

docs.title: 7. A book costs $40 to produce. Which price gives the seller a 20% profit margin?
docs.text:
1. $48
  2. $50
  3. $44
  4. $60
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Profit margin is the share of a price that is profit: price minus cost, divided by price. For a 20% margin the price is the cost divided by 0.80, so $40 ÷ 0.80 is $50, and the $10 profit is 20% of that price. Multiplying the cost by 1.20 gives $48, which is a 20% markup, measured against cost. That price yields a margin of only 16.7%, less than the seller intended.

Concept Tested: Profit Margin

See: Profit Margin

docs.title: 8. A unit generates for 2,000 hours a year at 150 W and idles for the other 6,760 hours at 40 W. About how much energy does it use in a year?
docs.text:
1. About 570 kWh
  2. About 300 kWh
  3. About 832 kWh
  4. About 1,314 kWh
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Electricity cost is energy consumed times the price of energy, and a machine that is on but not generating still draws idle power, so yearly energy has two terms. Generating: 2,000 h × 150 W = 300,000 Wh. Idle: 6,760 h × 40 W = 270,400 Wh. Together that is 570,400 Wh, or about 570 kWh. Counting only the generating hours gives 300 kWh and leaves out nearly half of the energy.

Concept Tested: Electricity Cost

See: Electricity Cost

docs.title: 9. In the reference case, changing the hardware price moves the cost per book by about ten percent, while changing operations labor moves it by up to a factor of two. What does this pattern tell a planner?
docs.text:
1. The hardware price should be negotiated before anything else
  2. The labor estimate deserves more scrutiny than the hardware price
  3. Both assumptions should be varied together to save time
  4. The cost model is too unreliable to support any decision
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Sensitivity analysis changes one assumption at a time and records how the output moves, so you learn which assumptions the answer depends on. Doubling operations labor raises the cost per book from $53 to $81 and removing it drops it to $25, while hardware price moves it by about ten percent. The ranking shows where attention belongs: on the labor estimate. Varying two assumptions together would hide which one moved the answer.

Concept Tested: Sensitivity Analysis

See: Sensitivity Analysis

docs.title: 10. A break-even calculation returns 426 books a year against a $20 alternative, but one unit can produce only 156 books a year. What does this result mean?
docs.text:
1. The unit breaks even once demand grows to 426 books
  2. The formula is invalid whenever the price is below $50
  3. The unit's variable cost per book has been overstated
  4. One unit cannot break even at any volume it can reach
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Break-even volume is the production level at which two options cost the same: the fixed cost divided by the saving on each book. A result above what the machine can produce is not a target to grow into. It means that against that alternative, one unit does not break even at any volume it can reach. The formula gives no warning, so always compare the result with capacity: generating hours divided by hours per book.

Concept Tested: Break-Even Volume

See: Break-Even Volume

docs.title: References: Cost, Price, and Quality
docs.text:
1. Total cost of ownership - Wikipedia - Defines TCO as an estimate of the direct and indirect costs of owning a product, and argues that ownership costs far exceed the purchase price. It supports the chapter's three-year TCO calculation.

  2. Break-even point - Wikipedia - Explains the point at which total cost equals total revenue, with sections on purpose, construction, and limitations. It underlies the chapter's break-even volume formula comparing a local machine's fixed cost with a per-book price.

  3. Depreciation - Wikipedia - Covers depreciation as both a fall in an asset's value and the allocation of its cost over its useful life, with the common calculation methods. It supports the chapter's even three-year spread of hardware cost.

  4. Quality Is Free: The Art of Making Quality Certain (1st Edition, 1979) - Philip B. Crosby - McGraw-Hill - Crosby defined quality as conformance to requirements and measured it by the price of nonconformance: rework, scrap, and lost customers. That idea shows why a cheaper local model whose output must be redone has not saved money.

  5. Horngren's Cost Accounting: A Managerial Emphasis (16th Edition) - Srikant M. Datar and Madhav V. Rajan (original author Charles T. Horngren) - Pearson - A long-running cost accounting text built on the theme "different costs for different purposes," a phrase credited to economist J. M. Clark. Its cost-volume-profit chapters match the chapter's fixed, variable, and break-even analysis.

  6. 3.2 Calculate a Break-Even Point in Units and Dollars - OpenStax - Free textbook section from Principles of Accounting, Volume 2 that derives break-even in units and dollars from fixed costs and contribution margin. It matches the chapter's break-even formula and worked examples.

  7. Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.6.B: Average Price of Electricity to Ultimate Customers by End-Use Sector - U.S. Energy Information Administration - Publishes year-to-date electricity prices in cents per kilowatthour by sector and state, including a commercial column and a U.S. total. It is the kind of source behind the chapter's per-kilowatthour electricity price.

  8. Pricing - Anthropic - Lists model prices per million tokens, with separate rates for input, output, and cached tokens. It is a concrete example of the per-token pricing that the chapter contrasts with subscription and per-seat charges.

  9. Markup - Corporate Finance Institute - Defines markup as profit over cost and contrasts it with gross margin, using a worked example in which a 20 percent markup yields a gross margin under 17 percent. It matches the chapter's margin-versus-markup table.

  10. Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide (GAO-20-195G) - U.S. Government Accountability Office - Best-practice guide to building and defending cost estimates, with steps for ground rules and assumptions, data collection, and sensitivity and risk analysis. It models the chapter's habit of stating assumptions and varying them.

docs.title: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
Summary
docs.text: This chapter teaches how to reach a remote machine securely. It covers SSH, key pairs, and unattended login, then explains how a WireGuard-based mesh VPN works and how Tailscale and the tailnet separate coordination from data transfer. Students finish able to describe the connection path between a laptop and a DGX.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 21 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Remote Access 210 SSH 31 Mesh VPN 170 Home Router 39 SSH Key Pair 15 SSH Port Forward 2 Host Key Fingerprint 1 WireGuard 85 Ed25519 Key 4 ssh-copy-id 3 NAT Traversal 3 Host Hygiene 1 Tailscale 81 Passphrase-Free Key 3 Tailnet 61 Data Plane 3 Unattended SSH Login 2 Coordination Plane 1 Peer-to-Peer Connection 1 DERP Relay 1 BatchMode 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 6: Cost, Price, and Quality

Reaching the Machine Without Opening a Door

The DGX is in one building and you are in another, with two home routers between you that neither of you controls. By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the exact path a command takes from your laptop to the machine, and say what each party on that path can see. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Everything after this chapter happens on a machine you reach over a network. If that connection is fragile, insecure, or impossible to script, every later step inherits the problem. The chapter therefore teaches the connection itself before any software is installed on the DGX.

It has two layers. The first is SSH, the protocol you use to run commands on a remote machine, and the key-based login that lets scripts and agents use it without a person typing a password. The second is the mesh VPN, the network layer that makes a machine behind someone else's router reachable at all. Chapter 9 installs and configures Tailscale. This chapter explains why it works, so the installation steps make sense.

docs.title: Remote Access
docs.text:
Remote access is the ability to use a computer that is not in front of you: to log in, run commands, move files, and watch its output. Every DGX evaluation needs it, because the machine is in a lab, a server room, or someone else's home, and the work of the evaluation runs for hours.

There are three common ways to arrange it, and they differ in what they expose to the public internet.

Approach How it works What is exposed Main drawback Port forwarding The router forwards a public port to the machine The machine's login service, to everyone on the internet Constant automated attacks, and it needs router access A conventional VPN Both sides connect to a central VPN server The VPN server All traffic passes through one point, and someone must run it A mesh VPN Each machine connects directly to the others Nothing on the machine's own address Depends on a coordination service

A worked decision shows how the three compare against this evaluation's actual constraints. The laptop and the DGX are on different home networks. Nobody involved controls both routers, and the person running the benchmark has no access to the DGX's router at all. Scripts and an AI agent must log in with no person present. And the machine must not become reachable by strangers, because it belongs to someone else.

Constraint Port forwarding Conventional VPN Mesh VPN No access to the DGX's router Fails: it needs a router change Works if the server is reachable Works Scripts must connect unattended Works Works Works Must not be reachable by strangers Fails: the login port is public Works Works No new server to run and patch Works Fails: someone runs the hub Works

Only the mesh VPN passes every row, which is why the Administrator chose Tailscale and why the rest of this chapter explains how it works.

Port forwarding is the approach a tutorial reaches for first, and it is the one this course does not use. A login service open to the whole internet receives guessing attempts within minutes of appearing, and exposing a DGX that way endangers the machine and the network it sits on.

docs.title: Home Router
docs.text:
A home router is the device that connects a local network to the internet and gives the devices behind it private addresses. It also performs network address translation, or NAT: many devices on the private side share one public address, and the router keeps a table that records which internal device each outgoing conversation belongs to.

NAT has a consequence that explains the whole chapter. A reply to a conversation you started is allowed back in, because the router remembers it. A new connection that arrives unprompted has no entry in the table, so the router drops it. Two machines behind two routers therefore cannot simply connect to each other: each router sees an unsolicited connection and refuses it.

Step What happens Result 1 The laptop at 192.0.2.10 opens a connection to a website The router records the conversation and sends it out under its public address 2 The website replies The router finds the record and forwards the reply to the laptop 3 A stranger sends a packet to the router's public address There is no record, so the router drops it 4 The DGX's router receives an unsolicited connection from the laptop's router Also no record, so it is dropped

The addresses in this chapter come from the ranges reserved for documentation, such as 192.0.2.0/24 and 198.51.100.0/24. A real address never appears in this book.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
SSH, short for Secure Shell, is a protocol for logging in to another computer and running commands there over an encrypted connection. The machine you want to reach runs an SSH server, your machine runs an SSH client, and the two negotiate encryption before anything is sent. The server listens on port 22 by default, and it is what runs underneath nearly every remote administration task on Linux.

The simplest use is a single command run on the remote machine, with its output printed on yours. The command below logs in as <user> on <dgx-host>, runs hostname, prints the result, and returns. The two angle-bracketed names are placeholders, and the book uses them for every login and every address.

ssh <user>@<dgx-host> hostname

The first time you connect, the client asks whether you trust the server's key, and later sessions skip the question. That prompt is the subject of the next concept, because answering it carelessly defeats the point of the protocol.

docs.title: Host Key Fingerprint
docs.text:
A host key fingerprint is a short value derived from the server's public key that identifies the server. The first time you connect, your client shows the fingerprint and asks you to accept it. It stores the key in a file called known_hosts, and on every later connection it checks that the server presents the same key.

The check protects against someone placing themselves between you and the server. If the key suddenly differs, the client refuses to continue and prints a loud warning. The warning has two ordinary causes and one serious one: the machine was reinstalled, its disk image was cloned onto another machine, or something is intercepting the connection. A fingerprint is useful only if you compare it, once, with a value the administrator gave you through another channel.

docs.title: SSH Key Pair
docs.text:
An SSH key pair is two linked files: a private key that stays on your machine and a public key that you give to servers. A server holding your public key can check that you hold the matching private key without the private key ever crossing the network. The check replaces a password, and it cannot be guessed by trying passwords against a login prompt.

The public key goes into a file on the server named authorized_keys. Anyone who holds the private key can log in as you, so the private key is the secret, and the public key is safe to share.

docs.title: Ed25519 Key
docs.text:
An Ed25519 key is a key using a modern elliptic-curve signature scheme. It produces short keys, which are 68 characters when printed, it is fast, and it is the default recommendation for new SSH keys. The older RSA type is still accepted but needs far longer keys for comparable strength. Create one with ssh-keygen -t ed25519.

The command writes two files in ~/.ssh: id_ed25519, the private key, and id_ed25519.pub, the public key. The permissions on the private file matter, and SSH refuses a key that other users on the machine can read.

docs.title: ssh-copy-id
docs.text:
ssh-copy-id installs your public key on a server's authorized_keys file. It logs in once with your password, appends the key, and sets the correct permissions. It is the standard way to move from password login to key login.

ssh-copy-id <user>@<dgx-host>

Run it once for each machine you want to reach. After it succeeds, the next login needs no password.

docs.title: Passphrase-Free Key
docs.text:
A passphrase is a password that encrypts the private key file on disk, so a stolen file is useless without it. A passphrase-free key has no such protection: the file alone is enough to log in. It is what makes unattended login possible, since a script cannot type a passphrase.

This is a trade, not a mistake, and the design choice in this evaluation was made knowingly. The scripts and the agent that ran the benchmark logged in unattended, so the key had no passphrase. The price is that the file on the laptop is as sensitive as a password.

A Key With No Passphrase Is a Password in a File

Anyone who copies the private key file can log in as you from anywhere, with nothing to guess. Keep it only on the machine that needs it, never commit it to a repository, and tell the administrator that you installed a key on their machine so they can remove it when the project ends.

docs.title: Unattended SSH Login and BatchMode
docs.text:
Unattended SSH login is a login that needs no person: the client authenticates with the key and runs the command. BatchMode is the SSH option that makes this explicit. It tells the client never to prompt for a password or a passphrase, and to fail at once if a prompt would be needed.

That failure is the useful property. A script that hangs waiting for a prompt nobody can see wastes hours, and a script that fails with an error in a second does not. The command below is also the standard test that key login works.

ssh -o BatchMode=yes <user>@<dgx-host> hostname

If it prints the machine's name, key login works. If it prints Permission denied, the key is not installed or is not the one the client offered.

Always Test Key Login With BatchMode

A normal ssh can fall back to asking for a password and appear to work, which hides a broken key. Add -o BatchMode=yes to the test and it either succeeds silently or tells you which part failed.

docs.title: SSH Port Forward
docs.text:
An SSH port forward carries traffic for one network port through an SSH connection, so a service on the remote machine appears as though it were on your own. In the first benchmark runs the model server on the DGX listened only on that machine's own loopback address, which no other machine can reach. A forward made it reachable from the laptop.

The command has three parts that need explaining before you read it. -N tells SSH not to run a remote command and only hold the tunnel open. -L creates the forward and takes the form local-port:destination:destination-port. The destination is resolved on the remote side, so 127.0.0.1 there means the DGX itself.

ssh -N -L 11434:127.0.0.1:11434 <user>@<dgx-host>

While that command runs, a request to port 11434 on the laptop reaches the model server on the DGX, and the traffic travels inside the encrypted SSH connection. Port 11434 is the port the Ollama model server uses by default. Chapter 13 sets it up.

docs.title: Host Hygiene
docs.text:
Host hygiene is the set of habits that keep a remote-access setup from becoming a liability. For this course five are enough.

  • Keep private keys private. Never copy id_ed25519 to another machine, a chat, or a repository.
  • Use one key per purpose. A separate key for the DGX project can be revoked without affecting anything else.
  • Remove what you added. When the project ends, delete your public key from the server's authorized_keys and ask the administrator to remove the account.
  • Tell the owner. Installing a key on a machine you do not own is a change to their security, and they are entitled to know.
  • Read the output before saving it. A pasted SSH session contains hostnames and addresses. Chapter 23 builds the review that catches them.

docs.title: Mesh VPN
docs.text:
A VPN, or virtual private network, is an encrypted virtual network built on top of the internet, so that devices far apart behave as if they shared one private local network. A mesh VPN is one in which every device can connect directly to every other device, with no central machine that all traffic must pass through.

The structure matters because a conventional VPN is hub-and-spoke: every device connects to one server, and traffic between two devices goes through it. A mesh removes the middle. The comparison below uses the three machines of this evaluation: the laptop and two DGX units.

Hub-and-spoke VPN Mesh VPN Path from laptop to a DGX Laptop → hub → DGX Laptop → DGX Number of hops Two One What fails if one machine fails The hub takes everything down Only that machine Who runs central infrastructure You A coordination service, which carries no traffic Direct links among 3 devices 3, all via the hub 3, each direct

The number of possible links among \( n \) devices is \( n(n-1)/2 \). Three devices have 3 pairs and ten devices have 45, which is why configuring a mesh by hand does not scale and why the coordination step in the next sections exists.

docs.title: WireGuard
docs.text:
WireGuard is a VPN protocol built around a small set of modern cryptographic choices and a short code base. Each device has a key pair, and a connection is defined by listing the other device's public key and the address to reach it at. It runs over UDP, it encrypts with ChaCha20-Poly1305, and it has been part of the Linux kernel since version 5.6, so on a current DGX OS the protocol is already present.

A minimal configuration shows what WireGuard asks of a person. Three things need defining before you read it. The [Interface] block describes this device, and its Address is the private address it takes inside the VPN. A [Peer] block describes one other device, identified by its public key. AllowedIPs lists the addresses that may be sent to that peer, and Endpoint is where the peer can be reached on the real network.

[Interface]
PrivateKey = <laptop-private-key>
Address    = 100.x.y.z/32

[Peer]
PublicKey  = <dgx-public-key>
AllowedIPs = 100.x.y.z/32
Endpoint   = <dgx-public-address>:51820

Every placeholder above is a value that someone has to generate, copy to the right place, and keep current. For two devices behind home routers it is worse: the Endpoint line assumes the DGX has a fixed public address that accepts connections, which a device behind a home router does not. WireGuard secures the connection and leaves finding and keying the peers to you.

docs.title: Tailscale
docs.text:
Tailscale is a service and a set of client programs that build a WireGuard mesh automatically. It does the work the configuration above asks of a person: it generates each device's keys, distributes the public keys to the devices that should have them, discovers each device's current address, and arranges the connection across the routers. The client software is open source, and the coordination service that ties devices together is hosted.

A device joins by signing in with an identity, and from then on the other devices in the same network can find it by name or by a private address. In this evaluation the laptop signed in with an account the Administrator had invited, and the two DGX units were already members, so a single status command listed all three. Chapter 9 performs those steps.

What you would do by hand with WireGuard What Tailscale does Generate a key pair on each device The client generates it at first start Copy each public key to every peer The coordination service distributes it Find each peer's current public address The coordination service tracks it Open a path through two routers The clients negotiate it, with a relay as fallback Write and update a config file per device None, the clients keep it current

docs.title: Tailnet
docs.text:
A tailnet is a private network of devices and users managed together under one Tailscale account or organization. Devices in a tailnet get stable private addresses from a reserved range that starts 100., and they get names that resolve only inside the tailnet. Only members can reach one another, and the administrator of the tailnet controls who is a member and what each may reach.

A tailnet also has a name, in the form <tailnet-name>.ts.net, which is part of every machine's full name. Like an address, it is a detail that helps a stranger locate the network, so it is a placeholder in this book.

Membership gives a device four things, and each one is a place where a setting can go wrong later.

  • A stable private address. The device keeps it as it moves between networks, so a script written against the address or name keeps working from a coffee shop or an office.
  • A name. Names resolve only inside the tailnet, through a feature called MagicDNS that Chapter 9 configures.
  • Access rules. The tailnet's administrator can restrict which devices and users may reach which machines and ports, using an access control list.
  • A key that expires. A device's credentials last for a period and then must be renewed, so a machine that has not been touched in months may have silently dropped off the network.

The machines in this evaluation sat in a tailnet that the Administrator ran. That is the fact behind two later cautions: the Administrator decides who joins, and the evaluator's laptop is a guest on a network the evaluator does not control.

docs.title: Coordination Plane and Data Plane
docs.text:
Tailscale's design separates two jobs that a conventional VPN combines. The coordination plane is the exchange of information needed to set up connections: who the devices are, their public keys, where they can currently be reached, and which devices are allowed to reach which. The data plane is the traffic itself: the packets that carry your commands, your prompts, and a model's replies.

The two planes use different paths. Coordination goes between each device and the coordination service. Data goes between the devices, and does not pass through the service.

Coordination plane Data plane Carries Public keys, addresses, access rules Your SSH sessions, prompts, and replies Goes between A device and the coordination service The two devices Volume Tiny As much as you send What the service learns Identities, keys, and addresses Nothing about the content

The Service Introduces You and Then Steps Aside

Think of the coordination service as a mutual friend who tells two strangers each other's names and phone numbers, then leaves the room. It knows who talked to whom, and it never hears the conversation. The privacy of your prompts rests on that second half, and it is why the data plane has to be encrypted device to device.

docs.title: NAT Traversal and the Peer-to-Peer Connection
docs.text:
NAT traversal is the set of techniques for opening a direct path between two devices that are each behind a router performing NAT. Recall that a router drops a connection nobody inside asked for, and that it accepts replies to conversations that started from inside. The traversal exploits that rule.

Following the sequence shows how it works. Each device learns, from the coordination service, the other's public address. Both then send a packet to the other's address at about the same moment. Each router sees an outgoing packet and records an entry for it, and each incoming packet from the other side now matches that entry and is let through. The result is a peer-to-peer connection: the two devices exchange packets directly, with no one between them.

The data plane then carries every packet encrypted by WireGuard, so the routers on the path see only that two public addresses exchanged data.

docs.title: DERP Relay
docs.text:
Sometimes the direct path cannot be opened: a strict firewall may block outgoing UDP, or a router may allocate a different port for each destination in a way the technique cannot predict. For those cases Tailscale runs relay servers called DERP servers, short for Designated Encrypted Relay for Packets. The two devices connect outward to a relay, and the relay forwards their packets.

Two properties make the relay safe to use. The packets are already encrypted by the devices, so the relay forwards data it cannot read. And the relay is only a fallback: the clients keep probing, and as soon as a direct path becomes possible they switch to it. A relayed connection is slower, because the traffic takes a longer route, and the status listing marks such connections so you can see which one you have.

The evaluation's laptop reached the DGX units across two home routers, and the status listing for one unit showed a relay in use instead of a direct connection. Chapter 9 shows how to read that listing.

docs.title: Diagram: Tailscale Connection Path
docs.text:
Run Tailscale Connection Path Fullscreen

Tailscale Connection Path

Type: microsim sim-id: tailscale-connection-path Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain how two devices behind NAT build an encrypted connection by predicting the path for 3 scenarios and assigning 3 messages to the coordination plane or the data plane, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: home router, NAT traversal, peer-to-peer connection, DERP relay, coordination plane, data plane (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner first steps through the five connection steps listed in Content. The learner then answers 6 items before any answer is revealed: three path predictions ("Direct" or "Relay") and three message assignments ("Coordination plane" or "Data plane"). An item is correct when the choice equals the Correct answer column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Stepping through is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The coordination service carries or can read the traffic. (2) A relay can read the traffic it forwards. (3) Two devices behind routers can never connect directly. (4) A relayed connection is not encrypted.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level explaining needs the learner to predict an outcome from the mechanism, so the path items are cases where the correct answer follows from the NAT and UDP rules of the chapter. Separating the planes in a second set of items checks that the learner assigns each message to the right path.

Content:

The five steps the learner steps through, in order:

  1. Both devices sign in to the coordination service and give it their public keys.
  2. The service gives each device the other's public key and its candidate addresses.
  3. Each device sends packets to the other's addresses at the same moment, so each router creates a table entry for the conversation.
  4. If those packets get through, the devices talk directly. If they do not, both connect outward to a relay.
  5. Everything the devices exchange is encrypted by the devices themselves, so neither the relay nor the service can read it.

The six items:

# Item shown to the learner Choices Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Laptop and DGX are each behind an ordinary home router. Direct or Relay Direct Ordinary NAT allows the simultaneous-send technique to open both routers. 2 The laptop is on a network whose firewall blocks all outgoing UDP. Direct or Relay Relay The direct path uses UDP, so the encrypted packets go through a relay instead. 3 Laptop and DGX are on the same local network. Direct or Relay Direct They can reach each other's local addresses without leaving the network. 4 A device uploads its public key. Coordination plane or Data plane Coordination plane It is setup information exchanged with the service. 5 A packet carrying part of a model's reply. Coordination plane or Data plane Data plane It is traffic between the two devices. 6 The list of which devices may reach which. Coordination plane or Data plane Coordination plane Access rules are distributed by the service to the devices.

Provenance: The items are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The mechanism comes from the sections of this chapter above.

Rules: A connection is Direct when a UDP path can be opened between the two devices, and Relay otherwise. A relay forwards only encrypted packets. Items are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6, and each item allows one final choice.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner presses Next to move through the five steps, with the devices, routers, service, and relay shown and the current step's message highlighted.
  2. After step 5 the learner begins the six items and reads item 1.
  3. For each item the learner chooses one of the two answers and confirms.
  4. The sim shows the correct answer and the Why text, and marks the item correct or incorrect.
  5. After item 6 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Six items, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct answer and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: The five-step walkthrough is at step 1 with the two devices, their routers, and the coordination service shown, and the question on screen is "How do these two devices end up able to talk?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a router drops unsolicited connections, that NAT traversal makes both routers create entries by sending at the same moment, that a relay forwards packets it cannot read, and that coordination carries keys, addresses, and rules while data carries content.

docs.title: What Each Party Can See
docs.text:
The reason to understand the path is to know who can see what. The table assigns each party on the way from the laptop to the DGX to its role.

Party What it can see Why The laptop's router That encrypted packets go to a public address It forwards packets and sees no content The coordination service Which devices exist, their public keys, and addresses It runs the coordination plane A DERP relay, if used Encrypted packets and the two endpoints It forwards without the keys The DGX's router That encrypted packets arrive from a public address Same as the first router The two devices Everything They hold the keys

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Remote access to a machine behind a home router fails by default, because the router drops connections nobody inside asked for. SSH gives an encrypted login, and a key pair gives a login that a script can use, at the price of a private key that must be protected like a password. A mesh VPN solves the routing problem: WireGuard provides the encryption, and Tailscale automates the key distribution, address discovery, and NAT traversal, falling back to an encrypted relay when a direct path cannot be opened. The coordination plane sets up the connection and the data plane carries the traffic, and the two are separate paths.

You Can Trace the Whole Path

You can now follow a command from your laptop through two routers to the DGX, say which party sees what, and explain why the privacy of your prompts does not depend on trusting the coordination service. Chapter 8 builds the Python environment that the tooling will live in.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
docs.text: Test your understanding of SSH, key-based login, mesh VPNs, and the connection path between a laptop and a DGX with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What distinguishes a mesh VPN from a hub-and-spoke VPN?
docs.text:
1. Each device connects directly to the others, with no central hub
  2. All traffic passes through one central server that someone must run
  3. The router forwards a public port to each member device
  4. Devices connect without encryption inside a private range
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A mesh VPN is one in which every device can connect directly to every other device, with no central machine that all traffic must pass through. A conventional VPN is hub-and-spoke: traffic between two devices goes through one server, and if the hub fails everything goes down. In a mesh the path from laptop to DGX is one hop, and the coordination service that sets up connections carries no traffic.

Concept Tested: Mesh VPN

See: Mesh VPN

docs.title: 2. In an SSH key pair, which key is the secret, and where does the other one go?
docs.text:
1. The public key is secret; the private key goes in known_hosts
  2. Both keys are secret and both stay in ~/.ssh on the laptop
  3. The private key is secret; the public key goes in authorized_keys
  4. The private key is copied to the server; the public key stays on the laptop
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An SSH key pair is two linked files. The private key stays on your machine and is the secret: anyone who holds it can log in as you. The public key is safe to share and goes into the server's authorized_keys file. The server uses it to check that you hold the matching private key, without the private key ever crossing the network. known_hosts is a different file, where the client stores server keys.

Concept Tested: SSH Key Pair

See: SSH Key Pair

docs.title: 3. What is a tailnet?
docs.text:
1. A relay server that forwards encrypted packets between peers
  2. A private network of devices and users under one Tailscale account
  3. A WireGuard configuration file listing each peer's public key
  4. A public address range that home routers assign to devices
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A tailnet is a private network of devices and users managed together under one Tailscale account or organization. Its devices get stable private addresses from a reserved range that starts 100. and names that resolve only inside the tailnet. Only members can reach one another, and the tailnet's administrator controls who is a member and what each may reach. A relay that forwards encrypted packets is a DERP server, a separate idea.

Concept Tested: Tailnet

See: Tailnet

docs.title: 4. Why can two machines behind two home routers not simply connect to each other?
docs.text:
1. Home routers block all encrypted traffic by default
  2. Each router drops incoming connections it has no record of
  3. The two machines are assigned the same private address
  4. SSH servers refuse logins that arrive from another network
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A home router performs NAT: many private devices share one public address, and the router keeps a table of the conversations that started from inside. A reply to such a conversation is let back in. A new connection that arrives unprompted has no entry in the table, so the router drops it. Two machines behind two routers each look like an unsolicited connection to the other's router, so neither gets through.

Concept Tested: Home Router

See: Home Router

docs.title: 5. What does Tailscale add to WireGuard?
docs.text:
1. Automatic key distribution, address discovery, and NAT traversal
  2. A stronger encryption scheme that replaces WireGuard's own
  3. A central server through which all device traffic is routed
  4. Password-based login for devices that have no key pair
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. WireGuard secures a connection and leaves finding and keying the peers to you: someone must generate keys, copy public keys, and know each peer's reachable address. Tailscale builds a WireGuard mesh automatically. It generates each device's keys, distributes the public keys, discovers current addresses, and arranges the connection across the routers. It does not replace WireGuard's encryption, and its coordination service carries no device traffic.

Concept Tested: Tailscale

See: Tailscale

docs.title: 6. Why does the privacy of your prompts not depend on trusting the coordination service?
docs.text:
1. Data travels encrypted between the devices, not through the service
  2. The service deletes every prompt as soon as it has finished forwarding it
  3. The service runs on hardware that the tailnet's owner controls
  4. Prompts are sent only while the coordination service is offline
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Tailscale separates two jobs. The coordination plane exchanges setup information between each device and the service: public keys, addresses, and access rules. The data plane carries your SSH sessions, prompts, and replies directly between the two devices, encrypted by WireGuard, and it does not pass through the service. The service learns identities, keys, and addresses, and nothing about the content. It knows who talked to whom and never hears the conversation.

Concept Tested: Data Plane

See: Coordination Plane and Data Plane

docs.title: 7. You want to confirm that key login works before a script depends on it. Which command is the standard test?
docs.text:
1. ssh-copy-id <user>@<dgx-host>, then enter the password
  2. ssh <user>@<dgx-host> hostname, with no extra options
  3. ssh -o BatchMode=yes <user>@<dgx-host> hostname
  4. ssh-keygen -t ed25519, then read the files in ~/.ssh
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. BatchMode tells the SSH client never to prompt for a password or passphrase and to fail at once if a prompt would be needed. The command prints the machine's name if key login works and Permission denied if the key is not installed or is not the one offered. A plain ssh can fall back to asking for a password and appear to work, which hides a broken key, so it is not a reliable test.

Concept Tested: BatchMode

See: Unattended SSH Login and BatchMode

docs.title: 8. While ssh -N -L 11434:127.0.0.1:11434 <user>@<dgx-host> runs, where does a request to port 11434 on the laptop go?
docs.text:
1. To port 11434 on the laptop itself, since 127.0.0.1 is local
  2. To port 22 on the DGX, where the SSH server answers it
  3. To the coordination service, which then relays it to the DGX
  4. To the model server on the DGX, through the SSH connection
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. An SSH port forward carries traffic for one port through an SSH connection. -N holds the tunnel open without running a remote command, and -L takes the form local-port:destination:destination-port. The destination is resolved on the remote side, so 127.0.0.1 there means the DGX itself, not the laptop. A request to port 11434 on the laptop therefore reaches the model server on the DGX, traveling inside the encrypted SSH connection.

Concept Tested: SSH Port Forward

See: SSH Port Forward

docs.title: 9. A status listing shows that your laptop reaches a DGX unit through a DERP relay instead of a direct connection. What should you conclude?
docs.text:
1. The relay can read the session, so stop sending prompts
  2. The coordination service is now carrying all of the traffic
  3. The unit's device key has expired and must be renewed
  4. The traffic is still encrypted by the devices but is slower
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A DERP relay is the fallback when a direct path cannot be opened, for example when a firewall blocks outgoing UDP. The packets are already encrypted by the devices, so the relay forwards data it cannot read. A relayed connection is slower because the traffic takes a longer route, and the clients keep probing and switch to a direct path as soon as one becomes possible. The coordination service still carries no traffic.

Concept Tested: DERP Relay

See: DERP Relay

docs.title: 10. The person running the benchmark cannot change the DGX's router, and the machine must not be reachable by strangers. Why does port forwarding fail both constraints?
docs.text:
1. It cannot carry SSH traffic, which a mesh VPN can carry
  2. It needs a router change and exposes the login port publicly
  3. It requires a central hub that someone has to run and keep patched
  4. It prevents scripts from connecting when no person is present to log in
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Remote access can be arranged by port forwarding, a conventional VPN, or a mesh VPN, and they differ in what they expose. Port forwarding needs a change on the DGX's router, which the evaluator cannot make, and it opens the machine's login service to everyone on the internet, where guessing attempts arrive within minutes. Running a hub is the drawback of a conventional VPN. Only the mesh VPN passed every constraint in this evaluation.

Concept Tested: Remote Access

See: Remote Access

docs.title: References: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
docs.text:
1. Secure Shell - Wikipedia - Describes the SSH protocol, its replacement of Telnet and rlogin, public-key authentication, and architecture. It supports the chapter's coverage of encrypted remote login, host keys, and key-based unattended access.

  2. WireGuard - Wikipedia - Covers the UDP-based VPN protocol, its design goals compared with IPsec and OpenVPN, and its inclusion in Linux 5.6. It supports the chapter's account of the encryption layer beneath Tailscale.

  3. Network address translation - Wikipedia - Explains how routers map private addresses to public ones, with a section on NAT types and NAT traversal. It underlies the chapter's explanation of why a home router drops unsolicited connections.

  4. Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (9th Edition) - James F. Kurose and Keith W. Ross - Pearson - The authors describe their book as breaking new ground by teaching networking top-down, starting at the application layer and working toward physical links. That order makes NAT, VPNs, and SSH concrete before the plumbing beneath them.

  5. SSH, The Secure Shell: The Definitive Guide (2nd Edition) - Daniel J. Barrett, Richard E. Silverman, and Robert G. Byrnes - O'Reilly Media - A widely used book-length reference on the SSH-2 protocol, covering key management, agents, and port forwarding. It is the deeper treatment behind the chapter's key pair, unattended login, and port-forward sections.

  6. How Tailscale Works - Tailscale - Avery Pennarun's 2020 post explains the WireGuard data plane, the coordination server that distributes public keys, NAT traversal, and DERP relays. It is the primary source for the chapter's coordination-plane versus data-plane distinction.

  7. How NAT Traversal Works - Tailscale - David Anderson's article walks through stateful firewalls, NAT, STUN, and hole punching, with relays as the fallback. It gives the step-by-step mechanism behind the chapter's simultaneous-send explanation of peer-to-peer connections.

  8. Protocol & Cryptography - WireGuard - The project's own overview of WireGuard's primitives (ChaCha20 with Poly1305, Curve25519, BLAKE2s), UDP transport, and Noise-based handshake. It backs the chapter's description of WireGuard's encryption and its key-based handshake.

  9. ssh(1) manual page - OpenBSD manual pages (OpenSSH) - Official OpenSSH client manual documenting options such as -L port forwarding, -N, and -o, plus known_hosts handling and host key verification. It is the authoritative reference for the commands the chapter shows.

  10. RFC 4251: The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Architecture - IETF - Standards-track description of SSH's transport, user authentication, and connection layers, with a discussion of host keys and the risk on first connection. It grounds the chapter's host key fingerprint warning.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter shows how an isolated conda environment makes an evaluation reproducible. Students create, activate, pin, export, and rebuild environments, handle architecture-specific wheels, and install CUDA-enabled PyTorch. They finish with an environment specification that can rebuild the full software stack on a fresh machine.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 21 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Python Environment 52 pip 9 Miniforge 29 Environment Isolation 18 requirements.txt 3 Architecture-Specific Wheels 3 PyTorch 3 Conda 28 Conda Create Command 25 Conda Versus pip 1 Package Channel 1 Dedicated Tool Environment 15 Conda Activate Command 5 Python Version Pinning 3 CUDA-Enabled PyTorch 2 Conda Remove Command 1 Conda List and Export 4 Reproducibility 2 environment.yml 3 Environment Rebuild 2 Install Script 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 5: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture

Build the Toolbox Once, Rebuild It Anywhere

An evaluation whose software cannot be rebuilt is a story, not a measurement, because nobody can check it. By the end of this chapter you will have an environment specification that rebuilds your tools on a fresh machine, and a way to prove that it did. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 7 reached the machine. This chapter prepares the software that will run against it. The aim is narrow: every Python tool in this course should run from an environment you can delete, rebuild, and compare, so that a surprising result can be traced to a cause instead of to "something I installed last week".

The chapter covers what an environment is and why isolating it matters, the conda tool that manages environments, and the difference between conda and pip. It then handles the two traps that DGX machines add, which are architecture-specific packages and CUDA-enabled PyTorch, and it ends with the specification file and install script that make a rebuild a single command.

docs.title: Python Environment
docs.text:
A Python environment is a self-contained directory that holds a Python interpreter and the packages installed for it, together with a script that points your shell at them. Activating an environment puts its interpreter and packages first on your path, so the python command runs that interpreter and import finds those packages and no others.

The need for one is easiest to see by what happens without it. Suppose two projects share one system Python. The first needs version 1 of a library and the second needs version 2, and a package can exist in only one version at a time in one place. Installing for the second project silently breaks the first. The break may not show up until a script that worked last month fails with an error about a function that no longer exists.

The table sets out what an environment contains, so that its parts are not mysterious later.

Part What it is Where it lives Interpreter The python executable, of one version Inside the environment directory Packages Libraries installed for that interpreter A site-packages folder in the environment Activation script Changes the shell's path to use the environment Run by the activate command Metadata A record of what was installed A conda-meta folder, for conda environments

An Environment Is a Directory You Can Throw Away

Once you see an environment as just a folder, the discipline follows. You never repair a broken one. You delete it and rebuild it from the specification, which is a faster and more trustworthy fix than finding the one package that drifted.

docs.title: Environment Isolation
docs.text:
Environment isolation is keeping each environment separate so that a change in one cannot affect another. It is what turns the list of packages from a shared, mutable pile into a record that belongs to one purpose.

A real instance from this course's tooling shows the stakes. Two documentation build tools each depend on the same markdown-extension package, and each pins a different version of it. Installed together in one environment, they cannot both be satisfied, and installing the second breaks the first. The fix was not a cleverer install. It was to give each tool its own environment, so that neither one had to agree with the other.

docs.title: Conda and Miniforge
docs.text:
Conda is a package and environment manager. It creates environments, installs packages into them, and records what it installed. Unlike a tool that handles only Python libraries, conda also installs the non-Python programs a library depends on, and Python itself, so an environment can contain a whole stack.

Miniforge is a minimal installer for conda that is set up to use the community-maintained conda-forge channel by default. It is the installer this course uses. The alternative, a distribution from a commercial vendor, brings a default channel with licensing terms that can require a paid license for larger organizations, and a book whose readers are professionals in unknown organizations should not depend on that.

docs.title: Package Channel
docs.text:
A package channel is a server that hosts packages for conda to download. When you ask for a package, conda searches the channels in order. The channel you use decides which packages and versions exist for you, and it decides who built them.

The course uses conda-forge, which is large, community-maintained, and builds packages for both x86_64 and aarch64. A specification should always name its channel explicitly, because an unnamed channel falls back to whatever a particular machine has configured, and two machines can then resolve the same list differently.

docs.title: The Create, Activate, and Remove Commands
docs.text:
The conda create command makes a new environment. Its parts are worth reading before you run it. -n dgx names the environment. -c conda-forge names the channel to search. Everything after is the packages to install, and a version after an equals sign pins it.

conda create -n dgx -c conda-forge python=3.12 psutil

The conda activate command switches your shell into the environment, and the prompt shows its name.

conda activate dgx

The conda remove command deletes the environment. conda env remove -n dgx removes the directory and its record, and it is the first step of a rebuild.

Activation Belongs to Interactive Shells

The conda activate function is defined by your shell's startup files, so a script or an agent running in a non-interactive shell may fail with a permission or "command not found" error. Call the environment's executables by their full path, or use conda run -n dgx <command>, and the failure goes away.

docs.title: Python Version Pinning
docs.text:
Python version pinning is fixing the interpreter's version in the environment's specification. Writing python=3.12 fixes the major and minor version, and conda chooses the newest 3.12 patch release. Writing python=3.12.4 fixes the patch release too.

Pinning matters because a minor release can change behavior, and a compiled package is built for one interpreter version. A machine that rebuilds your environment a year later without a pin gets a newer Python, which may not have wheels for every package you use.

docs.title: Dedicated Tool Environment
docs.text:
A dedicated tool environment is an environment that exists for one tool or one job and holds nothing else. In this evaluation the tools for reaching the DGX live in one, named dgx, which holds the Tailscale client and daemon and nothing else. The environment that builds this book is a different one.

The separation pays off three ways.

  • A break is contained. Breaking the build tool's environment cannot take out remote access.
  • The record is meaningful. The dgx environment's package list is exactly what reaching the DGX needs, with nothing accumulated from other work.
  • Removal is clean. When the project ends, one command removes everything it installed.

docs.title: Conda List and Export
docs.text:
The conda list command prints the packages in the active environment with their versions. The export command writes the environment to a file. The two forms of export differ in a way that decides whether the file can be used on another machine.

Export form What it records Portable across architectures? conda env export Every package, with exact builds No: the builds are specific to one platform conda env export --from-history Only the packages you asked for Yes: conda resolves the rest for the new platform

The listing has four columns that are worth knowing by name. The sanitized example below shows the dgx tool environment, with the filesystem path and the last digits of each version replaced.

# packages in environment at <conda-prefix>/envs/dgx:
#
# Name          Version    Build        Channel
python          3.12.4     h...         conda-forge
tailscale       1.xx.x     h...         conda-forge
tailscaled      1.xx.x     h...         conda-forge

Name and Version are what you pin. Build identifies the exact compiled variant, and it is the column that makes a full export platform-specific. Channel records where the package came from, which is how you notice a package that arrived from somewhere you did not intend. The environment holds only what the tool needs, which is the point of a dedicated environment.

A full export taken on a Mac with an Arm laptop chip lists builds that exist only for that platform. Rebuilding from it on a Linux aarch64 DGX fails with a list of packages that cannot be found. Exporting from history avoids this, at the price of letting each dependency resolve to whatever is current, unless you pin them in the file yourself.

docs.title: environment.yml
docs.text:
An environment.yml file is the specification of a conda environment. It names the environment, lists the channels in order, and lists the packages, with pins where you want them. It is the file that goes into the repository, because it is small, readable, and enough to rebuild.

name: dgx
channels:
  - conda-forge
dependencies:
  - python=3.12
  - tailscale
  - tailscaled

docs.title: requirements.txt and Conda Versus pip
docs.text:
A requirements.txt file is pip's equivalent: a list of Python packages, one per line, with optional version pins. It is created by pip freeze and installed with pip install -r requirements.txt.

pip installs Python packages from the Python Package Index. Conda versus pip is a question of scope: pip handles only Python packages, while conda handles Python, non-Python libraries, and tools. The rule that avoids most trouble is to install with conda first, and use pip only for what conda does not have, and to do the pip installs last. Going back and forth lets pip replace a package conda installed, and conda's record is then wrong about what is present.

conda pip Installs Python itself Yes No Installs non-Python programs Yes, such as Tailscale No Package source Channels such as conda-forge The Python Package Index Records its work in conda-meta and environment.yml requirements.txt Use it for The base of the environment Packages conda lacks, installed last

docs.title: Architecture-Specific Wheels
docs.text:
A wheel is the file format for a built Python package, and an architecture-specific wheel is one built for a particular processor architecture. Its filename says which. Reading a filename, simplified here for clarity, shows what an installer checks:

numpy-1.26.4-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_17_aarch64.whl
        |       |      |        |             |
        |       |      |        |             processor architecture
        |       |      |        operating system and library version
        |       |      application binary interface
        |       Python version (3.12)
        package version

On an aarch64 machine, pip accepts only wheels whose last tag is aarch64. If a package publishes only x86_64 wheels, pip falls back to compiling it from source, which is slow, needs a compiler, and can fail. Chapter 5 introduced the two architectures, and this is where the difference becomes a failed install.

docs.title: PyTorch and CUDA-Enabled PyTorch
docs.text:
PyTorch is a widely used library for numeric computing and neural networks. This course uses it for one narrow purpose: to confirm that the GPU is visible to Python's machine-learning stack. CUDA-enabled PyTorch is the build of PyTorch compiled to use an NVIDIA GPU. The default install on some platforms is a CPU-only build, and it imports without any error, so a missing GPU shows up only when you ask.

Two lines establish which build you have. The first prints the CUDA version the build was compiled for, which is None for a CPU-only build. The second asks whether a GPU is usable right now.

import torch
print(torch.version.cuda)          # for example '13.0'; None means a CPU-only build
print(torch.cuda.is_available())   # True only if the driver and a GPU are usable

Test the GPU, Not the Import

import torch succeeds on a CPU-only build, so it proves nothing about the GPU. Make torch.cuda.is_available() part of the rebuild check. A model that silently runs on the CPU looks like a performance problem when it is an install problem.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Reproducibility is the property that someone else, or you on another day, can repeat a procedure and get the same result. For an environment it means the same specification produces the same software. It is what makes a benchmark checkable: a result that cannot be reproduced cannot be disputed either, because nobody can tell what was measured.

An environment specification covers the interpreter version, the package versions, and the channel they came from. It does not cover the operating system, the GPU driver, the CUDA libraries installed by the system, or the model weights. Those are separate pieces of the stack, and Chapter 4's version pinning and Chapter 12's checksum verification handle them.

docs.title: Install Script
docs.text:
An install script is a program that takes a machine from its starting state to a working tool set with no manual steps. It is the written-down version of your setup, and it is the strongest form of reproducibility because it runs.

A good one pins what it installs and verifies what it downloads. The excerpt below is from this project's model-server installer. V pins the release version, and F is the archive for the machine's architecture. The script downloads a published list of checksums and the archive, computes the archive's SHA-256 value, and stops if the two differ.

V=v0.40.2
F=ollama-linux-arm64.tar.zst
expected=$(grep "$F\$" sha256sum.txt | awk '{print $1}')
actual=$(sha256sum "$F" | awk '{print $1}')
[ "$expected" = "$actual" ] || { echo "sha256 MISMATCH"; exit 1; }

Three habits make a script worth trusting: it stops at the first error, it pins every version it installs, and it prints the versions it ended up with, so a log shows what a run used.

docs.title: Environment Rebuild
docs.text:
An environment rebuild is creating an environment again from its specification and confirming that it matches the original. A specification you have never rebuilt from is an unverified claim. The rebuild is the test.

The sequence below creates a throwaway environment from the file, checks that it works, and compares its package list with the original's. Each command is explained before it runs: conda env create -f builds from the file, -n dgx-test gives it a different name so it does not overwrite the original, and conda list --export prints the packages in a comparable form.

conda env create -n dgx-test -f environment.yml
conda run -n dgx-test tailscale version
diff <(conda list -n dgx --export) <(conda list -n dgx-test --export)
conda env remove -n dgx-test

An empty diff means the rebuild matches. A few differing lines are the packages that were not pinned and resolved to a newer release, and they are exactly what to pin next.

docs.title: Diagram: Environment Reproducibility Auditor
docs.text:
Run Environment Reproducibility Auditor Fullscreen

Environment Reproducibility Auditor

Type: microsim sim-id: environment-reproducibility-auditor Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of 6 environment specifications rebuilds the same software on a second machine, and name the reason, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: environment.yml, Python version pinning, package channel, architecture-specific wheels, conda export forms, CUDA-enabled PyTorch, environment rebuild (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 specifications the learner commits a verdict ("Reproducible" or "Not reproducible") and, for a "Not reproducible" verdict, one reason from the five listed in Content, before the sim reveals the answer. An item is correct when the verdict equals the Correct verdict column and, if the verdict is "Not reproducible", the reason equals the Correct reason column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the specifications is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A file that lists packages is automatically reproducible. (2) A full export from one machine rebuilds on any machine. (3) A package that imports without error has the capabilities you need. (4) An unnamed channel is harmless.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level judging needs criteria applied to a case, so each specification fails, if it fails, for exactly one reason named in the chapter. A mix of failing and passing items prevents the learner from assuming every file is flawed.

Content:

The five reasons the learner can choose from: "Unpinned versions", "Platform-specific builds", "No channel named", "May install a CPU-only build", and "None, it is reproducible" (the last is valid only with the verdict "Reproducible").

# Specification shown to the learner Correct verdict Correct reason Why (shown as feedback) 1 Channels: conda-forge. Packages: python, numpy, psutil, no versions. Not reproducible Unpinned versions A rebuild installs whatever is newest on that day, which can differ from the original. 2 Channels: conda-forge. Packages: python=3.12.4, numpy=1.26.4, psutil=5.9.8. Reproducible None, it is reproducible The channel is named and every package is pinned. 3 A full conda env export taken on a Mac with an Arm laptop chip, used to rebuild on a Linux aarch64 machine. Not reproducible Platform-specific builds The export lists builds that exist only for the Mac's platform, so they cannot be found on Linux. 4 pip install torch run on an aarch64 machine with no index named and no CUDA check afterward. Not reproducible May install a CPU-only build The default build can lack CUDA, and the import succeeds anyway. 5 Packages: python=3.12, psutil=5.9.8, and no channel listed. Not reproducible No channel named The rebuild uses whatever channels the second machine has configured, so it may resolve differently. 6 An environment.yml exported with --from-history, naming conda-forge and pinned versions, plus an install script that creates the environment and then runs python -c "import psutil". Reproducible None, it is reproducible It is pinned, names its channel, is portable, and verifies itself.

Provenance: The specifications are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The package versions are illustrative.

Rules: Specifications are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6. For each, the learner chooses a verdict, and a reason when the verdict is "Not reproducible". A verdict of "Reproducible" is correct only with the reason "None, it is reproducible". Choices are final once confirmed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads specification 1.
  2. The learner chooses "Reproducible" or "Not reproducible", and if the latter, one of the four failure reasons, then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct verdict and reason with the Why text, and marks the item correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for specifications 2 to 6. After specification 6 the sim shows the score and, for each miss, the misconception behind it.

Feedback: Six items, fixed order, one confirmed pair of choices each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct verdict, the correct reason, and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: Specification 1 is shown with no verdict chosen, and the question on screen is "Would a second machine rebuild exactly this environment?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that an unpinned package, a platform-specific export, an unnamed channel, and a possibly CPU-only build each defeat a rebuild, and that --from-history is the portable export.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
An environment is a directory holding an interpreter and packages, and isolating one per purpose keeps a change in one place from breaking another. Conda creates, activates, exports, and removes environments, and installs non-Python software that pip cannot. A specification is reproducible only when it names its channel, pins the interpreter and its packages, and is exported in a form that crosses platforms. On a DGX the two extra traps are wheels built for the wrong architecture and a PyTorch build with no CUDA, and both are caught by checking, not by importing. A rebuild from the specification is the test, and an install script is the specification that runs.

You Can Rebuild Your Tools on Demand

You can now write an environment.yml that names its channel and pins its versions, rebuild it into a throwaway environment, and diff the result against the original. Chapter 9 uses the dgx environment to install Tailscale and take a first inventory.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
docs.text: Test your understanding of isolated environments, conda commands, portable specifications, and rebuild checks with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a Python environment?
docs.text:
1. A server that hosts packages for conda to download
  2. A file that lists packages with optional version pins
  3. A system-wide Python shared by every project on a machine
  4. A self-contained directory with an interpreter and its packages
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A Python environment is a self-contained directory that holds a Python interpreter and the packages installed for it, together with a script that points your shell at them. Activating it puts its interpreter and packages first on your path, so python runs that interpreter and import finds those packages and no others. Because it is only a directory, you never repair a broken one: you delete it and rebuild it from the specification.

Concept Tested: Python Environment

See: Python Environment

docs.title: 2. What is Miniforge?
docs.text:
1. A commercial Python distribution that requires a paid license
  2. A pip replacement that installs only Python packages
  3. A minimal conda installer that defaults to the conda-forge channel
  4. A build tool that compiles wheels for aarch64 machines
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Miniforge is a minimal installer for conda that is set up to use the community-maintained conda-forge channel by default, and it is the installer this course uses. The alternative, a distribution from a commercial vendor, brings a default channel whose licensing terms can require a paid license for larger organizations. A book whose readers work in unknown organizations should not depend on that, which is why Miniforge was chosen.

Concept Tested: Miniforge

See: Conda and Miniforge

docs.title: 3. Two documentation tools each pin a different version of the same package. Why does giving each tool its own environment fix the conflict?
docs.text:
1. Each environment downloads packages from a different channel
  2. Conda merges the two versions into one compatible build
  3. pip is allowed to override conda inside a shared environment
  4. Neither tool then has to agree with the other on one version
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Environment isolation keeps each environment separate so that a change in one cannot affect another. A package can exist in only one version at a time in one place, so two tools that pin different versions cannot both be satisfied in a shared environment: installing the second breaks the first. The fix was not a cleverer install. With one environment per tool, neither has to agree with the other.

Concept Tested: Environment Isolation

See: Environment Isolation

docs.title: 4. Why does the book advise installing with conda first and doing any pip installs last?
docs.text:
1. pip cannot run until conda has been removed from the path
  2. pip can replace a conda package, leaving conda's record wrong
  3. conda refuses to activate an environment that pip has touched
  4. pip installs Python itself, which must follow the packages
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Conda versus pip is a question of scope: pip handles only Python packages, while conda handles Python itself, non-Python libraries, and tools. The rule is to install with conda first, use pip only for what conda does not have, and do the pip installs last. Going back and forth lets pip replace a package that conda installed, and conda's record is then wrong about what is present in the environment.

Concept Tested: Conda Versus pip

See: requirements.txt and Conda Versus pip

docs.title: 5. Why is conda env export --from-history portable across architectures when a full export is not?
docs.text:
1. It records exact builds, which are identical on every platform
  2. It records only requested packages, so conda resolves the rest
  3. It converts each build string to the target architecture
  4. It leaves out the channel, so any server can supply packages
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The two export forms record different things. A full conda env export lists every package with its exact build, and builds are specific to one platform, so rebuilding on another platform fails with packages that cannot be found. Exporting with --from-history records only the packages you asked for, and conda resolves the rest for the new platform. The price is that each dependency resolves to whatever is current unless you pin it yourself.
