Concept Tested: Conda List and Export

See: Conda List and Export

docs.title: 6. You need a new environment named probe, built from conda-forge, with Python pinned to 3.12 and psutil installed. Which command does this?
docs.text:
1. conda activate probe -c conda-forge python=3.12 psutil
  2. conda env remove -n probe -c conda-forge python=3.12
  3. conda create -c probe -n conda-forge python psutil=3.12
  4. conda create -n probe -c conda-forge python=3.12 psutil
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The conda create command makes a new environment. -n probe names it, -c conda-forge names the channel to search, and everything after is the packages to install, with a version after an equals sign as a pin. Writing python=3.12 fixes the major and minor version, and psutil is left unpinned. conda activate only switches the shell into an existing environment, and conda env remove deletes one.

Concept Tested: Conda Create Command

See: The Create, Activate, and Remove Commands

docs.title: 7. A script running in a non-interactive shell fails at the line conda activate dgx with a "command not found" error. What should the script do instead?
docs.text:
1. Use conda run -n dgx <command> or the full executable path
  2. Put sudo in front of the conda activate dgx line
  3. Reinstall Miniforge so that the activate function exists
  4. Run conda env remove -n dgx and create the environment again
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The conda activate function is defined by your shell's startup files, so a script or an agent running in a non-interactive shell may fail with a permission or "command not found" error. The fix is to call the environment's executables by their full path, or to use conda run -n dgx <command>. Nothing is wrong with the environment or the installer, so removing or reinstalling either one does not address the cause.

Concept Tested: Conda Activate Command

See: The Create, Activate, and Remove Commands

docs.title: 8. After you install PyTorch on the DGX, import torch succeeds. How do you confirm that this build can use the GPU?
docs.text:
1. Check that torch.cuda.is_available() returns True
  2. Check that import torch finishes without any error
  3. Check that conda list shows a torch package entry
  4. Check that uname -m prints aarch64 on the machine
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. CUDA-enabled PyTorch is the build compiled to use an NVIDIA GPU. The default install on some platforms is a CPU-only build, and it imports without any error, so a successful import torch proves nothing about the GPU. torch.cuda.is_available() returns True only if the driver and a GPU are usable, and torch.version.cuda is None for a CPU-only build. A model that silently runs on the CPU looks like a performance problem when it is an install problem.

Concept Tested: CUDA-Enabled PyTorch

See: PyTorch and CUDA-Enabled PyTorch

docs.title: 9. On an aarch64 DGX, a pip install of one package runs for a long time, asks for a compiler, and then fails. What is the most likely cause?
docs.text:
1. The environment's Python version was pinned to 3.12
  2. The package was requested from the conda-forge channel
  3. The package has no aarch64 wheel, so pip built from source
  4. The NVIDIA driver is older than the package's CUDA build requires
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A wheel is a built Python package, and an architecture-specific wheel is built for one processor architecture, named in its filename. On an aarch64 machine pip accepts only wheels whose last tag is aarch64. If a package publishes only x86_64 wheels, pip falls back to compiling it from source, which is slow, needs a compiler, and can fail. That pattern points to a missing wheel, not to the Python pin or the GPU driver.

Concept Tested: Architecture-Specific Wheels

See: Architecture-Specific Wheels

docs.title: 10. After you rebuild environment.yml into a throwaway environment, the diff of the two package lists shows three differing lines. What do those lines indicate?
docs.text:
1. The rebuild ran on a different processor architecture
  2. The original environment is corrupted and must be removed at once
  3. Unpinned packages resolved to newer releases; pin them next
  4. The specification named a package channel that no longer exists
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An environment rebuild creates the environment again from its specification and compares it with the original. A specification you have never rebuilt from is an unverified claim, and the rebuild is the test. An empty diff means the rebuild matches. A few differing lines are the packages that were not pinned and resolved to a newer release, and they are exactly what to pin next. They do not mean the original environment is damaged.

Concept Tested: Environment Rebuild

See: Environment Rebuild

docs.title: References: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
docs.text:
1. Conda (package manager) - Wikipedia - Describes conda as a cross-platform package and environment manager, its channels, and its relation to Anaconda, Miniconda, and Miniforge. It frames the chapter's choice of conda and Miniforge for isolated environments.

  2. Pip (package manager) - Wikipedia - Explains pip as Python's package installer that fetches packages from the Python Package Index, with its history and command-line interface. It supports the chapter's conda-versus-pip rule and its requirements.txt discussion.

  3. Dependency hell - Wikipedia - Describes how packages needing incompatible versions of a shared library break one another, and lists solutions. It is the problem that the chapter's environment isolation and one-environment-per-tool rule solve.

  4. Effective Python: 125 Specific Ways to Write Better Python (3rd Edition) - Brett Slatkin - Addison-Wesley - Item 117 makes a self-contained case for virtual environments that give isolated and reproducible dependencies, in the book's short numbered-item format. It is a concise rationale for the chapter's disposable, rebuildable environments.

  5. Deep Learning with PyTorch - Eli Stevens, Luca Antiga, and Thomas Viehmann - Manning Publications - A widely used PyTorch introduction that starts from the tensor and includes a section on moving tensors to the GPU. It clarifies the CPU-versus-GPU distinction behind the chapter's CUDA-enabled PyTorch check.

  6. Managing environments - conda documentation - Official guide to creating, activating, cloning, exporting, and removing environments, including environment.yml files and the --from-history flag. It is the reference for every conda command in the chapter.

  7. Miniforge - conda-forge - README for the minimal conda installer that makes conda-forge its default and only channel, including a Linux aarch64 build. It documents the installer the chapter uses on the Arm-based DGX.

  8. A brief introduction to conda-forge - conda-forge - Explains the community channel, how to add it with strict channel priority, and which platforms it builds for. It supports the chapter's rule to name the channel explicitly in every specification.

  9. Get Started Locally - PyTorch - Official installer selector that offers CUDA, ROCm, or CPU builds with matching pip commands, and shows how to check a GPU with torch.cuda.is_available(). It is the source for the chapter's CUDA-enabled PyTorch check.

  10. Platform compatibility tags - Python Packaging User Guide - Specifies the Python, ABI, and platform tag triple, including manylinux tags, that installers use to choose a compatible wheel. It explains the filename anatomy behind the chapter's architecture-specific wheels.

docs.title: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
Summary
docs.text: This chapter puts the mesh VPN concepts to work. Students install Tailscale in a dedicated environment, authenticate the DGX, configure names and access controls, and test connectivity, then run read-only inventory commands over SSH. They finish with a verified, encrypted path to the machine and a first look at what it contains.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 18 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Linux Inventory Commands 7 Standard-Library-Only Python 2 Read-Only Inventory 5 Piping Scripts Over SSH 1 Tailscale Installation 14 MagicDNS 3 Access Control List 3 Tailscale Ping 2 Tailnet Invitation 1 Node Sharing 1 Tailscale Daemon 13 Tailscale SSH 1 Tailscale Authentication 9 Tailscale Up Command 3 Tailscale Auth Key 7 Tailscale Status Command 2 Device Key Expiry 1 Connectivity Test 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 6: Cost, Price, and Quality
  • Chapter 7: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
  • Chapter 8: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda

From Concept to a Working Connection

Chapter 7 explained the path, and now you build it, one step at a time with a test after each. By the end you will have a verified, encrypted route to the DGX and a first look at what is inside it, without having changed anything on the machine. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
This is the first hands-on chapter. It follows the order the evaluation itself used, and each step ends with a test, so that a failure appears at the step that caused it instead of three layers later. A step that "seems to work" without a test is the most common source of confusion later in a setup.

The chapter has two halves. The first half installs Tailscale in the dgx conda environment from Chapter 8, signs in, and proves the connection with three increasingly strong tests. The second half uses that connection to take a read-only inventory, which answers the hardware questions of Chapter 5 for the real machine without installing or changing anything on it.

Placeholders, not real values

This site is public, so every address, hostname, and login in this chapter is a placeholder: 100.x.y.z, <dgx-host>, <user>, and <tailnet-name>. Substitute the values your administrator gives you, and never copy your real ones into a file you plan to publish.

docs.title: Tailscale Installation
docs.text:
Tailscale installation here means installing the open-source command-line client and its daemon into a dedicated conda environment, so that the tooling for reaching the DGX is isolated and removable. The alternative is the graphical application for your operating system, which is simpler to run and sits outside the environment. This course uses the environment because Chapter 8's discipline of one environment per tool applies to the tool that every other step depends on.

The two conda-forge packages are named tailscale, the client, and tailscaled, the daemon. The client does nothing without the daemon, so install both, at the same version.

conda create -n dgx -c conda-forge tailscale tailscaled
conda activate dgx

The test is that both commands print the same version number.

tailscale version
tailscaled --version

docs.title: Tailscale Daemon
docs.text:
The Tailscale daemon, tailscaled, is the background process that creates the network interface, holds the encryption keys, and maintains the connections. The client program you type commands into only talks to the daemon.

Creating a network interface requires administrator rights on the laptop, so the daemon is started with sudo. A detail catches people here: sudo discards the conda PATH, so give it the full path to the binary. Run it in its own terminal tab and leave it running.

sudo "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/tailscaled"

A Daemon That Is Not Running Looks Like a Broken Network

If tailscale status says it cannot connect to the daemon, the cause is almost always that tailscaled is not running, for example because it does not survive a reboot or a closed tab. Restart it in its own tab before suspecting the DGX, the router, or your account.

docs.title: Tailscale Up Command
docs.text:
The tailscale up command brings the device onto the tailnet. Run in a second tab, with dgx activated, it asks the daemon to connect and sign in.

tailscale up

On the first run the command prints a sign-in address. It is the next concept.

docs.title: Tailscale Authentication
docs.text:
Tailscale authentication is proving who you are to the coordination service, so that your device is added to the right tailnet. The usual way is to open the sign-in address that tailscale up printed and log in with an identity account, in a browser. The device is then bound to that identity.

A mistake costs time and is easy to make. Signing in with a different account than the one the administrator invited creates or joins a different tailnet, and the DGX will not appear in your device list. If the listing shows only your own laptop, compare the account on the sign-in page with the one the invitation was sent to.

docs.title: Tailnet Invitation and Node Sharing
docs.text:
There are two ways to get a DGX that belongs to someone else onto your device list, and they are different arrangements.

A tailnet invitation adds you to the administrator's tailnet as a member. You then see every device the access rules allow, and you are subject to that tailnet's policy. This is how the evaluation was set up: the Administrator invited the Primary Author, and both units were already members.

Node sharing shares one specific device into your own tailnet, without making you a member of theirs. You see only the shared machine, and the owner keeps control of it. It suits a case where you have your own tailnet and need access to one machine for a limited time.

Tailnet invitation Node sharing You become A member of their tailnet A guest with access to one device You can see Whatever the access rules allow Only the shared device Whose policy applies Theirs Theirs, for that device Good for A team working on shared machines Giving one outsider temporary access

docs.title: Tailscale Auth Key
docs.text:
A Tailscale auth key is a pre-generated credential that lets a device join a tailnet without a person signing in through a browser. It exists for machines that nobody sits at, such as a server brought up by a script. Keys can be limited to one use, can expire, and can mark the device as temporary.

An auth key is equivalent to a password for joining the network. Treat it exactly that way: never put one in a repository, a chat, a screenshot, or a log, and prefer a key that expires soon and works once. The key is created by the tailnet's administrator, and an evaluator who is a guest of that tailnet usually does not need one.

docs.title: Device Key Expiry
docs.text:
Device key expiry is the limit on how long a device's credentials stay valid before it must sign in again. It is 180 days by default, and the tailnet's administrator can change it. A machine that is not used for months can have silently dropped off the network when its key expired, and the first sign is a device that shows as offline with no other explanation.

The fix is to sign in again from the device. For a machine you do not sit at, it is a reason to put a note on the calendar and a reason to tell the administrator who needs to know.

docs.title: MagicDNS
docs.text:
MagicDNS is Tailscale's feature that gives every device in a tailnet a name that resolves to its private address, so you type <dgx-host> and not 100.x.y.z. Names are stable even if the address changes, and a script written against the name keeps working.

A short name resolves from inside the tailnet, and the full name carries the tailnet's own name, in the form <dgx-host>.<tailnet-name>.ts.net. Both are identifying details, and in anything you publish, they are placeholders.

docs.title: Access Control List
docs.text:
An access control list, or ACL, is the tailnet's policy for who may reach what. It is a document kept by the tailnet's administrator, and it lists which users and devices may open connections to which machines and on which ports. A device that is in the tailnet but not permitted by the list simply cannot connect, and it shows no error beyond a timeout.

A minimal rule has three parts. Its action is accept. Its src lists who may connect, and its dst lists what they may reach, with a port after the colon.

{
  "acls": [
    { "action": "accept", "src": ["<tailnet-user>"], "dst": ["<dgx-host>:22"] }
  ]
}

That rule lets one user reach one machine on the SSH port and nothing else. A real policy file reveals which machines exist and which ports are open, so it is on the list of things that are never published.

docs.title: Tailscale SSH
docs.text:
Tailscale SSH is a feature in which Tailscale itself handles SSH authentication, using the tailnet identity in place of keys. It runs on the machine you are logging in to, and it needs to be turned on there with tailscale set --ssh. That change belongs to the administrator of the DGX.

This evaluation did not use it. The DGX accepted ordinary OpenSSH logins over the tailnet, so the key-based login of Chapter 7 was enough, and nothing had to change on the machine. Tailscale SSH is worth knowing about because it removes the private key as an asset to protect.

docs.title: Tailscale Status Command
docs.text:
The tailscale status command lists every device in your tailnet that you can see, with its private address, name, owner, operating system, and connection state. It is the first test after sign-in, and its output is the evidence that the DGX is reachable at all.

A sanitized listing looks like this. Each row has the address, the device name, the owner, the operating system, and the state.

100.x.y.z   <laptop-name>   <you>@    macOS   -
100.x.y.z   <dgx-host-a>    <admin>@  linux   active; direct 198.51.100.7:41641
100.x.y.z   <dgx-host-b>    <admin>@  linux   idle

The last column is the one to learn to read. A dash marks this device. active; direct means the two devices are exchanging data over a direct path, and an address after it shows where. active; relay means the traffic is going through a relay. idle means connected with nothing in flight, and offline with a time means the device has not been reachable.

docs.title: Tailscale Ping and the Connectivity Test
docs.text:
Tailscale ping tests the connection at the tailnet layer, below SSH. It sends a probe to the device and reports the path it used and the time it took. It is stronger than status, because status says a device is listed and ping shows that packets actually reach it.

pong from <dgx-host> (100.x.y.z) via DERP(<region>) in 38ms
pong from <dgx-host> (100.x.y.z) via 198.51.100.7:41641 in 12ms

The pair above shows a common sequence. The first reply went through a relay. A moment later the devices found a direct path and the following replies took it, which is NAT traversal from Chapter 7 happening in front of you.

A connectivity test is the complete check, and it has three steps in order, each one proving something the previous did not.

Step Command What it proves 1 tailscale status The device is listed and its state is not offline 2 tailscale ping <dgx-host> Packets reach the device, and which path they take 3 ssh -o BatchMode=yes <user>@<dgx-host> hostname The login works with a key, with no prompt

A failure at a step tells you which layer to look at. Step 1 failing points to your daemon or your account, step 2 to the network path or the access rules, and step 3 to the SSH server or your key.

docs.title: Diagram: Tailscale Status Reader
docs.text:
Run Tailscale Status Reader Fullscreen

Tailscale Status Reader

Type: microsim sim-id: tailscale-status-reader Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret 6 sanitized lines of Tailscale output by choosing the meaning of each, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: tailscale status command, tailscale ping, device key expiry, DERP relay, peer-to-peer connection (all defined in the sections above this block and in Chapter 7).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 lines the learner commits one meaning from the six listed in Content before the sim reveals the answer. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct meaning column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the line is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) idle means the device is down. (2) A relay connection is a failure. (3) A listed device is reachable. (4) A dash in the last column means something is wrong.

Instructional Rationale: Interpreting needs the learner to turn a terse string into a statement about the system, so each line is a realistic fragment with exactly one correct reading. Committing before the reveal separates reading from guessing.

Content:

The six meanings the learner chooses from: "This device", "Connected directly", "Connected through a relay", "Connected but idle", "Offline, not reachable", and "This device has not signed in".

# Line shown to the learner Correct meaning Why (shown as feedback) 1 100.x.y.z <laptop-name> <you>@ macOS - This device A dash in the state column marks the device running the command. 2 100.x.y.z <dgx-host> <admin>@ linux active; direct 198.51.100.7:41641 Connected directly direct followed by an address means a peer-to-peer path is in use. 3 100.x.y.z <dgx-host> <admin>@ linux active; relay "<region>" Connected through a relay relay means the encrypted traffic goes through a relay server. 4 100.x.y.z <dgx-host> <admin>@ linux idle Connected but idle idle means connected with no traffic in flight at the moment. 5 100.x.y.z <dgx-host> <admin>@ linux offline, last seen 13h ago Offline, not reachable offline with a time means the device has not been reachable for that long. 6 Logged out. This device has not signed in The daemon is running but this device has no identity on the tailnet.

Provenance: The lines are synthetic, modeled on the output format of the command, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". Addresses use placeholders and a documentation address range.

Rules: Lines are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6. Each line allows one final choice, and exactly one of the six meanings is correct for each line.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads line 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the six meanings and confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct meaning and the Why text, and marks the line correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for lines 2 to 6. After line 6 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Six lines, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct meaning and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: Line 1 is shown with no meaning chosen, and the question on screen is "What is this line telling you?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a dash marks this device, that active; direct means a peer-to-peer path, that relay means traffic goes through a relay server, that idle means no traffic at the moment, and that offline with a time means the device was not reachable for that long.

docs.title: Read-Only Inventory
docs.text: A read-only inventory is a survey of a machine's hardware and software made with commands that change nothing and need no administrator rights. It is the first thing to do on any machine you do not know, and it is the right first thing to do on one that belongs to someone else, because it answers the hardware questions of Chapter 5 without asking permission to install anything.

docs.title: Linux Inventory Commands
docs.text:
A small set of standard commands covers the questions. Each prints a few lines and writes nothing.

Question Command What to read Which operating system? grep PRETTY_NAME /etc/os-release Name and release Which kernel and architecture? uname -srm aarch64 or x86_64 Which processor? lscpu Core count, model name How much memory? free -h Total and available How much disk? df -h / Size and free space Which GPU and driver? nvidia-smi Name, driver, CUDA version Are containers available? docker --version Present or not Which groups am I in? id -nG Whether docker is listed

Run the Inventory Before You Install Anything

A five-minute read-only look tells you whether a plan is possible: the architecture, the free space, whether Docker answers. Finding out after a two-hour download that the disk is full is a much worse way to learn it.

docs.title: Piping Scripts Over SSH
docs.text:
Piping a script over SSH runs a local file on a remote machine without copying it there first. The shell on the DGX reads the script from its standard input, so nothing is written to the machine's disk. It is the right method for an inventory, because it leaves no trace and needs no permission to write anywhere.

The command below sends the local file inventory.sh to the remote bash, where -s tells it to read the commands from standard input, and saves the output on your own machine.

ssh <user>@<dgx-host> 'bash -s' < src/dgx-setup/inventory.sh > inventory.txt

docs.title: Standard-Library-Only Python
docs.text:
Standard-library-only Python is a script that imports only modules that ship with Python itself. It runs on a fresh machine with no pip install, no environment, and no administrator rights. Every script this project runs on the DGX is written this way, for exactly that reason: the machine needs nothing added before the first measurement.

The cost is real and accepted. Without the psutil package, memory and CPU figures are read from files such as /proc/meminfo, and GPU readings are parsed from the text of nvidia-smi. Chapter 10 builds probes that way and shows where the optional packages are worth adding.

Some system files contain identifiers

On DGX OS, /etc/dgx-release includes the unit's serial number. Read it with grep -v SERIAL /etc/dgx-release, and read any captured inventory before you save or share it. An inventory is a description of a specific machine, and Chapter 23 builds the review that makes it safe to publish.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
You installed the Tailscale client and daemon in a dedicated environment, brought the device onto the tailnet with tailscale up, and signed in with the account the administrator invited. Names come from MagicDNS, and an access control list decides who may reach what. The connectivity test proves the path in three steps: status lists the device, ping shows packets arriving and by which path, and a BatchMode login proves the key works. With that, a read-only inventory answers the hardware questions of Chapter 5, using standard commands and a standard-library-only script piped over SSH.

You Have a Verified Path and a First Look Inside

You can now bring a machine onto a tailnet, prove the connection at three layers, and take an inventory that changes nothing. Chapter 10 turns the inventory into repeatable Python probes.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
docs.text: Test your understanding of installing Tailscale, signing in, proving the connection, and taking a read-only inventory with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which two conda-forge packages does this course's Tailscale installation need?
docs.text:
1. tailscale, the client, and tailscaled, the daemon
  2. tailscale, the client, and wireguard, the protocol
  3. tailscaled, the daemon, and openssh, the login server
  4. tailscale, the client, and magicdns, the name service
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Tailscale installation here means installing the open-source command-line client and its daemon into a dedicated conda environment, so the tooling for reaching the DGX is isolated and removable. The two conda-forge packages are tailscale, the client, and tailscaled, the daemon. The client does nothing without the daemon, so install both at the same version. The test is that tailscale version and tailscaled --version print the same number.

Concept Tested: Tailscale Installation

See: Tailscale Installation

docs.title: 2. What is a read-only inventory?
docs.text:
1. A backup of the machine's disk taken before any install
  2. A list of the packages in a conda environment, with builds
  3. A survey made with commands that change nothing on the machine
  4. A log of every command an administrator has run on the unit
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A read-only inventory is a survey of a machine's hardware and software made with commands that change nothing and need no administrator rights. It is the first thing to do on any machine you do not know, and the right first step on one that belongs to someone else, because it answers the hardware questions without asking permission to install anything. Commands such as uname -srm, free -h, and df -h / print a few lines and write nothing.

Concept Tested: Read-Only Inventory

See: Read-Only Inventory

docs.title: 3. What does MagicDNS provide?
docs.text:
1. A name for each tailnet device that resolves to its private address
  2. A public DNS record that lets anyone find the device online
  3. A pre-generated credential that joins a device with no browser sign-in
  4. A policy document listing who may reach which machine and port
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. MagicDNS gives every device in a tailnet a name that resolves to its private address, so you type a name and not an address. Names are stable even if the address changes, so a script written against the name keeps working. A short name resolves only from inside the tailnet, and names appear as placeholders in anything published. A pre-generated credential is an auth key, and a policy document is an access control list.

Concept Tested: MagicDNS

See: MagicDNS

docs.title: 4. Why must a Tailscale auth key be handled like a password?
docs.text:
1. It encrypts every packet exchanged inside the tailnet
  2. It lets a device join the tailnet with no one signing in
  3. It grants administrator rights on every machine in the tailnet
  4. It can never be limited to one use or given an expiry
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A Tailscale auth key is a pre-generated credential that lets a device join a tailnet without a person signing in through a browser. It exists for machines nobody sits at. Because it is equivalent to a password for joining the network, it must never go in a repository, a chat, a screenshot, or a log. Keys can be limited to one use and can expire, and a key that expires soon and works once is the one to prefer.

Concept Tested: Tailscale Auth Key

See: Tailscale Auth Key

docs.title: 5. Why is tailscale ping a stronger test than tailscale status?
docs.text:
1. Ping proves that key-based SSH login works without a prompt
  2. Ping restarts the daemon whenever a device shows as offline
  3. Ping shows packets reach the device; status only lists it
  4. Ping checks the SSH server; status checks the access rules
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. tailscale status lists the devices you can see with their address, owner, and connection state, so it shows that a device is listed. Tailscale ping tests the connection at the tailnet layer, below SSH: it sends a probe and reports the path used and the time taken, which shows that packets actually reach the device. Neither one proves the login works. That takes the third step, an SSH command run with BatchMode.

Concept Tested: Tailscale Ping

See: Tailscale Ping and the Connectivity Test

docs.title: 6. Why is piping a script over SSH the right method for an inventory?
docs.text:
1. It is read from standard input, so nothing is written to disk
  2. The script runs with administrator rights on the remote machine
  3. The script is installed permanently, so later runs start faster
  4. The output is saved on the DGX, where the administrator can read it
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Piping a script over SSH runs a local file on a remote machine without copying it there first. The shell on the DGX reads the script from its standard input, so nothing is written to the machine's disk, and the output is saved on your own machine. That suits an inventory because it leaves no trace and needs no permission to write anywhere. It does not grant administrator rights.

Concept Tested: Piping Scripts Over SSH

See: Piping Scripts Over SSH

docs.title: 7. tailscale status reports that it cannot connect to the daemon. What should you do first?
docs.text:
1. Ask the administrator to restart the DGX unit
  2. Sign in again with the account that was invited
  3. Reboot the home router to clear its NAT table
  4. Check that tailscaled is running and restart it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Tailscale daemon is the background process that creates the network interface, holds the encryption keys, and maintains the connections; the client only talks to it. If tailscale status cannot connect to the daemon, the cause is almost always that tailscaled is not running, for example after a reboot or a closed tab. Restart it in its own tab, with sudo and the full path to the binary, before suspecting the DGX, the router, or your account.

Concept Tested: Tailscale Daemon

See: Tailscale Daemon

docs.title: 8. After you run tailscale up and sign in, tailscale status lists only your own laptop. What should you check?
docs.text:
1. Whether the DGX's device key expired 180 days ago
  2. Whether you signed in with the account that was invited
  3. Whether tailscaled was started with the full binary path
  4. Whether your SSH public key was installed with ssh-copy-id
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Tailscale authentication proves who you are to the coordination service so that your device is added to the right tailnet. Signing in with a different account than the one the administrator invited creates or joins a different tailnet, and the DGX will not appear in your device list. If the listing shows only your own laptop, compare the account on the sign-in page with the one the invitation was sent to. An expired key would show a listed device as offline.

Concept Tested: Tailscale Authentication

See: Tailscale Authentication

docs.title: 9. Before a large model download, you want to know how much disk space is free and whether your account is in the docker group. Which pair of commands answers both?
docs.text:
1. free -h and docker --version
  2. lscpu and uname -srm
  3. df -h / and id -nG
  4. nvidia-smi and free -h
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The Linux inventory commands each answer one question and write nothing. df -h / reports the disk's size and free space, and id -nG lists your groups, which shows whether docker is among them. free -h reports memory, not disk, and docker --version only shows whether Docker is present. Running these before a long download is how you learn in five minutes whether a plan is possible.

Concept Tested: Linux Inventory Commands

See: Linux Inventory Commands

docs.title: 10. In the three-step connectivity test, tailscale status lists the DGX and tailscale ping gets replies, but the BatchMode SSH command prints Permission denied. Which layer is at fault?
docs.text:
1. Your Tailscale daemon or your account
  2. The network path between the two routers
  3. The tailnet's access control list
  4. The SSH server or your key
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The connectivity test has three steps, each proving something the previous did not, so a failure tells you which layer to inspect. Status passing shows the device is listed and not offline, which clears your daemon and account. Ping passing shows packets reach the device, which clears the network path and the access rules. A failure at the third step, the BatchMode login, therefore points to the SSH server or your key.

Concept Tested: Connectivity Test

See: Tailscale Ping and the Connectivity Test

docs.title: References: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
docs.text:
1. Tailscale - Wikipedia - Covers the company and its open-source WireGuard-based mesh VPN, including NAT traversal, DERP relay fallback, and addresses from the RFC 6598 carrier-grade NAT space. It gives background for the chapter's installation and connectivity steps.

  2. Access-control list - Wikipedia - Defines an ACL as a list of permissions attached to a resource that says which subjects may perform which operations, and compares ACLs with role-based access control. It underlies the chapter's tailnet access rules.

  3. Domain Name System - Wikipedia - Explains the hierarchical naming system that maps names to IP addresses, with sections on structure, operation, and resource records. It provides the background for MagicDNS names that resolve only inside the tailnet.

  4. The Unix Programming Environment (1st Edition, 1984) - Brian W. Kernighan and Rob Pike - Prentice Hall - Argues that a system's power comes from the relationships among small programs, which filters and pipes connect. It is the classic grounding for the chapter's habit of piping a local script through SSH to a remote shell.

  5. Zero Trust Networks: Building Secure Systems in Untrusted Networks (2nd Edition) - Razi Rais, Christina Morillo, Evan Gilman, and Doug Barth - O'Reilly Media - Explains networks that grant access through authentication, authorization, and encryption on every connection instead of network location. It is the model behind a tailnet's identity-based access rules.

  6. Tailscale CLI - Tailscale - Reference for the tailscale command, including up, status, and ping, with status described as the state of your connections to other devices. It is the reference for the commands in the chapter's connectivity test.

  7. MagicDNS - Tailscale - Explains how each device gets a DNS name, a short name through search domains, and a fully qualified name ending in the tailnet's ts.net domain. It documents the naming behavior the chapter relies on.

  8. Manage permissions using ACLs - Tailscale - Describes the tailnet policy file and directional accept rules built from action, src, and dst, where devices cannot communicate unless a rule allows it. It matches the chapter's minimal access rule example.

  9. Auth keys - Tailscale - Explains pre-authentication keys for joining devices without a browser sign-in, with one-off, reusable, ephemeral, and pre-approved options, expiry, and storage guidance. It supports the chapter's warning to treat an auth key like a password.

  10. lscpu(1) - Arch Linux manual pages - Manual page for the util-linux tool that reports CPU architecture, counts, sockets, and cache sizes, with JSON output for parsing. It documents one of the read-only inventory commands in the chapter's table.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter turns hardware questions into measurements. Students write Python probes for CPU, RAM, storage, GPU, driver, CUDA, temperature, and power and combine them into a suite that emits a machine-readable report. They finish able to say what the machine really has and which setup branch applies.

docs.text:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 5: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
  • Chapter 8: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda

Let the Machine Answer for Itself

A specification sheet tells you what a machine was built to be, and a probe tells you what it is right now. By the end of this chapter you will have a script that reports your DGX's hardware as data, with nothing in it that you would be afraid to publish. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 5 listed the hardware questions, and Chapter 9 answered them by reading command output. That works once. This chapter makes the answers repeatable: a small Python program asks each question, records the answer in a file a machine can read, and can be run again after a driver update, a reboot, or a move to a different DGX.

The chapter builds the probes one at a time and then combines them. It ends with the habits that make a probe trustworthy, which are a test that the probe reads correctly, a report that leaves identifying details out by default, and a log that survives a machine that freezes.

docs.title: Hardware Probe
docs.text:
A hardware probe is a small, read-only measurement of one fact about a machine: how many cores it has, how much memory is free, which GPU is installed. The word "measurement" matters. A probe reads the value from the machine, so it reports what is true now, whatever the specification sheet or the last person's notes say.

A probe has three parts: the question, the source it reads, and the form of the answer. The table lists the probes this chapter builds, with the source of each.

Probe Question it answers Source it reads Answer CPU Which architecture, and how many cores? platform, os, lscpu Text and an integer RAM How much memory is total, and how much is available? /proc/meminfo Gibibytes Storage How big is the disk, and how much is free? shutil.disk_usage Gigabytes GPU Which GPU, driver, temperature, and power? nvidia-smi Fields per GPU CUDA Which CUDA version does the driver support? nvidia-smi header A version string Unified memory Does the GPU have its own memory? The GPU memory field True or false

docs.title: Probe Script
docs.text:
A probe script is a program that runs one or more probes and prints the results. A good one follows four rules, and each rule prevents a particular failure.

Rule Failure it prevents Read only, never write A probe that changes the machine it is measuring Standard library only A probe that cannot run on a fresh machine without an install Bounded run time A probe that hangs forever when a tool misbehaves Report unknown as null, never guess A report that looks complete and hides a failed measurement

The helper below is the base of every probe in this chapter. It runs a command and returns its text, or None if the command is missing, fails, or takes longer than timeout seconds. Every later probe goes through it, so a missing nvidia-smi on a machine without a GPU produces an empty answer instead of a crash.

import subprocess

def run(cmd, timeout=10):
    """Run a command and return its text output, or None if it fails."""
    try:
        out = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)
        return out.stdout if out.returncode == 0 else None
    except (OSError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired):
        return None

A Probe That Cannot Say 'I Don't Know' Will Lie

If a probe returns zero when it cannot read the value, a failed measurement looks like a machine with no memory. Return null for anything you could not read, and a reader can tell a missing measurement from a measured zero.

docs.title: The Processor, Memory, and Storage Probes
CPU Probe
docs.text:
The CPU probe reports the architecture and the core count. Both come from the standard library: platform.machine() returns aarch64 or x86_64, and os.cpu_count() returns the number of logical cores. The model name comes from the lscpu command, which on a machine with two kinds of core prints one Model name line for each.

import os, platform

def probe_cpu():
    models = []
    text = run(["lscpu"])
    if text:
        models = [l.split(":", 1)[1].strip() for l in text.splitlines()
                  if l.startswith("Model name")]
    return {"architecture": platform.machine(),
            "cores": os.cpu_count(),
            "model_names": models or None}

The answer drives the first branch of every setup: aarch64 selects aarch64 packages, as Chapter 5 and Chapter 8 explained.

docs.title: RAM Probe
docs.text:
The RAM probe reports the system memory. The kernel publishes it in the file /proc/meminfo, one Name: value kB line per figure, where kB is really kibibytes. Two names matter: MemTotal is all the memory the system can use, and MemAvailable is what a new program could use without pushing others out. Available is the number to watch, because a large total with little available is a machine about to struggle.

def probe_ram(meminfo_path="/proc/meminfo"):
    try:
        with open(meminfo_path) as f:
            kib = {}
            for line in f:
                key, rest = line.split(":", 1)
                kib[key] = int(rest.split()[0])
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        return {"total_gib": None, "available_gib": None}
    gib = lambda k: round(k / 1024 / 1024, 1)
    return {"total_gib": gib(kib["MemTotal"]),
            "available_gib": gib(kib["MemAvailable"])}

The path is a parameter on purpose. It lets a test hand the function a fake file, which the verification test below does.

docs.title: psutil
docs.text: psutil is a third-party Python package that reports CPU, memory, disk, and process information through one portable interface. It replaces the file parsing above with calls such as psutil.virtual_memory(). It is worth installing in an environment you control, and this course does not depend on it, because the probes must run on a machine with nothing installed.

docs.title: Storage Probe
docs.text:
The storage probe reports the size and free space of a filesystem. The standard library has shutil.disk_usage(path), which returns total, used, and free bytes for the disk that holds path. Disks are sold in decimal gigabytes, so the probe reports decimal values and says so.

import shutil

def probe_storage(path="/"):
    usage = shutil.disk_usage(path)
    gb = lambda b: round(b / 1e9, 1)
    return {"total_gb": gb(usage.total), "free_gb": gb(usage.free)}

docs.title: Disk Read Benchmark
docs.text: A disk read benchmark measures how fast the disk delivers data, which sets model load time as Chapter 5 described. It reads an existing large file for a fixed amount and divides the bytes by the seconds. The one trap is the operating system's page cache: a file read recently comes from memory, not the disk, and the number is far too high. Read a file that has not been touched since boot, such as a model file you have not loaded, and say so in the report.

docs.title: nvidia-smi and Its Output
docs.text:
nvidia-smi, the NVIDIA System Management Interface, is the command-line tool that reports a GPU's state. It is installed with the driver, so its presence on a machine is itself a probe: no nvidia-smi usually means no driver.

Run with no arguments it prints a table meant for people. Before reading the table you need names for its fields, and each is defined here. The driver version is the release of the NVIDIA driver. The CUDA version is the newest CUDA runtime the driver supports. Temperature is the GPU's reading in degrees Celsius. Power usage and cap is the power the board is drawing now and the limit it enforces, in watts. Memory usage is memory in use over total, in mebibytes. GPU utilization is the share of the last sampling period in which the GPU was running work.

The listing below is illustrative, for a machine with one discrete GPU, and it has had the serial number, unique identifier, and bus address removed.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| NVIDIA-SMI 580.xx.xx      Driver Version: 580.xx.xx    CUDA Version: 13.0 |
|-------------------------------+----------------------+----------------|
| GPU  Name                     | Temp  Perf  Pwr:Usage/Cap | Memory-Usage | GPU-Util |
|   0  NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3    | 41C   P0    70W / 700W    | 0MiB / 81559MiB | 0%   |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+

A person reads that table at a glance. A script should not parse it, because its layout changes between versions. Which leads to the query form in the next concept.

docs.title: GPU Probe
docs.text:
The GPU probe asks nvidia-smi for exactly the fields it wants, in a form that is easy to parse. --query-gpu names the fields, and --format=csv,noheader,nounits asks for one comma-separated line per GPU with no header and no unit suffixes. A field the GPU cannot report comes back as [N/A] or Not Supported, and the number helper turns anything that is not a number into None.

import re

def number(text):
    """Turn '45', '45.2', '[N/A]' or 'Not Supported' into a float or None."""
    try:
        return float(text)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return None

def probe_gpu():
    query = ("name,driver_version,temperature.gpu,power.draw,"
             "utilization.gpu,memory.total,memory.used")
    text = run(["nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=" + query,
                "--format=csv,noheader,nounits"])
    if not text:
        return {"gpus": [], "cuda_version": None, "unified_memory": None}
    gpus = []
    for line in text.strip().splitlines():
        f = [x.strip() for x in line.split(",")]
        gpus.append({"name": f[0], "driver": f[1],
                     "temperature_c": number(f[2]), "power_w": number(f[3]),
                     "utilization_pct": number(f[4]),
                     "memory_total_mib": number(f[5]),
                     "memory_used_mib": number(f[6])})
    header = run(["nvidia-smi"]) or ""
    m = re.search(r"CUDA Version:\s*([\d.]+)", header)
    unified = all(g["memory_total_mib"] is None for g in gpus)
    return {"gpus": gpus, "cuda_version": m.group(1) if m else None,
            "unified_memory": unified}

Five of the concepts in the chapter's list are read from this one function, and each is a field of the answer.

Concept Field in the answer Notes Driver version probe driver One string per GPU CUDA version probe cuda_version Parsed from the plain header, because the query form lacks it GPU temperature temperature_c Compare with the watchdog ceiling of Chapter 5 GPU power draw power_w The GPU's draw, not the whole machine's GPU memory total and free memory_total_mib, memory_used_mib None on unified memory

docs.title: GPU Memory Total and Free, and the Unified Memory Probe
docs.text:
GPU memory total and free is the memory the GPU reports for itself, and it is the figure that decides model fit on a machine with dedicated GPU memory. The unified memory probe is the check that those fields are missing. When every GPU's total comes back as None, the probe sets unified_memory to true, and the reader knows that the figure to use is the system RAM probe's available_gib.

This is a branch in the report, and the worked example is the whole reason the probe exists. On a discrete-GPU server, the usable model size is the GPU's free memory. On the unit in this evaluation, it is the system's available memory minus the headroom Chapter 11 introduces.

docs.title: NVML and the Python Bindings
docs.text:
NVML, the NVIDIA Management Library, is the C library that nvidia-smi itself is built on. It exposes the same readings through function calls. The NVML Python bindings, installed as the nvidia-ml-py package, let a Python program call it directly, which is faster than starting a new nvidia-smi process for every reading and gives access to fields the command does not print.

The cost is a dependency. This course uses the nvidia-smi query for the same reason it avoids psutil: it has to run on a fresh machine. In a long-running monitor, where a process starts every few seconds, the bindings are the better tool.

docs.title: PyTorch CUDA Check
docs.text:
The PyTorch CUDA check asks the machine-learning stack, not the driver, whether a GPU is usable. It is the probe that catches a CPU-only PyTorch build, which Chapter 8 warned about. It needs PyTorch installed, so it is the one probe here that belongs in a conda environment.

import torch
print(torch.cuda.is_available())            # True only if a GPU is usable
print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))        # for example 'NVIDIA GB10'

If nvidia-smi lists a GPU and this prints False, the driver is fine and the problem is the PyTorch build or its CUDA version.

docs.title: Probe Suite
docs.text:
A probe suite is a set of probes run together to produce one report. The suite below calls the four probes and returns their answers in one dictionary. Keeping the probes separate and the suite thin means a single failing probe cannot take the others with it, and each probe can be tested alone.

import json

def probe_suite():
    return {"cpu": probe_cpu(), "ram": probe_ram(),
            "storage": probe_storage(), "gpu": probe_gpu()}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(probe_suite(), indent=2))

Saved as probe_suite.py together with the functions above, the program runs on any machine with Python 3 and writes its report to standard output. It can be sent to a remote machine without being copied, with the pipe from Chapter 9.

ssh <user>@<dgx-host> 'python3 -' < probe_suite.py > report.json

docs.title: Machine-Readable Report and JSON Report
docs.text:
A machine-readable report is output in a form that a program can parse without guessing, in contrast to text written for a person. A JSON report is the form this course uses: nested key-value pairs in a plain text file, readable by every language and by people. The reason to produce one is that later steps consume it. A model-fit calculator reads available_gib, and a benchmark runner records the whole report beside each result so that a number is never separated from the machine that produced it.

The report below is illustrative. The values are plausible for a unified-memory machine and were not taken from a specific unit.

{
  "cpu":     { "architecture": "aarch64", "cores": 20,
               "model_names": ["Cortex-X925", "Cortex-A725"] },
  "ram":     { "total_gib": 119.0, "available_gib": 100.0 },
  "storage": { "total_gb": 1000.0, "free_gb": 780.0 },
  "gpu":     { "gpus": [ { "name": "NVIDIA GB10", "driver": "580.xx.xx",
                           "temperature_c": 44.0, "power_w": 4.0,
                           "utilization_pct": 0.0,
                           "memory_total_mib": null, "memory_used_mib": null } ],
               "cuda_version": "13.0", "unified_memory": true }
}

Two things in the report are worth noticing. The two null values in the GPU's memory fields are not an error: they are the unified-memory signature, and unified_memory is true because of them. And the report contains no hostname, no address, and no account name, which is deliberate.

docs.title: Hardware Variation Branching
docs.text:
Hardware variation branching is choosing the next setup step from the report instead of from assumption. The function below reads a report and returns the branches that apply. It is the Chapter 5 matcher as code, and the branches it names are the ones used throughout the later chapters.

def setup_branch(report):
    branches = []
    arch = report["cpu"]["architecture"]
    branches.append("aarch64 packages" if arch == "aarch64" else "x86_64 packages")
    gpu = report["gpu"]
    if not gpu["gpus"]:
        branches.append("no GPU: CPU only")
    elif gpu["unified_memory"]:
        branches.append("size models against system RAM")
    elif len(gpu["gpus"]) > 1:
        branches.append("plan to split across GPUs")
    else:
        branches.append("size models against one GPU's memory")
    return branches

docs.title: Redacted by Default
docs.text:
A report that is safe to publish is built from fields that are safe, not cleaned afterward. Redacted-by-default fields are the identifying details a probe never collects unless asked. The suite above reads no hostname, no username, no network address, no serial number, and no GPU unique identifier, so none can reach the file. A probe that never reads an identifier cannot leak it.

Collected by default Left out unless explicitly requested Architecture, core count, CPU model Hostname and domain name Total and available memory Account name and home directory Disk size and free space Network addresses and MAC addresses GPU name, driver, CUDA version Serial number, GPU unique identifier Temperature, power, utilization Tailnet name and access rules

Leaving a Field Out Beats Cleaning It Later

A report captured with every field and then edited by hand relies on you not missing one in four hundred lines. Decide the fields at the source: never read the identifier, and the review in Chapter 23 only has to confirm that you did not.

docs.title: Probe Verification Test
docs.text:
A probe verification test checks that a probe reads correctly by giving it input whose right answer is known. The RAM probe takes its file path as a parameter for exactly this reason: a test writes a small fake meminfo file with a total of 125,829,120 kB, which is 120 GiB, and an available figure of 104,857,600 kB, which is 100 GiB, and asserts what the probe returns.

import tempfile, os

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
path = os.path.join(d, "meminfo")
with open(path, "w") as f:
    f.write("MemTotal:       125829120 kB\n"
            "MemFree:             1000 kB\n"
            "MemAvailable:   104857600 kB\n")

assert probe_ram(path) == {"total_gib": 120.0, "available_gib": 100.0}
assert number("[N/A]") is None and number("45.2") == 45.2
print("probes read correctly")

The test also confirms the two behaviors that protect you from a silent wrong answer: a value that is not a number becomes None, and a missing file produces None fields, not an exception that stops the suite.

Test the Parser With Output That Lies

Feed each probe a deliberately awkward input: [N/A], an empty string, a missing file. The inputs a real machine produces on its worst day are the ones that break a parser, and you can write them down before that day.

docs.title: Vitals Logging
docs.text:
Vitals logging is recording a few measurements at a fixed interval while a long job runs, so that a machine that fails leaves its last readings behind. It uses the same probes in a loop. The loop below writes one JSON line every 30 seconds with the available memory, the GPU temperature, and the power draw. flush and fsync ask the operating system to put the line on the disk now, since a machine that freezes does not get to finish its buffers.

import json, os, time

with open("vitals.txt", "a") as out:
    while True:
        gpu = probe_gpu()["gpus"]
        row = {"t": int(time.time()),
               "mem_available_gib": probe_ram()["available_gib"],
               "gpu_temp_c": gpu[0]["temperature_c"] if gpu else None,
               "gpu_power_w": gpu[0]["power_w"] if gpu else None}
        out.write(json.dumps(row) + "\n")
        out.flush()
        os.fsync(out.fileno())
        time.sleep(30)

This is the same idea as the log_vitals.sh script in this project, which writes memory, GPU temperature, power, and load every 30 seconds. It was added after a unit stopped responding and left no record of why. Start it before any long run, and the last line it wrote becomes the evidence. Chapter 18 pairs it with a watchdog that acts on the same readings.

docs.title: Diagram: nvidia-smi Output Reader
docs.text:
Run nvidia-smi Output Reader Fullscreen

nvidia-smi Output Reader

Type: microsim sim-id: nvidia-smi-reader Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret 6 highlighted fields of an nvidia-smi listing by choosing what each one reports, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: nvidia-smi, driver version, CUDA version, GPU temperature, GPU power draw, GPU memory total and free, GPU utilization (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The sim shows the illustrative listing from Content with one field highlighted at a time. For each of the 6 highlighted fields the learner commits one meaning from the six listed before the sim reveals the answer. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct meaning column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the listing is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The CUDA version is the toolkit installed on the machine. (2) The power figure is the whole machine's draw. (3) A figure in MiB is the same as one in MB. (4) A GPU at 0% utilization is not working correctly.

Instructional Rationale: Interpreting a terse field needs the learner to attach a meaning and a unit to it, so each highlighted field is a case where a plausible wrong meaning exists in the choices. Committing before the reveal separates reading from guessing.

Content:

The illustrative listing, a machine with one discrete GPU, shown with the serial number, unique identifier, and bus address removed:

NVIDIA-SMI 580.xx.xx    Driver Version: 580.xx.xx    CUDA Version: 13.0
GPU  Name                  Temp  Perf  Pwr:Usage/Cap   Memory-Usage       GPU-Util
  0  NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3  41C   P0   70W / 700W      0MiB / 81559MiB    0%

The six meanings the learner chooses from: "The release of the NVIDIA driver", "The newest CUDA runtime the driver supports", "GPU temperature in degrees Celsius", "Power the board draws now over its power limit", "GPU memory in use over total memory", and "Share of the last sampling period the GPU was running work".

# Highlighted field Correct meaning Why (shown as feedback) 1 Driver Version: 580.xx.xx The release of the NVIDIA driver It names the installed driver, which is what the operating system uses to reach the GPU. 2 CUDA Version: 13.0 The newest CUDA runtime the driver supports It is a ceiling set by the driver, not the version of any toolkit installed on the machine. 3 41C GPU temperature in degrees Celsius The unit C marks Celsius, and it is the reading of the GPU, not the room. 4 70W / 700W Power the board draws now over its power limit The first value is current draw and the second is the cap, and neither is the whole machine's draw. 5 0MiB / 81559MiB GPU memory in use over total memory MiB are mebibytes, so the total is about 80 GiB, shown as in use over total. 6 0% Share of the last sampling period the GPU was running work A GPU with no running work reads 0%, which is normal for an idle machine.

Provenance: The listing is illustrative, written for this exercise, and the sim labels it "illustrative". Field meanings come from the "nvidia-smi and Its Output" section of this chapter.

Rules: Fields are highlighted in the fixed order 1 to 6, and each allows one final choice. Exactly one of the six meanings is correct for each field. A meaning may be used for only one field.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the listing with field 1 highlighted.
  2. The learner chooses one of the six meanings and confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct meaning and the Why text, and marks the field correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for fields 2 to 6. After field 6 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Six fields, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct meaning and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: The listing is shown with the driver version highlighted, and the question on screen is "What does this field report?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the CUDA version is the newest runtime the driver supports, that power usage and cap are in watts, that memory is in mebibytes, and that a field the GPU cannot report appears as [N/A] or Not Supported.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
A hardware probe is a read-only measurement, and a probe script gathers several under four rules: read only, standard library only, bounded time, and null for anything it could not read. The CPU, RAM, storage, and GPU probes answer the questions of Chapter 5, with nvidia-smi queried in its machine-readable form, and the missing GPU memory fields give the unified-memory probe. The suite writes a JSON report that omits identifying fields by default, and the setup branch is chosen from the report. A verification test feeds each probe known input, and a vitals log records the last readings before a machine fails.

The Machine Now Reports in Data

You can now write read-only probes, combine them into a suite that produces a JSON report without identifying fields, and branch your setup on what it says. Chapter 11 uses that report to predict whether a model will fit before you download it.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Python Hardware Probes
docs.text: Test your understanding of read-only probes, the nvidia-smi query, machine-readable reports, and vitals logging with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a hardware probe?
docs.text:
1. A specification sheet that the hardware's vendor has published
  2. A small, read-only measurement of one fact about a machine
  3. A stress test that loads the GPU until it throttles
  4. A background service that restarts a frozen machine
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A hardware probe is a small, read-only measurement of one fact about a machine: how many cores it has, how much memory is free, which GPU is installed. The word "measurement" matters. A probe reads the value from the machine, so it reports what is true now, whatever the specification sheet or the last person's notes say. It has three parts: the question, the source it reads, and the form of the answer.

Concept Tested: Hardware Probe

See: Hardware Probe

docs.title: 2. What does the absence of the nvidia-smi command on a machine usually mean?
docs.text:
1. The GPU has overheated and shut itself down
  2. The machine uses unified memory for its GPU
  3. The NVIDIA driver is not installed on the machine
  4. The account lacks administrator privileges
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. nvidia-smi, the NVIDIA System Management Interface, is the command-line tool that reports a GPU's state. It is installed with the driver, so its presence on a machine is itself a probe: no nvidia-smi usually means no driver. Unified memory shows up differently, as GPU memory fields that come back as Not Supported or [N/A] from a tool that is present and working.

Concept Tested: nvidia-smi

See: nvidia-smi and Its Output

docs.title: 3. Why is MemAvailable the number to watch in the RAM probe, and not MemTotal?
docs.text:
1. It is what a new program could use without pushing others out
  2. It is the only figure the kernel reports in gibibytes
  3. It includes the dedicated memory of every GPU on every kind of system
  4. It stays constant while a model server is running
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The RAM probe reads /proc/meminfo. MemTotal is all the memory the system can use, and MemAvailable is what a new program could use without pushing others out. Available is the number to watch, because a large total with little available is a machine about to struggle. On a unified-memory machine it is also the figure that model fit is judged against, since the GPU has no memory of its own.

Concept Tested: RAM Probe

See: RAM Probe

docs.title: 4. Why should a script avoid parsing the table that nvidia-smi prints when run with no arguments?
docs.text:
1. The table leaves out the GPU's temperature and power
  2. The table is printed only when the driver is missing
  3. The table can be read only with administrator rights
  4. The table's layout changes between versions
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Run with no arguments, nvidia-smi prints a table meant for people. A script should not parse it, because its layout changes between versions. The GPU probe instead asks for exactly the fields it wants with --query-gpu and --format=csv,noheader,nounits, which returns one comma-separated line per GPU. The table does show temperature and power, and it needs no administrator rights, so neither of those is the reason.

Concept Tested: nvidia-smi Output

See: nvidia-smi and Its Output

docs.title: 5. Why does the probe suite write a machine-readable report?
docs.text:
1. Later programs consume it, such as a model-fit calculator
  2. It is shorter than the table that nvidia-smi prints
  3. It can hold hostnames and serial numbers in a safely encoded form
  4. It lets a probe change the settings of the machine that it reads
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A machine-readable report is output a program can parse without guessing, in contrast to text written for a person. The reason to produce one is that later steps consume it: a model-fit calculator reads available_gib, and a benchmark runner records the whole report beside each result so a number is never separated from the machine that produced it. The report deliberately contains no hostname, address, or account name.

Concept Tested: Machine-Readable Report

See: Machine-Readable Report and JSON Report

docs.title: 6. A probe report shows memory_total_mib: null for the only GPU and unified_memory: true. Which figure should you use to judge whether a model fits?
docs.text:
1. The GPU's power_w reading from the same report
  2. The storage probe's free_gb for the root filesystem
  3. The RAM probe's total_gib, with nothing subtracted
  4. The RAM probe's available_gib, less some headroom
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The unified memory probe is the check that the GPU's own memory fields are missing. When every GPU's total comes back as None, the probe sets unified_memory to true, and the figure to use is the system RAM probe's available_gib, minus the headroom Chapter 11 introduces. The null values are not an error; they are the unified-memory signature. Using total_gib would ignore what the operating system and other programs already hold.

Concept Tested: Unified Memory Probe

See: GPU Memory Total and Free, and the Unified Memory Probe

docs.title: 7. You time a read of a model file that you loaded five minutes ago, and the measured speed is far higher than expected. What should you do?
docs.text:
1. Record the figure as the true read speed of the drive
  2. Rerun on a file that has not been read since boot
  3. Divide the result by the number of CPU cores
  4. Rerun the same file with the GPU sitting idle
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A disk read benchmark reads an existing large file and divides the bytes by the seconds. The one trap is the operating system's page cache: a file read recently comes from memory, not the disk, so the number is far too high. The fix is to read a file that has not been touched since boot, such as a model file you have not loaded, and to say so in the report.

Concept Tested: Disk Read Benchmark

See: Disk Read Benchmark

docs.title: 8. You are about to start a run that will last several hours on a unit that has stopped responding before. What should you start first?
docs.text:
1. A disk read benchmark on the largest model file
  2. A vitals log that writes and syncs a line every 30 seconds
  3. A probe verification test against a fake meminfo file
  4. A full nvidia-smi table, saved once before the run
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Vitals logging records a few measurements at a fixed interval while a long job runs, so a machine that fails leaves its last readings behind. The loop writes one line every 30 seconds with available memory, GPU temperature, and power draw, and flush and fsync put each line on the disk at once, because a machine that freezes does not get to finish its buffers. A single snapshot taken before the run records nothing about the failure.

Concept Tested: Vitals Logging

See: Vitals Logging

docs.title: 9. A probe returns 0 whenever it cannot read a value, and a report from a healthy machine shows available_gib: 0. What is wrong with this design?
docs.text:
1. Zero is not valid JSON, so the report cannot be parsed
  2. The probe should keep retrying until the value becomes nonzero
  3. A failed reading cannot be told apart from a measured zero
  4. The probe should have read the value with psutil
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A probe script should report an unknown value as null and never guess. If a probe returns zero when it cannot read a value, a failed measurement looks like a machine with no memory, and the report appears complete while hiding the failure. Returning null lets a reader tell a missing measurement from a measured zero. Retrying without limit is no fix, because a probe must also have a bounded run time.

Concept Tested: Probe Script

See: Probe Script

docs.title: 10. The suite runs on a machine with no GPU, where nvidia-smi is missing, yet the report still contains CPU, RAM, and storage results. Which design choices explain this?
docs.text:
1. The suite retries nvidia-smi until the GPU driver finally responds
  2. The suite copies GPU values from the last saved report
  3. The suite stops at the first error and prints whatever it has so far
  4. Separate probes and a helper that returns None on failure
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A probe suite runs a set of probes together to produce one report. Every probe goes through a helper that returns None when a command is missing, fails, or times out, so a missing nvidia-smi gives an empty GPU answer instead of a crash. Keeping the probes separate and the suite thin means a single failing probe cannot take the others with it, and each probe can be tested alone.

Concept Tested: Probe Suite

See: Probe Suite

docs.title: References: Python Hardware Probes
docs.text:
1. Procfs - Wikipedia - Describes the /proc pseudo-filesystem that presents kernel and process information as files in Unix-like systems. It explains where the RAM probe's reading of /proc/meminfo comes from.

  2. CUDA - Wikipedia - Covers NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and API, its history, supported GPUs, and version features. It gives context for the CUDA version that nvidia-smi reports and for the chapter's PyTorch CUDA check.

  3. JSON - Wikipedia - Explains the language-independent text format of name-value pairs and arrays, with its syntax and interoperability. It is the format of the chapter's machine-readable probe report.

  4. Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud (2nd Edition) - Brendan Gregg - Addison-Wesley - Gregg developed the USE Method, which checks utilization, saturation, and errors for every resource. That checklist maps directly onto the CPU, memory, storage, and GPU probes the chapter builds.

  5. Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software (2nd Edition) - Michael T. Nygard - Pragmatic Bookshelf - Martin Fowler credits Nygard with popularizing the Circuit Breaker pattern, and the book's stability chapters argue for timeouts on every outside call. That is the reasoning behind the probe helper's bounded run time.

  6. nvidia-smi: NVIDIA System Management Interface - NVIDIA - Official manual documenting --query-gpu and --format=csv,noheader,nounits, and noting that NVML is the better choice for tools needing stable output. It is the source for the chapter's GPU probe query.

  7. NVML API Reference Guide - NVIDIA - Reference for the C library behind nvidia-smi, used to query GPU temperature, power, memory, and clocks, and wrapped by the nvidia-ml-py Python bindings. It supports the chapter's NVML section.

  8. psutil: Process and System Utilities for Python - psutil project - Home page of the cross-platform library that reports CPU, memory, disk, network, and sensor data through functions such as virtual_memory() and disk_usage(). It is the optional package that the chapter's standard-library probes replace.

  9. The /proc Filesystem - Linux kernel documentation - Documents the /proc files, including the meminfo fields MemTotal, MemFree, and MemAvailable, an estimate of memory available for new applications without swapping. It is the source for the chapter's RAM probe.

  10. subprocess: Subprocess management - Python documentation - Documents subprocess.run with capture_output, text mode, return codes, and the timeout parameter that raises TimeoutExpired. It is the reference for the run() helper beneath every probe.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter predicts whether a model will fit before it is downloaded. It derives memory from parameter count, numeric precision, quantization, and KV cache, and adds runtime overhead and safety headroom. Students finish by building a model-fit calculator that returns a verdict for both dedicated and unified memory.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 5: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture

Do the Arithmetic Before the Download

A model that does not fit costs you a long download and a confusing failure, and a model that barely fits can freeze the whole machine. By the end of this chapter you will predict, to within a few gigabytes, whether a model will fit before you pull a single file. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 5 established that on a unified-memory machine everything shares one pool, and Chapter 10 built the probe that reports how much of it is free. This chapter supplies the other side of the comparison: how much memory a given model needs. With both numbers in hand, a fit decision becomes subtraction.

The estimate has three parts that behave differently. The weights are fixed by the model and its precision. The KV cache grows with the context you ask for. The runtime overhead is a small amount that the server adds on its own. The chapter builds each one, adds a safety margin, and ends with a calculator that returns a verdict. Measurements from this evaluation's own units appear alongside each formula, so you can see how close the estimate comes.

docs.title: Model Weights
docs.text:
Model weights are the learned numbers that make up a model. A language model is, concretely, a very large collection of them, and loading a model means placing every one of them in memory where the processor can read it. The count of weights is the model's parameter count, written in billions: a "27B" model has about 27 billion.

Weights dominate the memory budget, because every one must be resident for the model to run at full speed. The memory they take is the parameter count times the size of one number:

\[ \text{memory for weights} = \text{parameters} \times \text{bytes per weight} \]

A worked example makes the scale concrete. A 27-billion-parameter model stored at three precisions, which the next sections define, needs:

Precision Bytes per weight Memory for weights 16-bit 2 54 GB 8-bit 1 27 GB 4-bit 0.5 13.5 GB

The same model is a 54 GB problem or a 13.5 GB one, and which it is depends on a choice made when the file was produced. This is why the precision is part of a model's name in a library and why two files with the same parameter count can differ by a factor of four.

docs.title: Diagram: Parameters That Fit in Memory
docs.text:
Run the Parameters That Fit in Memory MicroSim fullscreen

Parameters That Fit in Memory (reused MicroSim)

Reused from this book's own MicroSims, which already exists locally, so no new specification is needed.

The sim shows only the weights, at one precision, with a fixed 20% kept free. The rest of this chapter adds the pieces it leaves out.

docs.title: Dense Model, Mixture of Experts, and Active Parameters
docs.text:
A dense model uses all of its parameters to produce every token. A mixture-of-experts model splits much of its parameters into many groups called experts, and for each token a routing step selects a small number of them. The parameters actually used for a token are its active parameters.

The distinction changes two things in opposite directions, and confusing them is a common mistake.

Dense model Mixture-of-experts model Memory needed All parameters All parameters, since any expert may be chosen Work per token All parameters Only the active parameters Speed Falls as the model grows Close to a much smaller dense model Example from this evaluation gemma4:31b, 30.7 billion gemma4:26b, 25.2 billion total, 3.8 billion active
