The two Gemma models are a clean comparison: similar total size, similar memory, and a threefold difference in speed. A mixture-of-experts model does not save memory. It saves time per token.

Memory Pays for the Whole Model, Speed Pays for the Active Part

A 26-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model still needs room for all 26 billion, because the router might pick any expert on the next token. What it saves is the work of reading them. Keep the two questions apart: does it fit, and how fast will it run.

docs.title: Numeric Precision, Bits per Parameter, and Bytes per Weight
docs.text:
Numeric precision is how many bits are used to store each number. More bits represent a number more finely and take more memory. Bits per parameter counts them, and bytes per weight is the same figure divided by 8, which is the one that multiplies the parameter count.

The common formats are few, and the table gives each a name and a size.

Format Bits Bytes per weight Used for FP32 32 4 Training and some calculations FP16, BF16 16 2 The usual full-precision release of a model 8-bit 8 1 A quantized file that keeps most quality 4-bit 4 0.5 The common local-inference choice

docs.title: FP16 and BF16
docs.text: FP16 and BF16 are the two 16-bit floating-point formats. Both take two bytes, so they cost the same memory. They differ in how they spend their 16 bits. FP16 keeps more digits of precision and a narrower range of values. BF16 keeps the wide range of the 32-bit format and fewer digits, which makes it more forgiving in training. A model released in BF16 is the reference that quantized versions are made from.

docs.title: Quantization, Quantization Level, 8-Bit and 4-Bit
docs.text:
Quantization is storing a model's weights with fewer bits than the original, trading a small loss of accuracy for a large saving in memory and a gain in speed. A quantization level names how aggressively: 8-bit keeps nearly all of the original's quality at half the 16-bit size, and 4-bit cuts it to a quarter with a loss that is small for most tasks and larger for hard reasoning.

File names for the common format carry the level in a code such as Q4_K_M or Q8_0, and the model library's default tag for a model is usually 4-bit. This evaluation's design choices page records the decision: every candidate ran at its default 4-bit, with an 8-bit retest left for the winner, since memory is not the constraint on this machine.

The effect on quality is not uniform, and it is an evaluation question, not a calculation. Chapter 15 returns to it with measurements.

docs.title: Quantized File Overhead, Size on Disk, and Memory for Weights
docs.text:
A "4-bit" file is not exactly 4 bits per parameter. A quantized file stores the scaling factors that let the small numbers be turned back into real ones, and it keeps some layers, often the ones most sensitive to precision, at a higher precision. Quantized file overhead is the extra that results. Size on disk is the file's actual size, and memory for weights is what that file takes once loaded, which is close to the same number.

This evaluation measured the overhead, and the measurements are the reason the calculator below does not use 4.0.

Model Parameters Formula at 4-bit Actual download Effective bits per parameter gemma4:26b 25.2 billion 13 GB 18 GB 5.7 qwen3.8:27b 27 billion 14 GB 17 GB 5.0 gemma4:31b 30.7 billion 15 GB 20 GB 5.2 gpt-oss:120b 117 billion 59 GB 65 GB 4.4

The last column is the download size times 8 divided by the parameter count. The four "4-bit" files work out to between 4.4 and 5.7 bits per parameter. A planner who used 4.0 would have underestimated the weights by 10 to 30 percent, in the direction that makes a machine look roomier than it is.

Use the File Size When You Can, 5 Bits When You Cannot

The download size on the library page is the best predictor of memory for weights, since it is what will load. When you only have a parameter count, multiply by about 5 bits and not 4, and your estimate will err on the safe side.

docs.title: KV Cache and Context Length Memory
docs.text:
The KV cache is the memory a model uses to remember the conversation so far. For every token already in the context, the model keeps two vectors at every layer, called the key and the value, so that it does not recompute them for each new token. The cache grows by a fixed amount per token, and context length memory is that amount times the number of tokens you allow.

The per-token amount comes from the model's shape. Each token stores a key and a value (2 vectors), at every layer, for each of the model's key-value heads, each of a fixed dimension, at the cache's precision:

\[ \text{KV bytes per token} = 2 \times \text{layers} \times \text{KV heads} \times \text{head dimension} \times \text{bytes per value} \]

A worked example uses an illustrative shape, not the published architecture of any candidate: 48 layers, 8 key-value heads, a head dimension of 128, and 2 bytes per value. That gives 2 × 48 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 196,608 bytes, or 192 KiB, for each token.

Context length KV cache Calculation 32,768 tokens 6.4 GB 32,768 × 196,608 bytes 131,072 tokens 25.8 GB 131,072 × 196,608 bytes 262,144 tokens 51.5 GB 262,144 × 196,608 bytes

The cache is allocated for the context length the server is configured with. It is not something you can ignore until the conversation gets long. This evaluation measured it: with a 20 GB model loaded and idle, one unit showed 66 to 71 GB in use at a 256,000-token setting, where the same model at 32,000 tokens took 29 GB. The difference is mostly the cache, and it is about twice the size of the model.

A Context Setting Is a Memory Reservation

Raising the context length does not make a model slower to load a little. It reserves tens of gigabytes before the first prompt, on the same pool the operating system lives in. Choose the smallest context the job needs, and raise it deliberately while watching available memory.

docs.title: Runtime Overhead
docs.text: Runtime overhead is the memory the inference server and the GPU stack use beyond the weights and the cache: the compute buffers, the CUDA context, and bookkeeping. It is small compared with the other two, and it is not zero. From the four measurements at a 32,000-token context, the weights plus the cache plus the overhead came to 24 to 69 GB where the weights alone were 17 to 65 GB, so the cache and overhead together were 4 to 9 GB. The calculator uses 3 GB for the overhead alone, which with a 6.4 GB cache gives 9.4 GB, at the top of that range and so on the cautious side.

docs.title: Safety Headroom
docs.text:
Safety headroom is memory deliberately left unused, as a margin against the things an estimate misses: the operating system, other processes, a cache that grows during a run, and an estimate that is simply low. It is expressed as a share of the memory, and this course uses 20% as the default.

On a unified-memory machine the headroom is not a nicety. Exhausting a pool that the operating system also runs on can freeze the whole machine instead of stopping one program, as Chapter 5 described. The memory watchdog of Chapter 18 enforces a floor in gigabytes for the same reason, and headroom is the planning-time version of that floor.

docs.title: Memory Estimation Formula
docs.text:
The memory estimation formula adds the three parts defined above. Weights depend on the model and its precision, the cache depends on the context you configure, and the overhead is a small constant:

\[ \text{memory needed} = \underbrace{\text{parameters} \times \tfrac{\text{bits}}{8}}_{\text{weights}} + \underbrace{\text{context} \times \text{KV bytes per token}}_{\text{KV cache}} + \text{overhead} \]

Each symbol has a unit. Parameters are in billions, so weights come out in gigabytes. Bits is the effective bits per parameter, 5.0 for a file labeled 4-bit, from the measurements above. Context is in tokens. KV bytes per token comes from the model's shape, or from the 192 KiB of the worked example if you do not know it. Overhead is in gigabytes.

docs.title: Model-Fit Calculation and Fit Verdict
docs.text:
A model-fit calculation compares the memory needed with the memory available, after setting aside the safety headroom. The comparison produces a fit verdict, and three verdicts are enough because each one calls for a different action.

Verdict Condition What to do Fits Needed ≤ memory × (1 − headroom) Proceed Fits without headroom memory × (1 − headroom) < needed ≤ memory Reduce context or choose a smaller file; do not run unattended Does not fit Needed > memory Choose a smaller model or lower precision

The middle verdict is the one that earns its place. A model in that zone loads, and then runs until something else asks for memory, which on a unified-memory machine can be the operating system itself. A calculation that returned only "fits" or "does not fit" would call it a success.

docs.title: Unified Memory Fit
docs.text:
Unified memory fit is the same calculation with the right number for memory. On a machine with dedicated GPU memory, the available memory is the GPU's free memory, per GPU. On a unified-memory machine it is the system's available memory from the RAM probe of Chapter 10, since that pool is the only one, minus the headroom.

This is why the report's unified_memory field mattered: it decides which number goes into the comparison. The same model can fit on a 128 GB unified-memory machine and not fit on a 24 GB discrete GPU with 512 GB of system RAM beside it.

docs.title: Model-Fit Calculator
docs.text:
A model-fit calculator is the formula and the verdict as a program. The function below takes the model and the machine and returns the memory needed, the usable limit, and the verdict. Its parameters, in order, are the parameter count in billions, the effective bits per parameter, the context in tokens, the KV cache bytes per token in KiB, the runtime overhead in gigabytes, the memory in gigabytes, and the headroom as a fraction.

def fit_verdict(params_b, bits, context, kv_kib_per_token,
                overhead_gb, memory_gb, headroom=0.20):
    weights = params_b * bits / 8                        # GB
    kv = context * kv_kib_per_token * 1024 / 1e9         # GB
    total = weights + kv + overhead_gb
    limit = memory_gb * (1 - headroom)
    if total <= limit:
        verdict = "Fits"
    elif total <= memory_gb:
        verdict = "Fits without headroom"
    else:
        verdict = "Does not fit"
    return round(total, 1), round(limit, 1), verdict

Two runs on this evaluation's machine, a 128 GB unified-memory unit, show it against the measurements. The model is gemma4:31b, with 30.7 billion parameters at 5.0 effective bits.

fit_verdict(30.7, 5.0, 32768, 192, 3, 128)    # (28.6, 102.4, 'Fits')
fit_verdict(30.7, 5.0, 262144, 192, 3, 128)   # (73.7, 102.4, 'Fits')

The first estimate, 28.6 GB, compares with the 29 GB measured at that context. The second, 73.7 GB, compares with the 71 GB measured with the model idle at 256,000 tokens. The estimates are within a few percent of the measurements, and both say "Fits".

The second result deserves a second look, because that configuration is the one where a unit stopped responding a few minutes into a long run. An estimate of the idle footprint is a floor, not a peak: the server's per-conversation state grows as a run proceeds, and the cause of the freeze was not confirmed. A "Fits" verdict at 73.7 GB with 102 GB of limit means the idle state fits, and it does not mean a long run is safe. This is why Chapter 18 adds a watchdog on top of the calculation.

The Formula Is Simple and the Judgment Is Not

If you got the arithmetic right and the machine still struggled, you have not made a mistake. An estimate predicts the starting footprint, and a long run adds to it. Treat the verdict as a gate on what to try, then measure what actually happens with the vitals log.

docs.title: Diagram: Model-Fit Calculator
docs.text:
Run Model-Fit Calculator Fullscreen

Model-Fit Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: model-fit-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/dgx-eval/tree/main/docs/sims/model-fit-by-memory Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the memory a model needs from its parameter count, precision, and context length, to within 1 GB, and state the fit verdict, for 3 challenges.

Prerequisites: model weights, numeric precision, quantization, KV cache, runtime overhead, safety headroom, fit verdict, unified memory fit (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 3 challenges the learner types the memory needed in gigabytes and chooses one of the three verdicts before the sim reveals the answer. A challenge is correct when the typed value is within 1 GB of the model value and the verdict matches. Mastery is 3 of 3. Changing the inputs in exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A 4-bit file uses exactly 4 bits per parameter. (2) The context length does not change memory until the conversation is long. (3) A model that loads has therefore fit. (4) A larger memory always means a bigger model can be run.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs the learner to combine three terms, so each challenge changes one input that moves a different term: context for the cache, memory for the verdict, and precision for the weights. The middle verdict is included so that the learner meets the zone where a model loads and is still unsafe.

Content:

The learner can change seven quantities:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Parameters 1 200 0.1 30.5 billions Precision 16, 8, or 4-bit file 4-bit Context length 4,096 262,144 4,096 32,768 tokens KV cache per token 32 512 32 192 KiB Runtime overhead 0 10 0.5 3 GB Memory 16 512 16 128 GB Headroom 0.05 0.40 0.05 0.20 share of memory

The effective bits per parameter for each precision are 16 for the 16-bit file, 8.5 for the 8-bit file, and 5.0 for the 4-bit file.

The three challenges, in this order:

# Parameters Precision Context Memory Model memory needed Verdict Feedback when wrong 1 30.7 4-bit 32,768 128 28.6 GB Fits Weights 30.7 × 5.0 ÷ 8 = 19.2 GB, cache 32,768 × 192 KiB = 6.4 GB, overhead 3 GB, total 28.6 GB, which is under the usable 102.4 GB. 2 30.7 4-bit 262,144 64 73.7 GB Does not fit Weights 19.2 GB, cache 262,144 × 192 KiB = 51.5 GB, overhead 3 GB, total 73.7 GB, which is above all 64 GB of memory. 3 110 8-bit 32,768 128 126.3 GB Fits without headroom Weights 110 × 8.5 ÷ 8 = 116.9 GB, cache 6.4 GB, overhead 3 GB, total 126.3 GB, which is under 128 GB and above the usable 102.4 GB.

Provenance: The effective bits for the 4-bit file are rounded from the measured range of 4.4 to 5.7 in this chapter's table. The 8-bit value of 8.5 and the cache shape of 192 KiB per token are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative, not a published figure". Challenge 1 compares with the measured 29 GB in this chapter.

Rules: Weights in GB = parameters × effective bits ÷ 8. Cache in GB = context × KV per token in KiB × 1,024 ÷ 10^9. Needed = weights + cache + overhead. Usable = memory × (1 − headroom). Verdict "Fits" when needed <= usable, "Fits without headroom" when usable < needed <= memory, and "Does not fit" when needed > memory. Values are shown to one decimal.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1, whose inputs are shown, and types the memory needed in GB.
  2. The learner chooses a verdict and presses Check.
  3. The sim reveals the model value, the verdict, and the Feedback text, and marks the challenge correct or missed.
  4. After all three challenges the exploration mode unlocks and the learner changes any of the seven quantities, watching a bar split into weights, cache, and overhead, with the usable limit and the memory marked.
  5. In exploration the learner should notice that raising the context moves the cache term far more than changing the precision of a small model.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: GB, ." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge. After the second wrong attempt the model value and the worked calculation are shown, and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with an empty answer box and its inputs displayed. The question on screen is "How much memory does this model need, and does it fit?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states 5.0 effective bits for a 4-bit file, 192 KiB of cache per token in the worked example, 3 GB of runtime overhead, a 20% headroom default, and the three verdicts; its worked results are 28.6 GB and 73.7 GB for the 30.7-billion-parameter model.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
A model's memory is its weights plus its KV cache plus a small runtime overhead. The weights are the parameter count times the bytes per weight, and a "4-bit" file measures nearer 5 bits per parameter once its scaling factors and higher-precision layers are counted. The cache grows with the context you configure, and it is reserved at the full setting. A mixture-of-experts model needs memory for all of its parameters while doing the work of only its active ones. A safety headroom turns the comparison into three verdicts, and on unified memory the memory to compare against is the system's available memory. The result is a prediction of the starting footprint, which a long run can exceed.

You Can Predict a Fit Before You Download

You can now estimate a model's weights, cache, and overhead, apply a headroom, and reach one of three verdicts that matches what this evaluation measured to within a few percent. Chapter 12 uses the calculation to choose which models are worth downloading at all.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Model Sizing and Fit
docs.text: Test your understanding of weights, quantization, the KV cache, headroom, and the model-fit calculation with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. How is the memory for a model's weights calculated?
docs.text:
1. Parameter count times bytes per weight
  2. Context length times KV bytes per token
  3. Download size times the number of layers
  4. Active parameters times bits per token
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Model weights are the learned numbers that make up a model, and loading a model means placing every one of them in memory. The memory they take is the parameter count times the size of one number, the bytes per weight. A 27-billion-parameter model needs 54 GB at 16-bit, 27 GB at 8-bit, and 13.5 GB at 4-bit. Context length times KV bytes per token gives the cache, a separate term in the estimate.

Concept Tested: Model Weights

See: Model Weights

docs.title: 2. What is the KV cache?
docs.text:
1. A disk folder where downloaded model files are stored
  2. Memory holding key and value vectors for tokens in the context
  3. The compute buffers and CUDA context the server allocates
  4. A table of scaling factors stored inside a quantized file
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The KV cache is the memory a model uses to remember the conversation so far. For every token already in the context, the model keeps two vectors at every layer, the key and the value, so it does not recompute them for each new token. The cache grows by a fixed amount per token. Compute buffers and the CUDA context are runtime overhead, and scaling factors are part of a quantized file's overhead.

Concept Tested: KV Cache

See: KV Cache and Context Length Memory

docs.title: 3. What is safety headroom in a fit calculation, and what default does this course use?
docs.text:
1. Memory the server uses for compute buffers; 3 GB
  2. Extra bits a quantized file stores per parameter; 5 bits
  3. Memory reserved for the KV cache; 192 KiB per token
  4. Memory deliberately left unused as a margin; 20%
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Safety headroom is memory deliberately left unused as a margin against what an estimate misses: the operating system, other processes, a cache that grows during a run, and an estimate that is simply low. It is expressed as a share of memory, and this course uses 20% as the default. On a unified-memory machine it is not a nicety, because exhausting a pool the operating system also runs on can freeze the whole machine.

Concept Tested: Safety Headroom

See: Safety Headroom

docs.title: 4. Why does a mixture-of-experts model not save memory compared with a dense model of similar total size?
docs.text:
1. Its experts are stored at a higher numeric precision
  2. Its router keeps a second full copy of every expert's weights
  3. Any expert may be chosen next, so all must stay in memory
  4. Its KV cache grows with the number of experts that it holds
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A dense model uses all of its parameters for every token. A mixture-of-experts model routes each token to a small number of expert groups, so only its active parameters do the work. Memory is another matter: any expert may be chosen on the next token, so all parameters must be resident. The two Gemma models show it: similar total size and memory, and a threefold difference in speed. The design saves time per token, not memory.

Concept Tested: Mixture of Experts

See: Dense Model, Mixture of Experts, and Active Parameters

docs.title: 5. Why does a file labeled 4-bit measure nearer 5 bits per parameter?
docs.text:
1. It stores scaling factors and keeps some layers at higher precision
  2. It bundles the whole KV cache needed for the model's full context length
  3. It includes a second copy of the weights for error checking
  4. It counts the tokenizer and license files as parameters
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A quantized file stores the scaling factors that let its small numbers be turned back into real ones, and it keeps some layers, often the most precision-sensitive, at higher precision. That extra is the quantized file overhead. The four "4-bit" files measured in this evaluation worked out to between 4.4 and 5.7 bits per parameter, so a planner using 4.0 would underestimate the weights by 10 to 30 percent and make the machine look roomier than it is.

Concept Tested: Quantized File Overhead

See: Quantized File Overhead, Size on Disk, and Memory for Weights

docs.title: 6. Why is a context-length setting described as a memory reservation?
docs.text:
1. The setting limits how many models the server can load
  2. The cache is written to disk and then read back for each new token
  3. The memory is claimed only once a conversation gets long
  4. The cache is allocated at the full setting before any prompt
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Context length memory is the per-token KV cache amount times the number of tokens you allow. The cache is allocated for the context length the server is configured with, so it is reserved before the first prompt and cannot be ignored until a conversation gets long. This evaluation measured it: a 20 GB model took 29 GB at a 32,000-token setting and 66 to 71 GB at 256,000 tokens while idle. Choose the smallest context the job needs.

Concept Tested: Context Length Memory

See: KV Cache and Context Length Memory

docs.title: 7. A 48-billion-parameter model comes as a file labeled 4-bit. At the planned context its KV cache is 6.4 GB, and runtime overhead is 3 GB. Using 5.0 effective bits for the 4-bit file, how much memory does the model need?
docs.text:
1. 33.4 GB
  2. 39.4 GB
  3. 30.0 GB
  4. 57.4 GB
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The memory estimation formula adds weights, KV cache, and overhead. Weights are parameters in billions times effective bits divided by 8, and a file labeled 4-bit uses 5.0 effective bits: 48 × 5.0 ÷ 8 = 30 GB. Adding the 6.4 GB cache and 3 GB of overhead gives 39.4 GB. Using exactly 4 bits gives 33.4 GB, which underestimates the weights, and 30 GB counts the weights alone.

Concept Tested: Memory Estimation Formula

See: Memory Estimation Formula

docs.title: 8. A model needs 110 GB on a 128 GB unified-memory machine, and the headroom is 20%. What is the verdict, and what should you do?
docs.text:
1. Fits; proceed with the run as planned
  2. Does not fit; choose a smaller model or lower precision
  3. Fits; raise the context length to use the spare memory
  4. Fits without headroom; reduce context or use a smaller file
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A model-fit calculation compares memory needed with memory available after setting aside headroom. Usable memory is 128 × (1 − 0.20) = 102.4 GB. A need of 110 GB is above that and below 128 GB, which is the middle verdict, "Fits without headroom". The action is to reduce context or choose a smaller file, and not to run unattended. Such a model loads and then runs until something else asks for memory, which can be the operating system itself.

Concept Tested: Fit Verdict

See: Model-Fit Calculation and Fit Verdict

docs.title: 9. A model needs 60 GB. Machine X has a 24 GB discrete GPU and 512 GB of system RAM. Machine Y has 128 GB of unified memory. On which machine does the model fit?
docs.text:
1. Only Y: the limit there is the shared pool, not a 24 GB GPU
  2. Only X: its 512 GB of system RAM exceeds what is needed
  3. Both: each machine has more than 60 GB of memory in total to draw on
  4. Neither: 60 GB exceeds a 20% headroom on both machines
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Unified memory fit is the same calculation with the right number for memory. With dedicated GPU memory, the available memory is the GPU's free memory, so machine X's limit is 24 GB whatever its system RAM. On a unified-memory machine it is the system's available memory minus headroom: 128 GB × 0.80 is 102.4 GB, which holds a 60 GB need. The same model can fit on Y and not fit on X.

Concept Tested: Unified Memory Fit

See: Unified Memory Fit

docs.title: 10. The calculator returned "Fits" at 73.7 GB against a 102.4 GB limit, yet a unit stopped responding a few minutes into a long run at that setting. What does this show about the verdict?
docs.text:
1. The formula's arithmetic is wrong for large context settings
  2. The 20% headroom should always be replaced by a 50% headroom
  3. The estimate is a floor for the idle state, not a peak
  4. The model's weights were really stored at 16 bits
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A fit verdict predicts the starting footprint. The 73.7 GB estimate matched the 71 GB measured with the model idle, so the arithmetic held. An estimate of the idle footprint is a floor, not a peak: the server's per-conversation state grows as a run proceeds. The cause of that freeze was not confirmed, so the lesson is limited: "Fits" means the idle state fits, not that a long run is safe, which is why a watchdog is added.

Concept Tested: Model-Fit Calculation

See: Model-Fit Calculator

docs.title: References: Model Sizing and Fit
docs.text:
1. Mixture of experts - Wikipedia - Explains how a gating function routes each input to a few expert networks, with examples such as Mixtral. It supports the chapter's point that such models need memory for all parameters but compute with only the active ones.

  2. bfloat16 floating-point format - Wikipedia - Describes the 16-bit format that keeps the exponent range of 32-bit floats while cutting the significand, covering bit layout and conversion rules. It shows the trade the chapter describes: two bytes per weight, with range kept and precision reduced.

  3. Quantization (signal processing) - Wikipedia - Defines quantization as mapping a large set of values onto a smaller set and relates bit depth to error and noise. It supplies the general theory behind trading fewer bits per weight for smaller size and some lost accuracy.

  4. Hands-On Large Language Models (1st Edition) - Jay Alammar and Maarten Grootendorst - O'Reilly Media - Alammar is known for The Illustrated Transformer, and this book carries that visual style to the whole model; Chapter 3 shows how caching keys and values speeds generation, the cache whose growth this chapter sizes.

  5. Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (3rd Edition) - Randal E. Bryant and David R. O'Hallaron - Pearson - Builds IEEE 754 floating point from a tiny 8-bit format with 4 exponent bits and 3 fraction bits, so every value can be listed by hand. That makes the exponent-versus-fraction trade behind FP16 and BF16 concrete.

  6. Model memory estimator - Hugging Face Accelerate Documentation - Shows how accelerate estimate-memory reports load size per dtype from float32 down to int4 without downloading weights, and warns to add up to 20 percent for inference. It is a ready-made version of this chapter's fit calculation.

  7. Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization - NVIDIA Technical Blog - Gives the per-token KV cache size formula from layers, heads, head dimension, and precision, with a Llama 2 7B example of about 2 GB at 4,096 tokens. It matches the chapter's cache arithmetic.

  8. A Visual Guide to Quantization - Maarten Grootendorst, Exploring Language Models - Diagrams the FP32, FP16, and BF16 bit layouts, works a 70-billion-parameter memory example, and walks from 8-bit to 4-bit methods including GGUF. It supports the chapter's precision and quantization sections.

  9. llama-quantize README - llama.cpp Project on GitHub - Tabulates quantization types such as Q4_K_M and Q8_0 with bits per weight, file size, and speed for an 8-billion-parameter model. Its figures, about 4.9 bits for Q4_K_M, show why a 4-bit file is not 4 bits per parameter.

  10. Mixture of Experts Explained - Hugging Face Blog - Explains routers and experts in sparse transformer layers and states that all parameters must be loaded in memory even though only some are used per token. It states the dense-versus-sparse memory trade-off this chapter works through.

docs.title: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
Summary
docs.text: This chapter moves from the question of fit to the choice of model. Students apply selection criteria, review licenses, compare publisher claims with measured behavior, and download models from the Hugging Face Hub with checksum verification. They finish with a documented shortlist of models that fit and are legal to use.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 23 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Apache 2.0 License 2 Hugging Face Hub 31 Model Repository 27 Safetensors Format 3 License Review 3 Model Leaderboard 3 Writing Quality 2 Gated Model Access 2 Publisher Provenance 2 Commercial Use Terms 1 Model Download 26 Model Selection Criteria 4 Tool-Calling Reliability 2 Public Benchmark Score 2 Access Token Handling 1 Checksum Verification 3 GGUF Format 2 Model Cache Directory 1 Publisher Claims 1 Exclusion Rationale 1 Storage Management 1 Model Shortlist 2 Model Comparison 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 5: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
  • Chapter 11: Model Sizing and Fit

A Shortlist You Can Defend

There are thousands of open-weight models and you have room for a handful. By the end of this chapter you will have a shortlist that fits your machine, that you are allowed to use, and whose exclusions you can explain in one sentence each. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 11 told you which models fit. This chapter decides which of those are worth the disk space and the testing time. The two questions are different: a model can fit and still be the wrong choice because its license forbids your use, its publisher cannot be identified, or its claims describe a task you are not doing.

The chapter follows a choice from criteria to files on disk. It sets the criteria the benchmark needs, shows where models are published and how to read a model page, reviews licenses and the claims a publisher makes, and ends with downloading safely, verifying that the file is the one intended, and recording why each candidate was included or left out.

docs.title: Model Selection Criteria
docs.text:
Model selection criteria are the requirements a model must meet to be worth testing. They come from the workload, not from a leaderboard. For this course's workload, which is running a long skill through an agent harness, the criteria were four, and each can be checked before downloading.

Criterion Why the workload needs it Where to check it Supports tool calling A harness acts only through tool calls The model page, then a test Context window of at least 64,000 tokens The harness prompt alone takes about 19,000 tokens The model page Fits with headroom A model that fits tightly can freeze a unified-memory machine Chapter 11's calculation Identifiable publisher and checkable terms A result cannot be recommended if readers cannot check the license The repository and its license file

docs.title: Tool-Calling Reliability and Writing Quality
docs.text:
Tool-calling reliability is how often a model produces a well-formed tool call when one is needed. It is the property that decides whether a harness run works at all, and it is rarely stated on a model page as a number. Writing quality is how good the prose is: clear, accurate, at the stated reading level, and sustained across thousands of words. A textbook is mostly prose.

Neither can be read from a model's name. Both are measured, in different places in this course. Chapter 19 builds a model-only test that exposes tool-calling failures in seconds, and Chapter 20 builds the scoring for prose. At selection time the right move is to prefer candidates whose publishers state tool-calling support, and to expect to discard some of them after testing.

docs.title: Hugging Face Hub and Model Repository
docs.text:
The Hugging Face Hub is the main public site for sharing machine-learning models, datasets, and demonstration apps. A model repository is one model's home on it: a versioned folder of files that holds the weights, the configuration, a README called the model card, and a license file.

A model repository page is a primary source, and reading it is the main selection skill. Five things are worth finding before you consider a download.

  • Who published it. An organization's verified account, or an individual who repackaged someone else's work.
  • The license, as a file and in the page's metadata, which can disagree.
  • The model card. Intended use, training notes, and the publisher's own benchmark claims.
  • The file list. Which formats exist and how large each is.
  • The history. When it was last updated and whether the files changed after publication.

docs.title: Publisher Provenance
docs.text: Publisher provenance is the answer to "where did these weights actually come from?" A file with a famous model's name can be a conversion by a third party, a fine-tune, or something else. For an evaluation that will be published, provenance matters because your recommendation is only as trustworthy as the file it was measured on. Prefer the original publisher's repository, and when you use a conversion, say who made it.

docs.title: Model Leaderboard and Public Benchmark Score
docs.text:
A model leaderboard ranks models by their scores on shared tests, and a public benchmark score is one model's result on one such test. They are cheap evidence and they answer a question that is rarely yours. A leaderboard of general knowledge or coding says little about whether a model follows a thousand-line skill file or keeps a blank line before every list.

Use them to build a long list, not to make the final decision. A published score is one more claim to be checked against what you measure, as the next concept describes.

docs.title: Publisher Claims and Model Comparison
docs.text:
Publisher claims are the statements a model's publisher makes about it: that it is built for agents, that it leads a benchmark, that it follows instructions better than its size suggests. They are useful as hypotheses, because they name the property the publisher optimized for.

A model comparison sets candidates side by side on the criteria that matter to you, with measured values where you have them and claims marked as claims where you do not. This evaluation's candidate page is one, and its habit is the one to copy: each section states the claim, then states what testing found.

Model Publisher's claim What testing found qwen3.8:27b Built for long agent tasks The cleanest learning graph, and by far the slowest gemma4:26b A fast mixture-of-experts model The fastest, with a graph that had 40 duplicate labels gpt-oss:120b Function calling and structured output Mixed: a tool call printed as plain text in one of two runs muse-glimmer:30b Top tool-use scores in its own comparison Lost the task after a few steps

A Claim Tells You What to Test, Not What You Will Get

A publisher states the property it optimized for, and that is useful. It does not state the conditions under which the property fails, and your workload may be one of them. Read each claim as the first line of a test plan.

docs.title: License Review and Commercial Use Terms
docs.text:
A license review is reading a model's license before relying on it, and recording what it permits. It is not optional for work you will publish, because a recommendation is only useful to readers who are allowed to follow it. Commercial use terms are the part of a license that says whether you may use the model, or what it writes, to make money, and under what conditions.

Three questions cover most reviews. May you use the model for your purpose? May you redistribute what it generates? And are there conditions, such as a revenue threshold above which different terms apply, a required notice, or a prohibited use list? A page's metadata may say one thing and the license file another, so read the file.

docs.title: Apache 2.0 License
docs.text:
The Apache 2.0 license is a permissive open-source license. It allows use, modification, and redistribution, including commercial use, and it includes an express grant of patent rights from the contributors. It requires you to keep the license and copyright notices and to state changes, and it provides no warranty.

For this evaluation it is the easy case: a model under Apache 2.0 raises no question about using its output in a published book. Several of the candidates carry it, and the candidate page records for each whether the license was checked against the file or reported only by secondary sources.

docs.title: Gated Model Access and Access Token Handling
docs.text:
Some publishers gate a model: you must be signed in and must accept their terms before the files can be downloaded. Gating is the publisher's way of recording who agreed to its license. A gated download needs an access token, a credential that identifies your account to the hub.

Access token handling is the discipline of treating that token as a secret. Keep it in an environment variable or the tool's credential store, not in a script. Never commit it, paste it into a chat, or let it appear in a log or a screenshot. Prefer a token limited to read access, and revoke it when the project ends. Chapter 23 returns to tokens as one of the categories that must never be published.

docs.title: Safetensors Format and GGUF Format
docs.text:
Two file formats cover almost every model you will download here.

Safetensors GGUF What it is A format that stores tensors and nothing executable A single file holding weights, tokenizer, and metadata Typical precision 16-bit, sometimes quantized Quantized, often 4-bit or 8-bit Used by Python frameworks and servers such as vLLM llama.cpp and Ollama Why you would pick it You will serve with a Python framework You will serve with Ollama or llama.cpp

The format has a cost that is easy to overlook. Two models in this evaluation were on disk in two formats, the standard one and one in the llama.cpp format, so each took twice its download size. The ten models together took about 397 GB, a good part of a 1 TB disk.

docs.title: Model Download
docs.text:
A model download is fetching a model's files to the machine. There are two routes in this course. The first is the model library of the inference server: for Ollama a single command pulls a named model and its quantization, and this project wraps that in a script that records when every download has finished. The second is the hub's own client, which fetches a repository's files into a cache directory.

ollama pull gemma4:31b

A download is large and takes a long time on a home connection, and it should run inside tmux so that a dropped SSH session does not stop it. Pull deliberately, and say what was pulled, because on a machine you do not administer the disk and the bandwidth are the Administrator's.

docs.title: Model Cache Directory
docs.text: The model cache directory is where a tool keeps downloaded models so that it does not fetch them twice. Ollama keeps its models under ~/.ollama/models by default, and the hub client keeps files under ~/.cache/huggingface. Both locations can be changed with an environment variable. Knowing the directory matters for two reasons: it is where the disk space went, and it is the folder to inspect when you ask whether a model is already present.

docs.title: Checksum Verification
docs.text:
A checksum is a fixed-length value computed from a file's bytes, such that any change to the file changes the value. Checksum verification is computing it for the file you received and comparing it with the value the publisher states. A match means the file is the one the publisher released, unaltered and complete.

sha256sum model.safetensors

The command prints a 64-character SHA-256 value. Compare it with the one on the publisher's file page, or in the checksum list beside the release. A mismatch means a corrupt or substituted file, and the right response is to delete it and download again. Ollama checks each layer's digest as it pulls, so for models fetched through it the verification is built in. For a file you fetch directly, you do it yourself. The install script of Chapter 8 shows the same check applied to a program.

docs.title: Storage Management
docs.text:
Storage management is keeping the disk from filling. A model download that runs out of space fails partway through and can leave a partial file. Check free space before a pull, list what is present with du -sh on the cache directory, and remove what you no longer need with the server's own command, such as ollama rm <model>.

Check Free Space Against the Largest File, Not the Average

Before a pull, run df -h and compare the free space with the model's download size plus a margin for a second format. A 65 GB model on a disk with 60 GB free fails after an hour, and the partial file stays behind.

docs.title: Model Shortlist and Exclusion Rationale
docs.text:
A model shortlist is the written list of candidates you will test, each with its reasons. An exclusion rationale is the reason a model was left off. The second is as important as the first, because a reader who sees a famous model missing will wonder whether you missed it. One line each, tied to a criterion, answers them.

The shortlist for this evaluation, and some of its exclusions, show the form.

Model Decision Rationale gpt-oss:120b Included The largest model that still runs at a usable speed on one unit qwen3.5:122b Left out At 81 GB it was the largest download, and gpt-oss:120b already covered the large tier qwen3-coder:30b Left out About a year old, replaced by newer releases from the same family nemotron3:33b Left out Aimed at understanding video, audio, and documents, which this benchmark does not use A model needing both units Left out The course does not cover multi-machine serving

Do Not Drop a Model for a Fault You Did Not Check

This evaluation set aside its fastest model partly for broken navigation files, and the fault turned out to be a faulty example in the skill that the model had copied. The model had not been retested. An exclusion based on a symptom needs the cause confirmed, and an exclusion that is not retested should say so in its rationale.

docs.title: Diagram: Model Shortlist Filter
docs.text:
Run Model Shortlist Filter Fullscreen

Model Shortlist Filter

Type: microsim sim-id: model-shortlist-filter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/dgx-eval/tree/main/docs/sims/model-fit-by-memory Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply four selection criteria to 8 candidate models for a 128 GB unified-memory machine, deciding shortlist or exclude and naming the first failed criterion, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: model selection criteria, tool-calling reliability, context window, safety headroom, publisher provenance, license review, exclusion rationale (all defined in the sections above this block and in Chapter 11).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 8 candidates the learner commits "Shortlist" or "Exclude" and, for "Exclude", the first failed criterion from the four listed, before the sim reveals the answer. A candidate is correct when the decision equals the Correct decision column and, for an exclusion, the criterion equals the Correct failed criterion column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the candidate cards is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A model that fits in raw memory is acceptable. (2) A large context window makes up for a missing tool-calling feature. (3) A missing license statement is as good as a permissive one. (4) A popular name is proof of provenance.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level work needs the learner to use criteria on new cases, so each candidate fails at most one criterion, and the check order is fixed so that exactly one answer is correct. Mixed shortlist and exclude cases prevent a habit of excluding everything.

Content:

The machine has 128 GB of unified memory, with a 20% headroom, so the usable memory is 102.4 GB. The memory figure on each card is the estimate at a 32,768-token context.

The four criteria, checked in this order: "Tool calling", "Context window", "Fit with headroom", "Publisher and terms". A model passes "Tool calling" when it supports tool calling, passes "Context window" when its window is at least 64,000 tokens, passes "Fit with headroom" when its memory is at most 102.4 GB, and passes "Publisher and terms" when its publisher is identified and its license can be read.

# Card shown to the learner Correct decision Correct failed criterion Why (shown as feedback) 1 Model A: tool calling yes; window 256,000; memory 29 GB; Apache 2.0; publisher identified Shortlist None It passes all four criteria. 2 Model B: tool calling no; window 128,000; memory 20 GB; Apache 2.0; publisher identified Exclude Tool calling A harness acts through tool calls, so a model without them cannot run a skill. 3 Model C: tool calling yes; window 32,000; memory 18 GB; Apache 2.0; publisher identified Exclude Context window 32,000 tokens is below the 64,000 minimum, and the harness prompt alone takes about 19,000. 4 Model D: tool calling yes; window 128,000; memory 118 GB; Apache 2.0; publisher identified Exclude Fit with headroom 118 GB is above the usable 102.4 GB, so it would run with no margin on a unified-memory machine. 5 Model E: tool calling yes; window 256,000; memory 40 GB; license not stated; publisher identified Exclude Publisher and terms Without a license the terms cannot be checked, so a result could not be recommended. 6 Model F: tool calling yes; window 128,000; memory 69 GB; Apache 2.0; publisher identified Shortlist None It passes all four criteria, and 69 GB is under 102.4 GB. 7 Model G: tool calling yes; window 256,000; memory 24 GB; Apache 2.0; publisher an unknown repackager Exclude Publisher and terms The weights cannot be traced to the original publisher, so the measurement would be of an unknown file. 8 Model H: tool calling yes; window 1,000,000; memory 25 GB; custom license published in the repository's license file; publisher identified Shortlist None The terms are readable, so they can be checked, and every other criterion passes.

Provenance: The candidates are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The criteria come from the "Model Selection Criteria" section of this chapter and the headroom from Chapter 11.

Rules: Candidates are shown in the fixed order 1 to 8. A candidate is excluded for the first criterion it fails in the listed order. A "Shortlist" decision is correct only when it passes all four. Each decision is final once confirmed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads card 1.
  2. The learner chooses "Shortlist" or "Exclude", and for "Exclude" the first failed criterion, then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct decision and criterion with the Why text, and marks the card correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for cards 2 to 8. After card 8 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Eight cards, fixed order, one confirmed decision each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct decision, the failed criterion, and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 8 correct".

Starting State: Card 1 is shown with no decision made, and the question on screen is "Does this model go on the shortlist, and if not, which criterion fails first?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that tool calling, a window of at least 64,000 tokens, a fit with headroom, and an identifiable publisher with readable terms are the four criteria, and that the usable memory of a 128 GB machine at 20% headroom is 102.4 GB.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Selection starts from the workload: tool calling, a context window of at least 64,000 tokens, a fit with headroom, and a publisher and license you can check. A model repository is the primary source, and provenance, license, and the model card are read there. Leaderboards and publisher claims are hypotheses to test, not results. Apache 2.0 is the easy license case, a gated model needs a token that is handled as a secret, and the file format decides which server can load it. A download goes into the cache directory, its checksum is compared with the publisher's, and the disk is watched. The shortlist records each decision and, for each exclusion, the criterion that caused it.

A Shortlist That Fits, Is Legal, and Is Explained

You can now turn a long list into a shortlist with a stated reason for every name left off, and download and verify a file safely. Chapter 13 puts a model behind a local endpoint you can send a first prompt to.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
docs.text: Test your understanding of selection criteria, license review, publisher claims, safe downloading, and the documented shortlist with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does a model repository on the Hugging Face Hub hold?
docs.text:
1. A ranked table of models scored on shared tests
  2. A versioned folder of weights, config, model card, and license
  3. A cache directory on your machine for downloaded files
  4. A credential that identifies your account to the hub
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The Hugging Face Hub is the main public site for sharing machine-learning models, and a model repository is one model's home on it: a versioned folder of files that holds the weights, the configuration, a README called the model card, and a license file. The repository page is a primary source, and reading it is the main selection skill. A ranked table of scores is a leaderboard, and a credential for the hub is an access token.

Concept Tested: Model Repository

See: Hugging Face Hub and Model Repository

docs.title: 2. What does the Apache 2.0 license allow?
docs.text:
1. Use for research only, with commercial use forbidden
  2. Use, modification, and redistribution, including commercial use
  3. Use only by organizations below a revenue threshold
  4. Use only after signing in and accepting the publisher's gating terms
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The Apache 2.0 license is a permissive open-source license. It allows use, modification, and redistribution, including commercial use, and it includes an express grant of patent rights from the contributors. It requires you to keep the license and copyright notices and to state changes, and it provides no warranty. For this evaluation it is the easy case: it raises no question about using a model's output in a published book.

Concept Tested: Apache 2.0 License

See: Apache 2.0 License

docs.title: 3. Why should a leaderboard be used to build a long list and not to make the final decision?
docs.text:
1. Its tests rarely measure what your own workload demands
  2. Its scores are computed only for closed models in the cloud
  3. Its rankings change each time a listed model is downloaded
  4. Its scores already include tool-calling reliability
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A model leaderboard ranks models by their scores on shared tests. Those scores are cheap evidence, and they answer a question that is rarely yours: a leaderboard of general knowledge or coding says little about whether a model follows a thousand-line skill file or keeps a blank line before every list. Use leaderboards to build a long list, and treat each published score as one more claim to check against what you measure.

Concept Tested: Model Leaderboard

See: Model Leaderboard and Public Benchmark Score

docs.title: 4. Why does publisher provenance matter for an evaluation that will be published?
docs.text:
1. A repackaged file always takes more space on disk
  2. Only the original publisher's files support tool calling
  3. A recommendation is only as trustworthy as the file measured
  4. A converted file cannot be verified with a checksum
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Publisher provenance answers the question "where did these weights actually come from?" A file with a famous model's name can be a conversion by a third party, a fine-tune, or something else. For an evaluation that will be published, your recommendation is only as trustworthy as the file it was measured on. Prefer the original publisher's repository, and when you use a conversion, say who made it.

Concept Tested: Publisher Provenance

See: Publisher Provenance

docs.title: 5. What does a matching SHA-256 checksum tell you about a downloaded model file?
docs.text:
1. The file is the one the publisher released, unaltered and complete
  2. The file's license permits commercial use of everything it generates
  3. The file will fit in memory with the default headroom
  4. The file is in the format the inference server expects
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A checksum is a fixed-length value computed from a file's bytes, and any change to the file changes the value. Checksum verification computes it for the file you received and compares it with the value the publisher states. A match means the file is the one the publisher released, unaltered and complete. A mismatch means a corrupt or substituted file, to be deleted and downloaded again. It says nothing about license terms or memory fit.

Concept Tested: Checksum Verification

See: Checksum Verification

docs.title: 6. A candidate supports tool calling, has a 48,000-token context window, needs 22 GB of memory, and carries Apache 2.0 from an identified publisher. What is the decision for this course's workload?
docs.text:
1. Shortlist it, because it passes all four selection criteria
  2. Exclude it, because it does not fit with headroom
  3. Exclude it, because its license terms cannot be checked
  4. Exclude it, because its window is under 64,000 tokens
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Model selection criteria come from the workload, not from a leaderboard. This course's workload needs tool calling, a context window of at least 64,000 tokens, a fit with headroom, and an identifiable publisher with checkable terms. This candidate passes three and fails the window test: 48,000 tokens is below the minimum, and the harness prompt alone takes about 19,000 tokens. A small memory footprint does not make up for a window that is too short.

Concept Tested: Model Selection Criteria

See: Model Selection Criteria

docs.title: 7. You are about to pull a 65 GB model, and df -h shows 60 GB free. What should you do?
docs.text:
1. Start the pull, since downloads are compressed on disk
  2. Start the pull inside tmux so it can finish overnight
  3. Free space first, for example with ollama rm <model>
  4. Pull the model in a second file format to save space
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Storage management is keeping the disk from filling. A download that runs out of space fails partway through and can leave a partial file behind, so a 65 GB model on a disk with 60 GB free fails after an hour. Check free space before a pull, and remove what you no longer need with the server's own command, such as ollama rm <model>. Running in tmux protects against a dropped session, not a full disk.

Concept Tested: Storage Management

See: Storage Management

docs.title: 8. A gated model needs an access token, and a script will run the download. Where should the token be kept?
docs.text:
1. In the script, as a variable near the top of the file
  2. In the repository's README, so collaborators can reuse it
  3. In the run log, so the download can be reproduced later
  4. In an environment variable or the tool's credential store
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A gated download needs an access token, a credential that identifies your account to the hub. Access token handling means treating it as a secret: keep it in an environment variable or the tool's credential store, not in a script. Never commit it, paste it into a chat, or let it appear in a log or a screenshot. Prefer a token limited to read access, and revoke it when the project ends.

Concept Tested: Access Token Handling

See: Gated Model Access and Access Token Handling

docs.title: 9. One model was claimed to be fast, tested fastest, and still wrote a graph with 40 duplicate labels. Another claimed top tool-use scores and lost the task after a few steps. What do these results show about publisher claims?
docs.text:
1. Claims are false and should be ignored during selection
  2. Claims are hypotheses to test against your own workload
  3. Claims are reliable whenever they concern model speed
  4. Claims remove the need for a model-only tool-calling test
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Publisher claims are statements a publisher makes about its model, and they are useful as hypotheses because they name the property the publisher optimized for. They do not state the conditions under which that property fails, and your workload may be one of them. One model was as fast as claimed and still produced duplicate labels; another claimed strong tool use and lost the task. A comparison therefore marks claims as claims and records what testing found.

Concept Tested: Publisher Claims

See: Publisher Claims and Model Comparison

docs.title: 10. The evaluation set aside its fastest model partly for broken navigation files, and the fault was later traced to a faulty example in the skill. What was the flaw in that exclusion?
docs.text:
1. The model was too large to fit with headroom on a single unit
  2. The model's license had not been reviewed beforehand
  3. The symptom's cause was unconfirmed and no retest was run
  4. The model's download had not been checksum-verified
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An exclusion rationale is the reason a model was left off the shortlist. Here the navigation fault came from a faulty example in the skill, which the model had copied, and the model had not been retested. An exclusion based on a symptom needs the cause confirmed, and an exclusion that is not retested should say so in its rationale. Otherwise a model is dropped for a fault that was never its own.

Concept Tested: Exclusion Rationale

See: Model Shortlist and Exclusion Rationale

docs.title: References: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
docs.text:
1. Hugging Face - Wikipedia - Covers the company's history, its platform for sharing models and datasets, and the software ecosystem around its Hub. It gives background on the main public repository that this chapter's selection and download steps depend on.

  2. Apache License - Wikipedia - Describes the permissive Apache License 2.0, including its patent grant and conditions, and its compatibility with other licenses. It explains why a model released under Apache 2.0 is the easy case in a license review.

  3. Cryptographic hash function - Wikipedia - Explains how a hash function maps any input to a fixed-size digest, the properties that make digests suitable for security, and their use in verifying file integrity. It underpins the chapter's SHA-256 checksum verification of downloaded model files.

  4. AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models (1st Edition) - Chip Huyen - O'Reilly Media - Huyen lays out a four-step model selection workflow: filter by hard attributes such as license and privacy, narrow with public benchmarks, test with your own evaluation, then monitor. It frames this chapter's criteria-first, claims-as-hypotheses approach.

  5. Natural Language Processing with Transformers (Revised Edition) - Lewis Tunstall, Leandro von Werra, and Thomas Wolf - O'Reilly Media - Widely praised as the practical reference for working with the Hub, written by Hugging Face engineers including co-founder Thomas Wolf. Its code-first chapters show how pretrained checkpoints are loaded from and shared to the Hub, the workflow behind this chapter.

  6. Model Cards - Hugging Face Hub Documentation - Describes the README that accompanies each model, its YAML metadata for license, datasets, base model, and evaluation results, and how custom licenses are declared. It is the primary source this chapter has you read for provenance, terms, and claims.

  7. Safetensors - Hugging Face Safetensors Documentation - Introduces a tensor file format that is safe, unlike pickle, and fast through zero-copy loading, with partial loading of individual tensors. It supports the chapter's comparison of safetensors and GGUF, including why a format that stores nothing executable matters.

  8. GGUF - Hugging Face Hub Documentation - Explains GGUF as a binary format holding both tensors and metadata for llama.cpp-style engines, with a Hub viewer and a table of quantization types and their bits per weight. It covers the format Ollama and llama.cpp load.

  9. Understand caching - Hugging Face Hub Python Library Documentation - Documents the default cache folder under .cache/huggingface in the home directory, how HF_HOME relocates it, and commands to list, verify checksums, and delete cached models. It matches the chapter's model cache directory and storage management sections.

  10. User access tokens - Hugging Face Hub Documentation - Defines read, write, and fine-grained token roles and recommends one token per use, fine-grained tokens for production, and revoking a leaked token. It supports the chapter's guidance to treat a hub token as a secret, preferably read-only.

docs.title: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
Summary
docs.text: This chapter installs the software that loads a model and exposes it through an API. Students configure Ollama, llama.cpp, or vLLM, bind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint to localhost, share it across the tailnet, and run a first-prompt smoke test from curl and Python. They finish with a working local endpoint.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 25 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score tmux Session 1 Inference Server 129 Local API Endpoint 44 Model Loading 20 Ollama 13 Runtime Installation 4 vLLM 2 Server Logs 2 GPU Offload 1 OpenAI-Compatible API 14 localhost Binding 6 Ollama Model Library 4 Runtime Configuration 2 Release Archive 2 llama.cpp 1 Model Keep-Alive 1 Anthropic-Compatible API 1 Chat Completions Endpoint 13 Tailscale Serve 3 Background Service 1 User-Space Installation 1 curl Request 6 Python Client 6 Endpoint Sharing 1 First-Prompt Smoke Test 5

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 4: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
  • Chapter 5: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
  • Chapter 7: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
  • Chapter 9: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
  • Chapter 11: Model Sizing and Fit
  • Chapter 12: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model

From Files on Disk to an Answer on the Wire

A model file does nothing until a server loads it and listens for requests. By the end of this chapter you will have a local endpoint that answers a prompt, bound so that only the right machines can reach it, and a smoke test that tells you in minutes whether it works. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
You have a machine that is reachable, probed, and sized for a model, and a shortlist of models. This chapter connects them with the software in the middle. An inference server loads a model's weights into memory and exposes an interface that other programs call, which is how the harness of Chapters 16 and 17 will eventually reach the model.

The chapter compares the three servers a DGX evaluator is likely to meet, installs one without administrator rights, and keeps it running in a way that survives a dropped connection. It then covers the interface it exposes, decides who may reach it, and ends with a first prompt sent from curl and from Python, and a smoke test that makes that first prompt a repeatable check.

docs.title: Inference Server
docs.text:
An inference server is a program that loads a trained model into memory and answers requests to generate text from it. It owns the hard parts of running a model, which are placing the weights on the GPU, managing the KV cache, scheduling requests, and turning the model's raw output into text, and it hides them behind a simple interface. Everything else in the stack talks to the server and never to the model directly.

Three servers matter for this course, and they differ in what they optimize.

Server What it is Strength Cost Ollama A server with a model library and one-command downloads The quickest path from nothing to an answer Less control over scheduling than the others llama.cpp A C++ inference engine for quantized models in the GGUF format Runs almost anywhere, and is what Ollama is built on You build it and fetch models by hand vLLM A high-throughput server for Python and GPU deployments Many concurrent requests served efficiently The usual route on this hardware is a container

This evaluation chose Ollama. It installs from one archive into a home directory, has the widest ready-made library, and offers an interface the harness can use directly. vLLM remains the candidate for a second pass on whichever model wins, because its strength, serving several sessions at once, is the lever for lowering cost per book.

The Server Is a Loader Plus an API

Hold two jobs in mind. One is the loader, which puts the weights and cache into memory and runs them on the GPU. The other is the interface, which accepts a request and returns text. Almost every problem in this chapter is a problem in one or the other, and knowing which halves your search.

docs.title: Ollama and the Ollama Model Library
docs.text: Ollama is the server this course uses. It runs as one background process, loads models on demand, and serves them over HTTP. The Ollama model library is its catalog of ready-to-pull models, named family:tag such as gemma4:31b, where the tag selects the size and the quantization. Pulling from the library gives you a file in the right format with its digests verified, which removes Chapter 12's download and verification steps for the common case.

docs.title: llama.cpp and vLLM
docs.text: llama.cpp is the C++ engine for running quantized models that Ollama wraps. It can be built and run directly when you need control over a setting that Ollama does not expose, at the price of fetching GGUF files and passing flags by hand. vLLM is a server built for throughput: it batches many requests together on the GPU, so it produces more total tokens per second when several sessions are active. For one benchmark session at a time the gain is small, and for a service that generates many books at once it is the main lever. Chapter 15 explains batching.

docs.title: Runtime Installation, Release Archive, and User-Space Installation
docs.text:
Runtime installation is putting the server on the machine. The usual instructions run an installer script with sudo, which creates a system-wide service. On a machine that belongs to someone else, that is a step you should not take on your own.

A release archive is the alternative: a compressed file of the program, published with a checksum. A user-space installation unpacks it into your own home directory, with no administrator rights and no system changes. This evaluation did exactly that: the pinned Ollama release was downloaded as an archive for the machine's architecture, its SHA-256 was compared with the published value, and it was unpacked under the home directory. The cost is that the server is not a system service and does not start on its own. The benefit is that removing it is deleting one directory.

ssh <user>@<dgx-host> 'bash -s' < src/dgx-setup/install_ollama.sh

docs.title: tmux Session and Background Service
docs.text:
A tmux session is a terminal that keeps running after you disconnect. It lets a server, a download, or a long benchmark continue when your SSH connection drops, and you can reattach later to see what it printed. A background service is the system-level equivalent, managed by the operating system, started at boot, and restarted if it fails.

This evaluation ran the server in a tmux session named ollama, bound to the loopback address, writing its output to a log file.

tmux new-session -d -s ollama \
  "$HOME/opt/ollama/bin/ollama serve > $HOME/opt/ollama/serve.log 2>&1"

The command creates a detached session, -d, named ollama, -s, which runs the server and sends its output to serve.log. Check it with tmux has-session -t ollama, and stop it with tmux kill-session -t ollama. The trade-off is the one that makes a service worth having: a tmux session does not survive a reboot, so after a restart the server is simply not running until someone starts it.

docs.title: Runtime Configuration and Model Keep-Alive
docs.text:
Runtime configuration is the settings that shape how the server runs, which Ollama reads from environment variables. Two matter most here. OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH sets the context window in tokens, which Chapter 11 showed is a memory reservation. OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE sets how long an idle model stays loaded.

Model keep-alive is that idle period. By default a model is unloaded after about five minutes without a request, which frees memory and means the next request pays the load time again. A benchmark that sends prompts minutes apart wants a longer keep-alive, and a machine that shares memory with other work may want a shorter one.

This project's start_ollama.sh takes the context length as an argument and restarts the server with it, so that the setting is chosen on purpose for each model and not inherited.

docs.title: GPU Offload and Model Loading
docs.text:
Model loading is reading a model's file from disk into memory and preparing it to run. It happens on the first request after a model is unloaded, and its duration is the storage read speed of Chapter 5 applied to the model's size. GPU offload is placing the model's layers on the GPU so that the GPU does the work. On a unified-memory machine every layer is offloaded, because the memory is shared.

The command ollama ps shows what is loaded, how much memory it holds, and the share running on the GPU.

ollama ps

A model that shows less than 100% on the GPU is partly running on the CPU, and will be much slower than the figures in this book. On a unified-memory machine that usually points to a context setting so large that the cache and weights no longer fit together.

docs.title: Server Logs
docs.text: Server logs are the text the server writes about what it did: when a model loaded, how much memory it requested, which request arrived, and any error. They are the first place to look when something fails, and the only place some information exists. The log in this project is serve.log beside the install. Two lines to learn to find are the one that reports a model finishing its load and the one that reports a request's timing. This evaluation relied on them to see that, with one model, the server re-read the conversation on every turn.

docs.title: Local API Endpoint
docs.text: A local API endpoint is the network address on the machine where the server accepts requests. Ollama's is 127.0.0.1 on port 11434, so the base address is http://127.0.0.1:11434. Programs on the machine call it as they would a web service, and the server answers with JSON.

docs.title: OpenAI-Compatible API and Chat Completions Endpoint
docs.text:
The OpenAI-compatible API is an interface that copies the request and response shapes of OpenAI's service, which became a de facto standard. A server that offers it can be called by any client written for that service, by changing only the base address. The chat completions endpoint is its main route, at /v1/chat/completions, and it accepts a list of messages and returns the model's reply.

A request has a model name and a list of messages, each with a role and content. The roles are system for standing instructions, user for the person's request, and assistant for the model's earlier replies.

docs.title: Anthropic-Compatible API
docs.text: The Anthropic-compatible API is the same idea with a different shape, copying Anthropic's messages interface. Ollama offers it too, and it is the interface that Claude Code uses, because Claude Code is built to talk to that shape. Chapter 17 points Claude Code at the local endpoint through this route. The model behind it is whichever local model you name, and no request leaves the machine.

docs.title: curl Request
docs.text:
A curl request is the simplest way to call the endpoint: one command, no code. It also removes every layer between you and the server, so a failure here is a failure of the server or the model and not of your program.

Before reading the command, three of its pieces need naming. -H adds a header, and Content-Type: application/json tells the server the body is JSON. -d supplies the body. In the body, model names the model, messages is the conversation, and "stream": false asks for the whole reply in one piece and not token by token.

curl http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "gemma4:31b", "stream": false,
       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the single word: ready"}]}'

The reply is a JSON object. The text is at choices[0].message.content, and a usage block reports prompt_tokens and completion_tokens, which are the two numbers every later performance measurement uses.

docs.title: Python Client
docs.text:
A Python client is a program that makes the same request. The version below uses only the standard library, so it runs on a fresh machine with no pip install. urllib.request.Request builds the call, json.dumps turns the dictionary into the body, and urlopen sends it.

import json, urllib.request

body = {"model": "gemma4:31b", "stream": False,
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the single word: ready"}]}
req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/chat/completions",
                             data=json.dumps(body).encode(),
                             headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=300) as r:
    reply = json.load(r)

print(reply["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
print(reply["usage"])

docs.title: First-Prompt Smoke Test
docs.text:
A smoke test is a quick check that a system is alive at all, named for the old practice of powering a circuit on and watching for smoke. A first-prompt smoke test sends one tiny request and checks four things: the server answered, the reply is not empty, the speed is plausible, and the model is running on the GPU.

The function below extends the client with timing. max_tokens caps the reply length so the test stays short. The speed is the output tokens divided by the elapsed seconds.

import json, time, urllib.request

def smoke(model, base="http://127.0.0.1:11434"):
    body = {"model": model, "stream": False, "max_tokens": 64,
            "messages": [{"role": "user",
                          "content": "Reply with the single word: ready"}]}
    req = urllib.request.Request(base + "/v1/chat/completions",
                                 data=json.dumps(body).encode(),
                                 headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    t0 = time.time()
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=600) as r:
        reply = json.load(r)
    seconds = time.time() - t0
    tokens = reply["usage"]["completion_tokens"]
    return {"reply": reply["choices"][0]["message"]["content"].strip(),
            "seconds": round(seconds, 1),
            "output_tokens": tokens,
            "tokens_per_second": round(tokens / seconds, 1) if seconds else None}

The First Request Includes the Model Load

The first prompt after a model is unloaded pays for reading the file from disk, so its tokens per second looks terrible and is not the model's speed. Send it twice and read the speed from the second. If the second is also slow, the cause is the model, the context, or the memory.

This project's own smoke test, ollama_smoke.py, goes further than one word. It runs five short tasks: Markdown writing, p5.js code, schema-constrained JSON, a tool call, and a 30,000-token prompt. It reports speed, memory, GPU power, and which format rules the output broke. Chapter 19 explains why a model gets tested alone, with a script like this, before it is tested in the harness.

docs.title: localhost Binding
docs.text:
localhost binding is configuring the server to accept connections only from the machine it runs on, by listening on the loopback address 127.0.0.1. A request from any other machine, including one on the same network, is refused before it reaches the server. This is the default and the setting this evaluation used.

The alternative is to bind to all interfaces, written 0.0.0.0, which accepts connections from any machine that can reach the port. That is sometimes what you want, and it is a security decision, because an inference endpoint has no login of its own. Anyone who can send it a request can use the machine's GPU and read whatever the model is allowed to read.

Start Closed and Open Deliberately

Leave the server on the loopback address, confirm that everything works there, and then decide who else needs access and how to give it to exactly them. Binding to every interface to make a tutorial command work is a decision you cannot easily see later.

docs.title: Endpoint Sharing and Tailscale Serve
docs.text:
