Endpoint sharing is making a local endpoint reachable from other machines. A harness on a laptop that needs the model on a DGX is the common reason, and so is a colleague who wants to try the model. There are three ways to do it, and they differ in who ends up able to reach the server.

Method How it works Who can reach the endpoint Changes on the DGX SSH port forward The laptop forwards a local port through an SSH login Only you, for as long as the forward runs None Tailscale Serve The Tailscale client publishes the local port to the tailnet Tailnet members the access rules allow Needs the client and a command on the DGX Bind to all interfaces The server listens on 0.0.0.0 Anyone who can reach the port A server setting

Tailscale Serve is the second route. A single command makes the loopback endpoint available to the tailnet over HTTPS under the machine's tailnet name, while the server itself stays bound to the loopback address. Access is limited to tailnet members, and the access control list of Chapter 9 still applies.

tailscale serve --bg 11434

The flags have changed across Tailscale versions, so check tailscale serve --help for yours.

This evaluation used the first method. A forward costs nothing on the DGX and exposes nothing, and the alternatives would have changed which services the Administrator's machine offers, which was the Administrator's decision to make. The first harness runs reached the model this way, and later runs moved the harness onto the DGX, so the port never needed to leave it.

An Open Inference Endpoint Is an Open GPU

The endpoint has no login. If you bind it to every interface on a network you share, anyone on that network can run prompts on your machine and tie up its memory. Prefer a forward or Tailscale Serve, and test from a second machine that the endpoint is refused where you expect it to be.

docs.title: Diagram: Inference Request Path
docs.text:
Run Inference Request Path Fullscreen

Inference Request Path

Type: workflow sim-id: inference-request-path Library: Mermaid Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/conversational-ai/tree/main/docs/sims/user-query-components Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain what each of 6 stages of a chat completion request does by opening each stage and then locating the stage responsible for each of 4 described events, with at least 3 of 4 correct.

Prerequisites: inference server, local API endpoint, chat completions endpoint, model loading, GPU offload, localhost binding, curl request (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner opens all 6 stages to read their descriptions, then answers 4 questions, each by choosing one of the 6 stages, before any answer is revealed. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct stage column. Mastery is 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Opening a stage is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The first request is slow because the GPU is slow. (2) A wrong model name is rejected by the model. (3) A refused connection is a model problem. (4) Token counts are computed by the client.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level explaining needs the learner to attribute an observed event to a part of the mechanism. Reading each stage first gives the vocabulary, and the questions then require the learner to place events in that structure.

Content:

The six stages, in order, with the description shown when a stage is opened:

# Stage Description shown 1 Client A program such as curl or a Python script builds a JSON body with a model name and messages, and sends it to the endpoint's address. 2 Endpoint The address 127.0.0.1 on port 11434, where the server listens. If nothing is listening, the client's connection is refused. 3 Request handler The server reads the body, checks that the named model exists, and counts the tokens in the prompt. An unknown model is rejected here. 4 Model loader If the model is not in memory, the server reads its file from disk and places it on the GPU. This is the slow part of a first request. 5 Generation The model produces the reply one token at a time on the GPU, reading the weights and the KV cache for each token. 6 Response The server returns JSON with the reply text and a usage block holding the prompt and completion token counts.

The four questions:

# Question shown to the learner Correct stage Why (shown as feedback) 1 The first request after the model was unloaded takes 40 seconds, and the second takes 2. Which stage accounts for the difference? Model loader The first request pays to read the model from disk into memory, which later requests skip. 2 A request names a model that was never pulled and returns "model not found". Which stage rejected it? Request handler The handler checks the model name before any loading or generation. 3 A request fails at once with "connection refused". Which stage is at fault? Endpoint Nothing is listening at the address, usually because the server is not running. 4 Which stage reports how many tokens the prompt and the reply used? Response The server returns the counts in the usage block of its reply.

Provenance: The stages and the questions are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The stage roles come from the "The Server" and "The Interface" sections of this chapter.

Rules: Stages may be opened in any order. The questions are asked in the fixed order 1 to 4, each allows one final choice from the six stages, and exactly one stage is correct for each question.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner opens each of the 6 stages in the flow diagram and reads its description. The questions unlock after all six have been opened.
  2. The learner reads question 1 and chooses the responsible stage, then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct stage and the Why text, and marks the question correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for questions 2 to 4. After question 4 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Four questions, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct stage and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 4 correct".

Starting State: The six-stage flow is shown with no stage opened, and the instruction on screen is "Open each stage to see what it does".

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the endpoint is 127.0.0.1 on port 11434, that the first request pays for model loading, that the usage block reports prompt and completion tokens, and that a connection is refused when no server is listening.

docs.title: Diagram: Endpoint Exposure Classifier
docs.text:
Run Endpoint Exposure Classifier Fullscreen

Endpoint Exposure Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: endpoint-exposure-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish, for 6 configurations of a local endpoint, whether a stated party can reach it, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: localhost binding, endpoint sharing, SSH port forward, Tailscale Serve, home router, access control list (all defined in this chapter and in Chapters 7 and 9).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 6 cases the learner commits "Can reach" or "Cannot reach" before the sim reveals the answer. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct answer column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the cases is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any machine on the same network can reach a localhost-bound server. (2) A port forward needs the server to listen on a network address. (3) Binding to every interface exposes the server to the whole internet regardless of the router. (4) Tailscale Serve opens the server to everyone.

Instructional Rationale: Analyzing exposure requires separating the server's binding, the path a connection takes, and the party's position, so each case varies one of them while the others are fixed. Committing before the reveal separates reasoning from pattern matching.

Content:

# Configuration and party shown to the learner Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 The server is bound to 127.0.0.1. A process running on the DGX itself sends a request to port 11434. Can reach The request comes from the same machine's loopback address, which is exactly what the binding allows. 2 The server is bound to 127.0.0.1. The laptop, on the same tailnet, sends a request to the DGX's tailnet address on port 11434. Cannot reach The server accepts connections only from the loopback address, and this one arrives on the network. 3 The server is bound to 127.0.0.1. The laptop runs an SSH port forward to the DGX and sends a request to its own local port. Can reach The SSH server on the DGX opens the connection from the DGX itself, so it arrives on the loopback address. 4 The server is bound to 0.0.0.0. A tailnet member whom the access rules permit sends a request to the DGX's tailnet address on port 11434. Can reach The server listens on every interface, including the tailnet's, and the rules allow the connection. 5 The server is bound to 0.0.0.0. The DGX is behind a home router with no forwarded port. A stranger on the internet sends a request to the router's public address. Cannot reach The router drops a connection that nobody inside started, so the request never arrives. 6 The server is bound to 127.0.0.1, and Tailscale Serve publishes port 11434 to the tailnet. A tailnet member whom the access rules permit sends a request to the DGX's tailnet name. Can reach Tailscale Serve relays permitted tailnet requests to the loopback address on the DGX's behalf.

Provenance: The cases are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The reasoning comes from Chapters 7 and 9 and the sections of this chapter above.

Rules: Cases are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6. Each allows one final choice. Two parties are never combined, and each case states the binding, the path, and the party in full.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads case 1.
  2. The learner chooses "Can reach" or "Cannot reach" and confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct answer and the Why text, and marks the case correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for cases 2 to 6. After case 6 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Six cases, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct answer and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: Case 1 is shown with no answer chosen, and the question on screen is "Can this party reach the endpoint?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a loopback binding accepts connections only from the same machine, that an SSH forward arrives from the DGX's own loopback address, that binding to every interface needs a decision about who can reach the port, and that Tailscale Serve limits access to permitted tailnet members.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
An inference server loads a model and exposes it behind an API, and the stack above it talks only to the server. Ollama installs without administrator rights from a release archive, runs in a tmux session on the loopback address, and is configured through environment variables for context length and keep-alive. Its OpenAI-compatible endpoint takes a model name and messages and returns the reply with token counts, and its Anthropic-compatible endpoint is the one Claude Code uses. A first-prompt smoke test checks that the server answers, that the reply is not empty, that the speed is plausible, and that the model is on the GPU. Binding to the loopback address keeps the endpoint private, and an SSH forward or Tailscale Serve shares it with only the machines that should have it.

A Local Endpoint That Answers and Stays Private

You can now install a model server without administrator rights, send it a first prompt from curl and Python, and say exactly who can reach it. Chapter 14 turns to the ten models this evaluation puts behind such an endpoint.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
docs.text: Test your understanding of inference servers, user-space installation, local endpoints, the first-prompt smoke test, and endpoint exposure with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is an inference server?
docs.text:
1. A program that trains a model's parameters from data
  2. A program that loads a model and answers generation requests
  3. A public hub that hosts model repositories for download
  4. A harness that runs an agent loop and executes its tools
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An inference server is a program that loads a trained model into memory and answers requests to generate text from it. It owns the hard parts of running a model: placing the weights on the GPU, managing the KV cache, scheduling requests, and turning raw output into text. Everything else in the stack talks to the server and never to the model directly. It does not train models, and the harness is a separate layer that calls it.

Concept Tested: Inference Server

See: Inference Server

docs.title: 2. What does an OpenAI-compatible API let you do with a local server?
docs.text:
1. Send requests to the server without naming a model
  2. Reach a localhost-bound server from any other machine you own
  3. Download models from the server's library by their tags
  4. Reuse OpenAI clients by changing only the base address
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The OpenAI-compatible API copies the request and response shapes of OpenAI's service, which became a de facto standard. A server that offers it can be called by any client written for that service, by changing only the base address. Its main route is the chat completions endpoint at /v1/chat/completions, which accepts a model name and a list of messages and returns the reply. Compatibility concerns the request format, not who can reach the server.

Concept Tested: OpenAI-Compatible API

See: OpenAI-Compatible API and Chat Completions Endpoint

docs.title: 3. What happens by default to a loaded model after about five minutes without a request?
docs.text:
1. It is unloaded, and the next request pays the load time again
  2. It is deleted from disk and must be pulled a second time before use
  3. It moves from the GPU to the CPU in order to save power
  4. It stays loaded until someone restarts the server
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Model keep-alive is how long an idle model stays loaded, set with OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE. By default a model is unloaded after about five minutes without a request, which frees memory and means the next request pays the load time again. A benchmark that sends prompts minutes apart wants a longer keep-alive, and a machine that shares memory with other work may want a shorter one. Unloading removes the model from memory, not from disk.

Concept Tested: Model Keep-Alive

See: Runtime Configuration and Model Keep-Alive

docs.title: 4. What is the cost of a user-space installation of the server, compared with the usual system-wide installer?
docs.text:
1. The server cannot use the GPU without root access
  2. The server is not a system service and will not start on its own
  3. The server can load only models smaller than system RAM
  4. The server must be reinstalled after each dropped SSH session ends
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A user-space installation unpacks a release archive into your own home directory, with no administrator rights and no system changes. The cost is that the server is not a system service and does not start on its own. The benefit is that removing it is deleting one directory. On a machine that belongs to someone else, a system-wide installer run with sudo is not a step to take on your own, so the trade is worth making.

Concept Tested: User-Space Installation

See: Runtime Installation, Release Archive, and User-Space Installation

docs.title: 5. Why is binding the server to 0.0.0.0 a security decision?
docs.text:
1. The endpoint has no login, so anyone who reaches it can use it
  2. The setting disables the encryption on the tailnet's whole data plane
  3. The setting sends each prompt to the model's publisher
  4. The endpoint then demands administrator rights per request
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Localhost binding makes the server listen only on the loopback address 127.0.0.1, so a request from any other machine is refused before it reaches the server. Binding to 0.0.0.0 accepts connections from any machine that can reach the port. That is a security decision because an inference endpoint has no login of its own: anyone who can send it a request can use the machine's GPU and read whatever the model is allowed to read.

Concept Tested: localhost Binding

See: localhost Binding

docs.title: 6. What does running the server in a tmux session protect against, and what does it not?
docs.text:
1. It survives a dropped SSH connection but not a reboot
  2. It survives a reboot but not a dropped SSH connection
  3. It restarts the server automatically whenever it fails
  4. It keeps other tailnet members from reaching the server
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A tmux session is a terminal that keeps running after you disconnect, so a server, a download, or a long benchmark continues when your SSH connection drops, and you can reattach later. It does not survive a reboot: after a restart the server is not running until someone starts it. Starting at boot and restarting after a failure are what a background service managed by the operating system provides.

Concept Tested: tmux Session

See: tmux Session and Background Service

docs.title: 7. Your first smoke-test request after a model was unloaded reports a very low tokens-per-second figure. What should you do before judging the model's speed?
docs.text:
1. Lower the context length and restart the server
  2. Switch to a smaller quantization of the same model
  3. Send the request again and read the second result
  4. Rebind the server to all interfaces and then try again
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A first-prompt smoke test sends one tiny request and checks that the server answered, the reply is not empty, the speed is plausible, and the model is on the GPU. The first prompt after a model is unloaded pays for reading the file from disk, so its tokens per second looks terrible and is not the model's speed. Send it twice and read the speed from the second. If the second is also slow, look at the model, the context, or the memory.

Concept Tested: First-Prompt Smoke Test

See: First-Prompt Smoke Test

docs.title: 8. On a unified-memory machine, ollama ps shows a loaded model at less than 100% on the GPU. What is the usual cause to check?
docs.text:
1. A keep-alive period that has been set too short
  2. A context setting too large for weights and cache to fit
  3. A server that is bound to the loopback address only
  4. A model that was pulled from the Ollama model library
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. GPU offload is placing the model's layers on the GPU, and on a unified-memory machine every layer is offloaded because the memory is shared. ollama ps shows what is loaded, how much memory it holds, and the share running on the GPU. A model below 100% is partly on the CPU and will be much slower. On a unified-memory machine that usually points to a context setting so large that the cache and weights no longer fit together.

Concept Tested: GPU Offload

See: GPU Offload and Model Loading

docs.title: 9. A permitted member of the tailnet needs to reach a local endpoint, and the server must stay bound to the loopback address. Which method fits?
docs.text:
1. Bind the server to 0.0.0.0 so every interface listens
  2. Forward a public port on the home router to the server
  3. Hand the member your private SSH key for a port forward
  4. Publish the port to the tailnet with Tailscale Serve
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Endpoint sharing makes a local endpoint reachable from other machines. Tailscale Serve publishes the loopback port to the tailnet over HTTPS while the server itself stays bound to the loopback address, and access is limited to tailnet members the access rules allow. Binding to 0.0.0.0 opens the port to anyone who can reach it, and a private key is never handed to another person. An SSH port forward reaches only the person who runs it.

Concept Tested: Tailscale Serve

See: Endpoint Sharing and Tailscale Serve

docs.title: 10. A Python program on the DGX gets no usable reply from the endpoint, but the same request sent with curl from the same machine succeeds. What does this tell you?
docs.text:
1. The model is not loaded on the GPU
  2. The server is bound to the wrong interface
  3. The server and model work; the fault is in the client
  4. The model's context window is too small for the prompt
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A curl request is the simplest way to call the endpoint: one command and no code. It removes every layer between you and the server, so a failure there is a failure of the server or the model and not of your program. Here curl succeeds from the same machine, so the server is running, the model answers, and the binding allows the request. What remains is the client program, such as its request body or how it reads the reply.

Concept Tested: curl Request

See: curl Request

docs.title: References: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
docs.text:
1. llama.cpp - Wikipedia - Describes the C++ library for running quantized language models locally, its architecture, and the GGUF file format it uses. It supports the chapter's account of llama.cpp as the engine that Ollama is built on.

  2. Ollama - Wikipedia - Covers the platform for running language models locally, its llama.cpp backend, model library, and REST API on port 11434, and reports of servers exposed by binding to 0.0.0.0. It backs the chapter's warning about opening an endpoint.

  3. Localhost - Wikipedia - Defines localhost as the hostname for the local computer, mapped to loopback addresses 127.0.0.1 and ::1, and covers name resolution and packet handling. It grounds the chapter's localhost binding and why other machines are refused.

  4. Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (9th Edition) - James F. Kurose and Keith W. Ross - Pearson - Kurose and Ross are known for teaching networking top-down, beginning with application-layer protocols such as HTTP and Python socket programming. That order mirrors this chapter's path from an API call to ports, binding, and reachability.

  5. TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols (2nd Edition) - Kevin R. Fall and W. Richard Stevens - Addison-Wesley Professional - Stevens taught protocols through captured packet traces from real systems, so each exchange can be read line by line. That method shows what a connection to a listening port, or a refused one, looks like on the wire.

  6. OpenAI compatibility - Ollama Documentation - Lists the /v1/chat/completions features Ollama supports, the local base URL, and runnable curl, Python, and JavaScript examples. It is the reference for the chapter's first-prompt requests and for pointing existing clients at a local model.

  7. Ollama FAQ - Ollama Documentation - Answers configuration questions: the default 127.0.0.1:11434 binding and OLLAMA_HOST, keep-alive, context length, reading ollama ps output, model storage paths, and running as a Linux service. It backs this chapter's runtime configuration and localhost binding sections.

  8. llama.cpp HTTP Server - llama.cpp Project on GitHub - Documents llama-server, which serves GGUF models through OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible routes with parallel decoding, continuous batching, prompt caching, and a default 127.0.0.1 binding. It shows the build-it-yourself alternative to Ollama.

  9. vLLM Documentation - vLLM Project - Introduces vLLM as a high-throughput serving library with PagedAttention, continuous batching, and an OpenAI-compatible API server. It supports the chapter's comparison of vLLM as the batching server for a second-pass evaluation.

  10. Tailscale Serve - Tailscale Documentation - Explains how tailscale serve shares a local service only within a tailnet, with HTTPS proxying and background mode, and how it differs from public Funnel. It is the reference for sharing an endpoint while the server stays on loopback.

docs.title: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the model families and the ten candidates under evaluation. It records what each family offers, where each candidate comes from, and why each was included or excluded. Students finish able to justify the candidate list with evidence rather than reputation.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 18 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Qwen Family 3 Gemma Family 3 Mistral Family 3 Nemotron Family 2 gpt-oss Family 2 Granite Family 2 Llama Family 1 Phi Family 1 devstral-small-2:24b 1 qwen3.6:35b 1 gemma4:26b 1 nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 1 mistral-medium-3.5:128b 1 gpt-oss:120b 1 granite4.2:30b 1 qwen3.8:27b 1 gemma4:31b 1 muse-glimmer:30b 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 11: Model Sizing and Fit
  • Chapter 12: Selecting and Downloading an Open-Weight Model
  • Chapter 13: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints

Ten Candidates, Each With a Reason

A list of model names tells you nothing until each one has a reason attached. By the end of this chapter you will be able to say, for every candidate in this evaluation, where it came from, why it was chosen, and what the first round of testing showed. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 12 gave you the criteria for choosing a model, and this chapter shows the criteria applied. It introduces the model families that publish open-weight models, then the ten candidates this evaluation tested, with the reason for each and the first-round result.

Two cautions apply to everything here. The first is that these are measurements from one set of runs, on one kind of machine, with one run of each test, and they are provisional. The second is that the model landscape changes within months, so the specific names will date. The reasoning the chapter models, which is a claim, a test, and a result for each candidate, is the part meant to last.

docs.title: The Families
docs.text: A model family is a series of models from one publisher that share a design lineage and a naming scheme. Members of a family usually differ in size and in whether they are specialized for code or for general use. Knowing the family tells you what to expect about licensing, tool-calling support, and how sizes relate to each other.

docs.title: Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral
docs.text:
The Qwen family comes from Alibaba. Its recent releases are aimed at long agent tasks and tool use, and a mid-2026 survey reported Qwen models holding most of the top places on a public function-calling leaderboard. It spans dense models and mixture-of-experts models. Two candidates are here: qwen3.8:27b and qwen3.6:35b.

The Gemma family comes from Google. It is offered in sizes that fit a single machine, with both a dense model and a mixture-of-experts model at similar total size in the Gemma 4 release, which makes a clean comparison of the two designs. Two candidates are here: gemma4:26b and gemma4:31b.

The Mistral family comes from Mistral AI, a French company. It includes a large dense general model and a smaller one built for coding agents. Two candidates are here: mistral-medium-3.5:128b and devstral-small-2:24b.

docs.title: Nemotron, gpt-oss, and Granite
docs.text:
The Nemotron family comes from NVIDIA, which also makes the hardware. Its models are positioned for agents and for efficient throughput, and its newer releases use mixture-of-experts designs with a very long context window. One candidate is here: nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b.

The gpt-oss family comes from OpenAI, and it is the company's open-weight release. It is a mixture-of-experts model released with function calling, structured output, and adjustable reasoning effort. One candidate is here: gpt-oss:120b.

The Granite family comes from IBM. It is positioned for enterprise use, with a plain Apache 2.0 license, structured output, and documentation of its training data governance. One candidate is here: granite4.2:30b.

docs.title: Llama and Phi
docs.text:
The Llama family is Meta's long-running open-weight line, and the one most tutorials were written for. None of the ten candidates carries the Llama name. The one Meta model on the list, muse-glimmer:30b, is a newer line that its publisher describes as built for local agents.

The Phi family is Microsoft's line of small models, designed to give strong results at a size that fits modest hardware. None of the ten candidates is a Phi model, because the benchmark's long skills and 64,000-token minimum favored larger models. A reader with less memory would start here.

Family Publisher Candidates in this evaluation Qwen Alibaba qwen3.8:27b, qwen3.6:35b Gemma Google gemma4:26b, gemma4:31b Mistral Mistral AI mistral-medium-3.5:128b, devstral-small-2:24b Nemotron NVIDIA nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b gpt-oss OpenAI gpt-oss:120b Granite IBM granite4.2:30b Llama Meta None Phi Microsoft None

The one remaining candidate, muse-glimmer:30b, is from Meta and is listed with the candidates below.

docs.title: The Ten Candidates
docs.text: Each entry gives the claim that put the model on the list and what the first round of testing found. The first round was one run of each test, so a result is a first observation, not a verdict.

docs.title: The Qwen Candidates
docs.text:
qwen3.8:27b is the newest Qwen release and is described by its publisher as improved for long-running agent tasks. It produced the cleanest learning graph of the first stage, with exactly 200 concepts, no cycles, and no duplicate labels. It took 102 minutes where the five others that finished took 6 to 22, because the server re-read almost the whole conversation on every turn. In the later chapter-writing stage it was too slow to finish a chapter inside 90 minutes.

qwen3.6:35b is the release before it, in a larger mixture-of-experts form with about 3 billion parameters active for each token. It was the best combination of speed and correctness in the first round: 83 to 105 tokens per second and a learning graph in 22 minutes with every file present. The graph is looser than the Qwen 3.8 one, with 19 concepts that have no prerequisite.

docs.title: The Gemma Candidates
docs.text:
gemma4:31b is a dense model of 30.7 billion parameters and the most consistent rule-follower in the tests. It passed every model-only rule twice and ended every smoke run with a site that builds. It ran at 28 to 40 tokens per second. Its first learning-graph attempt was lost when a machine froze at a context setting that is now treated as unsafe, and its second finished in 21 minutes without the taxonomy page or the navigation entries.

gemma4:26b is the mixture-of-experts sibling, with 25.2 billion parameters and 3.8 billion active. It was the fastest model tested at 86 to 130 tokens per second, and it finished the learning graph in under six minutes. That graph has 40 duplicate concept labels out of 200, which is a serious flaw. A model this fast can afford a second attempt, but something has to notice that one is needed.

docs.title: The Mistral Candidates
docs.text:
mistral-medium-3.5:128b is a dense model of 128 billion parameters, promoted for instruction and system-prompt adherence. It loaded and ran, at 3 tokens per second, and used 88 GiB at a 32,000-token context, so no context of 64,000 tokens or more would fit. On one unit of this hardware it is not usable.

devstral-small-2:24b is built to drive software-engineering agents and has a 384,000-token window in a 15 GB download. It did no work in either harness test: both times it wrote its first tool call as plain text, the harness saw no tool call, and the run ended after one turn.

docs.title: The Remaining Candidates
docs.text:
nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b is NVIDIA's model for always-on agents, with 3 billion active parameters and a one-million-token context window. It was as fast as claimed, at 84 to 105 tokens per second, and finished the learning graph in 18 minutes with 199 concepts, one short of the 200 asked for. It made 140 tool calls, nearly three times as many as any other model.

gpt-oss:120b is the largest model that still ran at a usable speed, at 38 to 44 tokens per second, because only about 5 billion of its 117 billion parameters are active. It finished the learning graph in 17 minutes with every tool call succeeding, and the graph is thin: 19 concepts connected to nothing. In one run it printed a tool call as plain text.

granite4.2:30b is the conservative choice, with a plain Apache 2.0 license and structured-output support. It was too slow to finish: 12 tokens per second, and it was stopped at the 150-minute limit having produced only the concept list.

muse-glimmer:30b is Meta's model, positioned around instruction following and recovery in unattended agent runs. It lost the task after a few steps in the harness, which looks like a context problem: its first prompt took 35,000 tokens where the others took 17,000 to 21,000.

docs.title: The First Round at a Glance
docs.text:
The table gathers the first-round measurements. It is the answer to the question this chapter began with, and it is also a reminder of how much of the ordering a single stage could not have predicted.

Model Parameters Download Speed (tokens/s) First-stage result qwen3.8:27b 27 billion 17 GB 26 200 concepts in 102 minutes, no structural fault gemma4:31b 30.7 billion, dense 20 GB 28–40 200 concepts in 21 minutes, two files missing muse-glimmer:30b 30 billion 18 GB 13 No graph; lost the task qwen3.6:35b 35 billion, about 3 active 22 GB 83–105 200 concepts in 22 minutes, 19 without prerequisites gemma4:26b 25.2 billion, 3.8 active 18 GB 86–130 200 concepts in under 6 minutes, 40 duplicate labels nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 30 billion, 3 active 25 GB 84–105 199 concepts in 18 minutes mistral-medium-3.5:128b 128 billion, dense 80 GB 3 Not run; no usable context fits gpt-oss:120b 117 billion, 5.1 active 65 GB 38–44 200 concepts in 17 minutes, 19 unconnected devstral-small-2:24b 24 billion 15 GB 15 No graph; tool call written as text granite4.2:30b about 30 billion, dense 17 GB 12 Stopped at 150 minutes; concept list only

The speed for qwen3.8:27b was measured on one long turn and is not a range, and the speeds of the three models with a failed first stage come from the model-only test.

One Run Is an Observation, Not a Ranking

Every figure in this table comes from a single attempt, and a model that failed once may succeed on a second try, as one candidate did after its skill was corrected. Treat the first round as a way to decide what to test further, and repeat a run before you write a sentence that begins "model X cannot".

docs.title: Diagram: Candidate Model Explorer
docs.text:
Run Candidate Model Explorer Fullscreen

Candidate Model Explorer

Type: chart sim-id: candidate-model-explorer Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/tracking-ai-course/tree/main/docs/sims/lm-arena-timeline Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare the ten candidate models on parameter count, generation speed, and download size by answering 5 questions from a bubble chart, with at least 4 of 5 correct.

Prerequisites: dense model, mixture of experts, active parameters, tokens per second, model download (all defined in Chapters 11 and 12 and in this chapter).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 5 questions the learner selects one model from the ten before the sim reveals the answer. A selection is correct when it equals the Correct model column. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Hovering over a bubble to read its values is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A bigger model is a faster model. (2) A bigger download means more parameters. (3) A mixture-of-experts model needs less memory. (4) The model with the most parameters is the best choice.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level comparing needs the learner to hold several dimensions at once, so a bubble chart places parameters, speed, and download size together, and questions that need two dimensions at a time prevent a single-dimension answer.

Content:

The chart plots each of ten models as a bubble. The horizontal position is the parameter count in billions, the vertical position is the generation speed in tokens per second, and the bubble's size is the download size in gigabytes.

Model Parameters (billions) Speed (tokens/s) Download (GB) qwen3.8:27b 27 26 17 gemma4:31b 30.7 34 20 muse-glimmer:30b 30 13 18 qwen3.6:35b 35 94 22 gemma4:26b 25.2 108 18 nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 30 95 25 mistral-medium-3.5:128b 128 3 80 gpt-oss:120b 117 41 65 devstral-small-2:24b 24 15 15 granite4.2:30b 30 12 17

The five questions:

# Question shown to the learner Correct model Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which model has the highest generation speed? gemma4:26b At 108 tokens per second it is the highest point on the chart. 2 Which model has the largest download? mistral-medium-3.5:128b At 80 GB it is the largest bubble. 3 Among models faster than 80 tokens per second, which has the largest download? nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b The three above 80 are 18, 22, and 25 GB, and 25 GB is the largest. 4 Which model has more than 100 billion parameters and runs faster than 30 tokens per second? gpt-oss:120b It has 117 billion parameters at 41 tokens per second, and the other model above 100 billion runs at 3. 5 Which model has the fewest parameters? devstral-small-2:24b At 24 billion it is the leftmost bubble.

Provenance: The values are the midpoints of the measured ranges in this chapter's table, rounded to whole tokens per second, and the sim labels them "measured, one run each, provisional". The speed for qwen3.8:27b was measured on one long turn. The speeds for muse-glimmer:30b, devstral-small-2:24b, granite4.2:30b, and mistral-medium-3.5:128b come from the model-only test.

Rules: Questions are shown in the fixed order 1 to 5. Each allows one final choice among the ten models. Exactly one model is correct for each question under the data in Content.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner hovers over bubbles to read each model's three values.
  2. The learner reads question 1 and clicks the bubble for the model they choose, then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct model and the Why text, and marks the question correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for questions 2 to 5. After question 5 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Five questions, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct model and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 5 correct".

Starting State: The chart is shown with all ten bubbles, no question answered, and the instruction on screen is "Hover over a bubble to read its values".

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states a fastest speed of 108 tokens per second for gemma4:26b, an 80 GB download for mistral-medium-3.5:128b, 117 billion parameters at about 41 tokens per second for gpt-oss:120b, and 3 tokens per second for the 128-billion-parameter model.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Eight families publish the open-weight models a DGX evaluator is likely to meet, and ten candidates from six of them were tested. Each had a claim that put it on the list and a first-round result that qualified the claim: the model built for agents was the cleanest and the slowest, the fastest model wrote a graph with duplicate labels, the largest dense model did not fit with a usable context, and two models wrote their tool calls as text and did no work at all. None of that could have been read from a name, a size, or a leaderboard.

Every Name Now Has a Reason

You can now say where each of the ten candidates came from, why it was tested, and what the first round showed, and you know that each number is one observation and not a ranking. Chapter 15 measures why the same model can be fast in one test and slow in another.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
docs.text: Test your understanding of the open-weight model families, the ten candidates, and what the first round of testing showed with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does the Gemma 4 release offer that makes a clean comparison of two model designs?
docs.text:
1. A coding model and a general model released under the same license
  2. Two dense models that differ only in context window
  3. A cloud model and a local model with identical weights
  4. A dense model and a mixture-of-experts model of similar size
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Gemma family comes from Google and is offered in sizes that fit a single machine. Its Gemma 4 release includes both a dense model and a mixture-of-experts model at similar total size, which makes a clean comparison of the two designs. The two candidates here are gemma4:31b, the dense one, and gemma4:26b, the mixture-of-experts sibling. A general model alongside a coding model describes the Mistral family's pair instead.

Concept Tested: Gemma Family

See: Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral

docs.title: 2. How is IBM's Granite family positioned?
docs.text:
1. For always-on agents, with a one-million-token context window
  2. For enterprise use, with a plain Apache 2.0 license
  3. For coding agents, with a 384,000-token context window
  4. For modest hardware, with strong results at a small size
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The Granite family comes from IBM. It is positioned for enterprise use, with a plain Apache 2.0 license, structured output, and documentation of its training data governance. Its one candidate here is granite4.2:30b, the conservative choice. Always-on agents and a one-million-token window describe NVIDIA's Nemotron candidate, and strong results at a size that fits modest hardware describe Microsoft's Phi family.

Concept Tested: Granite Family

See: Nemotron, gpt-oss, and Granite

docs.title: 3. Why is none of the ten candidates a Phi model?
docs.text:
1. Phi models carry a license that forbids published use
  2. The long skills and 64,000-token minimum favored larger models
  3. Phi models cannot be served through the Ollama library
  4. The Phi family has no model that supports tool calling
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The Phi family is Microsoft's line of small models, designed to give strong results at a size that fits modest hardware. None of the ten candidates is a Phi model because the benchmark's long skills and its 64,000-token minimum context favored larger models. That is a statement about this workload, not about the family's quality: a reader with less memory than this evaluation's unit would start with Phi.

Concept Tested: Phi Family

See: Llama and Phi

docs.title: 4. Why could gpt-oss:120b run at a usable speed despite having 117 billion parameters?
docs.text:
1. Only about 5 billion of its parameters are active per token
  2. Its weights are stored at 16 bits instead of 4 bits
  3. It ran on both DGX units at once to share the load
  4. Its context window was limited to 32,000 tokens
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. gpt-oss:120b is a mixture-of-experts model. Only about 5 billion of its 117 billion parameters are active for each token, so it ran at 38 to 44 tokens per second and was the largest model that still ran at a usable speed. The dense mistral-medium-3.5:128b, which uses all of its parameters for every token, ran at 3 tokens per second. Storing weights at 16 bits would add memory and no speed.

Concept Tested: gpt-oss:120b

See: The Remaining Candidates

docs.title: 5. Why did qwen3.8:27b take 102 minutes for the first stage when the five other models that finished took 6 to 22?
docs.text:
1. Its graph had 40 duplicate labels that had to be repaired by hand
  2. It was stopped and restarted at the 150-minute limit
  3. The server re-read almost the whole conversation each turn
  4. Its download was the largest of the ten candidates
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. qwen3.8:27b produced the cleanest learning graph of the first stage: exactly 200 concepts, no cycles, and no duplicate labels. It took 102 minutes where the five others that finished took 6 to 22, because the server re-read almost the whole conversation on every turn. The delay came from that repeated reading, not from a faulty graph, and in the later chapter-writing stage the model was too slow to finish a chapter inside 90 minutes.

Concept Tested: qwen3.8:27b

See: The Qwen Candidates

docs.title: 6. You want a first-stage model that combines speed with a complete, correct result, judging only by the first round. Which candidate fits best?
docs.text:
1. gemma4:26b: under 6 minutes, with 40 duplicate labels
  2. qwen3.8:27b: no structural fault, in 102 minutes
  3. granite4.2:30b: stopped at the 150-minute limit
  4. qwen3.6:35b: 22 minutes, with every file present
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. qwen3.6:35b was the best combination of speed and correctness in the first round: 83 to 105 tokens per second and a learning graph in 22 minutes with every file present. Its graph is looser than the Qwen 3.8 one, with 19 concepts that have no prerequisite, but the faster gemma4:26b wrote 40 duplicate labels and the cleaner qwen3.8:27b needed 102 minutes. Each figure is a single run, so the choice is provisional.

Concept Tested: qwen3.6:35b

See: The Qwen Candidates

docs.title: 7. You plan to use gemma4:26b for the learning-graph stage because it finishes in under six minutes. Given its first-round result, what should your pipeline add?
docs.text:
1. A longer time limit, since it ran out of time in that round
  2. A larger context window, since its first prompt was too long
  3. A check for duplicate labels that triggers a second attempt
  4. A second unit, since the model does not fit on one machine
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. gemma4:26b was the fastest model tested and finished the learning graph in under six minutes, but that graph has 40 duplicate concept labels out of 200, which is a serious flaw. A model this fast can afford a second attempt, but something has to notice that one is needed. A structural check for duplicate labels is that something. Time limits and memory were not its problem in the first round.

Concept Tested: gemma4:26b

See: The Gemma Candidates

docs.title: 8. granite4.2:30b was stopped at the 150-minute limit in its single first-round run. Which statement may a report make?
docs.text:
1. In one run it reached the time limit with only a concept list
  2. The model cannot produce a learning graph on this kind of hardware
  3. The model is ranked last among the ten candidates tested
  4. The Granite family is unsuitable for textbook generation
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Every first-round figure comes from a single attempt, so a result is a first observation, not a verdict. granite4.2:30b ran at 12 tokens per second and was stopped at the 150-minute limit having produced only the concept list, and a report may say exactly that. A model that failed once may succeed on a second try, so repeat a run before writing a sentence that begins "model X cannot". One run is not a ranking.

Concept Tested: granite4.2:30b

See: The First Round at a Glance

docs.title: 9. muse-glimmer:30b lost the task after a few steps in the harness. Which observation points to the likely cause?
docs.text:
1. It ran at only 3 tokens per second in the model-only smoke test
  2. Its download was the largest of the ten candidates
  3. Its first prompt took 35,000 tokens, far more than the others
  4. It wrote 40 duplicate concept labels into its own learning graph
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. muse-glimmer:30b lost the task after a few steps in the harness, which looks like a context problem: its first prompt took 35,000 tokens where the others took 17,000 to 21,000. That is a reading of the evidence, not a confirmed diagnosis. The other observations belong to different candidates: 3 tokens per second and the largest download were mistral-medium-3.5:128b, and the 40 duplicate labels were gemma4:26b.

Concept Tested: muse-glimmer:30b

See: The Remaining Candidates

docs.title: 10. What trade-off does the first round show between the dense gemma4:31b and its mixture-of-experts sibling gemma4:26b?
docs.text:
1. The dense model was faster, and the sibling followed rules better
  2. The dense model needed far more memory for the same speed
  3. Both ran at the same speed, and only their licenses differed
  4. The dense model was slower but the more consistent rule-follower
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. gemma4:31b is a dense model and was the most consistent rule-follower in the tests: it passed every model-only rule twice and ended every smoke run with a site that builds, at 28 to 40 tokens per second. Its mixture-of-experts sibling gemma4:26b was the fastest model tested, at 86 to 130 tokens per second, and wrote a graph with 40 duplicate labels. The pair trades speed against rule-following at a similar total size.

Concept Tested: gemma4:31b

See: The Gemma Candidates

docs.title: References: Open-Weight Model Families and Candidate Models
docs.text:
1. Gemma (language model) - Wikipedia - Covers Google DeepMind's Gemma family, from its February 2024 debut through its architecture and variants. It gives background on the family behind two of the ten candidates.

  2. Mistral AI - Wikipedia - Profiles the French company, its funding, and its models, including the Apache 2.0 Mistral 7B and Mixtral 8x7B and the Devstral coding models. It supplies context for the Mistral family and the two candidates drawn from it.

  3. Llama (language model) - Wikipedia - Traces Meta's Llama releases from 2023 through Llama 4, covering architecture, training data, and the licensing disputes over calling it open source. It backs the chapter's Llama entry and Chapter 12's license review.

  4. Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) - Sebastian Raschka - Manning - Widely praised for building a GPT-style model line by line; its companion repository extends the approach to Llama 3.2, Qwen3 dense and mixture-of-experts, and Gemma 3. That shows how the families differ from one baseline.

  5. AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models (1st Edition) - Chip Huyen - O'Reilly Media - Widely praised for treating model choice as an engineering trade-off; Chapter 2 covers model architecture and size, and Chapter 4 weighs building against buying. That frames why each family and size became a candidate.

  6. The Big LLM Architecture Comparison - Sebastian Raschka, Ahead of AI - Compares the architectures of recent open-weight models, including Qwen3, Gemma, Mistral Small, Llama 4, and gpt-oss, covering mixture-of-experts routing and attention variants that cut KV cache memory. It shows what separates the families the chapter lists.

  7. Ollama Model Library - Ollama - Catalogs ready-to-pull models by family and size, with capability tags such as tools, thinking, and vision and pull counts. It is where this chapter's family:tag names come from and where tool-calling support is checked before a download.

  8. Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard - UC Berkeley Gorilla Project - Ranks models on how accurately they call functions, across versions that add multi-turn and agentic evaluation, and reports estimated cost and latency. It is the kind of public function-calling leaderboard the chapter treats as a hypothesis, not a result.

  9. openai/gpt-oss - OpenAI on GitHub - Documents the gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b mixture-of-experts models, with 117 and 21 billion parameters, 5.1 and 3.6 billion active, an Apache 2.0 license, and Ollama and vLLM usage. It is the primary source for the chapter's gpt-oss candidate.

  10. Qwen3 - QwenLM on GitHub - Presents the Qwen3 dense models and mixture-of-experts models such as 30B-A3B, whose name marks 3 billion active parameters, all under Apache 2.0, with thinking mode and local-serving instructions. It shows how the Qwen family names its sizes.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter measures and tunes inference speed. Students collect tokens per second, time to first token, and latency, then adjust quantization, context length, batch size, concurrency, prompt caching, and sampling while watching GPU use, memory pressure, and thermal throttling. They finish able to break a run's wall-clock time into its causes.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 22 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Sampling Parameters 3 Temperature Setting 1 Top-p and Top-k 1 GPU Utilization 3 Prompt Processing Speed 15 Tokens per Second 11 Prompt Caching 9 Batch Size 4 Context Length Setting 1 Prompt Re-Reading 8 Model Load Time 8 Memory Pressure 5 Concurrency 3 Performance Optimization 1 Time to First Token 6 GPU Monitoring 2 Out-of-Memory Error 2 Batched Serving 1 Quantization Tradeoffs 1 Throughput 1 Latency 5 Thermal Throttling 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 5: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
  • Chapter 10: Python Hardware Probes
  • Chapter 11: Model Sizing and Fit
  • Chapter 13: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints

Find Out Where the Minutes Go

A model that benchmarks as fast can still take ninety minutes to do a job a slower model finishes in twenty. By the end of this chapter you will be able to split a run's wall-clock time into its causes and say which setting to change first. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Speed is the property most people ask about first and measure worst. A single "tokens per second" figure hides the fact that a run has several kinds of time in it, and which kind dominates depends on the workload. A chat answer is dominated by generating the reply. An agent session, which resends a growing conversation on every turn, is dominated by something else entirely.

The chapter defines each kind of time and the settings that move it. It follows the order a request meets them: loading the model, reading the prompt, generating the reply, and running the tool the reply asks for. Then it covers the limits that cut a run short, which are memory pressure, the out-of-memory error, and heat. The worked examples use this evaluation's own measurements, including the one case where re-reading a conversation cost more than everything else combined.

docs.title: Model Load Time
docs.text:
Model load time is how long the server takes to read a model from disk into memory and get it ready, and it is paid whenever a model is not already loaded. It is the storage read speed of Chapter 5 applied to the model's size, plus the setup of the GPU. A 20 GB model at 2 GB per second is about ten seconds of reading, and a larger one proportionally more.

It matters when it is paid repeatedly. A server that unloads an idle model and reloads it for the next request spends that time again, which is why the keep-alive setting of Chapter 13 exists. For a benchmark that runs for hours, one load is a rounding error, and a load before every request is not.

docs.title: Prompt Processing Speed and Time to First Token
docs.text:
Prompt processing speed is how fast the server reads the prompt, measured in input tokens per second. Reading is fast because the model can process all the prompt's tokens in parallel. Time to first token is the delay between sending a request and receiving the first token of the reply, and it is made up mostly of loading, if needed, and prompt processing.

A worked example from this evaluation: one model read a 30,000-token prompt in ten seconds, which is about 3,000 tokens a second, so its time to first token for that prompt was about ten seconds. The same prompt on a model that processes 500 tokens a second would take a full minute before a single word appeared.

docs.title: Tokens per Second
docs.text:
Tokens per second is the generation speed: how many output tokens the model produces each second once it has started. Generation is slower than reading because each token depends on the one before it, so the tokens are produced in sequence and each requires reading the model's active weights from memory.

The measured speeds in this evaluation spanned a factor of forty, from 3 tokens a second for the largest dense model to 130 for the fastest mixture-of-experts model. They are the figure behind every estimate of how long a chapter takes.

Reading Is Parallel and Writing Is Sequential

The model can look at an entire prompt at once, but it can only write one token at a time, because each depends on the last. That is why a prompt of 30,000 tokens is read in seconds and a reply of 600 tokens takes tens of seconds. Two different speeds govern two different halves of every request.

docs.title: Latency and Throughput
docs.text:
Latency is the total time for one request, from sending it to receiving the last token. Throughput is the total amount of work done per unit of time across all requests, usually tokens per second summed over everything in flight. They are different goals and often pull against each other. A setting that lowers one request's latency can lower the machine's total throughput, and the reverse.

For a single benchmark session, latency is what you feel and throughput is irrelevant, because only one request is in flight at a time. For a service that generates many books, throughput is the number that sets the cost per book.

docs.title: Why an Agent Turn Is Slow
Prompt Caching and Prompt Re-Reading
docs.text:
An agent harness resends the whole conversation on every turn: the system prompt, the skill, every earlier message, and every tool result. Prompt caching is the server's remedy: it keeps the already-computed internal state for the part of the prompt that has not changed, so each new turn only has to read what is new. With caching working, a turn that adds 2,000 tokens to a 50,000-token conversation reads 2,000.

Prompt re-reading is the failure of that remedy, where the server recomputes most of the conversation on each turn. This evaluation observed it. With one model under the Ollama version used, on every agent turn the server restored a saved state just past the 19,000-token system prompt and then re-read the rest of the conversation, which was 46,000 to 65,000 tokens, taking one and a half to two minutes per turn. A different model, on the same server, did not show it. The cause was not identified.

The effect on the cost of a run was larger than anything else. The first stage of one model took 102 minutes where the others took 6 to 22. Its 55 tool calls at 90 seconds each of re-reading account for about 83 of those minutes, and a single turn of reasoning accounts for another 19.

Quantity Value Source Tokens re-read per turn 46,000 to 65,000 Measured from the server log Time per turn spent re-reading 1.5 to 2 minutes Measured Tool calls in the stage 55 Measured Time from re-reading about 83 minutes 55 × 90 seconds One reasoning turn about 19 minutes Measured Stage total 102 minutes Measured

The sum of the two causes, 83 plus 19, is the 102 minutes. Neither cause was the model's speed.

Look for the Restore Line in the Server Log

If one model is slow and another on the same server is not, search the server log for lines that say a context checkpoint was restored, and compare how many tokens each turn then processed. A turn that re-reads most of the conversation is the signature, and it is a different problem from slow generation.

docs.title: Context Length Setting
docs.text:
The context length setting is the window size the server is configured with, and Chapter 11 showed that it reserves memory for the cache. It also bounds how large a conversation can get before the harness must shrink it. The setting is a trade between room for long conversations and memory for everything else.

This project's batch runner chooses it for each model from a memory estimate that keeps about 45 GiB free, and not a single value for all models. That is the Chapter 11 calculation applied as a setting.

docs.title: Batch Size, Batched Serving, and Concurrency
docs.text:
Batch size is how many tokens, or requests, the server processes together in one step. A larger batch uses the GPU more fully, because the same weights are read once and applied to many tokens. Batched serving is a server design that combines concurrent requests into batches so that several users share one pass over the weights. Concurrency is the number of requests being handled at once.

The three are one idea at three levels. Raising concurrency, in a server that batches, raises throughput, and it can raise each request's latency. For a benchmark that deliberately runs one session at a time, this is a lever left unused, which is why vLLM, Chapter 13's batching server, is the candidate for a second pass.

docs.title: Sampling Parameters, Temperature, Top-p, and Top-k
docs.text:
Sampling parameters are the settings that control how the next token is chosen from the model's probabilities. Temperature scales how adventurous the choice is: 0 always takes the most likely token, and higher values spread the choice. Top-k limits the choice to the k most likely tokens, and top-p limits it to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p.

They matter for two reasons. They change the output, so a benchmark must fix and record them or its runs are not comparable. And they interact with reasoning models, where a high temperature can lengthen a chain of thought. They have little effect on speed, and a reader looking for speed will not find it here.

docs.title: Quantization Tradeoffs
docs.text: Quantization tradeoffs are what you give and get by storing weights in fewer bits. A 4-bit file is smaller, loads faster, and reads fewer bytes per token, so it generates faster than the same model at 8 bits. It also loses some accuracy, more on hard tasks than easy ones. This evaluation ran every candidate at its default 4-bit and left an 8-bit retest for the winner. Whether the quality loss matters is a measurement, and it is the one dial in this chapter that changes the output and not only the speed.

docs.title: Memory Pressure
docs.text:
Memory pressure is the condition in which available memory is low enough that the system starts to struggle: it swaps data to disk, stalls, or kills a process. It builds gradually as the context grows, and the symptom is that the same job slows down for no obvious reason in the later part of a run.

The probe of Chapter 10 reports available memory directly, and the vitals log of the same chapter records it every 30 seconds, so the slope is visible. Take an illustrative run that begins with 72 GiB available and ends with 18. It has been under growing pressure, and the second number is the one a watchdog acts on.

docs.title: Out-of-Memory Error
docs.text: An out-of-memory error is the failure when a program asks for memory that is not there. On a machine with dedicated GPU memory it shows up as a message in the server log, such as a CUDA allocation failure, and it ends one request or one process. On a unified-memory machine, the same shortage is shared with the operating system, and it can end in a frozen machine instead of a clean error. The practical rule is the one of Chapter 11: leave headroom, and watch the available figure so that you act before the error arrives.

docs.title: GPU Utilization and GPU Monitoring
docs.text:
GPU utilization is the share of the time the GPU is busy. GPU monitoring is watching it, and the temperature, power, and memory, while a job runs. A low utilization during generation means the GPU is waiting: for the prompt to be read, for a tool to run, or for the CPU to hand it work. A high utilization during a long reply is normal and healthy.

A single command shows it, refreshed every five seconds. The query asks for utilization, temperature, and power, and -l 5 repeats it.

nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,power.draw \
           --format=csv -l 5

During this evaluation a reading at about 43 seconds into a heavy run was 92% utilization, 72 degrees, and 69 W. Those numbers describe a GPU working hard on a single request, not a ceiling.

docs.title: Thermal Throttling
docs.text:
Thermal throttling is the chip reducing its own speed to stay below a safe temperature. It shows up as a speed that falls over a long run with no change in the workload, and it is invisible in a short test. The only way to find it is to run long and read the temperature and tokens per second together. The watchdog ceiling in this project was 95 degrees Celsius, chosen to stop a run before the chip had to protect itself, and a speed that decays while the temperature climbs is the pattern to look for.

A Fast Short Test Can Hide a Slow Long Run

A thirty-second speed test finishes before the chassis has warmed and before the cache has grown. Measure speed again at the end of a long run, with the same prompt, and compare. If the two numbers differ, the difference is memory pressure or heat, and the first number was never the machine's real speed.

docs.title: Performance Optimization
docs.text:
Performance optimization is changing one setting at a time and measuring the result against a fixed baseline. The discipline is the same as the sensitivity analysis of Chapter 6: one change, one measurement, then restore. A comparison between two runs that differ in three settings tells you nothing about which one mattered.

Each setting in this chapter moves a different part of the time, and the table matches them so that you change the one aimed at your bottleneck.

Setting What it moves What it costs Quantization to fewer bits Generation speed up, memory down Some quality Context length down Memory down, room for the system up Smaller conversations Keep-alive up Fewer reloads Memory held while idle Prompt caching working Prompt processing time down per turn Nothing, when it works Batching and concurrency up Throughput up Latency per request Sampling parameters The output, not the speed Different results

docs.title: Time Breakdown for an Agent Turn
docs.text:
A time breakdown splits one turn into the parts above. For a turn that begins with a prompt, produces a reply, and runs one tool, the time is the sum of reading, writing, and tool execution:

\[ T_{\text{turn}} = \frac{\text{prompt tokens}}{\text{prompt processing speed}} + \frac{\text{output tokens}}{\text{tokens per second}} + T_{\text{tool}} \]

With caching working, the prompt tokens are only the new ones. With re-reading, they are most of the conversation, and the first term dominates.

The three cases below use measured speeds from this evaluation. In each, the tool takes 5 seconds.

Case Prompt tokens read Reading speed Reply tokens Writing speed Turn time Caching works, dense model 2,000 3,000 per second 600 34 per second 23.3 s Re-reading, a slower model 55,000 500 per second 600 26 per second 138.1 s Caching works, fast mixture-of-experts model 2,000 3,000 per second 600 108 per second 11.2 s

In the second case the reading takes 110 of the 138 seconds, and tripling the generation speed would barely change the turn. In the first, writing takes 17.6 of 23.3 seconds, and faster generation is the lever. The same model can be on either row depending on whether the server is caching.

docs.title: Diagram: Agent Turn Time Breakdown
docs.text:
Run Agent Turn Time Breakdown Fullscreen

Agent Turn Time Breakdown

Type: microsim sim-id: turn-time-breakdown Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the time of an agent turn from its prompt tokens, reply tokens, speeds, and tool time to within 1 second, and name the component that dominates it, for 3 challenges.

Prerequisites: prompt processing speed, tokens per second, prompt caching, prompt re-reading, latency, time breakdown (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 3 challenges the learner types the turn time in seconds and chooses the dominant component from "Reading the prompt", "Writing the reply", and "Running the tool" before the sim reveals the answer. A challenge is correct when the typed value is within 1 second of the model value and the dominant component matches. Mastery is 3 of 3. Changing sliders in exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Faster generation always makes a turn faster. (2) Prompt reading is negligible. (3) A model's speed is one number for every workload. (4) Re-reading happens only when the context is full.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs a stated formula and committed numbers, and the dominant-component question turns the arithmetic into a diagnosis. The three cases are chosen so that each has a different dominant component or a different cause for the same one.

Content:

The learner can change five quantities:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Prompt tokens read this turn 0 100,000 500 2,000 tokens Prompt processing speed 100 5,000 100 3,000 tokens per second Reply tokens 50 5,000 50 600 tokens Generation speed 5 150 1 34 tokens per second Tool time 0 60 1 5 seconds

The three challenges, in this order:

# Prompt tokens Reading speed Reply tokens Writing speed Tool time Model turn time Dominant component Feedback when wrong 1 2,000 3,000 600 34 5 23.3 s Writing the reply 2,000 ÷ 3,000 = 0.7 s, 600 ÷ 34 = 17.6 s, tool 5 s, total 23.3 s, and writing is the largest. 2 55,000 500 600 26 5 138.1 s Reading the prompt 55,000 ÷ 500 = 110 s, 600 ÷ 26 = 23.1 s, tool 5 s, total 138.1 s, and reading is the largest. 3 2,000 3,000 600 108 8 14.2 s Running the tool 0.7 s reading, 600 ÷ 108 = 5.6 s writing, tool 8 s, total 14.2 s, and the tool is the largest.

Provenance: The speeds and token counts are drawn from the measurements in this chapter and the cost analysis page: 3,000 tokens per second reading and 108 writing for the mixture-of-experts model, 34 writing for the dense model, 26 writing and about 500 reading with 55,000 tokens re-read for the slow case. Tool times are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative".

Rules: Turn time = prompt tokens ÷ reading speed + reply tokens ÷ writing speed + tool time, in seconds, shown to one decimal. The dominant component is the largest of the three terms; a tie is shown as "tie". Model load time is not included.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1, whose inputs are shown, and types the turn time in seconds.
  2. The learner chooses the dominant component and presses Check.
  3. The sim reveals the model value, the dominant component, and the Feedback text, and marks the challenge correct or missed.
  4. After the three challenges the exploration mode unlocks, with a stacked bar of the three components, and the learner changes any of the five quantities.
  5. In exploration the learner should notice that changing generation speed barely moves the bar when reading dominates.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: s, dominates." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that challenge. After the second wrong attempt the model value and the worked calculation are shown, and the challenge counts as missed. A running count "Challenges correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with an empty answer box and its inputs displayed. The question on screen is "How long does this turn take, and where does the time go?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states a 23.3-second turn with caching on a dense model, a 138.1-second turn with 55,000 tokens re-read, and 110 of those seconds spent reading, and that the stage total of 102 minutes was about 83 minutes of re-reading plus a 19-minute reasoning turn.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
A run's wall-clock time is made of loading the model, reading the prompt, writing the reply, and running tools, and each has its own speed and its own setting. Reading is parallel and fast, and writing is sequential and slow, so a turn that resends a long conversation can spend most of its time reading unless prompt caching holds. The server's caching can silently fail, as it did for one model in this evaluation, and the cost was larger than any difference in generation speed. The settings move different parts of the time and some move the output, and a measurement with one change at a time is the only way to know which. Memory pressure, out-of-memory errors, and heat set the limits, and a long run is the only test that finds them.

You Can Split a Run Into Its Causes

You can now take a slow run, separate loading, reading, writing, and tool time, and say which setting to change first. Chapter 16 opens up the harness itself to see where an agent turn spends its time and its context.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
docs.text: Test your understanding of the kinds of time in a run, prompt caching, the settings that move speed, and the limits that cut a run short with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does tokens per second measure?
docs.text:
1. How fast the server reads the tokens of the prompt
  2. How long the server takes to load a model from disk
  3. How many requests the server completes each second
  4. How many output tokens the model produces each second
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Tokens per second is the generation speed: how many output tokens the model produces each second once it has started. Generation is slower than reading because each token depends on the one before it, so tokens are produced in sequence and each requires reading the model's active weights from memory. Reading the prompt has its own, much higher figure, the prompt processing speed. The measured generation speeds in this evaluation ranged from 3 to 130 tokens a second.

Concept Tested: Tokens per Second

See: Tokens per Second

docs.title: 2. What is time to first token mostly made up of?
docs.text:
1. Model loading, if needed, and prompt processing
  2. Generating the reply and running the requested tool
  3. Sampling the next token at a high temperature
  4. Writing the vitals log and checking the watchdog
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Time to first token is the delay between sending a request and receiving the first token of the reply. It is made up mostly of loading the model, if it is not already loaded, and prompt processing. One model in this evaluation read a 30,000-token prompt at about 3,000 tokens a second, so its time to first token was about ten seconds. Generating the rest of the reply and running tools come after the first token.

Concept Tested: Time to First Token

See: Prompt Processing Speed and Time to First Token

docs.title: 3. What does a temperature setting of 0 do?
docs.text:
1. It limits the choice to the k most likely tokens
  2. It spreads the choice across less likely tokens
  3. It always takes the most likely next token
  4. It stops generation after the first token
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Sampling parameters control how the next token is chosen from the model's probabilities. Temperature scales how adventurous the choice is: 0 always takes the most likely token, and higher values spread the choice. Limiting the choice to the k most likely tokens is top-k, a different parameter. These settings change the output, so a benchmark must fix and record them, and they have little effect on speed.

Concept Tested: Temperature Setting

See: Sampling Parameters, Temperature, Top-p, and Top-k

docs.title: 4. How does prompt caching shorten an agent turn?
docs.text:
1. The server reuses saved state and reads only the new tokens
  2. The harness stops resending the conversation after the first turn
  3. The model writes several tokens of the reply in parallel
  4. The server stores finished replies and returns them on later turns
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An agent harness resends the whole conversation on every turn. Prompt caching is the server's remedy: it keeps the already-computed internal state for the part of the prompt that has not changed, so each new turn only has to read what is new. With caching working, a turn that adds 2,000 tokens to a 50,000-token conversation reads 2,000. The harness still resends everything, and replies are still written one token at a time.

Concept Tested: Prompt Caching

See: Prompt Caching and Prompt Re-Reading

docs.title: 5. Why is latency, and not throughput, the figure that matters for a single benchmark session?
docs.text:
1. Throughput can be measured only on dedicated GPU memory
  2. Throughput and latency are two names for the same figure
  3. Only one request is in flight at a time, so latency governs
  4. A benchmark session never generates more than one reply
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Latency is the total time for one request, from sending it to receiving the last token. Throughput is the total work done per unit of time across all requests in flight. For a single benchmark session only one request is in flight at a time, so latency is what you feel and throughput is irrelevant. For a service that generates many books at once, throughput is the number that sets the cost per book.

Concept Tested: Latency

See: Latency and Throughput

docs.title: 6. Why is thermal throttling invisible in a short speed test?
docs.text:
1. Throttling occurs only while the GPU is idle
  2. Throttling is reported only in the model card
  3. A short test reads the prompt but never writes a reply
  4. A short test ends before the chassis has warmed up
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Thermal throttling is the chip reducing its own speed to stay below a safe temperature. It shows up as a speed that falls over a long run with no change in the workload. A thirty-second test finishes before the chassis has warmed, so the only way to find throttling is to run long and read temperature and tokens per second together. A speed that decays while the temperature climbs is the pattern to look for.

Concept Tested: Thermal Throttling

See: Thermal Throttling

docs.title: 7. A server processes prompts at 500 tokens per second. Because of re-reading, each agent turn reads 55,000 tokens. How long does the reading take on each turn, before any reply token is written?
docs.text:
1. 11 seconds
  2. 55 seconds
  3. 110 seconds
  4. 275 seconds
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Prompt processing speed is how fast the server reads the prompt, in input tokens per second. Reading time is the tokens read divided by that speed: 55,000 ÷ 500 is 110 seconds, before a single reply token is written. That is why a turn that re-reads most of a conversation is dominated by reading. With caching working, the same turn would read only the new tokens, perhaps 2,000, in about four seconds at this speed.

Concept Tested: Prompt Processing Speed

See: Time Breakdown for an Agent Turn
