docs.title: 8. Two runs differ in quantization, context length, and keep-alive, and the second is faster. What should you do to learn which setting mattered?
docs.text:
1. Average the two runs and report the mean speed
  2. Change one setting at a time against a fixed baseline
  3. Keep all three changes, since the second run was faster
  4. Raise the temperature and see whether the speed changes
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Performance optimization is changing one setting at a time and measuring the result against a fixed baseline: one change, one measurement, then restore. A comparison between two runs that differ in three settings tells you nothing about which one mattered. Each setting moves a different part of the time, so the single-change discipline is also how you confirm that the setting aimed at your bottleneck is the one that helped.

Concept Tested: Performance Optimization

See: Performance Optimization

docs.title: 9. A vitals log shows available memory falling from 72 GiB at the start of a run to 18 GiB near the end, and the job has slowed. What is the condition, and which figure does a watchdog act on?
docs.text:
1. Memory pressure; the watchdog acts on the low, later figure
  2. Thermal throttling; the watchdog acts on the starting figure
  3. Prompt re-reading; the watchdog acts on tokens read per turn
  4. A model reload; the watchdog acts on the keep-alive period
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Memory pressure is the condition in which available memory is low enough that the system starts to struggle: it swaps, stalls, or kills a process. It builds gradually as the context grows, and the symptom is a job that slows for no obvious reason late in a run. The vitals log records available memory every 30 seconds, so the slope is visible. A fall from 72 GiB to 18 GiB is growing pressure, and the second number is the one a watchdog acts on.

Concept Tested: Memory Pressure

See: Memory Pressure

docs.title: 10. In a turn with prompt re-reading, reading takes 110 of the 138 seconds. What would tripling the generation speed do to that turn?
docs.text:
1. The turn would take about a third as long
  2. The turn would barely change, since reading dominates
  3. The turn would get slower, since the tool would then wait
  4. The turn would fail, since the KV cache would overflow
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A turn's time is reading plus writing plus tool time. With prompt re-reading, the server recomputes most of the conversation on each turn, so the first term dominates: 55,000 tokens at 500 per second is 110 of the 138 seconds. Tripling the generation speed would shorten only the 23 seconds of writing, so the turn would barely change. The setting to fix first is the one aimed at the bottleneck, which here is caching.

Concept Tested: Prompt Re-Reading

See: Time Breakdown for an Agent Turn

docs.title: References: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
docs.text:
1. Latency (engineering) - Wikipedia - Defines latency as the delay between a cause and its observed effect in networks, audio, and computing, including a section on tail latency. It supports the chapter's split between latency per request and throughput overall.

  2. Out of memory - Wikipedia - Describes the state in which a computer cannot allocate more memory because RAM and swap are exhausted, with its history, recovery behavior, and per-process limits. It grounds the chapter's out-of-memory error and memory pressure sections.

  3. Voltage and frequency scaling - Wikipedia - Explains how processors lower their frequency and voltage to manage power and heat, also called CPU throttling, and how temperature and stability interact. It explains the mechanism behind thermal throttling, which makes speed decay on long runs.

  4. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach (6th Edition) - John L. Hennessy and David A. Patterson - Morgan Kaufmann - Presents the Roofline model, introduced by Williams, Waterman, and Patterson, which plots attainable performance against arithmetic intensity under memory-bandwidth and compute ceilings. That lens shows why token generation is bound by memory bandwidth and why batching raises throughput.

  5. Systems Performance (2nd Edition) - Brendan Gregg - Addison-Wesley Professional - Gregg developed the USE Method, which checks every resource for utilization, saturation, and errors. Applied to a GPU, memory, and CPU, it turns this chapter's utilization, memory pressure, and out-of-memory symptoms into a repeatable checklist.

  6. LLM Inference Benchmarking: Fundamental Concepts - NVIDIA Technical Blog - Defines time to first token, end-to-end latency, intertoken latency, tokens per second, and requests per second, and shows how concurrency saturates throughput and raises TTFT. It supplies the metric vocabulary used throughout the chapter.

  7. How to generate text: using different decoding methods for language generation with Transformers - Hugging Face Blog - Explains greedy search, beam search, and sampling, then temperature, top-k, and top-p (nucleus) sampling with worked examples. It is a hands-on walk-through of the sampling parameters this chapter lists, which change output, not speed.

  8. Automatic Prefix Caching - vLLM Documentation - Describes how vLLM keeps the KV cache of earlier queries and reuses it when a request shares a prefix, helping multi-turn chats, though it speeds only prefill. It shows prompt caching, and the re-reading it prevents, in practice.

  9. How continuous batching enables 23x throughput in LLM inference while reducing p50 latency - Anyscale Blog - Compares static batching with continuous batching on a single A100, reporting throughput gains of up to 23 times, and argues that LLM inference is memory-IO bound so batch size sets throughput. It explains the chapter's batching and concurrency levers.

  10. NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) - NVIDIA Documentation - Documents querying GPU utilization, memory, temperature, slowdown thresholds, and power draw, and repeating a query on an interval with the loop option. It is the reference for the chapter's GPU monitoring command.

docs.title: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
Summary
docs.text: This chapter explains what an agent harness does between a prompt and a result. It covers the agent loop, tool definitions, file and shell tools, permissions, context management, compaction, truncation, and how orchestrators and subagents divide work. Students finish able to trace one agent turn and say where its time and context go.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score AI Agent Harness 173 Tool Definition 14 Agent Loop 29 File Editing Tool 6 Shell Execution Tool 6 Orchestrator 3 System Prompt 2 Agent Turn 11 Context Management 6 Permission Model 5 Subagent 1 Role Separation 1 Turn Overhead 7 Context Truncation 3 Peak Context Size 2 Context Compaction 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 4: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
  • Chapter 13: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
  • Chapter 15: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance

Follow One Turn All the Way Through

A model by itself only produces text, and an agent is the machinery that turns that text into actions. By the end of this chapter you will be able to trace one agent turn and say where its time and its context go. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 13 gave you an endpoint that answers a prompt. A textbook, though, is not one answer. It is hundreds of steps: read a file, plan a chapter, write it, build the site, notice an error, fix it. Something has to turn a model's single reply into that sequence, and that something is the AI agent harness.

This chapter takes the harness apart. It defines the loop at its center, the tools the model can call, and the permission rules that decide which calls are allowed. It then covers the part that most often limits a long session, which is the context, and what a harness does when the context grows too large. It ends with two ways of dividing work among several agents, which this evaluation used and which affect how its results should be read.

docs.title: AI Agent Harness
docs.text:
An AI agent harness is the program that wraps a language model so that it can act in the world. The model supplies language: given a conversation, it produces the next message. The harness supplies everything else: the system prompt that sets the task, the list of tools the model may call, the code that carries out those calls, the rules that allow or refuse them, and the bookkeeping that keeps the conversation going.

Claude Code is a harness. So are OpenCode, Codex CLI, and Goose, which Chapter 17 compares. They differ in their prompts and their tool sets, and they share one structure, which is the loop.

The harness is a separate piece of software from the model, and the distinction is the reason this evaluation can swap the model underneath. The harness stays the same, a different model answers its requests, and any difference in the result belongs to the model.

docs.title: Agent Loop and Agent Turn
docs.text:
The agent loop is the cycle at the harness's center. It sends the conversation to the model. If the reply contains a request to call a tool, the harness runs the tool, appends the result to the conversation, and sends the conversation to the model again. If the reply contains no tool call, the loop ends and the reply is the final answer.

An agent turn is one trip around that loop: one request to the model and one response, plus the tool call and result if there was one. A task that takes 55 tool calls takes at least 55 turns, and each is a full request to the model with everything so far.

conversation = [system prompt, user request]
repeat:
    reply = model(conversation)
    if reply has no tool call:
        stop, the reply is the answer
    result = run the tool the reply names
    conversation += [reply, result]

Four things follow directly from that sketch, and each has a chapter behind it.

  • The conversation only grows. Each turn appends a reply and a result, so the prompt of turn 40 contains everything in turns 1 to 39. This is why Chapter 15's prompt re-reading matters.
  • Every turn pays the model's latency. Reading the prompt, writing the reply, and running the tool happen in sequence, once per turn.
  • A single bad reply can end the run. If the model writes a tool call as plain text, the harness sees no tool call and the loop stops. Two of this evaluation's candidates failed exactly this way.
  • The model chooses the path. The harness never says which tool comes next. A model that picks poorly wastes turns, and one that loses the task stops making progress.

The Loop Is the Whole Idea

An agent is not a smarter model. It is an ordinary model inside a loop that feeds it the results of its own actions. The model's only job on each turn is to say what to do next, and the harness's job is to do it and report back, so most agent failures are failures to say it in the form the harness can run.

docs.title: System Prompt
docs.text:
The system prompt is the standing instruction that opens every conversation. In a harness it is long: it describes the task, the style, the rules, and the tools. It is resent at the start of every turn, and it is the same every time, which is what makes it cacheable.

Its size is a real cost for a local model. Claude Code's own instructions and tool definitions run to about 19,000 tokens, and they were written for Claude models. A local model that struggles in the harness may be struggling with that prompt and not with the task, which is one reason a model is tested alone first.

docs.title: Tool Definition
docs.text:
A tool definition is the description of one tool that the harness gives the model: its name, what it does, and the arguments it takes. The model never runs a tool. It writes a structured request that names a tool and supplies arguments, and the harness runs it.

The shape is the same across harnesses. This example defines a tool that reads a file. name is how the model refers to it. description tells the model when to use it. input_schema lists the arguments and their types, so that the harness can check a request before running it.

{
  "name": "read_file",
  "description": "Read a text file and return its contents.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "path": { "type": "string" } },
    "required": ["path"]
  }
}

A model's tool-calling reliability, from Chapter 12, is how often it writes a request that matches a definition like this one. A request with a missing argument or a wrong name is a malformed tool call, and Chapter 22 diagnoses them.

docs.title: File Editing Tool and Shell Execution Tool
docs.text:
Two kinds of tool do most of the work in a skill. A file editing tool reads, creates, and changes files in the working directory, and it is how a model writes a chapter or a learning graph to disk. A shell execution tool runs a command in a terminal and returns its output, and it is how a model builds the site, runs a script, or checks a result.

Between them they let a model do nearly everything a person at a keyboard can. That power is the reason the next two concepts exist.

docs.title: Permission Model
docs.text:
The permission model is the set of rules that decide whether a tool call is allowed. A rule can allow a call, forbid it, or require a person to approve it first. A harness that runs interactively asks, and a person answers. A harness that runs unattended has nobody to ask, so an approval rule stalls the run.

This evaluation met that directly. The benchmark prompts carry a standing answer to the skill's approval questions, because no one is present during a run, and a paused run measures nothing. The harness also ran inside a container, so that the agent could run any command and could write only to its run directory. Chapter 18 builds that boundary. The first runs, with the harness on a laptop and no sandbox, allowed the agent no shell commands at all, and most skills need them.

An Unattended Run Cannot Answer a Question

If a permission rule asks for approval and nobody is there, the run waits forever and produces nothing. Decide every approval in advance, either by allowing the call or by putting a standing answer in the prompt, and confirm with a short test run that nothing pauses.

docs.title: Context Management and Peak Context Size
docs.text:
Context management is how a harness keeps the conversation within the model's window. The window is a fixed limit, and the conversation only grows, so sooner or later it has to be reduced. Peak context size is the largest the conversation reached in a run, and it is the figure that tells you whether a window was big enough.

Measurements in this evaluation show the range. One model's first prompt took 35,000 tokens where the others took 17,000 to 21,000, and within eight turns it was at 120,000, the edge of its window. Two others peaked at 135,000 and 147,000 tokens in a single stage. A window of 128,000 would have cut both off.

Run Peak context Notes muse-glimmer:30b, harness test About 120,000 within eight turns Its first prompt was already 35,000 tokens qwen3.6:35b, stage 1 135,000 tokens Second largest of any run nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b, stage 1 147,000 tokens 140 tool calls, nearly three times any other

docs.title: Context Truncation and Context Compaction
docs.text:
When the conversation approaches the window, a harness has two ways to shrink it. Context truncation drops the oldest content, and it is crude: the beginning of the conversation, which holds the task, is exactly what disappears. Context compaction asks the model to summarize the earlier conversation into a short note and replaces the old content with it. Compaction keeps the thread and loses detail, and it costs a model call.

The two have a dangerous interaction with the server's window. Claude Code assumes a window of about 200,000 tokens. If the server was configured with a smaller one, the server truncates silently before the harness knows to compact, and the model loses the start of its own task without any message. This is why this evaluation raised the server's context setting to a large value, and why Chapter 11 warned that raising it has a memory cost.

docs.title: Turn Overhead
docs.text:
Turn overhead is the time in a turn that is not generating the reply: reading the new part of the prompt, running the tool, and the harness's own bookkeeping. Chapter 15 measured it. The cost analysis assumes 15 seconds per turn when caching works, and the one model whose server re-read the conversation each turn showed 90.

Overhead is easy to overlook because no single request looks slow. It is spread across hundreds of turns, and for the fast models in this evaluation it was longer than the generation itself.

docs.title: Orchestrator, Subagent, and Role Separation
docs.text:
An orchestrator is an agent, or a person, that starts work and coordinates it without doing it. A subagent is an agent started by another to handle one part of a task in its own conversation, and it returns a summary, so its working detail never enters the parent's context. Role separation is keeping the roles of those agents distinct and recording who did what.

This evaluation has two roles that must not be confused. The orchestrator is a Claude Code session using a cloud model, running on the laptop, and its job is to start runs, watch them, and score the results. The harness is Claude Code inside a container with a local model, and its job is to generate. The rule that holds the evaluation together is that the orchestrator never writes benchmark content, because the question is whether a local model can.

The skills themselves can use subagents. The chapter-content skill has a parallel mode that starts one agent per group of chapters, at a stated token cost. The benchmark does not use it: each chapter is a separate harness run, so that each has its own timing and token counts.

Role Fills it Where it runs May write benchmark content? Orchestrator A Claude Code session on a cloud model The laptop No Harness Claude Code in a container The DGX Only by calling the local model Model An open-weight model behind the endpoint The DGX GPU Yes, all of it

docs.title: Diagram: Agent Loop Stepper
docs.text:
Run Agent Loop Stepper Fullscreen

Agent Loop Stepper

Type: microsim sim-id: agent-loop-stepper Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-strategy-for-education/tree/main/docs/sims/ai-agent-anatomy Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain what the harness does after each of 6 model replies or tool results by choosing the outcome of each, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: AI agent harness, agent loop, agent turn, tool definition, permission model, context compaction, context truncation (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner first steps once through the five phases of one turn. The learner then answers 6 situations by choosing one of the six outcomes before any answer is revealed. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct outcome column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Stepping through is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The model runs its own tools. (2) A tool call written as text still runs. (3) The conversation is reset each turn. (4) A permission question is answered automatically.

Instructional Rationale: Explaining a mechanism needs the learner to predict its behavior in cases that differ in one detail, so each situation changes a single fact about the reply or the result, and the outcomes are the possible next states of the loop.

Content:

The five phases of one turn, shown as the learner steps through them:

  1. The harness sends the whole conversation to the model.
  2. The model writes a reply.
  3. The harness checks the reply for a tool call.
  4. If there is one, the harness checks the permission rules and runs the tool.
  5. The harness appends the reply and the result to the conversation, and the loop starts again.

The six outcomes the learner chooses from: "The harness runs the tool, appends the result, and calls the model again", "The loop ends and the reply is returned", "The harness sees no tool call and the loop ends early", "The conversation grows by the size of the result", "The harness compacts or truncates earlier content", and "The run stalls waiting for an approval".

# Situation shown to the learner Correct outcome Why (shown as feedback) 1 The reply contains a well-formed request to read a file. The harness runs the tool, appends the result, and calls the model again A tool call is exactly what the loop acts on. 2 The reply is a finished answer with no tool call. The loop ends and the reply is returned With no tool call the loop has nothing to run. 3 The reply writes the tool call out as plain text inside its answer. The harness sees no tool call and the loop ends early Only a structured request is a tool call, so the text is treated as a final reply. 4 A shell command returns 8,000 tokens of output. The conversation grows by the size of the result The result is appended, so every later turn reads it. 5 The conversation is about to exceed the model's window. The harness compacts or truncates earlier content The conversation has to shrink to fit, by summary or by dropping the oldest content. 6 A permission rule requires approval for the tool and nobody is present. The run stalls waiting for an approval An unattended run cannot answer, so it waits.

Provenance: The situations are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The mechanism comes from the sections of this chapter above.

Rules: Situations are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6. Each allows one final choice, and exactly one outcome is correct for each situation.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner presses Next to move through the five phases of one turn, with the conversation shown growing at phase 5.
  2. After phase 5 the learner begins the six situations and reads situation 1.
  3. The learner chooses one of the six outcomes and confirms.
  4. The sim shows the correct outcome and the Why text, and marks the situation correct or incorrect.
  5. After situation 6 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Six situations, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct outcome and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: The loop is shown at phase 1 with a short conversation, and the question on screen is "What does the harness do with the model's reply?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a tool call written as plain text ends the loop, that a tool result is appended and read by every later turn, that an approval rule stalls an unattended run, and that a conversation near the window is compacted or truncated.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
A harness is a loop around a model: it sends the conversation, runs the tool the reply asks for, appends the result, and repeats until a reply has no tool call. Tool definitions tell the model what it may ask for, file and shell tools give it reach, and the permission model decides what is allowed, which for an unattended run must be settled in advance. The conversation only grows, so the harness must truncate or compact it, and a server window smaller than the harness assumes cuts it off silently. The orchestrator, the harness, and the model are three roles, and the evaluation depends on the first never doing the work of the third.

You Can Trace One Turn

You can now follow a turn through the loop, say which tool and permission rule applied, and find where its context and its time went. Chapter 17 loads the benchmark workload, the skills, into a harness connected to your local model.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
docs.text: Test your understanding of the agent harness, the loop, tool definitions, permissions, context management, and role separation with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does an AI agent harness supply that the model does not?
docs.text:
1. The language ability that produces each next message in turn
  2. The trained weights that are loaded onto the GPU
  3. The GPU memory that holds the conversation's cache
  4. The tools, permission rules, and loop around the model
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. An AI agent harness is the program that wraps a language model so it can act in the world. The model supplies language: given a conversation, it produces the next message. The harness supplies everything else: the system prompt that sets the task, the list of tools, the code that carries out tool calls, the rules that allow or refuse them, and the bookkeeping that keeps the conversation going. Because it is separate software, the model underneath can be swapped.

Concept Tested: AI Agent Harness

See: AI Agent Harness

docs.title: 2. When does the agent loop end?
docs.text:
1. When the context window is completely full
  2. When the harness has run a fixed number of turns
  3. When a tool returns a result that has no errors
  4. When the model's reply contains no tool call
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The agent loop sends the conversation to the model. If the reply contains a request to call a tool, the harness runs the tool, appends the result, and sends the conversation again. If the reply contains no tool call, the loop ends and the reply is the final answer. That rule has a sharp edge: a model that writes a tool call as plain text ends the run early, because the harness sees no tool call.

Concept Tested: Agent Loop

See: Agent Loop and Agent Turn

docs.title: 3. Why does the prompt for turn 40 of an agent session contain everything from turns 1 to 39?
docs.text:
1. Each turn appends its reply and tool result to the conversation
  2. The model stores earlier turns in its parameters between requests
  3. The server merges all open sessions into a single prompt
  4. The harness resends only the system prompt on each turn
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An agent turn is one trip around the loop: one request to the model and one response, plus the tool call and result if there was one. Each turn appends a reply and a result, so the conversation only grows, and the prompt of turn 40 contains everything in turns 1 to 39. The model keeps nothing between requests. Every turn is a full request with everything so far, which is why prompt caching matters so much.

Concept Tested: Agent Turn

See: Agent Loop and Agent Turn

docs.title: 4. Why might a local model that struggles in the harness be struggling with the system prompt and not with the task?
docs.text:
1. The system prompt changes on every turn of the loop
  2. It runs to about 19,000 tokens and was written for Claude models
  3. The system prompt is sent only once, on the first turn
  4. It is truncated by the harness before the model reads it
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The system prompt is the standing instruction that opens every conversation. In a harness it is long, and it is resent at the start of every turn unchanged, which is what makes it cacheable. Claude Code's own instructions and tool definitions run to about 19,000 tokens, and they were written for Claude models. A local model may be struggling with that prompt and not with the task, which is one reason a model is tested alone first.

Concept Tested: System Prompt

See: System Prompt

docs.title: 5. How does context compaction differ from context truncation?
docs.text:
1. Compaction drops the oldest content; truncation summarizes it
  2. Compaction raises the server's window; truncation lowers it
  3. Compaction summarizes earlier content; truncation drops the oldest
  4. Compaction removes the tool definitions; truncation removes the replies
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. When a conversation approaches the window, a harness can shrink it in two ways. Context truncation drops the oldest content, which is crude: the beginning of the conversation, which holds the task, is exactly what disappears. Context compaction asks the model to summarize the earlier conversation into a short note and replaces the old content with it. Compaction keeps the thread and loses detail, and it costs a model call.

Concept Tested: Context Compaction

See: Context Truncation and Context Compaction

docs.title: 6. You are preparing an unattended overnight run of a skill that asks approval questions. What must you do beforehand?
docs.text:
1. Leave the approval rules on and check how the run went in the morning
  2. Settle every approval in advance and confirm with a short test
  3. Remove the shell execution tool so nothing needs approval
  4. Raise the context window so the questions fit in the prompt
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The permission model is the set of rules that allow a tool call, forbid it, or require a person to approve it first. An unattended run has nobody to ask, so an approval rule stalls it and it produces nothing. Decide every approval in advance, either by allowing the call or by putting a standing answer in the prompt, and confirm with a short test run that nothing pauses. Removing the shell tool is no answer, because most skills need it.

Concept Tested: Permission Model

See: Permission Model

docs.title: 7. A tool definition for read_file lists path under required in its input_schema. A model emits a structured request to read_file with no path. What is this request?
docs.text:
1. A valid call, because the tool name matches the definition
  2. A malformed call, because a required argument is missing
  3. A final answer, because it contains no structured request
  4. A permission error, because reading files needs approval
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A tool definition gives the model a tool's name, a description of when to use it, and an input_schema listing the arguments and their types, so the harness can check a request before running it. The read_file definition marks path as required. A request with a missing argument or a wrong name is a malformed tool call. A matching name is not enough, and a structured request is not a final answer.

Concept Tested: Tool Definition

See: Tool Definition

docs.title: 8. Two models peaked at 135,000 and 147,000 tokens of context in one stage. You plan to rerun that stage with a 128,000-token window. What should you expect?
docs.text:
1. Both runs would be cut off, since their peaks exceed the window
  2. Both runs would fit, since peak context is measured in words
  3. Both runs would fit, since only the first prompt must fit
  4. The harness would enlarge the server's window as needed
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Peak context size is the largest the conversation reached in a run, and it tells you whether a window was big enough. Context management must keep the conversation within the window, which is a fixed limit measured in tokens. Peaks of 135,000 and 147,000 tokens both exceed 128,000, so a window of that size would have cut both runs off. The harness cannot enlarge the server's window; that is a server setting with a memory cost.

Concept Tested: Peak Context Size

See: Context Management and Peak Context Size

docs.title: 9. Claude Code assumes a window of about 200,000 tokens, but the server is configured with a smaller one. What goes wrong?
docs.text:
1. The harness compacts too early and wastes model calls
  2. The server rejects every request with an explicit error message
  3. The model's tool definitions are dropped from each of its replies
  4. The server truncates silently before the harness compacts
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Truncation and compaction interact dangerously with the server's window. Claude Code assumes a window of about 200,000 tokens, so it does not compact until the conversation nears that size. If the server was configured with a smaller window, the server truncates silently before the harness knows to compact, and the model loses the start of its own task without any message. This is why the evaluation raised the server's context setting, at a memory cost.

Concept Tested: Context Truncation

See: Context Truncation and Context Compaction

docs.title: 10. Why must the orchestrator in this evaluation never write benchmark content?
docs.text:
1. The orchestrator has no file editing tool available to it
  2. The orchestrator runs inside the container on the DGX
  3. It uses a cloud model, and the test is of a local one
  4. It lacks the context window needed to hold a full chapter
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An orchestrator starts work and coordinates it without doing it. In this evaluation it is a Claude Code session using a cloud model on the laptop, which starts runs, watches them, and scores results. The harness on the DGX generates, by calling the local model. Role separation keeps these distinct: the orchestrator never writes benchmark content, because the question is whether a local model can. Content written by the cloud model would answer a different question.

Concept Tested: Orchestrator

See: Orchestrator, Subagent, and Role Separation

docs.title: References: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
docs.text:
1. Intelligent agent - Wikipedia - Defines an agent as an entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators, and classifies agents from simple reflex to learning. It supplies the general vocabulary behind this chapter's agent loop.

  2. Large language model - Wikipedia - Surveys how language models are built, run, and extended, including the context window, prompt engineering, tool use, and agency. It supplies the background on the model that this chapter's harness wraps and calls repeatedly.

  3. Principle of least privilege - Wikipedia - States that each module should access only the information and resources necessary for its legitimate purpose, and covers implementation. It underlies this chapter's permission model, which allows, forbids, or requires approval for each tool call.

  4. Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th Edition) - Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig - Pearson - Frames all of AI around the rational agent and describes each agent by its PEAS task environment (performance measure, environment, actuators, sensors) and its agent program. That framing underlies this chapter's loop of percept, decision, and action.

  5. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd Edition) - Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto - MIT Press - Presents the agent-environment interface as a loop diagram in which the agent chooses an action and the environment returns a reward and next state at each step. It is the standard picture behind this chapter's turn-by-turn loop.

  6. How Claude Code works - Claude Code Documentation - Explains the agentic loop of gathering context, taking action, and verifying results, the built-in tool categories, context-window compaction, and subagents. It is a concrete harness that this chapter's abstract loop, tools, and context management can be mapped onto.

  7. Building effective agents - Anthropic Engineering - Distinguishes workflows from agents and describes patterns such as prompt chaining, routing, orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer, with advice on tool design and stopping conditions. It supports this chapter's orchestrator and role-separation material.

  8. Effective context engineering for AI agents - Anthropic Engineering - Treats context as a finite resource, explains context rot, and describes compaction, structured note-taking, and sub-agent architectures for long tasks. It supports this chapter's account of context management, compaction, and why subagents return summaries.

  9. Tool use with Claude - Claude Platform Documentation - Shows how a tool is defined with a name, description, and input schema, how the model returns a structured tool_use request, and how the application returns a tool_result. It is the formal version of this chapter's tool definition.

  10. Configure permissions - Claude Code Documentation - Describes the tiered permission system, with deny, ask, and allow rules evaluated in that order, permission modes, tool-specific rules, and how permissions interact with sandboxing. It shows this chapter's permission model written as real harness settings.

docs.title: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
Summary
docs.text: This chapter connects the harness to the local model and the benchmark workload. Students learn the skill format, skill loading and installation, and the ibook-skills chain, then configure Claude Code or an alternative against the local endpoint and verify that a skill runs. They finish with a harness that executes skills end to end.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Agent Skill 74 Claude Code 38 AGENTS.md File 1 OpenCode 1 Codex CLI 1 Goose 1 ibook-skills Skill Chain 51 SKILL.md Format 21 Local Endpoint Connection 21 Harness Prompt Overhead 1 Harness Configuration 17 Skill Loading 10 Skill Installation 10 Harness on Laptop 1 Skill Execution Verification 9 Harness Compatibility Test 3

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 7: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
  • Chapter 13: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
  • Chapter 16: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context

Giving the Harness Something to Do

The harness is only a loop until you hand it a skill, and the skill is the benchmark. By the end of this chapter you will have a harness pointed at your local model, a skill installed where it can find it, and a three-minute test that proves the whole chain runs. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 16 explained the loop and Chapter 13 supplied the endpoint. This chapter joins them to the workload. A skill is a packaged set of instructions that a harness can load on demand, and the ibook-skills collection is the set of skills that turns a course description into a textbook. Running them against a local model is the whole benchmark.

The chapter defines the skill format, shows how a harness finds and loads one, and lays out the chain this book uses. It then configures Claude Code to talk to the local endpoint, names the alternatives, and ends with the verification step that you should never skip: a short skill run whose result you can check, before you commit hours to a long one.

docs.title: Agent Skill
docs.text:
An agent skill is a folder of instructions, and sometimes helper files, that teaches a harness how to carry out one kind of task well. It is a procedure written down so that a model can follow it: the steps, the order, the checks, and the formats of the files to produce. A skill does not add a capability the harness lacks. It supplies knowledge of how to use the capabilities it has.

The reason skills exist is that a model's general ability is not a procedure. A person who asks a model to "generate a learning graph" gets something plausible and unrepeatable. A skill pins down what a good learning graph is, how to build one, and how to check it, so that the same request gives a comparable result each time. That repeatability is what makes a skill usable as a benchmark.

A skill is a directory, and the layout is a convention that several harnesses share.

learning-graph-generator/
├── SKILL.md              the instructions, with a header the harness reads first
├── references/           longer documents, read only when a step needs them
│   ├── taxonomy.md
│   └── quality-checks.md
├── scripts/              helper programs the instructions tell the model to run
│   └── analyze-graph.py
└── assets/               templates and files copied into the project

The file names under references/, scripts/, and assets/ are illustrative. The table gives each part its job, because the loading mechanism in the next section depends on keeping them separate.

Part What it holds When the harness reads it SKILL.md header Name and a one-paragraph description At startup, for every installed skill SKILL.md body The step-by-step instructions When the skill is invoked references/ Long documents, standards, examples Only when a step names them scripts/ Programs the steps call When a step runs them assets/ Templates and fixed inputs When a step copies them

docs.title: SKILL.md Format
docs.text:
The SKILL.md format is a Markdown file that opens with a block of YAML metadata between two lines of three dashes. The block carries the fields a harness needs to decide whether the skill applies, and the Markdown below it carries the procedure. The header of a real skill from this project's chain, abbreviated, looks like this.

---
name: chapter-content-generator
description: Generates detailed chapter content for an intelligent textbook,
  with text, diagrams, MicroSims, and exercises at the appropriate Bloom's
  level. Use when a chapter's index.md exists with title, summary, and
  concept list.
license: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International
metadata:
  ibook.version: "1.11"
---

Two fields do the work. The name is the identifier, and it matches the directory name. The description is the text the harness uses to decide when the skill is relevant, so it must say both what the skill does and when to use it. A description that says only what the skill does gives the harness no way to tell when it applies.

The Description Is How a Skill Gets Chosen

A harness with thirty skills installed cannot read thirty full procedures on every request. It reads thirty one-paragraph descriptions and loads the one that fits. A skill with an unclear description is invisible, however good its body is, so the description is the part to write most carefully.

docs.title: Skill Loading
docs.text:
Skill loading is how a harness brings a skill into the conversation. It works in stages so that the context is not spent on instructions that are not needed. At startup the harness reads only the name and description of each installed skill and places those short entries in the system prompt. When the model, or the user's request, selects a skill, the harness loads that skill's SKILL.md body. The reference documents load later still, one at a time, when a step names them.

The staging has a consequence for a local model. A skill whose body runs past a thousand lines, with reference documents beside it, asks the model to find the right file at the right step. A model that does not look when it should will proceed without the reference and produce something that ignores a rule the reference stated. That is a failure of skill following, and it is one of the two abilities this benchmark tests.

docs.title: Skill Installation
docs.text:
Skill installation is placing the skill directories where the harness looks for them. For Claude Code that is a skills directory under its configuration folder in the home directory. This evaluation's skills live in one repository and are linked there, so that updating the repository updates every harness.

Inside the benchmark container the skills are mounted read-only. The agent can read every skill and cannot change any of them, which matters for the comparison: a model that rewrote a skill to make its own task easier would be measuring itself against a different test.

-v <skills-repo>/skills:/home/agent/.claude/skills:ro

The :ro suffix marks the mount read-only.

docs.title: ibook-skills Skill Chain
docs.text:
The ibook-skills skill chain is the ordered set of skills that builds an intelligent textbook. Each skill takes the previous one's output as its input, so the order is part of the design. The full chain has ten steps.

Step Skill What it produces 1 course-description-analyzer A validated course description, scored for completeness 2 learning-graph-generator The concept list and dependency graph 3 book-chapter-generator The chapter structure, one outline per chapter 4 chapter-content-generator The text of each chapter 5 microsim-generator The interactive simulations 6 glossary-generator Definitions of the concepts 7 faq-generator Frequently asked questions 8 quiz-generator Chapter quizzes 9 reference-generator Citations for each chapter 10 book-installer Site features such as the mascot and graph viewer

This benchmark runs three of the ten, steps 2 through 4, and uses step 1 as a short check that the wiring works. MicroSims, the glossary, the FAQ, and the quizzes are outside the benchmark. The worked example is the first stage's prompt, which is what a person would type to start the skill, plus a standing answer to its approval questions.

Run the learning-graph-generator skill on this project. The course
description is at docs/course-description.md. Generate 200 concepts.

I am not available to answer questions or to review intermediate results.
Whenever the skill tells you to ask me something, or to wait for my review
or approval, treat it as approved and continue. Work through every step of
the skill, and stop when the skill is complete. Do not start the next skill.

The second paragraph is the standing approval answer that Chapter 16's permission section called for. Without it, a skill that stops to ask "does this look right?" would wait forever in an unattended run.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Claude Code is Anthropic's command-line coding agent, and it is the harness this evaluation uses. It was chosen for a practical reason: the published comparison books were generated with it and the skills were written for it, so using it makes the model the only thing that changes. It runs interactively for a person and headlessly for a script, and the headless form is the one a benchmark needs.

It is worth being exact about what Claude Code is doing here. It is the agent loop and nothing more. Every token of the textbook comes from the local model behind the endpoint, and the harness is given a placeholder credential so that it cannot reach Anthropic's service even if it tried.

docs.title: Local Endpoint Connection and Harness Configuration
docs.text:
A local endpoint connection points the harness at your own server instead of the vendor's. It is done with environment variables, and the set below is the one this project's runner uses. Each variable is explained before the table puts them together.

ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is the address the harness sends requests to, which here is the Ollama endpoint on the same machine. ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN is the credential the harness presents, and a placeholder word is enough because the local server does not check it. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is left empty. The several ...MODEL variables tell the harness which model to use in each role, and setting all of them to the same local model prevents it from asking for a name that does not exist.

Variable Value Purpose ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL http://127.0.0.1:11434 Send requests to the local server ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN A placeholder word Satisfy the harness without a real credential ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Empty Make sure no real key is used ANTHROPIC_MODEL and the DEFAULT_*_MODEL variables The local model's tag Use the same model in every role CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC 1 Turn off the harness's optional network features API_TIMEOUT_MS A large value Allow a slow model a long time per request CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS 32000 Allow long replies without cutting them off

Harness configuration is the whole of those choices plus the command-line flags. The command that runs one stage reads the prompt from a file and writes every event to a log. -p runs it non-interactively, and --output-format stream-json --verbose writes each message, tool call, and result as a line of JSON, which is the record the later chapters analyze. --max-turns caps the loop so a confused model cannot run forever.

claude -p --model <model> \
  --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  --max-turns 150 --dangerously-skip-permissions \
  < prompt.txt > run.jsonl

That Last Flag Is Safe Only Inside the Sandbox

--dangerously-skip-permissions lets the agent run any command without asking, which an unattended run requires. It is acceptable here only because the container limits what the agent can touch to its own run directory. Never use it on a machine where the agent can reach files you care about, and Chapter 18 builds the boundary.

docs.title: Harness Prompt Overhead
docs.text: Harness prompt overhead is the number of tokens the harness's own instructions and tool definitions take before your task begins. For Claude Code it is about 19,000 tokens, and it was written for Claude models. Every turn carries it, and a local model's window and speed pay for it. In this evaluation the prompts of the models in the harness started at 17,000 to 21,000 tokens, and one model's started at 35,000, which was an early sign that it would run out of window.

docs.title: Harness on Laptop
docs.text: Harness on laptop is the arrangement in which the harness runs on the machine you sit at and reaches the model on the DGX through an SSH port forward. It was this evaluation's first arrangement, and it is the quickest way to try a model, because nothing is installed on the DGX but the server. It has two drawbacks. Prompts and tokens cross the network on every turn, and the harness has no sandbox, so it was allowed no shell commands, which most skills need. The later runs moved the harness into a container on the DGX, so that a run kept going with the laptop disconnected.

docs.title: Alternatives: OpenCode, Codex CLI, and Goose
docs.text:
Claude Code is not the only harness, and the skill format is shared enough that others can run the same skills. OpenCode is an open-source harness with a lighter prompt, and it is a good second harness for telling a model failure from a harness mismatch. Codex CLI is OpenAI's command-line agent, and Goose is an open-source agent from a different publisher. Both implement the same skill format.

Harness Publisher Why consider it Why this evaluation did not use it Claude Code Anthropic The comparison books and skills were made with it Chosen OpenCode Open source Lighter prompt A good second pass, not yet run Codex CLI OpenAI Implements the skill format Did not match how the comparison books were made Goose Open source Implements the skill format Did not match how the comparison books were made

docs.title: AGENTS.md File
docs.text: An AGENTS.md file is a plain Markdown file at the root of a project that gives any coding agent the project's standing instructions: how to build, which rules to follow, where things live. It is the cross-harness counterpart of a harness-specific instruction file, and this book uses one. Its CLAUDE.md contains only a pointer to it, so that Claude Code, Codex, and any other agent that looks for AGENTS.md read the same rules.

docs.title: Skill Execution Verification
docs.text:
Skill execution verification is confirming that a skill ran to completion and produced what it should. It is a separate check from the first-prompt smoke test of Chapter 13, which tested only the server. This one tests the harness, the model, and the skill together.

The check this project uses is a short skill run of about three minutes, the course-description analyzer, whose output can be inspected quickly. It passes when four things are true.

  • The report was written. The skill's output file exists.
  • A score was given. The report contains the quality score the skill is meant to assign.
  • The project files were updated. The frontmatter and the site navigation reflect the skill's work.
  • The site builds. A strict mkdocs build finishes with no errors.

A script, score_analyzer_runs.py, applies exactly these checks, so the verdict does not depend on someone reading the output.

docs.title: Harness Compatibility Test
docs.text:
A harness compatibility test runs the same short skill against several harness and model combinations, to find which pairs work at all before spending hours on any of them. Failures at this stage are cheap and informative. In this evaluation it showed a model that wrote its first tool call as plain text, and a model that lost the task after a few turns, both within minutes, and neither would have been found by a first-prompt smoke test.

Run the Three-Minute Test Before the Three-Hour One

A model that fails the short skill will fail the long one more slowly. Put the analyzer run, with its scripted checks, in front of every model you intend to benchmark, and discard the ones that fail for reasons you can name.

docs.title: Diagram: SKILL.md Anatomy
docs.text:
Run SKILL.md Anatomy Fullscreen

SKILL.md Anatomy

Type: infographic sim-id: skill-md-anatomy Library: html Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ibook-skills/tree/main/docs/sims/skill-file-anatomy-diagram Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify the part of a skill that answers each of 6 questions about how a harness uses it, with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: agent skill, SKILL.md format, skill loading, skill installation (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The sim shows an annotated skill folder with six labeled regions. For each of 6 questions the learner selects one region before the sim reveals the answer. A selection is correct when it equals the Correct region column. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Hovering over a region to read its label is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The harness reads every file in a skill at startup. (2) The body of SKILL.md is how a skill is chosen. (3) Reference documents are loaded with the instructions. (4) A skill's scripts run by themselves.

Instructional Rationale: Identifying a part at the Remember level needs a labeled structure and questions that name a function, so that the learner links each function to its place. The questions are phrased by what the harness does, which is the behavior the chapter taught.

Content:

The six regions of the annotated skill folder: "name field", "description field", "metadata field", "instruction body", "references folder", and "scripts folder".

# Question shown to the learner Correct region Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which part is the skill's identifier, matching the directory name? name field The name identifies the skill to the harness. 2 Which part does the harness read at startup to decide whether the skill applies? description field Only the name and description of each skill are loaded at startup. 3 Which part holds the step-by-step procedure, loaded when the skill is invoked? instruction body The body is loaded on selection, not at startup. 4 Which part holds long documents that are read only when a step names them? references folder References are loaded last, one at a time. 5 Which part holds helper programs that a step tells the model to run? scripts folder Scripts are run by a step, and they do not run on their own. 6 Which part records the skill's version? metadata field The version is carried in the metadata block of the header.

Provenance: The annotated folder and the questions are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The meanings of the parts come from the sections of this chapter above.

Rules: Questions are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6. Each allows one final choice among the six regions, and exactly one region is correct for each question. A region may be the answer to only one question.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner hovers over the regions of the annotated folder to read their labels.
  2. The learner reads question 1 and selects a region, then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct region and the Why text, and marks the question correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for questions 2 to 6. After question 6 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Six questions, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct region and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 6 correct".

Starting State: The annotated folder is shown with no region selected, and the instruction on screen is "Hover over a region to read its label".

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a harness reads only each skill's name and description at startup, loads the body when the skill is selected, and loads references only when a step names them, and that scripts run only when a step runs them.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
A skill is a folder whose SKILL.md header lets a harness choose it and whose body, references, and scripts supply the procedure in stages. The ibook-skills chain has ten steps, and the benchmark runs three of them, with a fourth used as a short wiring check. Claude Code connects to the local endpoint through environment variables that set its address, a placeholder credential, and the model in every role, and its headless flags write a full event log. Alternative harnesses read the same skills, and an AGENTS.md file gives all of them the project's rules. Skill execution verification applies four scripted checks to a three-minute run, and a harness compatibility test applies it across combinations, so that a failure costs minutes and not hours.

The Harness Runs a Skill End to End

You can now install a skill, point a harness at your own endpoint with a placeholder credential, and prove with a scripted three-minute run that the chain works. Chapter 18 builds the container and the boundaries that keep that run from reaching anything it should not.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
docs.text: Test your understanding of the skill format, the ibook-skills chain, connecting a harness to a local endpoint, and verifying that a skill runs with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is an agent skill?
docs.text:
1. A folder of instructions that teaches a harness one kind of task
  2. A new tool that adds a capability the harness lacked
  3. A fine-tuned model that replaces the default model inside the harness
  4. A log of the tool calls made during a finished run
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An agent skill is a folder of instructions, and sometimes helper files, that teaches a harness how to carry out one kind of task well. It is a procedure written down so a model can follow it: the steps, the order, the checks, and the formats of the files to produce. A skill does not add a capability the harness lacks. It supplies knowledge of how to use the capabilities it has, which makes results repeatable.

Concept Tested: Agent Skill

See: Agent Skill

docs.title: 2. Which steps of the ten-step ibook-skills chain does the benchmark run as its stages?
docs.text:
1. All ten, from the course description to the installer
  2. Three: the learning graph, chapter structure, and chapter content
  3. Two: the glossary and the chapter quizzes
  4. Five: every step up to and including the MicroSims
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The ibook-skills skill chain is the ordered set of ten skills that builds an intelligent textbook, each taking the previous one's output as its input. This benchmark runs three of the ten, steps 2 through 4: the learning graph, the chapter structure, and the chapter content. Step 1, the course-description analyzer, serves as a short check that the wiring works. MicroSims, the glossary, the FAQ, and the quizzes are outside the benchmark.

Concept Tested: ibook-skills Skill Chain

See: ibook-skills Skill Chain

docs.title: 3. Which two header fields of a SKILL.md file identify a skill and let a harness decide when it applies?
docs.text:
1. name and description
  2. license and metadata
  3. scripts and assets
  4. title and summary
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The SKILL.md format is a Markdown file that opens with a block of YAML metadata, followed by the procedure. Two fields do the work. The name is the identifier and matches the directory name. The description is the text the harness uses to decide when the skill is relevant, so it must say both what the skill does and when to use it. A skill with an unclear description is invisible, however good its body is.

Concept Tested: SKILL.md Format

See: SKILL.md Format

docs.title: 4. Why does a harness load skills in stages?
docs.text:
1. So each skill can be edited by the model between its loading stages
  2. So the model can run scripts before reading the header
  3. So skills from different harnesses do not overwrite each other
  4. So context is not spent on instructions that are not needed
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Skill loading works in stages so that context is not spent on instructions that are not needed. At startup the harness reads only each installed skill's name and description and places those short entries in the system prompt. It loads a skill's SKILL.md body when that skill is selected, and reference documents later still, one at a time, when a step names them. A harness with thirty skills cannot read thirty full procedures on every request.

Concept Tested: Skill Loading

See: Skill Loading

docs.title: 5. Why are the skills mounted read-only inside the benchmark container?
docs.text:
1. So the skills load faster at the start of every turn
  2. So a model cannot alter the test it is being measured against
  3. So the container can start up without any access to the network
  4. So the harness skips the skill descriptions at startup
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Skill installation places the skill directories where the harness looks for them. Inside the benchmark container the skills are mounted read-only, marked by the :ro suffix, so the agent can read every skill and cannot change any of them. That matters for the comparison: a model that rewrote a skill to make its own task easier would be measuring itself against a different test than the other models faced.

Concept Tested: Skill Installation

See: Skill Installation

docs.title: 6. Why was Claude Code chosen as the harness for this evaluation?
docs.text:
1. It has the lightest system prompt of the harnesses compared
  2. It is the only harness that implements the skill format
  3. It can reach Anthropic's service when a local model fails
  4. The comparison books and the skills were made with it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Claude Code is Anthropic's command-line coding agent and the harness this evaluation uses. It was chosen for a practical reason: the published comparison books were generated with it and the skills were written for it, so using it makes the model the only thing that changes. Its prompt is not the lightest; OpenCode's is lighter. It is also given a placeholder credential, so it cannot reach Anthropic's service even if it tried.

Concept Tested: Claude Code

See: Claude Code

docs.title: 7. You are configuring Claude Code to use a model served by a local endpoint. Which settings point it at the local server without a real credential?
docs.text:
1. ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to the local endpoint, with a placeholder token
  2. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to a real key, with the vendor's default base address
  3. API_TIMEOUT_MS to zero, with the vendor's address unchanged
  4. ANTHROPIC_MODEL to a cloud model name, with no base address
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A local endpoint connection points the harness at your own server through environment variables. ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is the address requests go to, here the local endpoint. ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN is a placeholder word, which is enough because the local server does not check it, and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is left empty so no real key is used. The model variables are all set to the same local model's tag, so the harness never asks for a name that does not exist.

Concept Tested: Local Endpoint Connection

See: Local Endpoint Connection and Harness Configuration

docs.title: 8. A three-minute run of the course-description analyzer has finished. Which set of checks tells you the skill executed correctly?
docs.text:
1. The server answered, and the reply was not empty
  2. The run log exists, and the run used fewer than 150 turns
  3. Report written, score given, files updated, strict build passes
  4. The model loaded on the GPU, and its speed was plausible
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Skill execution verification confirms that a skill ran to completion and produced what it should. It tests the harness, the model, and the skill together. The short analyzer run passes when four things are true: the report was written, a quality score was given, the frontmatter and navigation were updated, and a strict mkdocs build finishes with no errors. An answering server and a plausible speed belong to the first-prompt smoke test, which tests only the server.

Concept Tested: Skill Execution Verification

See: Skill Execution Verification

docs.title: 9. You want a headless stage run that records every message, tool call, and result as a line of JSON. Which flags of the claude command do that?
docs.text:
1. --max-turns 150 with --model <model>
  2. --dangerously-skip-permissions by itself
  3. -p with --output-format stream-json --verbose
  4. --verbose with the prompt typed into an interactive session
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Harness configuration is the environment variables plus the command-line flags. -p runs Claude Code non-interactively, and --output-format stream-json --verbose writes each message, tool call, and result as a line of JSON, which is the record later chapters analyze. --max-turns only caps the loop so a confused model cannot run forever, and --dangerously-skip-permissions removes approval prompts, which is acceptable only inside the sandbox.

Concept Tested: Harness Configuration

See: Local Endpoint Connection and Harness Configuration

docs.title: 10. A model passes the first-prompt smoke test and then fails the three-minute skill run by writing its tool call as plain text. What does this pattern show?
docs.text:
1. The smoke test was run with the wrong context length on the server
  2. The skill's description did not say when to use it
  3. The server lost the model between the two tests
  4. The smoke test covers only the server, not harness tool use
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A harness compatibility test runs the same short skill against several harness and model combinations to find which pairs work at all. The first-prompt smoke test checks only the server: that it answers and how fast. It does not exercise tool calls through the harness. In this evaluation the short skill run exposed a model that wrote its first tool call as plain text within minutes, a failure that a first-prompt smoke test would not have found.

Concept Tested: Harness Compatibility Test

See: Harness Compatibility Test

docs.title: References: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
docs.text:
1. YAML - Wikipedia - Covers the YAML data format, its indentation-based syntax, features, and comparison with JSON and TOML. It explains the syntax of the metadata block that opens every SKILL.md file and carries a skill's name and description.

  2. Environment variable - Wikipedia - Explains named values that a running program reads for configuration, how child processes inherit them, and how Unix shells assign and export them. It is the mechanism this chapter uses to point Claude Code at a local endpoint.

  3. Smoke testing (software) - Wikipedia - Defines smoke tests as quick, preliminary checks of a system's most important functions that decide whether a build merits deeper testing, and gives the term's etymology. It matches this chapter's three-minute analyzer run before any long skill.

  4. The Pragmatic Programmer: Your Journey to Mastery (20th Anniversary Edition) - David Thomas and Andrew Hunt - Addison-Wesley Professional - Popularized the "tracer bullets" metaphor: a thin, working end-to-end slice built first so feedback arrives early. That idea clarifies why this chapter runs a three-minute skill through the whole chain before committing to a long one.

  5. The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right - Atul Gawande - Metropolitan Books - Argues that short written checklists make expert work reliable, using the WHO surgical safety checklist and its pause points, and separates read-do lists from do-confirm lists. A skill is a read-do checklist for a model.

  6. Agent Skills - Claude Platform Documentation - Defines a skill as a directory with a SKILL.md file and YAML frontmatter, and explains progressive loading: metadata at startup, instructions when triggered, resources as needed. It is the reference for this chapter's skill loading and installation.

  7. Agent Skills Specification - agentskills.io - Specifies the SKILL.md frontmatter fields (name, description, license, compatibility, metadata), the optional scripts, references, and assets folders, and the recommended progressive-disclosure limits. It is the open format behind this chapter's SKILL.md header and folder layout.

  8. Anthropic compatibility - Ollama Documentation - Explains how Ollama serves a subset of the Anthropic Messages API: set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to the local server, use any placeholder key, and get streaming and tool calling. It is the endpoint side of this chapter's configuration.

  9. CLI reference - Claude Code Documentation - Lists command-line flags, including -p for non-interactive runs, --output-format stream-json, --max-turns, --model, and --dangerously-skip-permissions. It documents the headless flags in this chapter's run command and what each one does.

  10. AGENTS.md - AGENTS.md Project - Describes AGENTS.md, a plain Markdown file of project instructions for coding agents, with example sections for setup, code style, and testing, and a list of agents that read it. It is the cross-harness instruction file this chapter describes.

docs.title: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
Summary
docs.text: This chapter bounds what a harness running a model can reach. Students run the harness in a Docker sandbox with a non-root user, read-only skills, and a defined network boundary, then trace and verify what data leaves the machine. They finish with a contained run that does not freeze the host.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 18 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Docker 22 Docker Group Membership 1 NVIDIA Container Toolkit 1 Network Boundary 35 Data Egress Trace 33 Harness Container 19 Container Sandbox 2 Host Network Mode 2 Supervision Data Exposure 1 Harness on DGX 1 Non-Root Container User 1 Read-Only Skill Mount 1 Placeholder Credential 1 System Freeze 1 Telemetry Disabled 2 Network Sandbox Gap 1 Memory Watchdog 1 Packet Capture Verification 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 4: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
  • Chapter 5: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
  • Chapter 6: Cost, Price, and Quality
  • Chapter 7: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
  • Chapter 10: Python Hardware Probes
  • Chapter 13: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
  • Chapter 15: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
  • Chapter 16: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
  • Chapter 17: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model

Let the Agent Work, and Fence the Yard

An agent that can run any command is exactly as useful as it is dangerous, and the container is how you keep the first and limit the second. By the end of this chapter you will know what a contained run can and cannot touch, and how to check where its data goes. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 17 ended with a harness that runs a skill, and with a flag that lets the agent run any command without asking. That is only reasonable inside a boundary. This chapter builds the boundary and, just as important, states honestly where it has gaps.

There are two boundaries to keep apart. The first is the filesystem boundary: what files the agent can read and change. A container handles it well. The second is the network boundary: where the agent's traffic can go. A container handles it only if it is configured to, and the arrangement this evaluation used did not. The chapter closes with a third concern that has nothing to do with security, which is a run that exhausts the machine's memory and freezes it.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Docker is a tool that runs programs in containers. A container is an isolated process with its own view of the filesystem, built from an image, a packaged set of files and settings. It shares the host's operating system kernel and is not a full virtual machine, so it starts in a second and costs little. The isolation is real and it is partial, and what it covers depends on how the container is started.

For this evaluation Docker does three jobs. It gives every run the same software, because the image is built once with pinned versions. It limits what the agent can write to, by mounting only specified folders. And it can be killed cleanly, with every process the agent started, by killing the container.

docs.title: Docker Group Membership
docs.text:
Docker group membership is the permission that lets a user run docker commands on a Linux machine. Because the Docker service runs as root, a member of the group can start a container that mounts any directory of the host, which makes membership equivalent to administrator access.

That is the reason the Administrator, and not the evaluator, decided it. The benchmark account was at first in no group but its own, and every Docker command failed with permission denied. After the Administrator added the account to the docker group, new logins could run containers.

docs.title: NVIDIA Container Toolkit
docs.text: The NVIDIA Container Toolkit is the software that lets a container use the host's GPU. The harness container in this evaluation does not need the GPU, because the model runs in the server on the host and the container only calls it over the network. The toolkit was present on the units, and it matters for a reader who wants to run the model server itself in a container, as vLLM usually is.

docs.title: Harness Container, Container Sandbox, and Harness on DGX
docs.text:
The harness container is the container that holds the agent. The container sandbox is the boundary it creates: inside it the agent may run any command, and the only paths it can write to are the ones deliberately mounted in. Harness on DGX is the arrangement in which that container runs on the DGX itself, beside the model server, so that the harness and the model talk over the machine's own loopback interface.

The excerpt from this project's runner shows the boundary as code. Before the lines are read, three Docker options need defining. -v host:container mounts a host folder into the container, and a :ro suffix makes it read-only. -w sets the working directory. -e sets an environment variable inside.

docker run --rm -i --network host --name "harness-$label" \
  -v "$run":/work -w /work \
  -v "$state":/home/agent/.claude \
  -v "$skills_repo/skills":/home/agent/.claude/skills:ro \
  -e ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://127.0.0.1:$port" \
  -e ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=ollama \
  "$image" claude -p ...

Reading the excerpt as a list of what the agent can and cannot reach gives the table below.

Mount or setting What it grants What it prevents -v "$run":/work Read and write in this run's directory Touching any other directory on the host -v "$state":/home/agent/.claude Write the harness's own transcript Nothing else; it is a separate folder ...skills:ro Read the skills Changing a skill Non-root user in the image Ordinary file permissions Acting as root inside the container --rm The container is deleted when it ends Leaving a stopped container behind

docs.title: Non-Root Container User and Read-Only Skill Mount
docs.text:
A non-root container user is a user with ordinary permissions inside the container, created in the image with the same numeric user and group identifiers as the account that started the run. Two things follow. Files the agent writes into the run directory belong to the evaluator and not to root, so they can be read and deleted without special rights. And the agent cannot do the things only root can do, even inside its own container.

A read-only skill mount is the :ro on the skills folder. The agent can follow a skill and cannot alter it. Chapter 17 gave the reason: a model that could edit the skill would be measuring itself against a different test.

Make the Container's User Match Yours

Build the image with your own user and group identifiers, using the UID and GID build arguments. Otherwise every file the agent writes is owned by a different user, and you will need elevated rights to clean up a run.

docs.title: Placeholder Credential and Telemetry Disabled
docs.text:
A placeholder credential is a fake value in the place a real one would go. The harness insists on having a credential, and the local server does not check one, so the evaluation gave it a word that is not a secret. If the harness ever tried to reach the vendor's service, the request would fail for want of a real credential.

Telemetry disabled means turning off the harness's optional reporting and update checks, with the settings CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 and DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1. They remove two sources of network traffic that a local-only evaluation does not want. They are configuration, not a guarantee, which is what the next section addresses.

docs.title: Network Boundary
docs.text:
A network boundary is the line between traffic that stays on a machine, or on a network you control, and traffic that leaves it. The reason to run a model locally is to control that line, so the line has to be drawn and checked, not assumed.

Chapter 4 listed what data crosses it in each arrangement, and the testing-architecture diagram of this evaluation shows its own. The sim below is the existing diagram, embedded: step through it to see which machine does each job and what each outside party can see.

docs.title: Diagram: Testing Architecture
docs.text:
Run the Testing Architecture MicroSim fullscreen

Testing Architecture (reused MicroSim)

Type: microsim sim-id: testing-architecture Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: sims/testing-architecture/index.md in this book Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/dgx-eval/tree/main/docs/sims/testing-architecture Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain which machine performs each role in this evaluation and which outside parties can see which data.

Reused from this book's own MicroSims, which already exists locally, so no new specification is needed.

docs.title: Data Egress Trace
docs.text:
