A data egress trace is an accounting of every place a system's data goes when it leaves. It is built component by component, and for each one it records the destination, what is sent, and how often. The result is a table that can be checked against what actually happened.

The trace for this evaluation, for the generation loop itself, is short, and it is worth reading as a model of the form.

Component Sends to What When Harness The model server on the same machine Prompts and tool results Every turn, over loopback Model server A model registry A request for a file Once, at download Container build A package index and the vendor's installer host Requests for packages Once, at build Harness optional features The vendor's service Update checks and reports Disabled by configuration Laptop and DGX Each other, over the tailnet SSH sessions and fetched output Throughout, encrypted Orchestrator A cloud model's API Whatever it reads to monitor and score Throughout

docs.title: Supervision Data Exposure
docs.text:
Supervision data exposure is the data that reaches a third party because something is watching the run, even though the run itself is local. It is the row at the bottom of the table. The orchestrator is a cloud model, and everything it reads back to monitor or score a run, including generated text and log excerpts, goes to its service.

The generation loop kept its tokens local, and the supervision of it did not. Nothing about this is a flaw in the setup. It is a fact that has to be stated, because a claim of "everything stayed local" would have been false. A reader with strict data-sovereignty needs replaces the cloud orchestrator with a script or a local one, and Chapter 4's privacy table is the checklist for which parts to bring in.

'The Model Runs Locally' Is Not 'Nothing Leaves'

Whatever reads the output, whether a reviewer, a scoring script that uploads, or a supervising assistant, can send it away. Trace where the generated text travels after the model writes it, and put every destination in the trace table before you claim a boundary.

docs.title: Host Network Mode and the Network Sandbox Gap
docs.text:
Host network mode is the Docker setting, --network host, that makes a container share the host's network instead of having its own. The harness container was started this way so that it could reach the model server, which listens only on the host's loopback address. A container on its own network cannot see the host's loopback.

The cost is the network sandbox gap. A container in host network mode can reach anything the host can: the internet, other machines on the tailnet, and every service on the host's loopback. The container is a filesystem sandbox, not a network sandbox, and the project's runner says so in its own header. The agent can be told not to reach out, and a model that has been told is not a boundary.

Option What it does What it costs Host network mode, as used Container reaches the loopback server No network isolation A private network with no outside route, and the server on it too Container can reach only the server The server has to run in a container too A firewall rule limiting the container's traffic Container reaches only listed destinations Needs administrator rights on the host No network at all Nothing leaves The container cannot reach the model

docs.title: Packet Capture Verification
docs.text:
Packet capture verification is watching the network interface during a run and confirming that the only traffic is the traffic the trace says. It turns the table above from a claim into a result. It needs administrator rights, because reading raw packets is a privileged operation.

This evaluation did not do it. The configuration, which is a placeholder credential and the optional features turned off, is stated, and it was not confirmed with a capture. The book says so for the same reason it names the supervision exposure: a boundary that has not been verified is a hypothesis.

A lighter check needs no special rights and catches the gross cases. While a run is going, list the established connections on the machine and look for any peer that is not the loopback address.

ss -tnH state established | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -c

ss lists the machine's sockets. -t selects TCP, -n prints addresses numerically, -H drops the header line, and state established keeps only live connections. The fourth column is the peer. Any address you cannot account for is a line to add to the trace, and an address you capture is one to redact before it goes in a published document.

docs.title: Diagram: Data Egress Trace Classifier
docs.text:
Run Data Egress Trace Classifier Fullscreen

Data Egress Trace Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: egress-trace-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish, for 8 data flows in a local-generation setup, whether each stays on the DGX, goes to the evaluator's own machine, or goes to a third party, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: network boundary, data egress trace, supervision data exposure, host network mode, telemetry disabled (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 8 flows the learner commits one of three destinations before the sim reveals the answer. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct destination column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the flows is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A locally hosted model means no data leaves. (2) Traffic to the evaluator's own laptop is traffic to a third party. (3) A one-time download is not egress. (4) The supervising assistant's reads are local.

Instructional Rationale: Analyzing a boundary needs the learner to separate flows by where they end, so the three destinations are exclusive and each flow ends in exactly one. Mixed flows prevent the habit of answering "stays" or "leaves" for everything.

Content:

The three destinations the learner chooses from: "Stays on the DGX", "Goes to the evaluator's own machine", and "Goes to a third party".

# Flow shown to the learner Correct destination Why (shown as feedback) 1 The harness in the container sends a prompt to the model server at the loopback address. Stays on the DGX Both ends are on the same machine and the traffic never leaves its loopback interface. 2 The model server reads a model file from the DGX's disk. Stays on the DGX A disk read is internal to the machine. 3 The model server downloads a model file from the public model library. Goes to a third party The request and the file travel to and from the library's host. 4 The container build downloads a base image and the harness installer. Goes to a third party The requests go to the hosts that serve those files. 5 The orchestrator on the laptop reads a generated chapter and sends it to a cloud model to be scored. Goes to a third party The generated text ends at the cloud model's service. 6 The laptop fetches the finished book from the DGX over SSH on the tailnet. Goes to the evaluator's own machine The destination is the evaluator's laptop, and the connection is encrypted. 7 The harness's optional update check runs, with its optional features left on. Goes to a third party The check contacts the vendor's service. 8 The watchdog appends a line to its log file on the DGX. Stays on the DGX It is a local file write.

Provenance: The flows are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". They follow the egress table in this chapter.

Rules: Flows are shown in the fixed order 1 to 8. Each allows one final choice, and exactly one destination is correct for each. A flow's destination is where its data ends, not the first hop.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads flow 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the three destinations and confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct destination and the Why text, and marks the flow correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for flows 2 to 8. After flow 8 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Eight flows, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct destination and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 8 correct".

Starting State: Flow 1 is shown with no destination chosen, and the question on screen is "Where does this data end up?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the harness-to-server traffic stays on loopback, that downloads and container builds go to third parties, that the cloud orchestrator's reads reach its API, and that the fetch of the finished book goes to the evaluator's own laptop.

docs.title: System Freeze
docs.text:
A system freeze is the machine ceasing to respond entirely: no SSH, no network, no output. It is different from a crashed program. On a unified-memory machine it is a recognizable consequence of exhausting the shared pool, and it needs the Administrator to restart it, because nothing remote can reach a machine that is not answering.

This evaluation had one unit stop responding twice, each time a few minutes into a long run with the same model. The first was at a 256,000-token context. The second was at a smaller context with a watchdog running, and the watchdog logged no action, so memory exhaustion as the only cause is not confirmed. Heat, power, and the memory hardware itself were not ruled out.

docs.title: Memory Watchdog
docs.text:
A memory watchdog is a small program that watches memory and temperature and acts before they reach a dangerous level. This project's version checks available memory and GPU temperature every five seconds. When memory falls below a floor, or the temperature passes a ceiling, it kills the harness containers and unloads every model from the server, then keeps watching.

It takes two arguments: the floor in gibibytes and the ceiling in degrees Celsius, with defaults of 16 and 95. This evaluation ran it with a 20 GiB floor, which, on a 128 GB machine, leaves about 15% for the system.

src/dgx-setup/mem_watchdog.sh 20 95 &

A watchdog is a safeguard against the failure you expect, and it is not a diagnosis of the one you get. It does not replace the vitals log of Chapter 10, which records the readings that a frozen machine would otherwise take with it. Run both before any long run, and treat the pair as a precondition.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
A container gives an agent a filesystem sandbox: a pinned image, a non-root user whose files belong to the evaluator, a writable run directory, and read-only skills. It does not give a network sandbox when started in host network mode, which this evaluation used so the harness could reach a loopback-bound server, and the gap is stated. A data egress trace lists every destination, and it must include the supervision that reads the output, which in this evaluation was a cloud model. A packet capture would verify the trace, and a lighter ss check catches gross cases. A memory watchdog and a vitals log are preconditions for a long run on a unified-memory machine, and neither explains a freeze.

You Can Fence the Run and Say Where It Leaks

You can now run a harness in a sandbox that limits what it can write, draw the network boundary honestly, and put a watchdog under a long run. Chapter 19 designs the evaluation those runs will serve.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
docs.text: Test your understanding of the container sandbox, the network boundary, the data egress trace, and safeguards against a frozen host with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a Docker container?
docs.text:
1. An isolated process with its own view of the filesystem
  2. A full virtual machine with its own operating system kernel
  3. A background service that starts the model server at boot
  4. A firewall rule that limits where a process can connect
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Docker runs programs in containers. A container is an isolated process with its own view of the filesystem, built from an image, a packaged set of files and settings. It shares the host's operating system kernel and is not a full virtual machine, so it starts in a second and costs little. The isolation is real and it is partial, and what it covers depends on how the container is started.

Concept Tested: Docker

See: Docker

docs.title: 2. Inside the harness container, what may the agent do, and where can it write?
docs.text:
1. Run only pre-approved commands, and write anywhere on the host
  2. Run no shell commands, and write only to the skills folder
  3. Run any command as root, and write to the host's home directory
  4. Run any command, and write only to deliberately mounted paths
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The harness container holds the agent, and the container sandbox is the boundary it creates: inside it the agent may run any command, and the only paths it can write to are the ones deliberately mounted in. The run directory is mounted writable, the harness's own state folder is separate, and the skills are read-only. The image also uses a non-root user, so the agent cannot do what only root can do, even inside its own container.

Concept Tested: Harness Container

See: Harness Container, Container Sandbox, and Harness on DGX

docs.title: 3. Why was adding the benchmark account to the docker group a decision for the Administrator?
docs.text:
1. Group members can change the tailnet's access control list directly
  2. The group gives a user ownership of the model files
  3. A member can mount any host directory, like an administrator
  4. The group is required before a user can log in over SSH
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Docker group membership is the permission that lets a user run docker commands. Because the Docker service runs as root, a member of the group can start a container that mounts any directory of the host, which makes membership equivalent to administrator access. That is why the Administrator, and not the evaluator, decided it. Until the account was added, every Docker command failed with permission denied.

Concept Tested: Docker Group Membership

See: Docker Group Membership

docs.title: 4. Why was the harness container started with --network host?
docs.text:
1. So the agent could download packages while it runs
  2. So it could reach the server on the host's loopback address
  3. So the container would be isolated from the tailnet
  4. So the GPU would be visible inside the container
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Host network mode, set with --network host, makes a container share the host's network instead of having its own. The harness container was started this way so it could reach the model server, which listens only on the host's loopback address; a container on its own network cannot see the host's loopback. The harness container does not need the GPU at all, because the model runs in the server on the host.

Concept Tested: Host Network Mode

See: Host Network Mode and the Network Sandbox Gap

docs.title: 5. Why would a claim that "everything stayed local" be false for this evaluation?
docs.text:
1. The harness sent every prompt to the vendor's service
  2. The cloud orchestrator read output to monitor and score runs
  3. The model server uploaded its weights after each stage
  4. The coordination service stored a copy of each generated chapter
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Supervision data exposure is the data that reaches a third party because something is watching the run, even though the run itself is local. Here the orchestrator is a cloud model, and everything it reads back to monitor or score a run, including generated text and log excerpts, goes to its service. The generation loop kept its tokens local, and the supervision of it did not. That is not a flaw in the setup, but it has to be stated.

Concept Tested: Supervision Data Exposure

See: Supervision Data Exposure

docs.title: 6. After a run, the files in the run directory are owned by a different user, and you need elevated rights to delete them. What should you change?
docs.text:
1. Start the container without the --network host option
  2. Mount the skills folder without the :ro suffix
  3. Build the image with your own UID and GID arguments
  4. Add --rm so the container is deleted when it ends
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A non-root container user has ordinary permissions inside the container and is created in the image with the same numeric user and group identifiers as the account that started the run. Files the agent writes then belong to the evaluator and not to root, so they can be read and deleted without special rights. Build the image with your own identifiers, using the UID and GID build arguments, or cleanup needs elevated rights.

Concept Tested: Non-Root Container User

See: Non-Root Container User and Read-Only Skill Mount

docs.title: 7. You have no administrator rights but want a basic check of where a running harness connects. What can you do?
docs.text:
1. Run a full packet capture on the network interface
  2. List established connections with ss and check each peer
  3. Read the model card for a list of contacted hosts
  4. Set a placeholder credential and assume nothing leaves
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Packet capture verification watches the network interface during a run and confirms that the only traffic is what the trace says, but reading raw packets needs administrator rights. A lighter check needs none and catches the gross cases: while a run is going, list the established connections with ss -tnH state established and look for any peer that is not the loopback address. A placeholder credential is configuration, not verification, and an unverified boundary is a hypothesis.

Concept Tested: Packet Capture Verification

See: Packet Capture Verification

docs.title: 8. You are writing the egress trace for a local-generation setup in which a script uploads each generated chapter to a cloud scoring service. Where does this flow belong?
docs.text:
1. Nowhere, because the model itself runs locally
  2. Under loopback traffic, because the script itself runs on the DGX
  3. In the trace, as a third-party destination with what is sent
  4. Under one-time downloads, because uploads are counted only once
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A data egress trace is an accounting of every place a system's data goes when it leaves, built component by component with the destination, what is sent, and how often. Whatever reads the output, whether a reviewer, a scoring script that uploads, or a supervising assistant, can send it away. The upload therefore gets its own row as a third-party destination. "The model runs locally" is not the same claim as "nothing leaves".

Concept Tested: Data Egress Trace

See: Data Egress Trace

docs.title: 9. The harness container limits the agent's writes to the run directory, yet it is described as not being a network sandbox. What explains the difference?
docs.text:
1. Mounts bound the filesystem; host networking shares the host's reach
  2. The non-root user is allowed to change the host's firewall rules
  3. The read-only skills mount exposes the tailnet to the agent
  4. The placeholder credential opens the vendor's service to the agent's calls
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The mounts decide what files the agent can reach, so the container is a real filesystem sandbox. Host network mode is a separate setting: a container that shares the host's network can reach anything the host can, including the internet, other machines on the tailnet, and every service on the host's loopback. That is the network sandbox gap. The agent can be told not to reach out, and a model that has been told is not a boundary.

Concept Tested: Network Sandbox Gap

See: Host Network Mode and the Network Sandbox Gap

docs.title: 10. One unit stopped responding twice. The second time, a watchdog was running at a smaller context and logged no action. What does this evidence support?
docs.text:
1. The freeze was caused by the 256,000-token context setting
  2. The watchdog itself caused the machine to stop responding
  3. The model's weights were corrupted during the download
  4. Memory exhaustion as the sole cause is not confirmed
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A system freeze is the machine ceasing to respond entirely, which needs the Administrator to restart it. The first freeze was at a 256,000-token context. The second was at a smaller context with a watchdog running, and the watchdog logged no action, so memory exhaustion as the only cause is not confirmed. Heat, power, and the memory hardware itself were not ruled out. A watchdog guards against the failure you expect; it is not a diagnosis of the one you get.

Concept Tested: System Freeze

See: System Freeze

docs.title: References: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
docs.text:
1. Docker (software) - Wikipedia - Describes Docker's history, design, and components, including images as read-only templates and containers that share one operating system kernel. It supports this chapter's explanation of why a container is isolated but not a virtual machine.

  2. Sandbox (computer security) - Wikipedia - Surveys sandbox implementations, including Linux namespaces and seccomp, virtual machines, jails, and language runtimes, each limiting what untrusted code can reach. It frames this chapter's filesystem sandbox and why it differs from a network sandbox.

  3. Packet analyzer - Wikipedia - Defines packet analyzers as tools that intercept and log network traffic, covering their capabilities, uses, and notable examples such as Wireshark and tcpdump. It underlies this chapter's packet capture verification of what actually leaves the machine.

  4. Container Security: Fundamental Technology Concepts that Protect Containerized Applications (1st Edition) - Liz Rice - O'Reilly Media - Explains containers through Linux namespaces, control groups, and capabilities, with runnable examples, an approach she also showed in her live-coded "Containers from Scratch" talk. It clarifies why a container limits files but not, in host mode, the network.

  5. Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (8th Edition) - James F. Kurose and Keith W. Ross - Pearson - Teaches networking from the application layer downward and pairs chapters with Wireshark labs in which students capture and read real packets. That hands-on capture method clarifies this chapter's packet capture verification.

  6. Docker Engine security - Docker Documentation - Explains kernel namespaces, control groups, the root-privileged daemon and its attack surface, restricted Linux capabilities, and running processes as non-root users. It supports this chapter's Docker group, non-root user, and sandbox sections.

  7. Host network driver - Docker Documentation - Explains that --network host makes a container share the host's network stack, so no network isolation or port mapping applies. It documents the network sandbox gap this chapter names for its harness container.

  8. Development containers - Claude Code Documentation - Covers running Claude Code in a Docker dev container as a non-root user, restricting network egress with a firewall, disabling non-essential traffic, and the exfiltration limits of --dangerously-skip-permissions. It mirrors this chapter's sandbox and its stated gaps.

  9. NVIDIA Container Toolkit Overview - NVIDIA Documentation - Introduces the libraries and utilities for building and running GPU-accelerated containers, including the container runtime and the nvidia-ctk command-line tool. It documents the toolkit this chapter says a containerized model server needs and the harness container does not.

  10. Wireshark User's Guide - Wireshark Documentation - Documents capturing live network data, choosing capture interfaces, capture filters, and display filters for reading traffic. It shows how to carry out the privileged packet capture this chapter describes but did not run.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter turns the evaluation question into an experiment that can be defended. Students define the question and independent variable, control and record the other variables, fix inputs, repeat runs, and compare against a cloud baseline. They finish able to critique a design for uncontrolled variables and unfair comparisons.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 24 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Evaluation Question 183 Independent Variable 76 Metric Selection 72 Design Decision Record 3 Controlled Variables 75 Logging 19 Baseline Comparison 14 Decision Attribution 1 Fixed Inputs 38 Repeated Runs 20 Explicit Assumptions 9 Uncontrolled Variable 8 Fair Comparison 8 Run Variance 9 Measured Versus Assumed Values 8 Retest After Fix 2 Reproducible Experiment 1 Sample Size 8 Skill Defect Correction 1 Model-Only Test 4 Harness Smoke Test 2 Two-Layer Testing 1 Control Run 1 Long-Context Recall Test 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 4: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
  • Chapter 6: Cost, Price, and Quality
  • Chapter 8: Reproducible Python Environments with Conda
  • Chapter 13: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
  • Chapter 17: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model

A Result Is Only as Good as Its Design

Two people can run the same models on the same machine and reach opposite conclusions, and the difference is almost never the models. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a comparison that holds up, and critique one that does not. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Everything so far built capability: a reachable machine, a measured one, a model that fits, a server that answers, and a harness that runs a skill. This chapter decides what to do with it. The step from "it runs" to "it is better" is where evaluations most often go wrong, and it goes wrong in the design, long before any number is produced.

The chapter works through the parts of a design in the order a person makes them: the question, the one thing you vary, the things you hold fixed, the things you could not control and must record, and the measurements. It then covers how to know whether a result is repeatable, what to compare it against, and how to test in two layers so that failures are found cheaply. This evaluation's own choices appear throughout, including the ones that did not hold up.

docs.title: Evaluation Question
docs.text:
An evaluation question is the single, answerable question the experiment exists to answer. Everything else in the design follows from it, so a vague question produces a design that measures everything and decides nothing. A good one names what is being compared, on what task, under what conditions, and what would count as an answer.

This evaluation's question, in the Primary Author's words, is whether a local harness can execute the skills correctly. Stated as a full question, it is: can a DGX running an open-weight model, driven by a local harness, run the ibook-skills chain to produce an intelligent textbook without sending a token to the cloud, and how good is the result?

The difference between a good question and a poor one is easiest to see side by side.

Poor question Why it fails Better question Which model is best? Best at what, for whom? Which candidate completes stages 1 to 3 on Algebra I with the fewest structural faults on one DGX unit? Is local cheaper than cloud? Mixes cost and price, and ignores quality What is the cost per textbook of local generation at the measured speed, and what would a service charge at a 20% margin? Does the DGX work? Nothing could ever answer "no" Does a local model produce a learning graph that passes structural checks within a 150-minute limit?

The test of a question is whether you can imagine two different outcomes. If you cannot, it is not a question for an experiment.

docs.title: Independent Variable
docs.text:
The independent variable is the one thing the experiment deliberately changes, so that its effect can be observed. A comparison of ten models has a single independent variable, which is the model, and that single choice is what lets a difference in the results be attributed to it.

The discipline is to change one thing. A design that varies the model and the harness and the context length at once can report that the runs differ, and cannot say why. This is the same one-change-at-a-time rule that Chapters 6 and 15 applied to cost and speed, now applied to the whole experiment.

A worked example compares three designs for the same ten-model question. The first changes the model and nothing else. The second lets each model run at its own best context length and its own reasoning setting. The third runs half of the models on one DGX unit and half on the other.

Design What varies What a difference in results can be blamed on Model only The model The model Model, context, and reasoning Three things together Any of the three, or their combination, and you cannot say which Model, split across two units The model and the machine The model or the unit, and you cannot say which

Only the first can answer the question as asked. The second may still be worth running, as a second experiment about tuning, but its results must not be presented as a comparison of models.

docs.title: Controlled Variables
docs.text:
Controlled variables are everything else that could affect the result, which the design holds fixed on purpose. They are the reason a difference can be blamed on the independent variable. Each one is a decision, written down, and for this evaluation the list is long.

Variable How it was controlled Course One fixed course, Algebra I, an unchanged copy of its description Workload Three skills, with one fixed prompt per stage Harness Claude Code, pinned to one version Server Ollama, pinned to one release Skills One checkout, mounted read-only Hardware One DGX unit for all ten candidates Quantization Each model's default 4-bit file Starting state A fresh copy of the template workspace for every run Time limits 150 minutes for stage 1, a fixed limit per chapter

A controlled variable is a promise, and some promises were not kept. The next two sections name the ones that were not.

Every Fixed Thing Is a Claim You Must Be Able to Defend

Writing "same harness" in a design is a statement that you checked. Each controlled variable should have a line in the record that says what the value was and how you know. The ones you cannot back with a record are the ones a critic will find.

docs.title: Uncontrolled Variable
docs.text:
An uncontrolled variable is something that could affect the result and that the design did not hold fixed. Some cannot be controlled, and others were not noticed. The honest response is not to pretend they were controlled, but to record them and say which direction they might push.

This evaluation had at least three. Reasoning mode: the model-only tests ran with reasoning turned off to bound their time, and the harness runs used each model's own default, so one model spent nineteen minutes on a single turn and predictions from the model-only test did not match. Context length: it was chosen for each model from a memory estimate, so the models did not all run at the same setting. Server behavior: one model's server re-read the conversation on every turn, and the cause was not identified, so a speed difference could belong to the server and not to the model.

docs.title: Fixed Inputs
docs.text:
Fixed inputs are the exact files and prompts every run starts from. They are the most concrete controlled variable, and the cheapest to get right. In this evaluation the course description is an unchanged copy of a published description, the starting workspace is copied fresh for every run, and each stage has one prompt file, numbered in stage order.

Two habits make fixed inputs trustworthy. Keep them in version control so a change is visible. And copy them into each run instead of pointing to them, so that no run can alter the input of the next. The runner's header says it plainly: the start directory is copied to a fresh run directory, so a run never changes its input.

docs.title: Metric Selection
docs.text:
Metric selection is choosing what to measure, and it is as much a decision as choosing the question. A metric is only useful if it answers the question, if it can be computed the same way for every run, and if you decided it before you saw the data.

The metrics this evaluation collects fall into three groups, and the table gives each group's role.

Group Examples What it answers Completion Stage finished, files present, build succeeds Did the run do the task at all? Efficiency Wall-clock time, tool calls, failed tool calls, tokens, peak memory What did it cost to do it? Quality Structural checks, reading level, human review Is what it produced any good?

The groups differ in how much they can be trusted. Completion and efficiency are computed by a program and are repeatable. Quality is the one that matters most and the hardest to measure, which is the subject of Chapter 20. A design that reports only completion and efficiency has measured the cheapest things.

Do Not Pick the Metric After You See the Result

If you look at the data and then choose the measure that makes your favorite model look best, you have not run an experiment. Write the metrics and how each is computed into the record before the first run, and add new ones afterward only as clearly labeled extras.

docs.title: Repeated Runs, Run Variance, and Sample Size
docs.text:
A repeated run is running the same configuration more than once. Run variance is how much the results differ among them. A language model samples its output, and even at a low temperature a long agent session takes a path that depends on small differences early on, so two runs of the same configuration are not the same run.

Sample size is the number of runs behind a conclusion. A single run is a sample of one, and it supports a statement about that run only. Nearly every result in this evaluation so far is one run: each model attempted each stage once. That is enough to find what fails, and not enough to rank.

A worked illustration shows why. Suppose a model finishes a stage in 20 minutes on one run and 45 on another, because in the second it made a wrong turn and recovered. A second model finishes in 30 minutes on its one run. Ranking the second ahead of the first from those numbers is a coin flip. With five runs of each, the spread of each is visible and the comparison can be stated with its uncertainty.

Runs per configuration What you can say 1 What happened; which things failed outright 3 Whether the result is stable, roughly 5 or more A typical value and a range, with caution

docs.title: Control Run
docs.text:
A control run is a repeat of a run that should give the same answer, done to check the apparatus and not the subject. This project's model-test script ends with one: it runs its smoke test on two models as their downloads finish, then repeats the first as a control. If the control differs from the original by more than the expected variation, something in the setup changed in between, such as memory pressure, a thermal state, or a different server setting.

A control is cheap, and it is the first thing to do when a surprising number appears. It separates "this model really behaves this way" from "this machine behaved differently this afternoon".

docs.title: Reproducible Experiment
docs.text: A reproducible experiment is one that someone else can repeat from the record and obtain a comparable result. It is the combination of this chapter's parts: a stated question, a recorded configuration, fixed inputs under version control, pinned software, and logs that show what happened. Reproducibility is not a property of the result. It is a property of the record.

docs.title: Baseline Comparison and Fair Comparison
docs.text:
A baseline comparison judges a result against a reference produced under the same rules. Without one, "the local model's learning graph has 200 concepts" has no meaning, because nobody knows whether a cloud model's would too. A fair comparison is one in which the only meaningful difference between the two sides is the thing being compared.

This evaluation has a reference for scale, and not yet a baseline. A published Algebra I book was generated with cloud models, and it has 200 concepts and 13 chapters of about 55,000 words. It was made with earlier versions of the skills, and no timings or token counts were kept. It shows how large a finished book is. It cannot say how long a cloud model takes or how good its output is under these exact conditions. The cloud baseline remains to be run.

Requirement for a fair comparison Satisfied by the published book? Same course description Yes Same skill versions No, earlier versions Same prompts Not recorded Timings and token counts recorded No Same scoring applied Not yet

Ask Three Questions of Any Baseline

Did it use the same inputs? Is its configuration recorded? Was it scored by the same method as the thing you are comparing it to? A baseline that fails any of the three is a reference point, and the comparison should call it that.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Logging is recording what happened during a run, in enough detail to reconstruct it. The log is what lets a surprising result be investigated later, and it is the difference between a measurement and a memory.

The records this evaluation keeps for each run are worth listing, because each answers a specific later question.

Record What it holds Answers The event stream Every message, tool call, and result What did the agent actually do? The final result Turns, token counts, timings How much did it use? The status file Exit code and wall-clock seconds Did it finish, and how long did it take? The server log Loads, memory, request timings Why was it slow? The vitals log Memory, temperature, power every 30 seconds What did the machine look like? The configuration Versions, settings, dates Can this be repeated?

docs.title: Explicit Assumptions and Measured Versus Assumed Values
docs.text:
Explicit assumptions are the things the analysis takes as true without having tested them, stated as such. Measured versus assumed values is the distinction applied to each number: a measured value came from an observation in this evaluation, and an assumed one came from a rule, a published figure, or a guess.

The cost analysis is the model for this. Its tables label every speed as measured, or as assumed equal to a measured model. Six of the ten speeds are assumed. It also tests its own rule against the one case it can check: the rule predicted 34 tokens a second for one model, and the measured figure was 26. Reporting the miss is what makes the other assumptions credible.

docs.title: Design Decision Record and Decision Attribution
docs.text:
A design decision record is a written account of each choice in the design: what was chosen, what else was considered, and why. Decision attribution is recording who made each decision, because a choice made by a person with a goal and a choice made by an assistant filling a gap deserve different scrutiny.

This book's design-choices page is such a record, and it has a table of who decided what. Three parties appear in it: the Primary Author, the Administrator, and the AI assistant that built and ran the tests under the Primary Author's direction. It also has a section on the choices that did not hold up, which is the part that earns the reader's trust.

docs.title: Two-Layer Testing, Model-Only Test, and Harness Smoke Test
docs.text:
Two-layer testing is testing a model alone first, and then inside the harness. The model-only test sends a model short, fixed tasks directly through the server, with no harness, and checks the output against rules. The harness smoke test is the three-minute skill run of Chapter 17, which checks the model, the harness, and a skill together.

The layers differ in what a failure costs and what it can tell you.

Layer Time per model What a failure means Model-only test Minutes The model cannot follow a rule on its own, such as a blank line before a list Harness smoke test About three minutes The model cannot work through a skill with tools Full stage Tens of minutes to hours The model fails at scale, or is too slow

The benefit is isolation. A model that fails the first layer fails in seconds and for a reason you can name, and a model that passes it and fails the second fails for a reason that involves the harness. Going straight to the full pipeline makes every failure slow and mixes the causes. The model-only test in this project has five tasks: Markdown writing, p5.js code, schema-constrained JSON, a tool call, and a 30,000-token prompt.

docs.title: Long-Context Recall Test
docs.text:
A long-context recall test checks that a model can find a specific fact in a long prompt. A value is placed in a long block of text, and the model is asked to return it. It is the model-only test's way of asking whether a model that advertises a large window can use it.

It found something the other tasks did not. One model returned the wrong value from a long prompt in two of its model-only runs and again in a third. A model that misreads a long prompt is a poor fit for long skills, and that is a hypothesis to test in the harness, not a conclusion.

docs.title: Skill Defect Correction and Retest After Fix
docs.text:
A skill defect correction is fixing a fault in the skill or in the test, and not in the model that revealed it. A retest after fix is running the affected models again once the fault is corrected, so that an early conclusion does not stand on a broken check.

Two cases in this evaluation show the need. A faulty example in a skill produced navigation files that would not build, and a fast model that copied it was set aside. The skill was corrected. The model was retested afterward, passed the short skill test, and finished the learning graph in under six minutes, and it was the graph itself, with 40 duplicate labels, that remained a serious fault. Separately, the first versions of three model-only checks were too strict and failed correct output. Each was fixed and the saved output was scored again.

Finding Your Own Bug Is Part of the Method

If a result turns out to come from a faulty check or a broken example, that is the evaluation working. Record the defect, fix it, rerun what it touched, and note which conclusions changed. The report that says so is more trustworthy than one that never found a mistake.

docs.title: Diagram: Experiment Variable Role Sorter
docs.text:
Run Experiment Variable Role Sorter Fullscreen

Experiment Variable Role Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: variable-role-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate the role of each of 10 items in a model-comparison experiment as independent variable, controlled variable, measured result, or uncontrolled variable, with at least 9 of 10 correct.

Prerequisites: independent variable, controlled variables, uncontrolled variable, metric selection, fixed inputs (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 10 items the learner commits one of four roles before the sim reveals the answer. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct role column. Mastery is 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the items is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Anything that is the same in every run is controlled, whether or not it was decided. (2) A measured result can also be the independent variable. (3) A variable that cannot be controlled can be ignored. (4) The model's default setting counts as controlled.

Instructional Rationale: Differentiating roles needs the learner to ask two questions of each item, who set it and whether it was held the same, so the items cover all four roles and include two that look controlled and are not.

Content:

The four roles the learner chooses from: "Independent variable", "Controlled variable", "Measured result", and "Uncontrolled variable".

The experiment: ten candidate models each run the same three skills on one DGX unit, and the question is how well each completes them.

# Item shown to the learner Correct role Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which model is loaded for the run Independent variable It is the one thing the experiment deliberately changes. 2 The course description, an unchanged copy for every run Controlled variable It was held fixed on purpose. 3 The harness version, pinned to one release Controlled variable It was held fixed on purpose. 4 Wall-clock time of the stage Measured result It is an outcome recorded for every run. 5 Which DGX unit a run happened on, when runs were spread across both with no plan Uncontrolled variable It varied without being decided, so a difference could belong to the unit. 6 The prompt text for each stage Controlled variable It was held fixed on purpose. 7 Number of tool calls that failed Measured result It is an outcome recorded for every run. 8 Other work running on the machine during the run Uncontrolled variable It varied without being managed. 9 Quantization, each model's default 4-bit file Controlled variable The same level was chosen for every model. 10 Whether a model's reasoning mode is on, when each model uses its own default Uncontrolled variable It differs by model without being decided, so it is mixed with the independent variable.

Provenance: The items are synthetic but drawn from this evaluation's design, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The roles come from the sections of this chapter above.

Rules: Items are shown in the fixed order 1 to 10. Each allows one final choice, and exactly one role is correct for each. A variable is "Controlled" only if the design held it fixed on purpose, and "Uncontrolled" if it varied without being decided.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads item 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the four roles and confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct role and the Why text, and marks the item correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for items 2 to 10. After item 10 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Ten items, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct role and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 10 correct".

Starting State: Item 1 is shown with no role chosen, and the question on screen is "What role does this play in the experiment?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the model is the single independent variable, that the course description, harness version, prompts, and quantization are controlled, and that reasoning mode, context length, and server behavior were uncontrolled.

docs.title: Diagram: Evaluation Design Flaw Finder
docs.text:
Run Evaluation Design Flaw Finder Fullscreen

Evaluation Design Flaw Finder

Type: microsim sim-id: design-flaw-finder Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/statistics-course/tree/main/docs/sims/experimental-designs-compare Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: critique Learning Objective: The learner will critique a described evaluation by judging each of 8 statements about it as a flaw or not a flaw, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: evaluation question, controlled variables, fixed inputs, repeated runs, sample size, fair comparison, bias, limitations statement (all defined in this chapter and in Chapter 20).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner reads the described evaluation, then judges each of 8 statements as "Flaw" or "Not a flaw" before the sim reveals the answer. A judgment is correct when it equals the Correct judgment column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Re-reading the description is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A comparison of two systems needs no controls if one is clearly stronger. (2) A single run is enough to rank. (3) A result scored by the system that produced it is neutral. (4) Having a method is the same as having a fair method.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluating a design needs criteria applied to a case, so the description contains five real flaws and three sound practices, which prevents answering "flaw" to everything.

Content:

The described evaluation, shown in full to the learner:

"A team compares a local model and a cloud model on textbook generation. They run the local model once on Monday on a machine that is also running a database backup, using the Algebra I course description, with the same harness and the same skills as the cloud run. They run the cloud model once on Friday using a rewritten course description that adds a glossary requirement. They score both outputs with the cloud model that wrote the cloud result. The team recorded the model names, versions, and dates of both runs, and stated its evaluation question before running anything. They report that the cloud model is better, without further comment."

# Statement shown to the learner Correct judgment Why (shown as feedback) 1 Each model was run once. Flaw One run gives no estimate of run variance, so a difference may be noise. 2 The two runs used different course descriptions. Flaw The inputs were not fixed, so a difference could come from the description and not the model. 3 The local model ran while a backup ran on the same machine. Flaw Competing load is an uncontrolled variable that can slow or starve the run. 4 Both runs used the same harness and the same skills. Not a flaw Holding these fixed is exactly what a fair comparison requires. 5 The cloud model's output was scored by the cloud model that wrote it. Flaw A model judging its own work is a source of bias, so the score is not neutral. 6 The team recorded the model names, versions, and dates of both runs. Not a flaw A record of the configuration is what makes an experiment reproducible. 7 The team stated its evaluation question before running anything. Not a flaw Fixing the question first prevents choosing a measure after seeing the data. 8 The result was reported as "the cloud model is better" with no limitations. Flaw A claim from one run per side needs a limitations statement that says so.

Provenance: The described evaluation and statements are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The criteria come from the sections of this chapter above.

Rules: Statements are shown in the fixed order 1 to 8. Each allows one final judgment, and exactly one of "Flaw" or "Not a flaw" is correct for each. The description contains five flaws and three sound practices.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the described evaluation.
  2. The learner reads statement 1 and chooses "Flaw" or "Not a flaw", then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct judgment and the Why text, and marks the statement correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for statements 2 to 8. After statement 8 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Eight statements, fixed order, one confirmed judgment each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct judgment and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 8 correct".

Starting State: The described evaluation is shown with statement 1 beneath it and no judgment made, and the question on screen is "Is this a flaw in the design?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that one run per side gives no run variance, that inputs must be fixed, that uncontrolled load is a variable, that a model should not score its own output, and that a result needs a limitations statement.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
A defensible evaluation starts from a question that could have different answers, and changes one thing. It holds everything else fixed on purpose, records the variables it could not hold, and chooses its metrics before it sees data. A result from one run is an observation. Repeated runs, control runs, and a stated sample size are what turn it into evidence, and a baseline is only a baseline if it was produced under the same rules. A record of the configuration, the assumptions, and the decisions, with who made each, is what makes the experiment reproducible. Testing in layers finds cheap failures first, and a defect found in the checks, once corrected, means a retest and a note of what changed.

You Can Defend a Design and Attack One

You can now turn a question into a design with named variables, say which were controlled and which were not, and critique a comparison that skipped the steps. Chapter 20 turns to the hardest measurement in the design, which is how good the output is.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Designing a Fair Evaluation
docs.text: Test your understanding of evaluation questions, variables, fixed inputs, repeated runs, baselines, and layered testing with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What are controlled variables?
docs.text:
1. The outcomes that are recorded in the same way for each and every run
  2. The factors that changed without anyone deciding they should
  3. The factors that could affect the result, held fixed on purpose
  4. The single factor that the experiment deliberately changes
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Controlled variables are everything other than the independent variable that could affect the result, which the design holds fixed on purpose. They are the reason a difference can be blamed on the independent variable. In this evaluation they include the course, the prompts, the harness and server versions, the skills, the hardware, and the quantization. Each one is a written decision, and a factor that varied without being decided is an uncontrolled variable.

Concept Tested: Controlled Variables

See: Controlled Variables

docs.title: 2. What are fixed inputs?
docs.text:
1. The exact files and prompts that every run starts from
  2. The metrics chosen after the first results are seen
  3. The hardware settings that differ from one model to the next
  4. The logs that each run writes while it is still in progress
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Fixed inputs are the exact files and prompts every run starts from. They are the most concrete controlled variable and the cheapest to get right. Here the course description is an unchanged copy, the starting workspace is copied fresh for every run, and each stage has one prompt file. Keep them in version control so a change is visible, and copy them into each run so that no run can alter the input of the next.

Concept Tested: Fixed Inputs

See: Fixed Inputs

docs.title: 3. Why must metrics be chosen before the data is seen?
docs.text:
1. Metrics chosen later cannot be computed by a program
  2. Completion metrics are available only before a run starts
  3. The server discards token counts once a run has ended
  4. Choosing afterward lets you pick what flatters a favorite
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Metric selection is choosing what to measure, and a metric is useful only if it answers the question, can be computed the same way for every run, and was decided before you saw the data. If you look at the data and then choose the measure that makes your favorite model look best, you have not run an experiment. Write the metrics into the record before the first run, and add new ones later only as clearly labeled extras.

Concept Tested: Metric Selection

See: Metric Selection

docs.title: 4. What is the purpose of a control run?
docs.text:
1. To give a slow model a second chance to finish its stage in time
  2. To check the apparatus by repeating a run that should match
  3. To compare a local model's output with a cloud model's
  4. To measure how a model behaves with its reasoning mode turned off
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A control run is a repeat of a run that should give the same answer, done to check the apparatus and not the subject. If the control differs from the original by more than the expected variation, something in the setup changed in between, such as memory pressure, a thermal state, or a server setting. It is cheap, and it separates "this model really behaves this way" from "this machine behaved differently this afternoon".

Concept Tested: Control Run

See: Control Run

docs.title: 5. A team proposes the evaluation question "Is our new model good?" Which revision makes it a question an experiment can answer?
docs.text:
1. "Is our new model really good across the tasks that matter to us?"
  2. "Does it finish stage 1 with no structural faults within 150 minutes?"
  3. "Is our new model better than most people would expect it to be?"
  4. "Does our new model work well on the machine we already own?"
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An evaluation question is the single, answerable question the experiment exists to answer. A good one names what is being compared, on what task, under what conditions, and what would count as an answer. The test is whether you can imagine two different outcomes. Only the revision with a named stage, a structural-fault criterion, and a time limit can come out "yes" or "no". The others still leave "good", "better", and "well" undefined.

Concept Tested: Evaluation Question

See: Evaluation Question

docs.title: 6. You have ten new candidate models and limited time. Following two-layer testing, what do you run first?
docs.text:
1. Short fixed tasks sent to the server, with no harness
  2. The full three-stage pipeline, run for each model in turn
  3. The three-minute skill run through the harness
  4. A cloud baseline run of all three benchmark stages
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Two-layer testing tests a model alone first and then inside the harness. The model-only test sends short, fixed tasks directly through the server, with no harness, and checks the output against rules. It takes minutes, and a failure there has a cause you can name. Going straight to the full pipeline makes every failure slow and mixes the causes. The three-minute harness smoke test is the second layer, for the models that pass the first.

Concept Tested: Model-Only Test

See: Two-Layer Testing, Model-Only Test, and Harness Smoke Test

docs.title: 7. The model-only tests ran with reasoning turned off, and the harness runs used each model's own default. One model then spent nineteen minutes on a single turn. What role does reasoning mode play in this design?
docs.text:
1. An uncontrolled variable that is mixed with the model itself
  2. The independent variable that the design deliberately set out to change
  3. A controlled variable, since each model used its default
  4. A measured result that is recorded for every run
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An uncontrolled variable is something that could affect the result and that the design did not hold fixed. Reasoning mode was off in the model-only tests and left at each model's own default in the harness runs, so it differed by model without being decided. It is therefore mixed with the independent variable, and predictions from the model-only test did not match the harness runs. Using each model's default is not control; control is a deliberate, recorded choice.

Concept Tested: Uncontrolled Variable

See: Uncontrolled Variable

docs.title: 8. Model X finishes a stage in 20 minutes on one run and 45 on another. Model Y finishes in 30 minutes on its only run. What can be concluded about which model is faster?
docs.text:
1. X is faster, because its best run beat Y's run
  2. Y is faster, because it beat X's average of 32.5 minutes
  3. They are equal, because the three run times average out evenly
  4. Neither claim holds; X's spread spans Y's single result
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Run variance is how much results differ among repeated runs of the same configuration. A single run is a sample of one and supports a statement about that run only. X's two runs span 20 to 45 minutes, and Y's single 30-minute run falls inside that spread, so ranking either ahead of the other is a coin flip. With five runs of each, the spread is visible and the comparison can be stated with its uncertainty.

Concept Tested: Run Variance

See: Repeated Runs, Run Variance, and Sample Size

docs.title: 9. Why is the published Algebra I book a reference for scale and not yet a baseline for the local runs?
docs.text:
1. It used a different course description from the local runs
  2. It used earlier skill versions and kept no timings or token counts
  3. It was written by a local model on a different DGX unit
  4. It has fewer concepts and chapters than the local runs produced
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A baseline comparison judges a result against a reference produced under the same rules. The published Algebra I book used the same course description, but it was made with earlier versions of the skills, its prompts were not recorded, and no timings or token counts were kept. It shows how large a finished book is. It cannot say how long a cloud model takes or how good its output is under these conditions, so the cloud baseline remains to be run.

Concept Tested: Baseline Comparison

See: Baseline Comparison and Fair Comparison

docs.title: 10. Three designs are proposed for comparing ten models. Design 1 changes only the model. Design 2 also lets each model use its own best context length and reasoning setting. Design 3 splits the models across two DGX units. Which design best answers "which model performs best on this task", and why?
docs.text:
1. Design 2, because each model is shown at its tuned best
  2. Design 3, because two units finish the runs in half the time
  3. Design 1, because any difference can be blamed on the model
  4. Design 2, because more settings give more data per run
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The independent variable is the one thing the experiment deliberately changes, and the discipline is to change one thing. Design 1 varies only the model, so a difference in results can be attributed to it. Design 2 varies three things together, and design 3 mixes the model with the machine, so neither can say why runs differ. Design 2 may be worth running as a separate experiment about tuning, but not presented as a comparison of models.

Concept Tested: Independent Variable

See: Independent Variable

docs.title: References: Designing a Fair Evaluation
docs.text:
1. Design of experiments - Wikipedia - Covers Fisher's principles of randomization, replication, and blocking, how independent variables and controls are set, and statistical control of spurious variables. It frames this chapter's independent variable, controlled variables, and repeated runs.

  2. Scientific control - Wikipedia - Explains controlled experiments, confounding, and positive and negative controls, which check that an experiment can detect an effect and is not producing a false one. It supports this chapter's control run and its warning about uncontrolled variables.

  3. Reproducibility - Wikipedia - Distinguishes reproducibility from replicability and repeatability, covers measures of each, and describes reproducible research practices such as documenting code and using version control. It supports this chapter's point that reproducibility is a property of the record.

  4. The Design of Experiments (1st Edition, 1935) - Ronald A. Fisher - Oliver and Boyd - Introduced the "lady tasting tea" experiment, eight cups in random order with a 1-in-70 chance of guessing all correctly, to show why randomization makes a comparison fair. It is the original worked example for this chapter's fair comparison.

  5. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing - Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang, and Ya Xu - Cambridge University Press - Widely praised for explaining A/B testing through its pitfalls, with Twyman's law (a surprising result is usually wrong) and the A/A test, which runs identical variants to validate the apparatus. The A/A test clarifies this chapter's control run.

  6. What is experimental design? - NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods - Defines experimental design as a plan written before the experiment, and distinguishes controllable factors the experimenter varies from uncontrolled factors and the measured responses. It supports this chapter's independent, controlled, and uncontrolled variables.

  7. A statistical approach to model evaluations - Anthropic Research - Recommends treating eval scores as estimates with standard errors and confidence intervals, comparing models with paired differences, and using power analysis to choose how many questions are needed. It supports this chapter's run variance and sample size discussion.

  8. Holistic Evaluation of Language Models - arXiv - Liang et al. evaluate 30 language models across 42 scenarios on seven metrics, including accuracy, robustness, and efficiency, under standardized conditions, and release raw prompts and completions. It models this chapter's metric selection and fixed inputs.

  9. Improving Reproducibility in Machine Learning Research - Journal of Machine Learning Research - Pineau et al. report the NeurIPS 2019 reproducibility program: a code submission policy, a reproducibility challenge, and a checklist for papers. It supports this chapter's reproducible experiment, which depends on a recorded configuration and logs.

  10. Deep Reinforcement Learning that Matters - arXiv - Henderson et al. show that non-determinism and variance can obscure whether a reported improvement is real, and propose significance metrics and standardized reporting. It illustrates this chapter's run variance and why one run cannot rank candidates.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers how generated output is scored and how the scores can mislead. Students apply rubrics, automated checks, and blind human review, account for bias such as LLM-as-judge scoring, and apply structural checks to generated learning graphs. They finish able to report provisional and negative results honestly.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 24 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Dependency Reasoning 1 Markdown Validity 1 Schema-Constrained JSON 1 MicroSim Code Correctness 1 Scoring Rubric 27 Reading Level Measure 1 Faithfulness to Description 1 Mathematical Notation 1 Bias in Evaluation 12 Structural Checks 11 Blind Human Review 3 LLM-as-Judge 1 Scoring Check Calibration 1 Automated Quality Score 1 Duplicate Concept Labels 1 Orphaned Concepts 1 Dependency Cycle Check 1 CSV-JSON Agreement 1 Label Length Limit 1 Provisional Results 7 Human Quality Score 2 Experimental Design Critique 7 Negative Result Reporting 1 Limitations Statement 6

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 2: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 6: Cost, Price, and Quality
  • Chapter 19: Designing a Fair Evaluation

A Score Is a Claim About Quality

A program can tell you quickly whether a learning graph has a cycle, and it cannot tell you whether the concepts are the right ones. By the end of this chapter you will know which questions a script can answer, which need a person, and how to report a result without claiming more than it shows. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 19 listed quality as one of three groups of metrics and called it the hardest. This chapter takes it on. It starts with the scoring rubric, the written definition of what good means. It then covers structural checks, the part of quality a program can verify, with the learning graph as the worked example. It moves on to the harder part, which is the judgment of whether prose is good, and the ways that judgment is biased. It ends with how to report a result that is provisional, or negative, or limited.

One distinction runs through all of it. A check answers a question that has a right answer, such as whether two concepts have the same label. A judgment answers a question that does not, such as whether an explanation is clear. A pipeline of checks can be automated and is fast. A judgment needs a person, or a model whose own bias you have accounted for.

docs.title: Scoring Rubric
docs.text:
A scoring rubric is a written description of what a result must have to earn each score. It makes a judgment repeatable: two reviewers using the same rubric on the same chapter should give scores that are close. Without one, "good" means whatever the reviewer felt that day.

A rubric needs dimensions, a scale, and a description of each level. The table gives the dimensions this evaluation cares about for a generated chapter, with the way each is measured. They come from the qualities that matter for a textbook, as this book's model candidates page lists them.

Dimension What it asks Measured by Faithfulness to the description Does it cover what the course says, and stay within its limits? Human review Dependency reasoning Does each concept come after the ones it depends on? Structural check, then human Writing quality Is the prose clear, accurate, and at the stated reading level? Reading-level measure, then human Schema-constrained output Are CSV, JSON, and YAML valid and consistent? Structural check Markdown validity Does the file render and the site build? Build and a script Mathematical notation Are formulas correct in the notation the site renders? Script for form, human for correctness MicroSim code correctness Does the code run in the browser? Run it

A worked use shows the mechanics. Suppose each dimension is scored 0, 1, or 2, where 0 means absent or broken, 1 means present with problems, and 2 means correct. A chapter that builds, has valid files, and covers its concepts, but whose notation has two errors and whose prose runs two grade levels above the target, might score 2, 2, 2, 1, 1 on five of the dimensions. The total of 8 out of 10 is less useful than the profile, which says where to fix it.

docs.title: Structural Checks
docs.text:
Structural checks are the checks a program can run on the form of the output, without judging its meaning. They answer questions with right answers: does the file exist, does it parse, does it agree with its twin. They are cheap, repeatable, and fast, and they find the failures that would otherwise waste a reviewer's time.

They are also limited in a way that is easy to forget. A structural pass does not mean the content is good. A learning graph can have no cycles and no duplicates and still be a graph of the wrong concepts. The checks are a gate, and the grade is a separate matter.

The learning-graph checks this project applies show what a structural check looks like. Each is a short test of one property.

Check What it tests A failure looks like Concept count The number of concepts equals the target 199 concepts when 200 were asked for Duplicate concept labels No two concepts share a label, ignoring case 40 of 200 labels duplicated Orphaned concepts Every concept has a prerequisite or a dependent 19 concepts connected to nothing Dependency cycle check No chain of dependencies loops back Three concepts each depending on the next CSV-JSON agreement The two files describe the same graph A concept in one and not the other Label length limit Labels are at most 32 characters A 64-character label that breaks the viewer

docs.title: Duplicate Labels, Orphans, and Label Length
docs.text:
Duplicate concept labels are concepts that share a label, compared without regard to case. They matter because the label is how a reader and a downstream tool refer to the concept, and two nodes with one name cannot be told apart. Orphaned concepts are concepts with no prerequisite and no dependent, so they are connected to nothing and cannot be reached from the rest of the graph. They are different from foundational concepts, which have no prerequisites and do have dependents.

The label length limit is the cap on label size, 32 characters in this project, which exists because longer labels do not fit in the graph viewer. It is a pragmatic limit and not a deep one, and it is a good example of a check whose threshold is a decision.

docs.title: Dependency Cycle Check and CSV-JSON Agreement
docs.text:
The dependency cycle check confirms that the graph is acyclic. A cycle means concept A depends on B, B on C, and C on A, so no order of study satisfies all three. The check repeatedly removes the concepts that have no remaining prerequisites. If everything can be removed, the graph is acyclic. Whatever is left sits on a cycle.

The excerpt from this project's scorer does exactly that. remaining maps each concept to the set of prerequisites not yet satisfied. Each pass takes the concepts whose set is empty, removes them, and deletes them from every other concept's set.

remaining = {c: set(ds) for c, ds in deps.items()}
while True:
    ready = [c for c, ds in remaining.items() if not ds]
    if not ready:
        break
    for c in ready:
        del remaining[c]
    for ds in remaining.values():
        ds.difference_update(ready)

is_dag = not remaining        # anything left is on a cycle

CSV-JSON agreement checks that the two files a skill writes, one for people and tools and one for the viewer, describe the same graph. Disagreement is a symptom of a model that updated one file and not the other, and it silently breaks whichever tool reads the stale one.

A Check Tests a Property, Not a Value

"No cycles" is a property of a whole graph, and it holds or it does not. A graph can satisfy every property you check and still be the wrong graph. Read a column of green checks as "nothing obviously broken", which is worth knowing and is not the same as "good".

docs.title: Scoring Check Calibration
docs.text:
Scoring check calibration is testing the checks themselves, on inputs whose answers you know, before you trust them on real output. A check can be wrong in two directions: it can pass a bad result, or it can fail a good one. Both are expensive, and the second is easy to miss because it looks like a model failure.

This evaluation met the second kind. The first versions of three model-only checks were too strict and failed output that was correct. Each was fixed, and the saved output was scored again. Without that step, a model would have been marked down for a defect in the test. Chapter 19's retest after fix is the same idea at the level of the experiment.

The calibration for a check is a small set: a known-good input that must pass, a known-bad input that must fail for the reason it should, and an edge case at the threshold, such as a label of exactly 32 characters and one of 33.

docs.title: Reading Level Measure
docs.text:
A reading level measure is a formula that estimates the school grade needed to read a text, from the lengths of its sentences and words. The common one, the Flesch-Kincaid grade, is computed by a script, so it is cheap and repeatable. This project's chapter-metrics pages report it for every generated chapter, using a shared function from the book-installer skill.

It is a measure of form and nothing more. A passage can score at grade 10 and be nonsense, and a clear explanation can score high because it uses necessary technical terms. Its right use is as a flag: a chapter written for adults that scores at grade 4 is probably padded with short sentences, and one that scores at grade 20 is probably unreadable.

docs.title: Faithfulness to Description, Mathematical Notation, and MicroSim Code
docs.text:
Three rubric dimensions cannot be fully automated, and each has a partial script and a human remainder.

Faithfulness to the description is whether the output covers what the course description lists and respects what it excludes. A script can check that each listed topic is mentioned. Whether the treatment matches the description's intent needs a reader. Mathematical notation is whether formulas are written in the notation the site renders, with the right delimiters, and are correct. A script can find malformed delimiters, and only a person can say whether the formula is right. MicroSim code correctness is whether the JavaScript runs in a browser without errors. It can be tested by loading the page, and it is the dimension where code that looks right and fails when run is worse than no simulation at all.

docs.title: Bias in Evaluation
docs.text:
Bias in evaluation is a systematic tilt in the scoring that favors some results over others for reasons unrelated to quality. It is distinct from noise. Noise averages out over many runs and bias does not, and it points the same way every time.

Four sources are worth naming. The scorer's own preferences: whoever scores brings habits, and a reviewer who expects a certain structure will prefer it. Order and position: the first of two answers read tends to be preferred. Length: longer answers look more thorough. Knowing the source: a reviewer who knows which model wrote a text, or that it came from a cloud service, is influenced by the name.

docs.title: LLM-as-Judge
docs.text:
LLM-as-judge is using a language model to score another model's output. It is attractive because it is fast, cheap, and scales to thousands of outputs. It is also the largest source of bias in this kind of evaluation. A model tends to prefer text that resembles its own, it favors longer answers, it is sensitive to the order in which candidates are shown, and it can be impressed by confident prose that is wrong.

There is also a cost that has nothing to do with accuracy. Sending a local model's output to a cloud model to be scored sends the text to the cloud, which undoes the reason for generating it locally. The design choices page records this as the reason this evaluation did not use it as its scoring method.

Weakness What it does to a score Mitigation Self-preference Rates output like its own higher Use a different model family as judge Verbosity Rewards length Control for length, or score against a rubric Position Prefers the first candidate Randomize order and score twice Confidence Rewards fluent errors Require evidence for each rubric score Data exposure Sends generated text to a service Use a local judge, or do not use one

A Judge Model Is Another Model Under Test

Treat an LLM judge as an instrument that has to be calibrated against human scores on a sample before you trust it on the rest. If its scores disagree with the people's on the cases you checked, it has told you something about itself, and not about the outputs.

docs.title: Blind Human Review and the Human Quality Score
docs.text:
Blind human review is a person scoring output against the rubric without knowing which model produced it, with the order randomized. It is the right test of quality, and it is slow and costs money: the cost analysis prices ten hours of subject-expert review at $900, seventeen times the cost of generating the book.
