The human quality score is the result: a set of rubric scores for each output from each reviewer. Two reviewers on a sample, with their disagreement recorded, is better than one reviewer on everything, because the disagreement is itself a measurement of how much the rubric leaves to taste.

At the time of writing, this evaluation had no completed human review. The Primary Author reads the generated chapters on their own machine, and the status page says "not yet" where a human score belongs.

docs.title: Automated Quality Score
docs.text:
An automated quality score is a single number a program computes from the checks, so that outputs can be ranked at a glance. It is tempting and dangerous for the reasons above: one number hides the profile, and a weighting that favors the checks that are easy to run will quietly define quality as whatever is easy to measure.

This evaluation has not defined one. Each model has a learning-graph quality report and a page of chapter metrics, and they have not been combined into a number. When one is defined, it should be a documented formula over the rubric dimensions, published with its weights, and reported beside the profile, not instead of it.

docs.title: Provisional Results
docs.text: Provisional results are results that are real observations and not yet established, because they rest on too few runs, an unvalidated check, or an incomplete review. The honest label is the one in this book's candidate page: a first round is one run of each test, so every result is provisional. A provisional result is useful for deciding what to test next, and not for writing a recommendation.

docs.title: Negative Result Reporting
docs.text:
Negative result reporting is stating what did not work, and why, with the same care as what did. A failure is data. A model that lost the task after a few steps, another that wrote its first tool call as plain text so the run ended after one turn, and a third that could not fit a usable context are all findings, and a reader choosing a model for their own machine needs them more than they need the successes.

Omitting negative results makes a field look easier than it is, and it makes the next person repeat them. The guide is to report the failure, the evidence, and your best account of the cause, with its confidence stated, since several causes in this evaluation were never identified.

docs.title: Limitations Statement
docs.text:
A limitations statement says what the result does not show. It is the section that tells a reader how far to trust the rest. The one this evaluation needs to carry is concrete.

  • Each model was run once. Run variance is unknown, so rankings are not supported.
  • One course, one machine type, one harness, one skills version. Nothing generalizes beyond them without more runs.
  • Structural checks only. No quality judgment from a person has been completed.
  • No cloud baseline. The published book is a reference for scale, not a controlled comparison.
  • Six of ten speeds in the cost analysis are assumed.
  • Reasoning mode was not held constant between the model-only tests and the harness runs.

docs.title: Experimental Design Critique
docs.text:
An experimental design critique is applying the standards of Chapter 19 to your own evaluation, in writing, before someone else does. The useful form pairs each flaw with its effect and its repair.

Flaw Effect on the results What would repair it One run per model Rankings could be noise Three to five runs each Reasoning mode differed between layers Model-only speeds did not predict harness speeds Fix the mode, or test with each model's default in both Context length chosen per model Models were not compared at one setting Add a run at a common context A cloud model supervised the runs Generated text reached a cloud service Use a local or scripted supervisor A model set aside for a skill defect Its result may have been wrong Retest it, which was done for one model

docs.title: Diagram: Learning Graph Defect Finder
docs.text:
Run Learning Graph Defect Finder Fullscreen

Learning Graph Defect Finder

Type: graph-model sim-id: learning-graph-defect-finder Library: vis-network Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/microsims/tree/main/docs/sims/graph-viewer Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine a 16-concept dependency graph and mark the concepts that have one of four structural defects, finding all 4 defects with no more than 1 false flag.

Prerequisites: duplicate concept labels, orphaned concepts, dependency cycle check, label length limit, structural checks (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner flags concepts and assigns each flag a defect type from "Duplicate label", "Orphan", "Cycle", and "Label too long", then submits. A defect is found when every concept in the answer key for that defect is flagged with that type. Mastery is all 4 defects found, with no more than 1 flag on a concept that is not in the answer key. Exploring the graph, without flagging, is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A concept with no prerequisites is always a defect. (2) A label at the limit is over it. (3) Two concepts whose labels differ only in case are different. (4) A cycle is visible only as one edge.

Instructional Rationale: Examining a structure for faults needs the learner to apply each check to the whole graph, so each of the four defects is seeded once and two legitimate look-alikes are included to prevent flagging everything unusual.

Content:

The graph has 16 concepts. Each row lists its identifier, its label, and the identifiers of the concepts it depends on. The Note column is the answer key and is never shown to the learner. Label lengths are in characters.

ID Label Depends on Note 1 Numbers none A foundational concept with dependents. Not a defect. 2 Variables 1 3 Expressions 2 4 Equations 3 5 Linear Equations 4 6 Slope 5 Duplicate label with concept 7, ignoring case. 7 slope 5 Duplicate label with concept 6, ignoring case. 8 Graphing Lines 6 9 Systems of Equations 5, 8 10 Inequalities 4 11 Factoring 13 On the cycle 11, 12, 13. 12 Quadratic Expressions 11 On the cycle 11, 12, 13. 13 Polynomials 12 On the cycle 11, 12, 13. 14 Scientific Notation none Orphan: nothing depends on it and it depends on nothing. 15 Representing Linear Relationships in Tables Graphs and Equations 5 64 characters, over the 32-character limit. 16 Absolute Value Function Examples 4 Exactly 32 characters. Not a defect.

The answer key: "Duplicate label" is concepts 6 and 7; "Cycle" is concepts 11, 12, and 13; "Orphan" is concept 14; and "Label too long" is concept 15. Concepts 1 and 16 are legitimate look-alikes.

Provenance: The graph is synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels it "synthetic example". The defect definitions and the 32-character limit come from this chapter.

Rules: A duplicate is two labels equal when compared without regard to case. An orphan has no prerequisites and no dependents. A cycle is a set of concepts that cannot be ordered so that every concept follows its prerequisites. A label is too long when it has more than 32 characters. A flag has one concept and one type, and a concept in a cycle or duplicate pair is flagged individually.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner views the graph, with each concept's label and its edges shown, and may click a concept to read its label length and its prerequisites and dependents.
  2. The learner selects a concept and chooses a defect type, which places a flag. The learner may remove a flag.
  3. When satisfied, the learner submits.
  4. The sim marks each defect found or missed, lists any false flags, and shows the one-sentence reason for each defect.

Feedback: One submission, with unlimited flag changes before it. After submission: for each of the four defects, "Found" or "Missed" with its reason; for each false flag, the reason that concept is not a defect (concept 1 is foundational and has dependents, concept 16 is exactly at the limit, and so on). The score reads "n of 4 defects found, m false flags".

Starting State: The graph is shown with no flags and the instruction "Find the four structural defects in this learning graph".

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states a 32-character label limit, that duplicates are compared without regard to case, that an orphan is connected to nothing while a foundational concept has dependents, and that a cycle makes no study order possible.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
A rubric defines quality dimension by dimension, and structural checks cover the part a program can verify: the count, duplicate labels, orphans, cycles, file agreement, and label length. They calibrate on known inputs, because a check can fail a good result as easily as pass a bad one. The rest of quality needs judgment, which has biases: a model judging its own family, preferring length, favoring the first answer, and sending the text to a cloud service. Blind human review is the right test and the expensive one, and an automated quality score hides the profile behind one number. Results are labeled provisional until repeated, negative results are reported with the same care, and a limitations statement and a design critique tell the reader how far to trust the rest.

You Can Say What a Score Does and Does Not Show

You can now separate checks from judgments, calibrate a check before trusting it, name the biases in a judge, and write a limitations statement. Chapter 21 uses all of it to run the benchmark.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
docs.text: Test your understanding of rubrics, structural checks, calibration, bias in judging, and honest reporting with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a scoring rubric?
docs.text:
1. A script that checks whether an output file parses
  2. A single number computed from all automated checks
  3. A written description of what earns each score
  4. A list of the models ranked by first-round results
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A scoring rubric is a written description of what a result must have to earn each score. It makes a judgment repeatable: two reviewers using the same rubric on the same chapter should give scores that are close. A rubric needs dimensions, a scale, and a description of each level. Without one, "good" means whatever the reviewer felt that day. A single computed number is an automated quality score, which hides the per-dimension profile.

Concept Tested: Scoring Rubric

See: Scoring Rubric

docs.title: 2. Why does passing every structural check not mean a learning graph is good?
docs.text:
1. Structural checks are too slow to run on a whole graph
  2. The checks test form, so the concepts may still be wrong ones
  3. Structural checks can be run only by a human reviewer
  4. The checks pass any graph that has exactly 200 concepts
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Structural checks are the checks a program can run on the form of the output without judging its meaning: does the file exist, does it parse, does it agree with its twin. They are cheap, repeatable, and fast. A structural pass does not mean the content is good: a learning graph can have no cycles and no duplicates and still be a graph of the wrong concepts. The checks are a gate, and the grade is a separate matter.

Concept Tested: Structural Checks

See: Structural Checks

docs.title: 3. Why should a report state what did not work with the same care as what did?
docs.text:
1. Failures are rare, so listing them costs a report very little space
  2. A failure is data that readers need and others would repeat
  3. Negative results raise a report's automated quality score
  4. Failures prove that local models cannot generate usable textbooks
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Negative result reporting is stating what did not work, and why, with the same care as what did. A failure is data: a model that lost the task, one that wrote its tool call as plain text, and one that could not fit a usable context are all findings, and a reader choosing a model needs them. Omitting them makes a field look easier than it is and makes the next person repeat them.

Concept Tested: Negative Result Reporting

See: Negative Result Reporting

docs.title: 4. In a generated graph, concept X has no prerequisites, and three other concepts depend on it. Concept Y has no prerequisites and no dependents. How should each be classified?
docs.text:
1. Both are orphans, because neither has a prerequisite
  2. X is an orphan, and Y is a foundational concept
  3. X is foundational, and Y is an orphan
  4. Both are foundational, because neither has a prerequisite
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Orphaned concepts have no prerequisite and no dependent, so they are connected to nothing and cannot be reached from the rest of the graph. They are different from foundational concepts, which have no prerequisites and do have dependents. X has three dependents, so it is foundational and not a defect. Y is connected to nothing, so it is an orphan. Flagging every concept without a prerequisite would mark the graph's legitimate starting points as faults.

Concept Tested: Orphaned Concepts

See: Duplicate Labels, Orphans, and Label Length

docs.title: 5. You have written a check for the 32-character label limit. Which calibration set should you run before trusting it on real output?
docs.text:
1. The ten candidate graphs, accepting whatever the check reports
  2. A single 64-character label that is certain to fail
  3. A good label, a bad label, and labels of 32 and 33 characters
  4. The longest label found in the published reference book
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Scoring check calibration tests the checks themselves on inputs whose answers you know, before you trust them on real output. A check can pass a bad result or fail a good one, and the second looks like a model failure. The calibration set is small: a known-good input that must pass, a known-bad input that must fail for the right reason, and an edge case at the threshold, such as a label of exactly 32 characters and one of 33.

Concept Tested: Scoring Check Calibration

See: Scoring Check Calibration

docs.title: 6. In a graph, D needs E, A needs B, B needs C, C needs A, and E needs nothing. The cycle check repeatedly removes every concept with no remaining prerequisites. What is left when it stops?
docs.text:
1. Nothing remains, so the graph is acyclic
  2. Only E remains, because it has no prerequisites
  3. D and E remain, because they form a single chain
  4. A, B, and C remain, so the graph has a cycle
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The dependency cycle check repeatedly removes the concepts that have no remaining prerequisites. E needs nothing, so it goes first, and D then has no remaining prerequisite and goes next. A, B, and C each wait on another of the three, so none ever becomes ready. If everything can be removed the graph is acyclic. Here three concepts are left, and they form the cycle, so no order of study satisfies all of them.

Concept Tested: Dependency Cycle Check

See: Dependency Cycle Check and CSV-JSON Agreement

docs.title: 7. A team scores two models' chapters with an LLM judge and always shows model 1's chapter first. Model 1 wins nearly every comparison. Which weakness of the judge could produce this pattern regardless of quality?
docs.text:
1. Position bias: the judge tends to prefer the first candidate
  2. Data exposure: the judge sends the text to a cloud service
  3. Calibration: the judge's label limit is set too strictly
  4. Run variance: the judge was given only one chapter to read
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. LLM-as-judge is using a language model to score another model's output. It is fast and cheap, and it is the largest source of bias in this kind of evaluation: a judge tends to prefer text like its own, favors longer answers, is sensitive to the order in which candidates are shown, and rewards confident prose that is wrong. A candidate always shown first can win on position alone. The mitigation is to randomize the order and score twice.

Concept Tested: LLM-as-Judge

See: LLM-as-Judge

docs.title: 8. A reviewer who knows which model wrote each chapter scores the cloud model's chapters higher across many chapters, even when order and length are matched. What is this tilt, and what addresses it?
docs.text:
1. Bias from knowing the source; blind review removes the name
  2. Noise from sampling; more chapters will average it out
  3. A calibration fault; the check's threshold should be loosened
  4. Run variance; each model should be run five more times
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Bias in evaluation is a systematic tilt in scoring that favors some results for reasons unrelated to quality. Noise averages out over many runs; bias does not, and it points the same way every time. One named source is knowing the source: a reviewer who knows which model wrote a text, or that it came from a cloud service, is influenced by the name. Blind review, in which the reviewer does not know the model, removes that influence.

Concept Tested: Bias in Evaluation

See: Bias in Evaluation

docs.title: 9. A team must judge the writing quality of locally generated chapters. The text must not leave the site, and the team wants the most trustworthy measure of quality. Which option best meets both criteria?
docs.text:
1. A cloud LLM judge, because it scales to thousands of outputs
  2. A Flesch-Kincaid grade, because a script computes it cheaply
  3. A single automated score, because it ranks outputs at a glance
  4. Blind human review against the rubric, in randomized order
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Blind human review is a person scoring output against the rubric without knowing which model produced it, with the order randomized. It is the right test of quality, though slow and costly. A cloud LLM judge sends the text to a service, which undoes the reason for generating locally, and it carries its own biases. A reading-level formula measures form only, and a single automated score hides the profile. Under these two criteria, only blind review qualifies.

Concept Tested: Blind Human Review

See: Blind Human Review and the Human Quality Score

docs.title: 10. You are asked to design an automated quality score that ranks outputs without hiding where each one is weak, and without defining quality as whatever is easy to measure. Which design meets those requirements?
docs.text:
1. A weighted sum of the checks that are fastest to run
  2. One number that replaces the per-dimension profile
  3. A score assigned by the same model that wrote the chapters
  4. A published rubric formula, reported beside the profile
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. An automated quality score is a single number a program computes from the checks. It is tempting and dangerous: one number hides the profile, and a weighting that favors the easy checks quietly defines quality as whatever is easy to measure. A sound design is a documented formula over the rubric dimensions, published with its weights, and reported beside the profile, not instead of it. A score from the generating model would add self-preference bias.

Concept Tested: Automated Quality Score

See: Automated Quality Score

docs.title: References: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
docs.text:
1. Rubric (academic) - Wikipedia - Defines a scoring rubric and distinguishes holistic, analytic, and developmental types, with steps for building one. It supports this chapter's rubric dimensions, scale, and level descriptions that make two reviewers' scores comparable.

  2. Flesch–Kincaid readability tests - Wikipedia - Gives the Flesch Reading-Ease score and grade-level formulas built from words per sentence and syllables per word, and their limitations. It grounds this chapter's reading level measure as a cheap flag for form, not a verdict on quality.

  3. Blinded experiment - Wikipedia - Explains single and double blinding, the sources of bias they control, and unblinding. It supports this chapter's blind human review, where reviewers score output without knowing the producing model and with the order randomized.

  4. Introduction to Rubrics (2nd Edition) - Dannelle D. Stevens and Antonia J. Levi - Stylus Publishing - Presents a rubric as a four-part grid of task description, scale, dimensions, and descriptions of the dimensions, with worked examples. This structure clarifies how this chapter's rubric defines each dimension and level.

  5. Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment - Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony, and Cass R. Sunstein - Little, Brown Spark - Separates judgment error into bias, a systematic offset, and noise, scatter, using shots at a target, and proposes decision hygiene such as structured processes and aggregated judgments. It frames this chapter's point that bias does not average out.

  6. Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena - arXiv - Zheng et al. examine using strong language models to score other models' answers and measure position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases against human preferences. It is a widely cited reference for this chapter's LLM-as-judge weaknesses and mitigations.

  7. LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations - arXiv - Panickssery, Bowman, and Feng show that language models can recognize their own outputs and rate them higher, a bias called self-preference. It supports this chapter's advice to use a judge from a different model family.

  8. graphlib: Functionality to operate with graph-like structures - Python Documentation - Documents TopologicalSorter, which orders nodes by their dependencies and raises CycleError, reporting the cycle, when no valid order exists. It is a ready-made form of this chapter's dependency cycle check for learning graphs.

  9. Creating and Using Rubrics - Carnegie Mellon University Eberly Center - Explains rubric components (criteria, descriptors, and performance levels), their benefits for consistent grading across reviewers, and sample rubrics for papers, projects, and presentations. It shows how this chapter's writing quality and faithfulness dimensions can be written down.

  10. Model Cards for Model Reporting - arXiv - Mitchell et al. propose short documents that accompany a model and state its intended use, evaluation procedure, and performance limits. It is a template for this chapter's limitations statement and honest reporting of provisional results.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter executes the textbook pipeline as a benchmark. Students prepare the workspace, run each stage with fixed prompts, retrieve outputs, and collect per-stage metrics and wall-clock time. They finish with a complete, logged run that is ready to be diagnosed and scored.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 25 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Pipeline Stage 28 Textbook Benchmark 22 Per-Stage Metrics 9 Standing Approval Answer 2 Required Output Files 2 Stage Sensitivity 1 Textbook Preview 1 Benchmark Runner 11 Algebra I Benchmark 7 Wall-Clock Time 4 Evaluation Status Tracking 1 Skill Completion Rate 1 Build Success 1 Structural Validity 1 Stage Prompt 1 Navigation Entries 1 Run Event Stream 7 Benchmark Workspace Template 5 Run Output Retrieval 3 Run Time Limit 1 Reference Book for Scale 1 Stage Chaining 4 Per-Chapter Generation Run 3 Chapter Completion Criterion 1 Chapter Dependency Check 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 2: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
  • Chapter 6: Cost, Price, and Quality
  • Chapter 7: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
  • Chapter 13: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
  • Chapter 15: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
  • Chapter 16: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
  • Chapter 17: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
  • Chapter 18: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
  • Chapter 19: Designing a Fair Evaluation
  • Chapter 20: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks

From a Design to a Run You Can Check

You have a question, a design, a harness, and a way to score. Now you run it, and the discipline is that every run leaves a record complete enough to diagnose later. By the end of this chapter you will have run each stage with fixed prompts and collected its metrics. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
This is the execution chapter. It takes the pieces that the previous chapters built and runs them as a benchmark: a fixed starting workspace, one prompt for each stage, stages chained so that each starts from the last one's output, and a runner that records what happened. It then covers how a long stage that runs once per chapter is organized, what limits a run's time, and how the output gets back to the laptop.

Two ideas hold the chapter together. The first is that a run must not change its input, so that a run can be repeated and a failed one cannot corrupt the next. The second is that a stage is only finished when its output passes a stated criterion, and not when the model says it is done. A model that announces completion has told you what it believes, and the criteria tell you what happened.

docs.title: Textbook Benchmark and the Algebra I Benchmark
docs.text:
A textbook benchmark is a fixed task that asks a system to generate a textbook, with a fixed input and a fixed way of scoring what comes out. The Algebra I benchmark is this evaluation's instance: the input is the description of a high school Algebra I course, and the task is to produce its learning graph, its chapter structure, and the content of its chapters.

The course was chosen for a practical reason. A published Algebra I book already exists, so its size can serve as a reference for scale, and Algebra I is familiar enough that a reviewer can judge the output without special expertise. The scope was set deliberately narrow: three skills, and no MicroSims, glossary, FAQ, or quizzes. The benchmark tests whether a local harness can execute those skills correctly.

docs.title: Reference Book for Scale
docs.text: The reference book for scale is the published Algebra I book, used to say how big a finished textbook is. The numbers that matter for the three stages are a learning graph of 200 concepts with 277 dependencies, and 13 chapters of about 55,000 words. It is a reference and not a baseline: it was generated with earlier skill versions, and no timings or token counts were kept.

docs.title: Pipeline Stage, Stage Chaining, and Stage Sensitivity
docs.text:
A pipeline stage is one skill run, with defined inputs and outputs. Stage chaining is the arrangement in which each stage starts from the previous stage's output directory, so that the work accumulates. The three stages, in order, and what each starts from and produces:

Stage Skill Starts from Produces 1 learning-graph-generator The benchmark workspace template 200 concepts, dependencies, taxonomy, learning-graph.json 2 book-chapter-generator The stage 1 run directory The chapter structure: a directory and outline per chapter 3 chapter-content-generator The previous run's directory, once per chapter The text of one chapter, added to the book so far

Stage sensitivity is how much a stage's result depends on the capability of the model, and the stages differ. The learning graph asks for dependency reasoning across 200 concepts, which punishes a model that cannot hold a structure in mind. The chapter structure asks for assignment and ordering, which a small error in stage 1 turns into a failed dependency check. The chapter text asks for sustained, accurate prose at a stated level. A model that does one of these well can fail another, and the results of this evaluation say so.

docs.title: Benchmark Workspace Template
docs.text:
The benchmark workspace template is the starting directory for stage 1: a minimal book project holding the course description and the site configuration. The runner copies it fresh for every run, so no run sees another's output. The template contains an unchanged copy of the published course description, and that is the single input to the whole chain.

The Template Is Never the Working Copy

A run works on a copy, and the original stays byte for byte what it was. That is the whole mechanism by which a failed run, a killed run, or a run that wrote garbage cannot reach the next one. If a run changes its own starting point, you can never again say what it started from.

docs.title: Stage Prompt and Standing Approval Answer
docs.text:
A stage prompt is the text that starts a stage, and there is one per stage, fixed. It is what a person would type to begin the skill, with the course description's location and the target. A standing approval answer is the paragraph in the prompt that tells the agent how to handle the skill's questions when no one is there. Without it, a skill that pauses for review stalls an unattended run.

The three prompts differ only in which skill they name. The shared closing is the part that matters: it says nobody is available, that every approval request counts as approved, to work through every step of the skill, and to stop when the skill is complete without starting the next one. That last clause keeps each stage's metrics separate.

docs.title: Benchmark Runner
docs.text:
The benchmark runner is the script that executes one stage. It takes a model, a label for the run, a prompt file, and a starting directory, and it does five things in order.

  • It copies the starting directory to a fresh run directory.
  • It starts the harness container with that directory mounted and the model's tag set.
  • It feeds the prompt file in and captures every event.
  • It stops the run at its time limit if the limit is reached.
  • It records the exit code and the wall-clock seconds.
src/harness/run_skill.sh <model> s1-<label> \
  benchmark/algebra-1/prompts/01-learning-graph-generator.txt \
  benchmark/algebra-1/template

The label, s1-<label>, names the run and every file it produces. The starting directory is the template for stage 1, and for each later stage it is the previous stage's run directory.

docs.title: Run Event Stream and Run Time Limit
docs.text:
The run event stream is the log the harness writes as it works, one JSON object per line: each message, each tool call, and each result. It is the complete record of what the agent did, and every later diagnosis reads it. It is kept outside the repository, because it holds local paths and has not been sanitized.

The run time limit is the longest a run may take before the runner stops it. A model that is stuck or merely very slow would otherwise occupy the machine for hours. A run stopped by the limit exits with code 124, and what it wrote so far is kept, so a timeout is a result and not a lost run. The limits in this evaluation were 150 minutes for stage 1, 2 hours for stage 2, and 90 minutes for each chapter in stage 3.

Output file What it holds <label>/ The run directory after the run, with the generated files <label>.jsonl The event stream <label>.json The final result: turns, token counts, timings <label>.status The exit code and wall-clock seconds <label>.stderr Anything the harness wrote to its error stream

docs.title: Wall-Clock Time
docs.text: Wall-clock time is the elapsed real time of a run, from start to finish, as measured by a clock on the wall. It is the figure a person waits for and the one the cost model uses. It includes everything: loading, reading, writing, tools, and waiting. Chapter 15 splits it into those causes, and the runner records the total in the status file.

docs.title: Per-Chapter Generation Run
docs.text:
A per-chapter generation run is a stage 3 run for a single chapter. The chapter-content skill is run once for each chapter, in order, each starting from the book as it stands. The reason is isolation: each chapter gets its own timing, token counts, and time limit, and a failure on one chapter does not discard the others.

A model stops after two time-outs in a row, because a model that cannot finish two chapters in 90 minutes each will not finish twelve, and the remaining runs would only occupy the machine. The runs not made are recorded as not run, with the reason.

docs.title: Chapter Completion Criterion
docs.text: The chapter completion criterion is the rule that says a chapter counts as written: its placeholder text is gone and it has at least 1,000 words. It exists because "the model said it finished" is not evidence. A model that announces it is running a skill and ends its turn without writing anything has not written a chapter, and the criterion catches it.

docs.title: Chapter Dependency Check
docs.text: The chapter dependency check is a step in the chapter-content skill that verifies that each chapter's concepts depend only on concepts in earlier chapters. If the check finds a violation, the skill stops and says so. In three of one model's runs it did exactly that, because the model's own chapter structure from stage 2 had placed concepts out of order. The failure is real and the stage that caused it was the earlier one, which is why chained stages must be diagnosed from the start.

docs.title: What a Stage Must Leave Behind
Required Output Files and Navigation Entries
docs.text:
Required output files are the files a skill is supposed to produce, and checking that they exist is the cheapest verification there is. The learning-graph stage has seven: the concept list, the dependency graph as CSV and as JSON, the concept taxonomy, a quality-metrics report, a taxonomy-distribution report, and an index page.

Navigation entries are the lines in the site configuration that make the new pages reachable. A page that exists on disk and is missing from the navigation is invisible to readers, and a strict build can fail on it. Several models left the entries out, even when they wrote the files, which is why this is a check of its own.

docs.title: Per-Stage Metrics
docs.text:
Per-stage metrics are the measurements recorded for each stage of each run, so that stages can be compared across models. They fall into the three groups of Chapter 19, and the table defines each metric in terms of something a program can compute.

Metric Definition Group Skill completion rate Stages that ended on their own with every required file, divided by stages attempted Completion Build success The strict site build exits with no errors Completion Structural validity The structural checks of Chapter 20 pass Completion Wall-clock time Real elapsed time of the run Efficiency Tool call count and failed tool calls From the event stream Efficiency Tokens Input and output, from the final result Efficiency Words and reading level For chapters, from the chapter-metrics script Quality

A worked example uses one model's actual results, from this book's model results page. The model is gemma4:26b, run on one DGX unit at a 163,840-token context.

Stage Produced Time 1. Learning graph 200 concepts, 483 dependencies, 40 duplicate labels 6 minutes 2. Book structure 14 chapters, 160 of 200 concepts assigned 4 minutes 3. Chapter content 10 of 14 chapters written, 27,217 words 100 minutes in 14 runs

Each row carries something a person would miss on a reading. The stage 1 row has a fault in it, 40 duplicate labels, that the structural check found. The stage 2 row says that 40 of the 200 concepts were not assigned to any chapter, which will limit what stage 3 can write. And the stage 3 row says four of 14 chapters were not written, for reasons the event streams explain. Chapter 22 reads them.

Write the Metric Definitions Down Before the First Run

Ten minutes spent writing "build success means a strict build exits zero" saves the argument, later, about whether a run that built with warnings counts. Put the definitions in the same record as the prompts, and score every run with the same script.

docs.title: Run Output Retrieval
docs.text:
Run output retrieval is bringing the run directories and event streams back from the DGX to the laptop, where they are reviewed and scored. This project's script copies each unit's run directory with rsync, which transfers only new and changed files and never deletes. The hosts come from an environment variable, so no address is written into the script.

export DGX_HOSTS="<user>@<dgx-host-a> <user>@<dgx-host-b>"
src/orchestration/fetch_runs.sh --watch 300

With --watch it fetches again every 300 seconds, and stops when a book or a phase finishes, when a host that was answering fails twice in a row, or when no run is going. The last two conditions are the useful ones: a unit that has frozen announces itself by failing to answer.

The fetched output is not sanitized. It holds local paths and, in the event streams, whatever the commands printed. It stays outside the repository, and only the learning graph and the chapter text are published, through a script that leaves out any file with an address, a host name, or a home-directory path.

docs.title: Textbook Preview
docs.text: A textbook preview is building the generated book and reading it as a reader would. It is the only way to see the rendered result, with its navigation, its tables, and its admonitions, and not the Markdown. The book is a project like any other, so mkdocs build --strict builds it, and a model's output can be previewed on the laptop after retrieval, with no need to reach the DGX at all.

docs.title: Evaluation Status Tracking
docs.text: Evaluation status tracking is a single table that shows, for each model, how far it has got. This book's status page is the form: one row per model, one column per stage, with a check, a cross, a count such as "10 of 14", "Running", or a dash for not started. It is updated after each run, and it carries a "last updated" line. It records that a stage finished and nothing about how good the output is, and the page says so.

docs.title: A Queue of Runs
docs.text:
A benchmark of ten models is a queue, and a queue needs more than the runner. This project's batch script works through a list of models one at a time, in phases: download and model-only test, harness smoke test, then stages 1, 2, and 3. A run that already has a status file is skipped, so a stopped queue restarts where it left off. An empty file named skip-<model> in the runs directory makes a running queue pass over a model.

Three practices make a long queue survivable. The queue runs in a tmux session named bench, with the watchdog in a session named watchdog, so that a dropped connection stops neither. The script restarts the model server for each model with a context chosen from a memory estimate that keeps about 45 GiB free. And each model's results are fetched back as it finishes, so that a unit that freezes does not take unfetched results with it.

docs.title: Diagram: Benchmark Stage Pipeline
docs.text:
Run Benchmark Stage Pipeline Fullscreen

Benchmark Stage Pipeline

Type: workflow sim-id: benchmark-stage-pipeline Library: Mermaid Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-graphs/tree/main/docs/sims/book-build-workflow-pipeline Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain how the three benchmark stages chain by opening each of 7 elements of the pipeline and then answering 4 questions about what starts from what, with at least 3 of 4 correct.

Prerequisites: pipeline stage, stage chaining, benchmark workspace template, per-chapter generation run, run time limit, run event stream (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner opens all 7 elements to read their descriptions, then answers 4 questions, each by choosing one element, before any answer is revealed. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct element column. Mastery is 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Opening an element is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Every stage starts from the template. (2) Stage 3 is one run for the whole book. (3) A run that hits its time limit loses what it wrote. (4) A run can change its starting directory.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level explaining of a chained process needs the learner to place inputs and outputs, so each element's description names where it starts from and what it leaves, and the questions ask the learner to locate a fact in that structure.

Content:

The seven elements, in order, with the description shown when an element is opened:

# Element Description shown 1 Template workspace The fixed starting directory with the course description. It is copied for each run and never changed. 2 Stage 1 run Runs the learning-graph skill on a copy of the template, with a 150-minute limit. 3 Stage 1 output The run directory holding the seven required files of the learning graph. 4 Stage 2 run Runs the chapter-structure skill on a copy of the stage 1 output, with a 2-hour limit. 5 Stage 2 output The run directory holding one directory and outline per chapter. 6 Stage 3 runs One run per chapter, each on a copy of the book so far, with a 90-minute limit each. 7 Finished book The run directory after the last chapter, which is the book the model wrote.

The four questions:

# Question shown to the learner Correct element Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which element is the starting point of stage 2? Stage 1 output Each stage starts from a copy of the previous stage's output. 2 Which element runs once for each chapter? Stage 3 runs The chapter skill is run once per chapter so each gets its own timing and limit. 3 Which element must never be changed by a run? Template workspace It is copied for each run, so every run starts from the same input. 4 Which element holds the seven required files of the learning graph? Stage 1 output The seven files are the required output of stage 1.

Provenance: The elements and limits come from the benchmark's runner and prompts and from the sections of this chapter above. The questions are synthetic, written for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example".

Rules: Elements may be opened in any order. The questions are asked in the fixed order 1 to 4, each allows one final choice among the seven elements, and exactly one element is correct for each question.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner opens each of the 7 elements of the pipeline and reads its description. The questions unlock after all seven have been opened.
  2. The learner reads question 1 and chooses an element, then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct element and the Why text, and marks the question correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for questions 2 to 4. After question 4 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Four questions, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct element and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 4 correct".

Starting State: The pipeline is shown with no element opened, and the instruction on screen is "Open each element to see what it does".

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that each stage starts from a copy of the previous stage's output, that the template is never changed, that stage 3 runs once per chapter, and that the limits are 150 minutes, 2 hours, and 90 minutes per chapter.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
The benchmark runs three chained stages from a fixed template with one prompt each, and a runner that copies the starting directory so no run changes its input. Each run leaves an event stream, a result, and a status file, and a time limit turns a stuck run into a recorded result. Stage 3 runs once per chapter, with a completion criterion in place of the model's own claim. A stage must leave its required files and navigation entries, and its metrics are defined before the first run and computed by the same script every time. Outputs come back to the laptop by a script that never deletes, a status table tracks progress, and a queue is made survivable by tmux, a watchdog, per-model context choice, and fetching as it goes.

You Have a Complete, Logged Run

You can now run the three stages from a fixed template, bound each by a time limit, retrieve the outputs, and record per-stage metrics against definitions you wrote first. Chapter 22 turns those raw records into a diagnosis and a decision.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Running the Textbook Benchmark
docs.text: Test your understanding of the benchmark stages, the runner, time limits, completion criteria, per-stage metrics, and output retrieval with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does the benchmark runner do first when it executes a stage?
docs.text:
1. Copies the starting directory to a fresh run directory
  2. Deletes the previous stage's run directory to save space
  3. Scores the generated files against the written scoring rubric
  4. Uploads the event stream to the public repository
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The benchmark runner is the script that executes one stage. It takes a model, a label, a prompt file, and a starting directory, and its first act is to copy the starting directory to a fresh run directory. It then starts the harness container, feeds in the prompt and captures every event, stops the run at its time limit if needed, and records the exit code and wall-clock seconds. Because it works on a copy, a run never changes its input.

Concept Tested: Benchmark Runner

See: Benchmark Runner

docs.title: 2. What happens to a run that reaches its time limit?
docs.text:
1. It is restarted from the template with a longer limit
  2. It continues, and the overrun is recorded only as a warning
  3. It exits with code 124, and what it wrote so far is kept
  4. It is deleted, and the model is then removed from the queue
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The run time limit is the longest a run may take before the runner stops it, so a stuck or very slow model cannot occupy the machine for hours. A run stopped by the limit exits with code 124, and what it wrote so far is kept, so a timeout is a result and not a lost run. The limits were 150 minutes for stage 1, 2 hours for stage 2, and 90 minutes for each chapter in stage 3.

Concept Tested: Run Time Limit

See: Run Event Stream and Run Time Limit

docs.title: 3. Why was Algebra I chosen as the benchmark course?
docs.text:
1. It needs MicroSims, a glossary, and quizzes to be complete
  2. It is the shortest course the skills are able to generate
  3. A published book gives a scale reference, and reviewers know it
  4. Its concepts have no dependencies, so stage 1 is simple
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The Algebra I benchmark is this evaluation's instance of a textbook benchmark: the input is a high school Algebra I course description, and the task is its learning graph, chapter structure, and chapter content. The course was chosen for a practical reason. A published Algebra I book already exists, so its size is a reference for scale, and the subject is familiar enough that a reviewer can judge the output without special expertise.

Concept Tested: Algebra I Benchmark

See: Textbook Benchmark and the Algebra I Benchmark

docs.title: 4. Why does the benchmark use a chapter completion criterion instead of the model's own statement that it finished?
docs.text:
1. The model's final message is not saved in the event stream
  2. A model's claim shows its belief, not what was actually written
  3. The criterion gives slower models some extra time for each chapter
  4. The harness cannot detect when the model ends its turn
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter completion criterion says a chapter counts as written when its placeholder text is gone and it has at least 1,000 words. It exists because "the model said it finished" is not evidence. A model that announces completion has told you what it believes, and the criterion tells you what happened. It catches a model that announces it is running a skill and then ends its turn without writing anything.

Concept Tested: Chapter Completion Criterion

See: Chapter Completion Criterion

docs.title: 5. You are starting stage 2 for a model whose stage 1 run is labeled s1-<label>. Which starting directory do you pass to the runner?
docs.text:
1. The stage 1 run directory for that model
  2. The benchmark workspace template
  3. An empty directory created for stage 2
  4. The published reference book's repository
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Stage chaining is the arrangement in which each stage starts from the previous stage's output directory, so the work accumulates. The starting directory is the template for stage 1 only; for each later stage it is the previous stage's run directory. The runner copies whatever directory it is given, so the stage 1 output itself is left unchanged. Starting stage 2 from the template would give the chapter-structure skill no learning graph to organize.

Concept Tested: Stage Chaining

See: Pipeline Stage, Stage Chaining, and Stage Sensitivity

docs.title: 6. A model attempted three stages. Stage 1 ended on its own with all seven required files. Stage 2 ended on its own but left out one required file. Stage 3 was stopped at its time limit. What is its skill completion rate?
docs.text:
1. 0 of 3
  2. 1 of 3
  3. 2 of 3
  4. 3 of 3
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Per-stage metrics are defined so that a program can compute them. Skill completion rate is the number of stages that ended on their own with every required file, divided by the stages attempted. Only stage 1 meets both conditions. Stage 2 ended on its own but is missing a required file, and stage 3 did not end on its own because the limit stopped it. The rate is therefore 1 of 3.

Concept Tested: Skill Completion Rate

See: Per-Stage Metrics

docs.title: 7. In stage 3, the chapter-content skill stops and reports that a chapter's concepts depend on concepts placed in later chapters. Which stage caused the failure?
docs.text:
1. Stage 3, because the chapter text was written incorrectly
  2. Stage 1, because the template was changed during the run
  3. The runner, because it copied the wrong prompt file
  4. Stage 2, because its chapter structure ordered concepts wrongly
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter dependency check is a step in the chapter-content skill that verifies each chapter's concepts depend only on concepts in earlier chapters, and it stops the skill when it finds a violation. In three of one model's runs it did so because the model's own chapter structure from stage 2 had placed concepts out of order. The failure appears in stage 3, and the stage that caused it was earlier, which is why chained stages must be diagnosed from the start.

Concept Tested: Chapter Dependency Check

See: Chapter Dependency Check

docs.title: 8. In the worked example, a model's stage 2 produced 14 chapters with 160 of the 200 concepts assigned. What does this imply for stage 3?
docs.text:
1. Stage 3 will run faster, because it has fewer chapters
  2. Stage 3 will fail its strict build on the very first chapter
  3. Stage 3 cannot cover the 40 concepts no chapter contains
  4. Stage 3 will reassign the concepts as it writes each chapter
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Each stage starts from the previous stage's output, so a gap carries forward. In the worked example, stage 2 produced 14 chapters with 160 of the 200 concepts assigned, which means 40 concepts were not assigned to any chapter. That limits what stage 3 can write. A per-stage record makes the gap visible at the stage where it arose, before anyone reads the chapter text, which is the reason metrics are kept per stage.

Concept Tested: Per-Stage Metrics

See: Per-Stage Metrics

docs.title: 9. During a queue of runs, the fetch script running with --watch stops because a host that had been answering failed twice in a row. What does this most likely indicate?
docs.text:
1. The unit has stopped responding and may be frozen
  2. The book on that unit has finished generating
  3. The queue reached a model marked with a skip file
  4. The script deleted the run directory on that unit
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Run output retrieval brings run directories and event streams back to the laptop with rsync, which copies new and changed files and never deletes. With --watch the script fetches repeatedly and stops when a book or phase finishes, when a host that was answering fails twice in a row, or when no run is going. A unit that has frozen announces itself by failing to answer, so that stop condition is the signal to check on the machine.

Concept Tested: Run Output Retrieval

See: Run Output Retrieval

docs.title: 10. A model has timed out on two chapters in a row at 90 minutes each, and twelve chapters remain. Which course of action is best justified?
docs.text:
1. Run all twelve, since each chapter is an independent run
  2. Double the time limit for that model's remaining chapters
  3. Delete the model's earlier results, since the book is incomplete
  4. Stop the model and record the remaining runs as not run
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A per-chapter generation run gives each chapter its own timing and limit, and a failure on one chapter does not discard the others. The rule is that a model stops after two time-outs in a row: a model that cannot finish two chapters in 90 minutes each will not finish twelve, and the remaining runs would only occupy the machine. The runs not made are recorded as not run, with the reason. Changing the limit for one model would break a controlled variable.

Concept Tested: Per-Chapter Generation Run

See: Per-Chapter Generation Run

docs.title: References: Running the Textbook Benchmark
docs.text:
1. Benchmark (computing) - Wikipedia - Describes how benchmarks run standard tests to compare systems, and lists principles including relevance, repeatability, and transparency. It frames this chapter's fixed Algebra I textbook benchmark and why every run must start from the same input.

  2. Rsync - Wikipedia - Covers the rsync tool and its delta-transfer algorithm, which sends only new and changed data, with usage examples. It explains how this chapter's run output retrieval copies run directories from the DGX without resending everything.

  3. JSON streaming - Wikipedia - Compares ways to stream a sequence of JSON values, including newline-delimited JSON (JSON Lines) with one object per line. It explains the format of this chapter's run event stream and why it can be read mid-run.

  4. Continuous Delivery: Reliable Software Releases through Build, Test, and Deployment Automation (1st Edition) - Jez Humble and David Farley - Addison-Wesley Professional - Develops the deployment pipeline, an automated sequence of stages from check-in to release in which each stage builds on the last and a failure stops the line. It clarifies this chapter's stage chaining and fail-fast stage gates.

  5. The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis (1st Edition) - Raj Jain - Wiley - Widely praised for opening with a catalog of common performance-evaluation mistakes, such as no goals, biased goals, and unrepresentative workloads, followed by a systematic approach. It guides the benchmark discipline this chapter applies.

  6. timeout invocation (GNU Coreutils) - GNU Project - Documents the timeout command, which stops a command after a time limit, with signal and kill-after options and exit status 124 on timeout. It matches this chapter's run time limit, where a timeout is recorded as a result.

  7. Run Claude Code programmatically - Claude Code Documentation - Explains non-interactive runs with the -p flag, exit codes, and the stream-json output format that emits one JSON event per line. It describes how this chapter's runner can feed a stage prompt unattended and capture every event.

  8. Bind mounts - Docker Documentation - Explains how a host directory is mounted into a container with --mount or -v, including read-only mounts. It underlies this chapter's runner, which mounts a fresh copy of the run directory into the harness container.

  9. tmux Wiki - tmux Project - Introduces tmux as a terminal multiplexer whose programs can be detached to keep running in the background and reattached from another terminal. It supports this chapter's named bench and watchdog sessions that survive a dropped connection.

  10. Command Line Interface - MkDocs Documentation - Documents the mkdocs build command and its strict mode, which aborts the build on any warning. It is the command behind this chapter's build success metric, where a strict build must exit with no errors.

docs.title: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
Summary
docs.text: This chapter turns raw run data into a decision. Students diagnose failures from logs, compute throughput, tool-call success, and energy, compare against the cloud baseline, and estimate cost per textbook. They finish able to write an evidence-based recommendation for a local, cloud, or hybrid workflow.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 26 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Malformed Tool Call 3 Text-Emitted Tool Call 1 Whole-Book Time Estimate 6 Context Overflow 2 Harness Misconfiguration 2 Task Loss 1 Cost per Textbook 4 DGX Sufficiency Judgment 3 Baseline Textbook 2 Books per Year 1 Failure Diagnosis 1 Premature Turn Termination 1 Cost per Chapter 1 Quality-Adjusted Cost 1 Service Price Calculation 1 Human Review Cost 1 Time Breakdown 1 Energy per Textbook 1 Tool Call Count 5 Evaluation Report 5 Failed Tool Calls 2 Run Report 1 Recommendation 2 Tool-Call Success Rate 1 Report Structure 1 Local Cloud or Hybrid Decision 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
  • Chapter 3: Small Language Models
  • Chapter 4: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
  • Chapter 6: Cost, Price, and Quality
  • Chapter 10: Python Hardware Probes
  • Chapter 11: Model Sizing and Fit
  • Chapter 13: Inference Servers and Local API Endpoints
  • Chapter 15: Optimizing Small Language Model Performance
  • Chapter 16: The Agent Loop, Tools, and Context
  • Chapter 17: Agent Skills and Connecting a Harness to a Local Model
  • Chapter 19: Designing a Fair Evaluation
  • Chapter 20: Scoring, Bias, and Structural Checks
  • Chapter 21: Running the Textbook Benchmark

Raw Logs In, A Decision Out

A folder of event streams is not an answer. By the end of this chapter you will turn one into a diagnosis of why a run failed, a cost per textbook, and a recommendation you can defend. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
Chapter 21 ended with complete, logged runs. This chapter is what you do with them. It has three parts, in the order the work goes. First, diagnose: for each run that failed, work out why from the evidence, because a failed run is a result and the cause decides what to do next. Second, compute: from the measured times and speeds, work out the time, the energy, and the cost of a textbook. Third, decide: assemble the evidence into a report with a recommendation.

The discipline that runs through all three is to keep what was measured separate from what was assumed. Where this evaluation could only assume, such as the time for stages it had not yet run, the chapter says so, and the recommendation carries the same caveat.

docs.title: Failure Diagnosis
docs.text:
Failure diagnosis is working from the symptoms in the logs to the cause of a failed run. The skill is to ask what the evidence rules out and not what the failure feels like, because several different causes produce runs that look similar from the outside: a run that ended early, a stage with nothing written, a model that seems to have given up.

The evidence is the run event stream, the final result, and the server log, and the questions are the same in every case. How many turns were taken? How many tool calls, and how many failed? What was the last thing the model said? What was the peak context size, against the window? Did the run end on its own, or was it stopped?

docs.title: Tool Call Count, Failed Tool Calls, and Tool-Call Success Rate
docs.text:
The tool call count is the number of tool calls a model made in a run, and failed tool calls is how many of them returned an error. The tool-call success rate is the successful share. All three come straight from the event stream, and the run-report script prints them.

The measured values in this evaluation's first stage show how different runs can look.

Model Tool calls Failed Success rate Reading gpt-oss:120b 28 0 100% Few calls, none failed qwen3.8:27b 55 1 98% Careful and slow gemma4:31b 50 8 84% Eight failures in fifty calls nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 140 not recorded here n/a Nearly three times as many calls as any other model

A number alone does not diagnose. 100% success on 28 calls is not better than 84% on 50 if the 28 calls never reached the step that writes the file. The count is the prompt for a question, and the event stream holds the answer.

docs.title: Malformed Tool Call and Text-Emitted Tool Call
docs.text:
A malformed tool call is a tool call with a wrong name, a missing argument, or an argument of the wrong type. The harness returns an error, the model usually reads it and tries again, and it counts as a failed tool call. It is a nuisance, and a run can recover from it.

A text-emitted tool call is a tool call that the model writes out as ordinary text in its reply, in the shape of a call but not as a call. The harness sees no tool call and treats the reply as a final answer, so the run ends. Two of this evaluation's candidates failed this way: one wrote its first tool call as text in both harness tests and did no work, and another did so in one of two runs and stopped after a single turn. The signature is a run of one turn whose last message contains something that looks like a call.

docs.title: Premature Turn Termination and Task Loss
docs.text:
Premature turn termination is the model ending its turn before the work is done, with no error. In this evaluation one model, in four of its ten chapter runs, announced that the skill was running, as if something else would do the work, and ended its turn without writing the chapter. The signature is a final message that describes work and no file that contains it.

Task loss is the model abandoning the task and answering something unrelated. One candidate, after a few steps, answered with a greeting as if the conversation had just begun. It is usually a context problem: that model's first prompt took 35,000 tokens where the others took 17,000 to 21,000, and within eight turns it was at 120,000, the edge of its window.

docs.title: Context Overflow and Harness Misconfiguration
docs.text:
Context overflow is the conversation exceeding the model's window, so that earlier content is dropped or the request is rejected. Its signature is a run that does well for a while and then behaves as if it had forgotten the task, with a peak context size close to the window.

Harness misconfiguration is a fault in how the harness was set up and not in the model: a wrong address, a model name that the server does not have, a skill folder that was not mounted, or a permission rule that stalls. The signature is a failure at the very first turn, for every model, with an error message that names the configuration. A failure that is identical across all models is a configuration fault until shown otherwise.

Symptom Likely cause First thing to check One turn, last message looks like a call Text-emitted tool call The final message in the event stream An error, then a correct retry Malformed tool call The failed call's arguments Ends after announcing, no file written Premature turn termination The last message and the run directory Answers a greeting after several turns Task loss Peak context size against the window Forgets the task late in the run Context overflow Peak context size against the window Same error at turn one for every model Harness misconfiguration The base address, model name, and mounts

Check Whether Every Model Failed the Same Way

A failure that appears for every model at the same place is almost never the models. Before you write that a model "cannot" do something, run the failing step with a model that is known to work. If it fails there too, you have found a configuration or skill fault, and the models were innocent.

docs.title: Diagram: Failure Diagnosis Chooser
docs.text:
Run Failure Diagnosis Chooser Fullscreen

Failure Diagnosis Chooser

Type: microsim sim-id: failure-diagnosis-chooser Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: attribute Learning Objective: The learner will attribute each of 8 failed-run symptoms to its most likely cause from a list of 8, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: malformed tool call, text-emitted tool call, premature turn termination, task loss, context overflow, harness misconfiguration, prompt re-reading, chapter dependency check (all defined in this chapter and in Chapters 15, 16, and 21).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 8 symptoms the learner commits one cause from the eight listed before the sim reveals the answer. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct cause column. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the symptoms is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A failure that ends a run is always a model failure. (2) A tool error means the run cannot recover. (3) A slow run is a failed run. (4) A model that says it is doing the work has done it.

Instructional Rationale: Attributing a symptom to a cause needs the learner to use the discriminating detail in each case, so each symptom has exactly one cause and the eight causes are different enough to confuse only if the detail is missed.

Content:

The eight causes the learner chooses from: "Text-emitted tool call", "Malformed tool call", "Task loss", "Context overflow", "Harness misconfiguration", "Premature turn termination", "Slow turns from prompt re-reading", and "Upstream stage fault".

# Symptom shown to the learner Correct cause Why (shown as feedback) 1 The run ended after one turn. Its last message contains text shaped like a tool call, written as ordinary prose. Text-emitted tool call The harness saw no real tool call, so it treated the reply as the final answer. 2 The harness reported invalid arguments for a file write. On the next turn the model sent a correct call and the run went on. Malformed tool call The call was ill-formed and the model recovered after the error. 3 After about eight turns the model answers "Hello, how can I help?" and ignores the skill. Task loss The model has dropped the task, which is usually a sign of a context that was too large for it. 4 The conversation reached 127,000 tokens in a 128,000-token window, and the model began to contradict its own earlier instructions. Context overflow The window was close to full, so earlier content was lost. 5 Every request returns "model not found" at turn one, for every model tried. Harness misconfiguration The same failure at the first turn for every model points at the setup, not a model. 6 The final message says "I will now run the chapter skill", with no tool call made and no file written. Premature turn termination The model described the work and ended its turn without doing it. 7 Four of 14 chapters were not written. The skill's own dependency check reported that each chapter needed concepts placed in later chapters, and stopped. Upstream stage fault The chapter structure from stage 2 was the cause, so the stage 3 failure is a symptom of it. 8 The stage hit its 90-minute limit after about twenty tool calls. Each turn took close to two minutes, and the server log shows most of that reading the prompt. Slow turns from prompt re-reading The time went to the server recomputing the conversation, not to the model's generating.

Provenance: The symptoms are synthetic but follow failures observed in this evaluation, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The causes come from this chapter and Chapters 15, 16, and 21.

Rules: Symptoms are shown in the fixed order 1 to 8. Each allows one final choice, and exactly one cause is correct for each. A cause is the correct answer for exactly one symptom.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads symptom 1.
  2. The learner chooses one of the eight causes and confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct cause and the Why text, and marks the symptom correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for symptoms 2 to 8. After symptom 8 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Eight symptoms, fixed order, one confirmed choice each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct cause and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 8 correct".

Starting State: Symptom 1 is shown with no cause chosen, and the question on screen is "What most likely caused this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a text-emitted tool call ends a run after one turn, that a malformed call is recoverable, that a failure identical for every model at turn one is a configuration fault, and that a dependency-check stop in stage 3 traces back to stage 2.

docs.title: Computing the Cost of a Book
Time Breakdown and Whole-Book Time Estimate
docs.text:
A time breakdown splits a run's wall-clock time into loading, reading, writing, and tools, as Chapter 15 did for one turn. A whole-book time estimate extrapolates the time for the whole book from the stages that were measured, and it is the number the cost model needs.

The benchmark covers three stages, which the Primary Author set at 10% of the cost of a whole book, because the learning graph, the chapter design, and the chapter content are one tenth of the work; the MicroSims, glossary, FAQ, quizzes, and references are the rest. The estimate follows:

\[ T_{\text{book}} = \frac{T_{\text{three stages}}}{0.10} \]

For the reference model, the three stages take 2.8 hours, so a whole book is about 28 hours of machine time. The estimate rests on an assumption about stages that have not been run, and a reader should treat it as a model to adjust. If the three stages were 5% of the book, the estimate doubles.

docs.title: Energy per Textbook
docs.text: Energy per textbook is the electricity a book takes. It is the generating power times the generating time. At 150 W for 28 hours it is 4.2 kWh, which at $0.1385 per kWh is about 58 cents. It is the smallest cost in the model, and the reason to compute it is to be able to say so with a number.

docs.title: Cost per Textbook, Cost per Chapter, and Books per Year
docs.text:
The cost per textbook is the machine's yearly cost spread over the books it makes, which comes down to the book's hours times the cost of a generating hour. The cost per chapter divides it by the number of chapters, and books per year is the generating hours in a year divided by the hours for one book.

generating hours per year  = 8,760 × utilization
cost per generating hour   = yearly cost ÷ generating hours per year
cost per book              = whole-book hours × cost per generating hour
cost per chapter           = cost per book ÷ chapters
books per year             = generating hours per year ÷ whole-book hours

The reference case gives each. At 50% utilization there are 4,380 generating hours, and with a yearly cost of $8,275 each is $1.89. A 28-hour book costs $52.92, a 13-chapter book is $4.07 a chapter, and the unit makes 156 books a year.

docs.title: Service Price Calculation and Quality-Adjusted Cost
docs.text:
The service price calculation is the price a book-generation service would have to charge to keep a stated margin: the cost divided by one minus the margin. At a 20% margin, $52.92 becomes $66.15.

Quality-adjusted cost corrects the cost for how much of the output is usable. A book generated for $53 of which only 10 of 14 chapters are written has not cost $53 for a book. One way to express it is the cost per usable chapter, which is the cost divided by the chapters that met the completion criterion. A cheap model that writes 6 of 10 chapters is more expensive per chapter than the arithmetic of its speed suggests.

Case Cost to generate Usable chapters Cost per usable chapter All 13 chapters complete $52.92 13 $4.07 10 of 13 complete $52.92 10 $5.29 6 of 13 complete $52.92 6 $8.82

docs.title: Human Review Cost
docs.text: Human review cost is the price of the person who judges quality. It is not in the generation cost and it can be much larger. Ten hours of subject-expert review at $90 an hour is $900, seventeen times the $53 generation cost. A quality-adjusted comparison that leaves it out has priced the book as though nobody had to read it.

docs.title: Diagram: Cost per Textbook Calculator
docs.text:
Run Cost per Textbook Calculator Fullscreen

Cost per Textbook Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: cost-per-textbook-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/economics-course/tree/main/docs/sims/opportunity-cost-calculator Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the cost per textbook and the price at a stated margin to within 1 dollar for 3 scenarios.

Prerequisites: utilization rate, whole-book time estimate, cost per textbook, service price calculation, margin versus markup (all defined in this chapter and in Chapter 6).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 3 scenarios the learner types the cost per textbook and the price at the stated margin, in dollars, before the sim reveals the answers. A scenario is correct when both typed values are within $1 of the model values. Mastery is 3 of 3. Changing sliders in exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A faster model always lowers the cost per book. (2) The cost is set by the electricity. (3) A 20% margin means a 20% markup. (4) A machine's cost per book does not depend on how often it is used.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs a formula the learner commits to, and the three scenarios isolate the two inputs that move the answer most, utilization and the hours per book, so exploration can then confirm that hardware price moves it far less.

Content:

The learner can change five quantities:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Yearly cost 2,000 20,000 25 8,275 dollars a year Utilization 0.05 0.95 0.05 0.50 share of 8,760 hours Whole-book hours 5 100 1 28 hours Margin 0 0.50 0.05 0.20 share of price Chapters 5 30 1 13 chapters

The three scenarios, in this order:

# Yearly cost Utilization Whole-book hours Margin Model cost per book Model price Feedback when wrong 1 8,275 0.50 28 0.20 $52.9 $66.1 8,760 × 0.50 = 4,380 hours, $8,275 ÷ 4,380 = $1.89 an hour, × 28 = $52.9, ÷ 0.80 = $66.1. 2 8,275 0.25 28 0.20 $105.8 $132.2 8,760 × 0.25 = 2,190 hours, $8,275 ÷ 2,190 = $3.78 an hour, × 28 = $105.8, ÷ 0.80 = $132.2. 3 8,275 0.50 17 0.20 $32.1 $40.1 $1.89 an hour × 17 = $32.1, ÷ 0.80 = $40.1.

Provenance: The yearly cost, utilization, and whole-book hours are the reference and sensitivity values of the cost analysis page. The scenario 3 hours of 17 are the whole-book estimate for a mixture-of-experts model in that analysis. The sim labels them "estimate, not a measurement".

Rules: Generating hours = 8,760 × utilization. Cost per generating hour = yearly cost ÷ generating hours. Cost per book = whole-book hours × cost per generating hour. Price = cost per book ÷ (1 − margin). Cost per chapter = cost per book ÷ chapters. Books per year = generating hours ÷ whole-book hours, rounded down. Dollars are shown to one decimal.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads scenario 1, whose inputs are shown, and types the cost per book and the price.
  2. The learner presses Check.
  3. The sim reveals the model values and the Feedback text, and marks the scenario correct or missed.
  4. After all three scenarios the exploration mode unlocks, with a readout of cost per chapter and books per year, and the learner changes any of the five quantities.
  5. In exploration the learner should notice that halving utilization doubles the cost per book, and that a 10% change in yearly cost moves it by 10%.

Feedback: Three scenarios, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: cost $, price $." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that scenario. After the second wrong attempt the model values and the worked calculation are shown, and the scenario counts as missed. A running count "Scenarios correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Scenario 1 is shown with empty answer boxes and its inputs displayed, and the question on screen is "What does one textbook cost, and what must it sell for?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states $1.89 per generating hour, $52.92 per 28-hour book, $66.15 at a 20% margin, 156 books a year at 50% utilization, and that halving utilization doubles the cost per book.

docs.title: Run Report and Baseline Textbook
docs.text:
A run report is the summary of one run produced from its event stream: turns, tool calls, failed tool calls, tokens, and time. This project's run_report.py produces it, and it works on a run that is still going, which makes it the tool for deciding whether to wait or to stop one.

A baseline textbook is the comparison book generated by a cloud model under the same rules, and it is what lets a local result be judged against something. This evaluation has a reference book for scale and has not yet generated a baseline. Until it does, the report can state costs and structural results and cannot state a quality gap, and it says so.

docs.title: DGX Sufficiency Judgment
docs.text:
A DGX sufficiency judgment is the answer to the question the evaluation was set up to ask: is this machine, with these models and this harness, enough to generate the textbook? It is a judgment and not a calculation, and it should be made against criteria written down before the data arrived.

The criteria this evaluation can state are concrete. Does at least one model complete all three stages without a fault that makes the output unusable? Does it do so within a time and cost the user can accept? Does the quality, once reviewed, meet the standard the course sets? The honest answer at any given moment can be that the first is established, the second is estimated, and the third is not yet known, and a report says which.

Sufficient Is a Threshold You Set, Not a Number You Find

A machine is sufficient for a purpose, and the purpose has to say how fast, how good, and at what cost. Write the thresholds down first. If you decide what counts as enough after seeing what the machine can do, the answer is always yes.

docs.title: Evaluation Report and Report Structure
docs.text:
An evaluation report is the document that carries the evaluation to a reader who was not there. A report structure is the order of its parts, and the five parts below are the ones that let a reader judge the conclusion for themselves.

Part What it states The question a reader asks of it Question What was being evaluated, for whom Is this my question? Method The design: variables, inputs, runs, metrics Could I repeat it, and was it fair? Results What was measured, with the assumed marked What actually happened?
