Limitations What the results do not show How far can I trust this? Recommendation Local, cloud, or hybrid, and the conditions What should I do?

The order matters. A reader who meets the recommendation before the method has nothing to judge it with, and a report that puts limitations at the end after a confident recommendation has buried the part that tempers it.

docs.title: Recommendation and the Local, Cloud, or Hybrid Decision
docs.text:
A recommendation is the action the evidence supports, stated with its conditions. The local, cloud, or hybrid decision is its most common form for this course: which of the three workflows to adopt for textbook generation, or which parts of the workflow go where.

The decision follows from the evidence in a way that can be written as rules, and the rules are better than the verdict, because a reader can apply them to their own circumstances. The table gives the structure, with the evidence it needs, and an illustrative reading from this evaluation's provisional results.

If the evidence shows Then the recommendation leans A local model completes every stage, at a cost per book below the service price, and review finds the quality acceptable Local No local model completes a stage that the skills need Cloud for that stage Local completes the high-volume or sensitive stages and fails a hard one Hybrid, routed by stage Quality is acceptable and the cost depends on utilization the user cannot reach Cloud, or a shared unit

An illustrative reading, and not a conclusion, uses the first round's pattern. Several models completed the learning-graph and chapter-structure stages, and the stage that exposed capability differences was the chapter text. That pattern would point to a hybrid workflow: the structural stages local, with a stronger model for the hard prose, until a local model's prose is reviewed and shown to be acceptable. It is provisional, because every result is one run and no human review has been finished.

Writing the Recommendation Is the Hard Part, and That Is Normal

After all the measuring, a recommendation can feel like a leap, and it is meant to. If the evidence is mixed, say so and state the conditions under which each answer holds. A recommendation that says "local for this, cloud for that, and here is what would change my mind" is a good one.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Failure diagnosis starts from the event stream and asks what the evidence rules out. A text-emitted tool call ends a run after one turn, a malformed one is recoverable, premature termination and task loss leave no work behind, context overflow shows as forgetting late in a run, and a failure identical for every model at the first turn is a configuration fault. A failure in stage 3 can be a symptom of stage 2. The cost of a book comes from the whole-book time estimate, itself an assumption about the unrun stages, times the cost of a generating hour, and quality adjusts it for how much was usable, while human review is a separate and larger cost. The report states the question, method, results, limitations, and recommendation in that order, and the recommendation is a set of conditions and not a verdict.

From Run Logs to a Defensible Recommendation

You can now diagnose a failed run from its evidence, compute cost and energy per book, adjust for quality, and structure a report whose recommendation states its conditions. Chapter 23 makes that report safe to publish.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
docs.text: Test your understanding of failure diagnosis, the cost of a textbook, sufficiency judgments, and evidence-based recommendations with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a text-emitted tool call?
docs.text:
1. A call with a wrong name or a missing argument
  2. A call the harness refuses under a permission rule
  3. A call written as ordinary text, which the harness does not see
  4. A call that returns more output than the window can hold
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A text-emitted tool call is a tool call that the model writes out as ordinary text in its reply, in the shape of a call but not as a call. The harness sees no tool call and treats the reply as a final answer, so the run ends. Its signature is a run of one turn whose last message contains something that looks like a call. A call with a wrong name or a missing argument is a malformed tool call, which is usually recoverable.

Concept Tested: Text-Emitted Tool Call

See: Malformed Tool Call and Text-Emitted Tool Call

docs.title: 2. Why is a 100% tool-call success rate on 28 calls not necessarily better than 84% on 50 calls?
docs.text:
1. A success rate is meaningful only above 100 tool calls per run
  2. Failed tool calls are never recorded in the run's event stream
  3. A higher call count always means a more careful model
  4. The 28 calls may never have reached the file-writing step
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The tool call count, the failed tool calls, and the success rate all come straight from the event stream, and a number alone does not diagnose. 100% success on 28 calls is not better than 84% on 50 if the 28 calls never reached the step that writes the file. The count is the prompt for a question, and the event stream holds the answer: what the calls did, and whether the work was finished.

Concept Tested: Tool-Call Success Rate

See: Tool Call Count, Failed Tool Calls, and Tool-Call Success Rate

docs.title: 3. Why does an evaluation report put the method before the recommendation?
docs.text:
1. A reader needs the method in order to judge the recommendation
  2. The method is the shortest part and is the quickest to read
  3. The recommendation cannot be drafted until the report is printed
  4. The method lists the limitations, which must always come first
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A report structure is the order of an evaluation report's parts: question, method, results, limitations, recommendation. The order matters because each part answers a reader's question in turn. A reader who meets the recommendation before the method has nothing to judge it with, and a report that puts limitations after a confident recommendation has buried the part that tempers it. Limitations are their own part, placed before the recommendation, not inside the method.

Concept Tested: Report Structure

See: Evaluation Report and Report Structure

docs.title: 4. A model's three benchmark stages take 4 hours. With the three stages set at 10% of the work of a whole book, what is the whole-book time estimate?
docs.text:
1. 4.4 hours
  2. 40 hours
  3. 14 hours
  4. 400 hours
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A whole-book time estimate extrapolates from the measured stages. The three benchmark stages were set at 10% of the work of a whole book, so the estimate is the three-stage time divided by 0.10: 4 hours ÷ 0.10 is 40 hours of machine time. The figure rests on an assumption about stages that have not been run, so treat it as a model to adjust. If the three stages were 5% of the book, the estimate would double.

Concept Tested: Whole-Book Time Estimate

See: Time Breakdown and Whole-Book Time Estimate

docs.title: 5. A 13-chapter book costs $52.92 to generate, and 8 of its chapters meet the completion criterion. What is the cost per usable chapter?
docs.text:
1. $4.07
  2. $6.62
  3. $10.58
  4. $52.92
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Quality-adjusted cost corrects the cost for how much of the output is usable. One way to express it is the cost per usable chapter: the generation cost divided by the chapters that met the completion criterion. Here $52.92 ÷ 8 is about $6.62. Dividing by all 13 chapters gives $4.07, which prices chapters that were never written. A cheap model that leaves chapters unwritten is more expensive per chapter than its speed suggests.

Concept Tested: Quality-Adjusted Cost

See: Service Price Calculation and Quality-Adjusted Cost

docs.title: 6. Every model you try fails at the first turn with the same "model not found" error. What should you do before concluding anything about the models?
docs.text:
1. Record that none of the models can run the skill
  2. Raise the time limit and rerun every model once more
  3. Compare each model's peak context with its window
  4. Check the base address, model name, and mounts first
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Harness misconfiguration is a fault in how the harness was set up and not in the model: a wrong address, a model name the server does not have, a skill folder that was not mounted, or a permission rule that stalls. Its signature is a failure at the very first turn, for every model, with an error that names the configuration. A failure identical across all models is a configuration fault until shown otherwise, so check the setup before blaming any model.

Concept Tested: Harness Misconfiguration

See: Context Overflow and Harness Misconfiguration

docs.title: 7. A run's final message says the chapter skill is now running. No tool call follows, and no chapter file exists in the run directory. Which cause does this evidence point to?
docs.text:
1. Premature turn termination: work described but not done
  2. Malformed tool call: an argument had the wrong type
  3. Context overflow: the conversation exceeded the model's window
  4. Harness misconfiguration: the skill folder was not mounted
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Premature turn termination is the model ending its turn before the work is done, with no error. Its signature is a final message that describes work and no file that contains it. Here the model announced the skill, made no tool call, and wrote nothing. A malformed call would show an error and usually a retry, context overflow shows late forgetting with a peak near the window, and a misconfiguration fails at turn one for every model.

Concept Tested: Premature Turn Termination

See: Premature Turn Termination and Task Loss

docs.title: 8. The cost model assumes the three benchmark stages are 10% of a whole book. If they are really 5%, how does the cost per textbook change, and why?
docs.text:
1. It halves, because fewer stages remain to be run
  2. It doubles, because the whole-book hours double
  3. It is unchanged, because the yearly cost is fixed
  4. It rises by 5%, matching the change in the share
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The cost per textbook is the whole-book hours times the cost of a generating hour. The whole-book hours come from dividing the measured three-stage time by the share of the book those stages represent. Halving that share from 10% to 5% doubles the whole-book hours, so the cost per book doubles, from about $53 to about $106 in the reference case. The yearly cost is fixed, but it is spread over half as many books.

Concept Tested: Cost per Textbook

See: Cost per Textbook, Cost per Chapter, and Books per Year

docs.title: 9. One model completes all three stages, the cost is estimated at $53 per book, and no human review has been finished. Which sufficiency statement is best supported by this evidence?
docs.text:
1. The DGX is sufficient, because one model finished every single stage
  2. The DGX is insufficient, because no human review has been completed
  3. The DGX is sufficient, because $53 is below any service price
  4. Completion is established, cost is estimated, quality is unknown
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A DGX sufficiency judgment answers whether this machine, with these models and this harness, is enough to generate the textbook. It is a judgment made against criteria written down beforehand: completion without an unusable fault, acceptable time and cost, and reviewed quality that meets the standard. The honest answer can be that the first is established, the second is estimated, and the third is not yet known. Declaring the machine sufficient or insufficient outright claims more than this evidence shows.

Concept Tested: DGX Sufficiency Judgment

See: DGX Sufficiency Judgment

docs.title: 10. Local models complete the learning-graph and chapter-structure stages, the chapter-text stage exposes capability differences, and every result is one run with no finished human review. Which recommendation design fits this evidence?
docs.text:
1. Local for every stage, stated as a final verdict
  2. Cloud for every stage, since one stage showed weakness
  3. A provisional hybrid routed by stage, with its conditions stated
  4. No recommendation until each model has been run five times
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A recommendation is the action the evidence supports, stated with its conditions. When local models complete the structural stages and a hard stage exposes differences, the rules lean toward a hybrid routed by stage: structural stages local, a stronger model for the prose. Because every result is one run and no human review is finished, the recommendation must be labeled provisional and say what would change it. A flat verdict or a refusal to recommend both serve the reader worse.

Concept Tested: Recommendation

See: Recommendation and the Local, Cloud, or Hybrid Decision

docs.title: References: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook
docs.text:
1. Root-cause analysis - Wikipedia - Defines root-cause analysis as finding the fundamental cause of a fault, with methods such as the five whys and fault trees and the difference between causes and causal factors. It underpins this chapter's failure diagnosis from run evidence.

  2. Total cost of ownership - Wikipedia - Explains total cost of ownership as an estimate of direct and indirect costs beyond purchase price, including hardware and staffing in IT, and its limitations. It supports this chapter's cost per textbook and the separate human review cost.

  3. Sensitivity analysis - Wikipedia - Describes how uncertainty in a model's output is divided among its inputs, including one-at-a-time variation. It applies to this chapter's whole-book time estimate, which doubles if the three stages are 5% of the book, not 10%.

  4. Debugging: The 9 Indispensable Rules for Finding Even the Most Elusive Software and Hardware Problems - David J. Agans - AMACOM - Organizes troubleshooting into nine rules, including Make It Fail, Divide and Conquer, and Check the Plug. It clarifies this chapter's habit of checking whether every model failed the same way before blaming a model.

  5. How to Measure Anything: Finding the Value of Intangibles in Business (3rd Edition) - Douglas W. Hubbard - Wiley - Shows how to turn an unmeasured quantity into a calibrated range, using 90% confidence intervals and the Rule of Five for small samples. It clarifies this chapter's separation of measured values from assumed ones in cost estimates.

  6. Effective Troubleshooting - Google SRE Book - Presents a hypothesis-driven troubleshooting method: report the problem, triage, examine logs and metrics, diagnose by simplifying and bisecting, then test and treat. It matches this chapter's evidence-first reading of event streams and server logs.

  7. Tool calling - Ollama Documentation - Shows how a model returns tool_calls that the client executes and answers with tool messages in a multi-turn loop. It shows the structured call that a text-emitted tool call fails to produce and a malformed one gets wrong.

  8. Context length - Ollama Documentation - Explains context length as the tokens a model can hold in memory, the VRAM-based defaults, the OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH setting, and checking allocation with ollama ps. It supports diagnosing this chapter's context overflow and task loss.

  9. Holistic Evaluation of Language Models - arXiv - Liang et al. evaluate 30 models across scenarios on seven metrics, including accuracy, robustness, and efficiency, and release raw prompts and completions. It models this chapter's reporting of several measurements side by side instead of one score.

  10. Prices and factors affecting prices - U.S. Energy Information Administration - Reports average U.S. retail electricity prices in cents per kilowatthour by sector and state, and the factors that drive them. It is a source for the electricity price used in this chapter's energy-per-textbook calculation.

docs.title: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
Summary
docs.text: This chapter makes the evaluation safe to share. Students catalog the details that make a device easier to find, reach, or log in to, redact probe reports, logs, and screenshots with placeholders, scan for secrets, and review every artifact before publication. They finish by publishing the capstone report with the sensitive details removed.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 28 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Git History Persistence 3 Sanitization 31 Device-Identifying Details 17 Redaction 8 Raw Output Isolation 2 Public Repository Risk 1 Keys and Tokens 6 IP Address 2 Hostname 2 Hardware Identifiers 2 Placeholder Conventions 2 Redacted-by-Default Fields 1 Tailnet Name 1 Usernames and Passwords 1 Access Configuration 1 Screenshot Redaction 1 Sanitized Sample Output 1 Gitignore Rules 1 Secret Scanning 5 Documentation Address Ranges 1 Hosts via Environment Variable 1 Identifiers in System Files 1 Pre-Commit Scan 3 Results Publishing 2 gitleaks 1 Publication Safety Review 2 Home Directory Paths 1 Capstone Evaluation 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Prerequisites and the Intelligent Textbook
  • Chapter 4: Local SLMs Versus Cloud LLM Services
  • Chapter 5: NVIDIA DGX Hardware Architecture
  • Chapter 7: Remote Access, SSH, and Mesh VPN Concepts
  • Chapter 9: Installing Tailscale and Taking a Read-Only Inventory
  • Chapter 10: Python Hardware Probes
  • Chapter 18: Containing the Harness: Containers and Network Boundaries
  • Chapter 19: Designing a Fair Evaluation
  • Chapter 21: Running the Textbook Benchmark
  • Chapter 22: Diagnosing Failures, Reporting, and Cost per Textbook

The Last Step Is the One You Cannot Undo

Everything in this course produces output that describes a real machine, and publishing it is the one step you cannot take back. By the end of this chapter you will have a routine that keeps the device's details out of anything you share, and a review that catches the ones that slip through. Measure first, then decide!

docs.title: What This Chapter Covers
docs.text:
An evaluation report is meant to be shared, and the raw material behind it is not safe to share. Probe reports, command output, logs, and screenshots all carry addresses, names, and identifiers that make the tested machine easier to find and reach. In an evaluation of a machine that belongs to someone else, a leak is not an embarrassment. It is harm done to a third party.

The chapter has three parts. First, a catalog of what must never be published, so that you know what you are looking for. Second, the methods that keep it out: placeholders, redaction, isolation of raw output, and rules about what the repository may contain. Third, the checks that catch what the methods miss: scans, and a review before publication. It closes with the capstone, which brings the whole course together into one published evaluation.

This chapter practices what it teaches. Every address, name, and identifier in it is a placeholder or from a range reserved for documentation, and none belongs to any real machine.

docs.title: Sanitization
docs.text: Sanitization is the process of removing or replacing the details in an artifact that could identify, locate, or give access to a device or a person, so that the artifact can be shared. It is a step in the pipeline, with its own checks, and not a final polish. The goal is stated in terms of the reader: after sanitization, someone who reads the artifact should learn how the evaluation was done and what it found, and nothing that makes the tested machine easier to find, reach, or log in to.

docs.title: Public Repository Risk
docs.text: Public repository risk is the exposure that comes from publishing a repository and its site. A public repository is readable by anyone, indexed by search engines, and scanned continuously by automated tools that look for credentials and addresses. Secrets committed to a public repository are often found and tried within minutes. A deployed documentation site is a second copy that is indexed in its own right.

docs.title: Device-Identifying Details
docs.text:
Device-identifying details are the facts that help a stranger find or reach a specific machine. The list for this course is fixed, and it appears in the project's own instructions so that every contributor, human or automated, reads the same rules.

Category Examples Why it matters Network addresses Tailnet addresses, public addresses, IPv6 addresses Tells a scanner where to look Names Hostnames, MagicDNS names, the tailnet's name Locates the machine and the network Accounts Usernames, passwords, passphrases The login itself, or half of it Keys and tokens SSH keys, Tailscale auth keys, model-hub tokens Access without a password Hardware identifiers Serial numbers, GPU unique identifiers, MAC addresses Identifies the physical unit Access configuration The access control policy, open ports, firewall rules Shows exactly how to get in Raw logs Unedited command output and run logs Contains any of the above, unpredictably

Each of the next sections takes one row that deserves a closer look.

docs.title: IP Address and Hostname
docs.text:
An IP address is the numeric network address of a machine, and a hostname is its name. Either one tells a stranger where to send a connection. A private address, such as one inside a home network, is less revealing than a public one and is still a detail of your network. A tailnet address, which begins 100., only works inside the tailnet, and it is still an identifier that should not be published, because it names a specific device in a specific network.

A hostname is often more informative than an address, since it can carry a purpose, a location, or an owner. The full name of a machine in a tailnet, <dgx-host>.<tailnet-name>.ts.net, combines the machine's name with the tailnet's, and so it names both.

docs.title: Tailnet Name
docs.text: The tailnet name is the identifier of the whole private network, and it forms the suffix of every machine's full name. It is easy to forget, because it appears only in full names and in the sign-in page. Revealing it is revealing the network that holds every machine in it.

docs.title: Usernames and Passwords
docs.text: Usernames and passwords are the account on the machine. Linux login names are case-sensitive and each one is a valid target. A password does not belong in any file, message, or screenshot at all. The same applies to a passphrase. The rule has no exception for "test" values that might be real.

docs.title: Keys and Tokens
docs.text: Keys and tokens are credentials that grant access without a password. An SSH private key is a login. A Tailscale auth key joins a machine to a network. A model-hub access token authorizes downloads and can authorize more. They are long random strings, easy to paste by accident in a command or an environment listing, and each has a recognizable shape that a scanner can find.

docs.title: Hardware Identifiers
docs.text: Hardware identifiers are values that identify a physical unit: serial numbers, GPU unique identifiers, and network card addresses. They are not secrets that give access, and they are identifying details that tie a document to one machine. A GPU's identifier is printed by a common nvidia-smi command, and a serial number is written in a system file on the machine.

docs.title: Access Configuration
docs.text: Access configuration is the description of how a machine can be reached: the tailnet's access control policy, the ports that are open, the firewall rules, and the SSH server's settings. It is the most useful single document to someone planning an attack, because it lists what is allowed. It is therefore never published, in whole or in part, for a real device.

docs.title: Identifiers in System Files
docs.text:
Identifiers in system files are the places a machine records who it is. The serial number sits in /etc/dgx-release. A unique machine identifier sits in /etc/machine-id. The list of hosts you have connected to is in ~/.ssh/known_hosts, and the commands you have run are in the shell history. A reader who copies any of these files, or a long command's output that includes them, copies the identifiers with it.

Read What You Captured Before You Keep It

A command that looks harmless can print an identifier on a line you did not expect, such as a serial number in a release file or a unique identifier in a listing. Treat every captured output as unsafe until you have read each line of it. Filter the known sources at capture time, for example with grep -v SERIAL, and then read it anyway.

docs.title: Home Directory Paths
docs.text: A home directory path is a file path that begins with a user's home directory, and it carries the username. A log of a run shows /home/<user>/... on every line that touches a file, so a single log excerpt can reveal an account name dozens of times. Replace the home directory with a placeholder, and prefer paths relative to the project root, which carry no account at all.

docs.title: Placeholder Conventions and Documentation Address Ranges
docs.text:
Placeholder conventions are the agreed replacement values that stand in for real details, used the same way everywhere so that a reader can follow an example and a scan can recognize a placeholder. The conventions in this book are the ones the project's own instructions set.

Real detail Placeholder A machine's name <dgx-host> A login name <user> An administrator's account <admin> The tailnet's name <tailnet-name>.ts.net A tailnet address 100.x.y.z A home directory <home> or a path relative to the project

Documentation address ranges are blocks of addresses reserved so that examples never point at a real machine. When an example needs an address that looks concrete, use one of them: 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, or 203.0.113.0/24 for IPv4, and 2001:db8::/32 for IPv6. A placeholder in angle brackets is clearer for a name, and a documentation range is clearer for an address that must still parse as one.

A rule of thumb for a placeholder is that it should be impossible to mistake for a real value. A fake value that looks real is worse than a placeholder, because someone will eventually try it, and because a scan cannot tell it from a leak.

docs.title: Redaction and Sanitized Sample Output
docs.text:
Redaction is replacing a detail in a specific artifact with a placeholder or removing it. It is what you do to a piece of captured output after the fact. Sanitized sample output is the result: an example of command output that shows the format and the meaning and none of the identifiers.

The example shows the transformation for a status listing. The raw version below is synthetic, with values from reserved ranges, and the sanitized version is what would go in the book.

# raw (synthetic)
198.51.100.31  example-host-01.example-tailnet.ts.net  exampleuser@  linux  active; direct 203.0.113.9:41641

# sanitized
100.x.y.z      <dgx-host>                          <admin>@  linux  active; direct 198.51.100.7:41641

Three things changed. The address became the placeholder, the full name became the machine placeholder, and the account name became the administrator placeholder. The remote endpoint was replaced with an address from a documentation range, because the placeholder form would not read as an address.

docs.title: Redacted-by-Default Fields
docs.text: Redacted-by-default fields are details a tool never collects unless explicitly asked, which is the strongest form of sanitization because nothing has to be removed afterward. The probe suite of Chapter 10 reads no hostname, no account name, no address, no serial number, and no GPU identifier, so its report cannot leak them. Where a tool must gather something sensitive, make the sensitive field opt-in and not opt-out.

docs.title: Screenshot Redaction
docs.text:
Screenshot redaction is removing identifying details from an image. A screenshot of a terminal or an admin console carries more than the lines you meant to show: window titles, tab names, the address bar of a browser, a prompt that includes the username and hostname, and a sidebar listing every other machine.

Three rules cover most of it. Crop first, to the smallest region that makes the point, so most of the window never enters the file. Cover with a solid fill, not a blur, because a blur can be partly reversed. And check the result at full size, including the edges, since a prompt line at the very bottom is easy to miss.

docs.title: Raw Output Isolation and Gitignore Rules
docs.text:
Raw output isolation is keeping unsanitized output in a place that is never published, so that nothing has to be removed from the repository because it never entered it. In this project, run output lives under a directory in the home folder, outside the repository, and model tests write to another. Only a script that copies selected, safe files can bring anything in.

Gitignore rules back that up. A .gitignore file lists patterns that git will refuse to add, so a careless git add . cannot pick up a log. The rules worth having for this kind of work are few.

*.log
*.jsonl
.env
id_*
*.pem
dgx-eval-runs/

A gitignore is a safety net and not a control. It does nothing for a file that is already tracked, and it will not stop an explicit git add -f.

docs.title: Hosts via Environment Variable
docs.text:
Hosts via environment variable is passing real machine addresses to scripts through the environment and not writing them in the script. This project's orchestration scripts read DGX_HOSTS, a space-separated list of login targets, so the real values exist only in the shell of the person running them, and the script in the repository contains <user>@<dgx-host>.

export DGX_HOSTS="<user>@<dgx-host-a> <user>@<dgx-host-b>"

The same technique handles the other direction. The script that publishes results takes a blocklist of real host names and logins from an environment variable, as a pattern, at run time, and refuses to copy any file that matches it. The real names are never stored in a file.

docs.title: Secret Scanning and gitleaks
docs.text:
Secret scanning is running a tool over files or history that looks for strings with the shape of a credential. gitleaks is an open-source scanner that does this for git repositories, with built-in rules for the common key and token formats. It can scan the working tree, the staged changes, or the whole history.

gitleaks detect --source . --redact

detect scans the repository, and --redact hides the matched secret in the report so that the report is not itself a leak. The subcommands have changed between versions, so check gitleaks --help for yours. A scanner finds credentials with a known shape. It does not find an IP address in a paragraph or a hostname in a caption, so it is one layer and not the whole defense.

docs.title: Pre-Commit Scan
docs.text:
A pre-commit scan checks the changes about to be committed and refuses the commit if it finds a detail that should not go in. It is the last cheap check before a mistake becomes history. The script below is a small, project-specific version. Each pattern is explained before it appears: the first matches an IPv4 address, the second a tailnet name, the third a private key header, the fourth a Tailscale auth key, the fifth a model-hub token, the sixth a home-directory path, and the last two a serial number line and a GPU identifier.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
patterns='([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}|[A-Za-z0-9-]+\.ts\.net|BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY|tskey-[A-Za-z0-9-]+|hf_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}|/home/[a-z_][a-z0-9_-]*|SERIAL=|GPU-[0-9a-f]{8}-'
allowed='192\.0\.2\.|198\.51\.100\.|203\.0\.113\.|100\.x\.y\.z|127\.0\.0\.1|0\.0\.0\.0'
hits=$(git diff --cached -U0 | grep -E '^\+' | grep -Ev '^\+\+\+' \
       | grep -E "$patterns" | grep -Ev "$allowed")
if [ -n "$hits" ]; then
  echo "Possible device details in staged changes:"; echo "$hits"; exit 1
fi

The script looks only at lines being added, and it allows the documentation ranges and the loopback address. A hit is a prompt to read the line, not proof of a leak: a version number can match the address pattern. It is placed in .git/hooks/pre-commit, or run by hand before every commit and before every publish.

Make the Scan Part of the Publish Command

A check you must remember to run will be skipped on the tired evening that matters most. Put the scan in the same script as git commit and the site deploy, so that publishing without it is not something you can do by accident.

docs.title: Git History Persistence
docs.text:
Git history persistence is the fact that a commit stays in a repository's history after a later commit removes its content. Deleting a leaked file in the next commit changes the latest version and leaves the leak in every earlier one, which anyone can read with git log -p. Every clone and fork made before the deletion keeps its own copy, and a deployed site is a separate copy again, with search engines holding their own.

The consequences set the order of operations.

  • Prevent, do not repair. The cheap time to catch a leak is before the commit.
  • If something sensitive has been committed, stop and tell the person responsible for the repository. Do not try to hide it with a quick follow-up commit.
  • Treat any leaked credential as compromised. Rotate it, because removing it from history does not un-expose it.
  • Rewriting history is a last resort. It is disruptive, it needs a force-push, and it still does not reach the copies made earlier.

docs.title: Results Publishing
docs.text:
Results publishing is the controlled path by which evaluation results enter the book. In this project it is one script that rebuilds the results pages from fetched run output. It copies only three kinds of file: a model's learning graph, its chapter text, and the course description. It leaves out any file that holds an address, a host name, or a home-directory path, and it counts what it removed so the omission is visible.

The design is the one this chapter argues for. A narrow, automated path with a blocklist beats a broad copy followed by cleaning, because it fails closed: a file it does not recognize is left out.

docs.title: Publication Safety Review
docs.text:
A publication safety review is a final read of everything about to be published, by a person, against the catalog of what must not leave. It is the check that does not depend on a pattern. A reviewer reads for the things scanners miss: a hostname in a caption, a screenshot with a visible title bar, a number that is a serial number in disguise, and a description that, taken together, identifies the machine.

The review is a checklist, and the items are short.

  1. The diff has been read line by line, and not skimmed.
  2. Every address, name, and identifier is a placeholder or from a documentation range.
  3. No file under a raw-output location has been added.
  4. The scan and the secret scanner have both been run, and every hit has been explained.
  5. Every screenshot has been cropped, covered, and checked at full size.
  6. Nothing describes the access configuration of the real device.
  7. A second person has read the changes, if there is one.

docs.title: Diagram: Redaction Reviewer
docs.text:
Run Redaction Reviewer Fullscreen

Redaction Reviewer

Type: microsim sim-id: redaction-reviewer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge each of 10 lines of captured output as safe to publish or in need of redaction, and name the category of any detail to redact, with at least 9 of 10 correct.

Prerequisites: device-identifying details, IP address, hostname, tailnet name, hardware identifiers, keys and tokens, home directory path, placeholder conventions, documentation address ranges (all defined in the sections above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 10 lines the learner commits "Safe to publish" or "Redact" and, for "Redact", one category from the five listed, before the sim reveals the answer. A line is correct when the decision equals the Correct decision column and, for "Redact", the category equals the Correct category column. Mastery is 9 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the lines is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A private address is not identifying. (2) A serial number or unique identifier is harmless because it grants no access. (3) A line already shown in a tutorial is safe. (4) Placeholders and documentation ranges still need redacting.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level judging needs the learner to apply the catalog of details to each line and to leave alone what is safe, so the lines mix four kinds of identifier with six safe lines, and include a line that is already a placeholder.

Content:

The five categories the learner chooses from: "Network address", "Name or tailnet", "Hardware identifier", "Account or home path", and "Key or token".

# Line shown to the learner Correct decision Correct category Why (shown as feedback) 1 Architecture: aarch64 Safe to publish None It describes the processor type and identifies no unit. 2 inet 198.51.100.24/24 brd 198.51.100.255 scope global eth0 Redact Network address An interface address places the machine on a network. 3 Hostname: example-host-01.example-tailnet.ts.net Redact Name or tailnet The full name carries both the machine's and the tailnet's name. 4 SERIAL=EXAMPLE-0000-0000 Redact Hardware identifier A serial number ties the output to one physical unit. 5 GPU 0: NVIDIA GB10 (UUID: GPU-00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000) Redact Hardware identifier The unique identifier of a GPU identifies that unit. 6 Driver Version: 580.xx.xx CUDA Version: 13.0 Safe to publish None Version numbers describe the software, not a specific machine. 7 /home/exampleuser/dgx-eval-runs/s1-model/run.jsonl Redact Account or home path The path contains an account name. 8 export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Redact Key or token A model-hub token authorizes access to an account. 9 MemAvailable: 104857600 kB Safe to publish None It is a memory figure and identifies no unit. 10 100.x.y.z <dgx-host> <admin>@ linux active; direct Safe to publish None Every identifying value is already a placeholder.

Provenance: The lines are synthetic, written for this exercise, with addresses from the documentation ranges and obviously inert names, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The categories come from this chapter's catalog.

Rules: Lines are shown in the fixed order 1 to 10. A line is "Redact" if it contains any value from the five categories that is not already a placeholder or a documentation-range address presented as an example. Each line has exactly one category or none.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads line 1.
  2. The learner chooses "Safe to publish" or "Redact", and for "Redact" one of the five categories, then confirms.
  3. The sim shows the correct decision and category with the Why text, and marks the line correct or incorrect.
  4. The learner repeats for lines 2 to 10. After line 10 the sim shows the score and the misconception behind each miss.

Feedback: Ten lines, fixed order, one confirmed decision each, no second attempt. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct decision, category, and the Why text. The final score reads "n of 10 correct".

Starting State: Line 1 is shown with no decision made, and the question on screen is "Is this line safe to publish?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the seven categories of detail that must not be published, that a serial number and a GPU identifier are hardware identifiers, that a home path carries an account name, and that a value already replaced by a placeholder is safe.

docs.title: Capstone Evaluation
docs.text:
The capstone evaluation is the course's final project: a complete, objective evaluation of a DGX system, published. It uses every chapter, and it is the only way to know that the pieces fit together. It is also, by design, a project in which sanitization is a graded step and not an afterthought.

The steps follow the order of the book, and each names the chapter that taught it.

  1. Reach the machine. Join the tailnet, prove the connection at three layers, and log in without a password (Chapters 7 and 9).
  2. Probe the hardware. Run the probe suite and produce a report with identifying fields left out by default (Chapters 5 and 10).
  3. Choose and install a model. Compute the fit, select and download a model, and put it behind a local endpoint that only you can reach (Chapters 11 to 13).
  4. Connect and contain the harness. Install the skills, point a harness at the endpoint, run it in a container, and start the watchdog and the vitals log (Chapters 16 to 18).
  5. Design the experiment. State the question, the variable, the controls, and the metrics before running anything (Chapter 19).
  6. Run and score. Run each stage from a fixed template, apply the checks, and calibrate them (Chapters 20 and 21).
  7. Diagnose, cost, and decide. Explain each failure, compute cost per textbook, compare with a baseline, and write the report (Chapter 22).
  8. Sanitize and publish. Redact, scan, review, and publish only what passes (this chapter).

The capstone is finished when the report is public and the review has found nothing in it that makes the machine easier to find, reach, or log in to.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Sanitization removes or replaces every detail that could identify, locate, or give access to a device: addresses, names, the tailnet's name, accounts, keys and tokens, hardware identifiers, and access configuration, along with the raw logs and system files that contain them. Placeholders and documentation address ranges replace them in examples, tools collect identifying fields only on request, screenshots are cropped and covered with solid fills, and raw output lives outside the repository. A gitignore, an environment variable for hosts, a narrow publishing script, a secret scanner such as gitleaks, and a pre-commit scan each catch a different kind of slip, and a person's review catches what patterns cannot. Because git history persists, prevention is the only real remedy, and a credential that has leaked is rotated and not merely deleted.

A Report You Can Publish Without Looking Over Your Shoulder

You can now catalog the details that make a machine easier to reach, keep them out with placeholders, redaction, isolation, and scans, and review an artifact before it goes public. That completes the course: you can probe a DGX, run a textbook benchmark on it, decide what the results mean, and share them safely. Measure first, then decide!

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
docs.text: Test your understanding of device-identifying details, placeholders and redaction, scanning, git history, and the publication safety review with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is the goal of sanitization, stated in terms of the reader?
docs.text:
1. The reader learns the method and findings, not how to reach the machine
  2. The reader can reproduce the run on the same physical machine
  3. The reader sees every raw log in full, with only the passwords taken out
  4. The reader can verify each result by logging in to the device
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Sanitization is the process of removing or replacing the details in an artifact that could identify, locate, or give access to a device or a person, so the artifact can be shared. The goal is stated in terms of the reader: someone who reads the artifact should learn how the evaluation was done and what it found, and nothing that makes the tested machine easier to find, reach, or log in to. It is a pipeline step with its own checks, not a final polish.

Concept Tested: Sanitization

See: Sanitization

docs.title: 2. What are documentation address ranges?
docs.text:
1. Addresses that a tailnet assigns to its member devices
  2. Addresses that home routers give to devices behind them
  3. Addresses that a scanner skips when it reads a repository
  4. Addresses reserved so that examples never point at a real machine
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Documentation address ranges are blocks of addresses reserved so that examples never point at a real machine. When an example needs an address that looks concrete, use one of them, such as 192.0.2.0/24 or 198.51.100.0/24. A placeholder in angle brackets is clearer for a name, and a documentation range is clearer for an address that must still parse as one. A fake value that looks real is worse, because someone will eventually try it and a scan cannot tell it from a leak.

Concept Tested: Documentation Address Ranges

See: Placeholder Conventions and Documentation Address Ranges

docs.title: 3. Why must a serial number be redacted even though it grants no access?
docs.text:
1. It can be used in place of a password at the SSH login prompt
  2. It identifies the physical unit and ties the document to it
  3. It reveals which ports are open on the machine's firewall
  4. It lets a stranger join the tailnet without needing an invitation
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Hardware identifiers are values that identify a physical unit: serial numbers, GPU unique identifiers, and network card addresses. They are not secrets that give access, but they are identifying details that tie a document to one machine. A serial number sits in a system file on the machine, and a GPU's identifier is printed by a common command, so both slip into captured output easily. Open ports and firewall rules are a different category, access configuration.

Concept Tested: Hardware Identifiers

See: Hardware Identifiers

docs.title: 4. Why does this project keep raw run output in a directory outside the repository?
docs.text:
1. Nothing has to be removed, because it never entered the repository
  2. The repository has a size limit that run logs would exceed
  3. Git cannot store files that are written in JSON lines format
  4. The logs must stay on the DGX so that the Administrator can read them
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Raw output isolation is keeping unsanitized output in a place that is never published, so that nothing has to be removed from the repository because it never entered it. In this project, run output lives under a directory in the home folder, outside the repository, and only a script that copies selected, safe files can bring anything in. This matters because git history persists: a file that was committed once stays readable in earlier commits.

Concept Tested: Raw Output Isolation

See: Raw Output Isolation and Gitignore Rules

docs.title: 5. You are sanitizing a status line that shows a tailnet address, the machine's full name, the administrator's account, and a remote endpoint that must still read as an address. Which replacements follow the book's conventions?
docs.text:
1. Invented values that look realistic, for all four of the fields
  2. 100.x.y.z, <dgx-host>, <admin>, and a documentation-range address
  3. A blur over all four fields in a screenshot of the terminal
  4. The real tailnet address, since it works only from inside the tailnet itself
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Redaction replaces a detail in a specific artifact with a placeholder or removes it. Following the conventions, the tailnet address becomes 100.x.y.z, the full name becomes <dgx-host>, and the administrator's account becomes <admin>. The remote endpoint takes an address from a documentation range, because a placeholder there would not read as an address. Invented realistic values are worse than placeholders, and a tailnet address still names a specific device in a specific network.

Concept Tested: Redaction

See: Redaction and Sanitized Sample Output

docs.title: 6. You need a screenshot of a terminal for the report. Which steps should you follow?
docs.text:
1. Crop first, cover with a solid fill, then check at full size
  2. Blur the prompt, then shrink the image so that details are small
  3. Keep the full window, and cover only the password line
  4. Capture the whole screen, and rely on the secret scanner
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Screenshot redaction removes identifying details from an image, which carries more than the lines you meant to show: window titles, tab names, and a prompt with the username and hostname. Three rules cover most of it. Crop first, to the smallest region that makes the point. Cover with a solid fill, not a blur, because a blur can be partly reversed. And check the result at full size, including the edges, where a prompt line is easy to miss.

Concept Tested: Screenshot Redaction

See: Screenshot Redaction

docs.title: 7. A repository passes a gitleaks scan with no findings, yet a figure caption in a chapter contains the machine's hostname. Why did the scanner miss it?
docs.text:
1. The scanner reads only the files listed in .gitignore
  2. The --redact flag removed the hostname from the report
  3. The scanner checks only the commits older than the current one
  4. A hostname in prose has no credential shape for it to match
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Secret scanning runs a tool over files or history that looks for strings with the shape of a credential, and gitleaks has built-in rules for the common key and token formats. A scanner finds credentials with a known shape. It does not find an IP address in a paragraph or a hostname in a caption, so it is one layer and not the whole defense. A person's publication safety review exists to catch what patterns cannot.

Concept Tested: Secret Scanning

See: Secret Scanning and gitleaks

docs.title: 8. A log file was committed last week. Today you add *.log to .gitignore, but git still tracks the file and its changes. Why?
docs.text:
1. The pattern must list each log file by its full name
  2. The .gitignore file applies only to the deployed site
  3. A gitignore does nothing for a file that is already tracked
  4. The pre-commit scan re-adds any files that match its patterns
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Gitignore rules list patterns that git will refuse to add, so a careless git add . cannot pick up a log. A gitignore is a safety net and not a control. It does nothing for a file that is already tracked, and it will not stop an explicit git add -f. The committed log also remains in the repository's history, so adding the pattern afterward neither untracks the file nor removes what was already recorded.

Concept Tested: Gitignore Rules

See: Raw Output Isolation and Gitignore Rules

docs.title: 9. A log excerpt has had every hostname and address replaced, yet it still reveals an account name on dozens of lines. Where is the name coming from?
docs.text:
1. The model tag that appears on each line of the run log
  2. The documentation-range addresses left in the excerpt
  3. The version numbers of the driver and the server
  4. The home directory paths on lines that touch a file
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A home directory path is a file path that begins with a user's home directory, and it carries the username. A run log shows /home/<user>/... on every line that touches a file, so a single excerpt can reveal an account name dozens of times even after hostnames and addresses are gone. Replace the home directory with a placeholder, or prefer paths relative to the project root, which carry no account at all.

Concept Tested: Home Directory Paths

See: Home Directory Paths

docs.title: 10. An access token was committed and pushed to the public repository an hour ago. Which response is best justified?
docs.text:
1. Delete the file in a new commit and push it at once
  2. Rewrite history with a force-push and tell no one
  3. Stop, tell the repository's owner, and rotate the token
  4. Add the file's pattern to .gitignore and carry on
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Git history persistence means a commit stays in history after a later commit removes its content, and clones, forks, and the deployed site keep their own copies. So the order of operations is fixed: stop and tell the person responsible for the repository, and do not try to hide the leak with a quick follow-up commit. Treat the credential as compromised and rotate it, because removing it from history does not un-expose it. Rewriting history is a last resort.

Concept Tested: Git History Persistence

See: Git History Persistence

docs.title: References: Sanitizing Evaluation Artifacts and Publishing the Report
docs.text:
1. Redaction - Wikipedia - Covers removing sensitive information from documents, with failures such as text left under black boxes in PDFs and data kept in revision history. It supports this chapter's cropping, solid fills, and review of redacted artifacts.

  2. List of reserved IP addresses - Wikipedia - Tabulates IPv4 and IPv6 blocks set aside for special uses, including the documentation ranges 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, and 2001:db8::/32. It lists the safe example addresses this chapter uses in place of real ones.

  3. Data loss prevention software - Wikipedia - Describes tools that detect and block unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data, including content-aware detection and the problem of false positives. It frames this chapter's pre-commit scan, whose hits need human reading.

  4. Threat Modeling: Designing for Security (1st Edition) - Adam Shostack - Wiley - Introduces a four-question framework for threat modeling: what are you building, what can go wrong, what should you do about it, and did you do a decent job of analysis. It maps onto this chapter's catalog, methods, and review.

  5. Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Scott Chacon and Ben Straub - Apress - Widely praised for explaining Git as a set of snapshots stored as linked objects, with a chapter on internals. It clarifies why this chapter's leaked file stays in history after a later commit deletes it.

  6. Gitleaks - GitHub - README for the open-source scanner that finds passwords, API keys, and tokens, with git, dir, and stdin scan modes, a pre-commit hook, and --redact. It documents the secret scanner this chapter names, and the newer commands replacing detect.

  7. Removing sensitive data from a repository - GitHub Docs - Explains rewriting history with git-filter-repo, its side effects on forks and cached views, and the advice to treat exposed credentials as compromised and revoke or rotate them. It supports this chapter's git history persistence rules.

  8. githooks - Git Documentation - Reference for Git hooks, including pre-commit, which runs before a commit is created and aborts it on a non-zero exit, and the --no-verify bypass. It documents the mechanism behind this chapter's pre-commit scan script.

  9. Secrets Management Cheat Sheet - OWASP Cheat Sheet Series - Covers keeping secrets out of code and logs, rotation and revocation, detecting secrets with pre-commit checks, and responding when one is exposed. It supports this chapter's rules for keys and tokens.

  10. Tailnet names and types - Tailscale Documentation - Explains the tailnet DNS name ending in .ts.net, the per-device machine name, and the tailnet ID. It shows why this chapter treats the tailnet name and hostnames as device-identifying details to replace with placeholders.

docs.title: Why This Mascot
docs.text: A robot suits a book about machines, and a measurement-focused one reinforces the book's stance of answering questions with measurements instead of opinions. The name echoes tera, the prefix behind terabytes and tera-operations, and the tool belt of benchmarking instruments gives every pose a visual tie to the evaluation work. Animal mascots were considered and rejected as too common and too cute for a professional audience.

docs.title: Learning Graph for DGX Evaluation for Textbook Generation
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

You can explore the finished graph in the interactive Learning Graph Viewer. It has 506 concepts, 824 dependencies, and 14 categories.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 12 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MOSC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Concept List
docs.text:
The numbered concepts below are the nodes of the learning graph for DGX Evaluation for Textbook Generation. Each number is the ConceptID used in learning-graph.csv. Most sections follow the 16 topics in the course description. Three sections hold concepts taken from the book's own pages: Prerequisite Skills, Candidate Models Under Evaluation, and Testing Architecture and Containment.

The course is DGX-model-agnostic, so the hardware concepts list both branches of each variation (CPU architecture and memory layout) and not the specifications of any one DGX model.

docs.title: Course Description Assessment
docs.text:
Course: DGX Evaluation for Textbook Generation

Assessed file: docs/course-description.md

Skill: Course Description Analyzer, version 0.04

Date: 2026-10-09

docs.title: Overall Score
docs.text:
100 / 100 — Excellent. Ready for learning graph generation.

The description was written against this rubric in the same session, so a full score is expected and says only that every required element is present. The open decisions listed under Gap Analysis are not measured by the rubric and matter more than the score.

docs.title: Detailed Scoring Breakdown
docs.text: Element Points Earned Notes Title 5 5 Matches site_name in mkdocs.yml. Target Audience 5 5 Professional development, with four named roles. Prerequisites 5 5 Five items, including an explicit "not required" statement. Main Topics Covered 10 10 16 topics, each with its sub-topics spelled out. Topics Excluded 5 5 10 exclusions, each with a one-line reason. Learning Outcomes Header 5 5 "After completing this course, students will be able to:" Remember 10 10 9 outcomes. Understand 10 10 9 outcomes. Apply 10 10 9 outcomes. Analyze 10 10 7 outcomes. Evaluate 10 10 7 outcomes. Create 10 10 6 outcomes plus a capstone project. Descriptive Context 5 5 Five-paragraph overview plus a software-stack table. Total 100 100

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
No rubric element scored below full points.

Decided: the course is DGX-model-agnostic. The author confirmed on 2026-10-09 that no specific DGX model is named. The description states this in the overview and in the hardware topic. The consequence for downstream content is that the conda, probe, and model-fit chapters must cover both x86_64 and aarch64 CPUs and both dedicated GPU memory and unified memory, with the probe report deciding which branch a reader follows.

Added: sanitization before publication. On 2026-10-09 the author asked for a sanitization topic, because the book is public and the tested DGX is a real machine. Topic 16 and one outcome at each of the Remember, Understand, Apply, and Evaluate levels cover it. The probe-suite outcome now redacts identifying fields by default, and the capstone sanitizes every artifact before publishing.

Three decisions are still open. None of them blocks concept enumeration, but each one changes specific chapters.

  1. The model and harness lists are candidates, not selections. The software-stack table names model families and four agent harnesses as examples. Whether each harness loads the ibook-skills skills unmodified against a local endpoint has not been tested and is itself part of the evaluation.
  2. The cloud baseline is not fixed. Four cloud services are named for the pros-and-cons discussion. The benchmark needs one specific model and harness as the quality reference.
  3. The benchmark book is not chosen. The capstone generates "a small intelligent textbook". The subject and size of that book determine run time and cost per chapter.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
Listed in order of impact on downstream content.

  1. Pick the cloud baseline (one model, one harness) and add it to the Objective evaluation methodology topic.
  2. Choose the benchmark book and record its subject, target concept count, and chapter count.
  3. After the first probe run, replace the model-family examples with the shortlisted models that fit the measured GPU memory.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
1. Have a person review the questions. The 91/100 score is mechanical. After generation, 48 of the 230 questions were read against the chapter text: all of chapters 11, 14, 22, and 23, and the numeric questions in chapters 6, 15, and 21. Every figure in them matched its chapter. The other 182 questions passed the format checks and were not read a second time.
  2. Concept coverage is below the 75% target. Ten questions cover 36% to 62% of a chapter's concepts, and 230 of the book's 506 concepts (45%) have a question. An average chapter has 22 concepts, so reaching 75% would take about 17 questions per chapter. A second question set per chapter is the direct fix.

docs.title: What the Columns Mean

• Written. The chapter's placeholder is gone and it has at least 1,000 words. A chapter marked No is still the outline from stage 2.

docs.title: Algebra I
docs.text: Course Title: Algebra I Target Audience: Junior High or High School Students (Grades 8–10) Prerequisites: Successful completion of Pre-Algebra or equivalent foundational mathematics course, including proficiency in arithmetic operations, fractions, decimals, ratios, and basic geometry.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
Algebra I is a foundational mathematics course designed to transition students from arithmetic reasoning to abstract algebraic thinking. This course introduces variables, functions, and relationships among quantities, emphasizing the ability to represent real-world situations using mathematical models. Students will develop fluency in manipulating algebraic expressions, solving equations and inequalities, analyzing patterns, and interpreting data.

Algebra I serves as the gateway to higher-level mathematics such as Geometry, Algebra II, Trigonometry, and Calculus. Students will explore both symbolic and graphical representations of relationships and will use technology and reasoning to analyze linear, quadratic, and exponential functions. The course encourages mathematical communication, critical thinking, and problem-solving, aligning with the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (CCSSM) and the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) recommendations.

docs.title: Intended Audience
docs.text: This course is intended for students who are beginning formal study in algebra, typically in Grades 8 through 10. It provides essential preparation for college- and career-readiness by building the quantitative reasoning skills required in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) disciplines.

docs.title: 1. Algebra Foundations
docs.text:
• Properties of operations and order of operations
  • Writing, expanding, and factoring algebraic expressions
  • Evaluating expressions with variables and exponents

docs.title: 2. Exponents and Radicals
docs.text:
• Integer and rational exponents
  • Laws of exponents
  • Simplifying and interpreting exponential expressions

docs.title: 3. Linear Equations and Inequalities
docs.text:
• Solving one-step, two-step, and multi-step equations
  • Literal equations and formulas
  • Solving and graphing linear inequalities and absolute value equations

docs.title: 4. Functions and Relations
docs.text:
• Understanding the function concept
  • Function notation, domain, and range
  • Interpreting graphs and tables
  • Piecewise and step functions

docs.title: 5. Linear Relationships
docs.text:
• Slope and rate of change
  • Writing linear equations in multiple forms (slope-intercept, point-slope, standard)
  • Graphing lines and modeling linear relationships
  • Solving and interpreting systems of linear equations and inequalities

docs.title: 6. Polynomials and Factoring
docs.text:
• Adding, subtracting, and multiplying polynomials
  • Factoring by GCF, trinomials, and difference of squares
  • Using factoring to solve quadratic equations

docs.title: 7. Quadratic and Exponential Functions
docs.text:
• Graphing quadratic functions and identifying vertex and axis of symmetry
  • Solving quadratics by factoring, square roots, completing the square, and the quadratic formula
  • Modeling real-world data using quadratic and exponential functions

docs.title: 8. Statistics and Data Analysis
docs.text:
• Creating and interpreting data displays and scatterplots
  • Analyzing correlation and line of best fit
  • Comparing linear and exponential models
  • Arithmetic and geometric sequences

docs.title: Concepts Not Included
docs.text:
• Calculus
  • Integrals
  • Derivatives

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: After this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remembering
docs.text:
• Recall and apply key algebraic properties (commutative, associative, distributive)
  • Identify the components of expressions, equations, and inequalities
  • Recognize linear, quadratic, and exponential forms

docs.title: Understanding
docs.text:
• Explain the meaning of variables, constants, coefficients, and exponents
  • Describe relationships between graphical, tabular, and symbolic representations
  • Interpret slope and intercepts in context of real-world problems

docs.title: Applying
docs.text:
• Solve linear, quadratic, and exponential equations using multiple methods
  • Model real-world problems with algebraic equations and functions
  • Apply rules of exponents and factoring in simplifying expressions

docs.title: Analyzing
docs.text:
• Compare characteristics of linear, quadratic, and exponential functions
  • Decompose complex expressions into simpler components
  • Analyze the effects of changing parameters on graphs of functions

docs.title: Evaluating
docs.text:
• Justify solutions to equations and systems through substitution and verification
  • Evaluate the appropriateness of mathematical models in context
  • Critically assess data to determine correlation and causation

docs.title: Creating
docs.text:
• Construct new equations or inequalities to represent unfamiliar problems
  • Design and interpret linear and quadratic models from real data
  • Integrate algebraic methods to solve multi-step, multi-concept problems

docs.title: Alignment to Common Core Domains
docs.text: Domain Description A-SSE (Seeing Structure in Expressions) Interpret, simplify, and factor expressions A-APR (Arithmetic with Polynomials) Perform operations on polynomials A-CED (Creating Equations) Create and solve equations and inequalities to model real situations A-REI (Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities) Understand and solve equations and systems logically F-IF (Interpreting Functions) Understand functions and their representations F-BF (Building Functions) Write, transform, and compose functions F-LE (Linear, Quadratic, and Exponential Models) Model growth and decay phenomena S-ID (Statistics and Probability) Analyze data using scatterplots, correlation, and regression

docs.title: Course Outcomes Summary
docs.text:
By the end of Algebra I, students will be able to:

  • Translate real-world scenarios into algebraic representations.
  • Use graphs, tables, and equations to model and analyze data.
  • Solve and interpret linear, quadratic, and exponential equations and inequalities.
  • Reason quantitatively, verify solutions, and communicate mathematical thinking clearly.
  • Build confidence and curiosity for further study in mathematics and STEM disciplines.

Standards Alignment: Aligned with the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (CCSSM), High School Algebra and Functions Domains.
