docs.title: Content
docs.text: Before we begin graphing, let's define two foundational terms that will appear throughout this chapter: coordinate an ordered pair (x, y) that specifies a location on a plane, and scatterplot a graph that displays the relationship between two quantitative variables by plotting ordered pairs as points. Understanding these basics will help us make sense of the more complex ideas ahead.

docs.title: 1. Create Scatterplot
docs.text:
[Tier A: E(c) = 0.558, Target: 500-750 words, Required: worked example + diagram/chart]

Imagine you have collected data on students' study hours and their quiz scores. You suspect there might be a relationship — perhaps more study leads to higher scores. To visualize this, you would plot each student's (study_hours, quiz_score) as a point on a coordinate plane. The collection of all such points forms a scatterplot.

Worked Example: Suppose we have the following data for 5 students:

Student Study Hours (x) Quiz Score (y) Alice 2 65 Bob 4 75 Carol 6 85 Dave 8 90 Eve 10 95

To create a scatterplot, we plot each (x, y) pair: Alice at (2, 65), Bob at (4, 75), and so on. Using graph paper or software, we mark each point. Looking at the pattern, we see that as study hours increase, quiz scores tend to increase as well — this suggests a positive association.

Before we examine the scatterplot diagram below, let's recall: a scatterplot displays the relationship between two quantitative variables. Each point represents one observation's values on both variables. The overall pattern (form, direction, strength) helps us understand whether and how the variables are related.

docs.title: Diagram: Scatterplot of Study Hours vs. Quiz Scores
docs.text:
Scatterplot: Study Hours vs. Quiz Scores

![Scatterplot showing positive association between study hours and quiz scores]{ class="mascot-admonition-img" }

The scatterplot above displays 5 data points: (2, 65), (4, 75), (6, 85), (8, 90), and (10, 95). We can see a clear upward trend — as study hours increase, quiz scores tend to increase. This positive association suggests that more study time is related to higher quiz scores.

Key observation: The points roughly follow a linear pattern, indicating a linear relationship between study hours and quiz scores. The strength appears moderate to strong, as the points are fairly close to an imaginary straight line through them.

MicroSim Specification:

Create Scatterplot Interactive Simulation

Type: microsim Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Create Bloom Verb: create Learning Objective: The learner will create a scatterplot given a set of bivariate data, plotting each (x, y) point accurately on a coordinate plane.

Prerequisites: Coordinate pairs (x, y), horizontal axis (x-axis), vertical axis (y-axis), scale and units

Evidence of Mastery: The learner accurately plots at least 8 out of 10 given (x, y) points on a coordinate plane, with each point positioned at the correct horizontal and vertical position.

Misconceptions: Confusing the x- and y-coordinates; plotting points by counting total distance from origin rather than horizontal then vertical distance; assuming any pattern in a scatterplot implies causation.

Instructional Rationale: Creating scatterplots requires the learner to transform tabular data into a visual representation, integrating knowledge of coordinate systems with the ability to recognize patterns in bivariate data. This hands-on construction builds deeper understanding than simply viewing a pre-made graph.

Content: The learner is given a table of 10 (x, y) values ranging from (1, 2) to (10, 18). They must plot each point on a blank coordinate grid with axes labeled and scaled from 0 to 11. After plotting, they verify their work by checking that each point's horizontal position matches its x-value and vertical position matches its y-value.

Provenance: Example adapted from Illustrative Mathematics, Algebra I, Unit 1, Lesson 1; synthetic data with seed 2026-AlgebraI-CH4.

Rules: - Each point's x-coordinate determines horizontal position: position_x = x * step_size + origin_x - Each point's y-coordinate determines vertical position: position_y = -y * step_size + origin_y (negative because screen y increases downward) - Default step size: 40 pixels per unit; origin at center (200, 200) - Adjustable parameters: num_points (2-20, step 2), x_range (2-20, step 2), y_range (2-20, step 2) - Default values: num_points = 5, x_range = 10, y_range = 18 - Tie-break: If two points have the same coordinates, display them slightly offset with a small gap

Learner Activity: 1. Enter 10 (x, y) points from a given table into the simulation 2. Click "Plot Points" to display each point on the coordinate grid 3. Use the "Check Answers" button to see which points are correct and which need adjustment 4. Notice the overall pattern/cluster/direction of the plotted points 5. Adjust the point positions until all 10 are in the correct locations

Feedback: - After each attempt, the learner receives immediate feedback: "Correct!" if all points are within ±1 pixel of the target position, or "Check the position of point #3 — it's too far left/right/up/down." if any point is incorrect. Correct answers are revealed after 3 attempts.

Starting State: The learner sees a blank coordinate grid with axes labeled "Study Hours" (x) and "Quiz Score" (y), ranging from 0 to 11 and 0 to 20 respectively. A table of 5 (x, y) values is shown, with the first value (1, 2) highlighted. The question posed: "Plot the first point (1, 2) on the grid."

Chapter Anchors: - The chapter states that "scatterplots display the relationship between two quantitative variables" - "A positive association means both variables tend to increase together" - "Looking at the overall pattern (form, direction, strength) helps us understand the relationship" - The scatterplot MicroSim will demonstrate these properties with the study hours/quiz scores data

Now let's look at the scatterplot diagram more closely. The diagram above shows the 5 points from our worked example. Notice how they form an upward-left-to-downward-right pattern, indicating a positive association. The x-axis represents study hours (2, 4, 6, 8, 10) and the y-axis represents quiz scores (65, 75, 85, 90, 95).

docs.title: Comparing Linear and Exponential Models for Scatterplot Data
docs.text:
When a scatterplot shows a linear pattern, we often want to fit a line through the points to make predictions. This is called the line of best fit (or trend line). For the study hours/quiz scores data, the line of best fit might have equation ŷ = 5x + 55, where ŷ is the predicted quiz score and x is study hours.

If the data shows a curve rather than a straight line, we might use an exponential model instead, such as y = a ⋅ bˣ. For example, population growth or compound interest often follows an exponential pattern.

Before we examine the comparison table below, let's recall: a linear model has constant rate of change (same increase in y for each unit increase in x), while an exponential model has constant percent rate of change (y multiplies by same factor for each unit increase in x).

Model Type Equation Form Rate of Change When It's Used Linear y = mx + b Constant: m units of y per 1 unit of x Relationship appears as straight line in scatterplot Exponential y = a ⋅ bˣ Constant factor: b multiplier per 1 unit of x Relationship appears as curve in scatterplot; y changes by constant percentage

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at the sequences concepts, which deal with ordered lists of numbers following specific patterns.

docs.title: 2. Interpret Scatterplot
docs.text:
[Tier B: E(c) = 0.471, Target: 250-400 words, Required: worked example]

A scatterplot helps us see patterns in bivariate data. When we look at a scatterplot, we ask three main questions:

  1. Form: Is the pattern linear (straight), curved, circular, or something else?
  2. Direction: Does y tend to increase (positive association), decrease (negative association), or show no clear pattern as x increases?
  3. Strength: Do the points cluster closely around a pattern (strong), or are they widely scattered (weak)?

Worked Example: Consider this scatterplot description: "The points form a rough upward-slanting cloud, with higher y-values tend accompanying higher x-values. The points are somewhat close to an imaginary straight line through them."

Interpretation: This scatterplot shows a positive association with linear form and moderate strength. As the x-variable increases, the y-variable tends to increase as well. The moderate strength means the points follow the general trend but with some variation.

Bridge sentence: Let's now look at correlation coefficient, which quantifies the strength and direction of a linear association.

docs.title: 3. Correlation Coefficient
docs.text:
[Tier B: E(c) = 0.373, Target: 250-400 words, Required: worked example]

The correlation coefficient (denoted r) is a number between -1 and 1 that measures the strength and direction of a linear association between two quantitative variables. The value of r tells us:

  • r > 0: Positive association — as x increases, y tends to increase
  • r < 0: Negative association — as x increases, y tends to decrease
  • r close to 1: Strong positive linear relationship
  • r close to -1: Strong negative linear relationship
  • r close to 0: Little or no linear relationship

Worked Example: Suppose we compute the correlation coefficient for the study hours/quiz scores data and get r = 0.88. This means:

  • There is a strong positive linear association between study hours and quiz scores
  • About 77% of the variation in quiz scores (r² = 0.88² ≈ 0.77) can be attributed to variation in study hours (this quantity r² is called the coefficient of determination)
  • The remaining 23% of the variation is due to other factors not captured by study hours alone

Bridge sentence: Now let's examine the line of best fit, which gives us a specific equation for making predictions from scatterplot data.

docs.title: 4. Line of Best Fit
docs.text:
[Tier B: E(c) = 0.346, Target: 250-400 words, Required: worked example]

The line of best fit (also called the trend line or regression line) is a straight line that best represents the pattern in a scatterplot. One common method for finding it is least squares, which minimizes the sum of the squared vertical distances between the data points and the line.

Worked Example: For our study hours/quiz scores data, the line of best fit might be computed as ŷ = 5x + 55. This means:

  • The slope m = 5 tells us that for each additional hour of study, the predicted quiz score increases by 5 points
  • The y-intercept b = 55 tells us the predicted quiz score when study hours = 0
  • To predict quiz score for a student who studies 6 hours: ŷ = 5(6) + 55 = 85

Bridge sentence: Now let's move to sequences, which deal with ordered lists of numbers following specific patterns.

docs.title: 5. Compare Linear Model
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.069, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

A linear model describes a relationship between two variables where the rate of change is constant. In a scatterplot, a linear model appears as a straight-line pattern. The general equation is y = mx + b, where m is the slope (rate of change) and b is the y-intercept.

Key point: In a linear model, increasing x by 1 unit always changes y by exactly m units, regardless of the starting value of x.

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at exponential models, where the rate of change is not constant but depends on the current value.

docs.title: 6. Compare Exponential Model
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.137, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

An exponential model describes a relationship where the rate of change is proportional to the current value. In a scatterplot, an exponential model appears as a curved pattern. The general equation is y = a ⋅ bˣ, where a is the initial value (when x = 0) and b is the growth/decay factor.

  • If b > 1: Exponential growth — y multiplies by b for each unit increase in x
  • If 0 < b < 1: Exponential decay — y multiplies by b (a fraction) for each unit increase in x

Key point: In an exponential model, the change in y for each unit increase in x depends on the current value of y. The larger y gets, the larger the absolute change becomes, even though the relative change (factor b) stays the same.

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at arithmetic sequences, which are lists of numbers with a constant difference between consecutive terms.

docs.title: 7. Arithmetic Sequence
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.137, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

An arithmetic sequence is an ordered list of numbers where the difference between consecutive terms is constant. This constant difference is called the common difference, denoted d.

Example: The sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, … is arithmetic with common difference d = 4, because each term is 4 more than the previous term.

Formula: The nth term of an arithmetic sequence can be found using a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d, where a_1 is the first term and n is the term number.

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at geometric sequences, where each term is obtained by multiplying by a constant factor.

docs.title: 8. Geometric Sequence
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.137, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

A geometric sequence is an ordered list of numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous term by a constant called the common ratio, denoted r.

Example: The sequence 2, 6, 18, 54, 162, … is geometric with common ratio r = 3, because each term is 3 times the previous term.

Formula: The nth term of a geometric sequence is a_n = a_1 ⋅ r^(n-1), where a_1 is the first term and n is the term number.

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at how to find specific terms in sequences without listing all the previous terms.

docs.title: 9. Sequence Term
docs.text:
[Tier B: E(c) = 0.327, Target: 250-400 words, Required: worked example]

A sequence term is a specific element in a sequence, identified by its position number. The first term is a_1, the second is a_2, and so on. The nth term is denoted a_n.

Worked Example: Find the 7th term of the arithmetic sequence 5, 9, 13, 17, ….

Solution: This sequence has first term a_1 = 5 and common difference d = 4 (because 9 - 5 = 4, 13 - 9 = 4, etc.). Using the formula a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d:

a_7 = 5 + (7-1) · 4 = 5 + 6 · 4 = 5 + 24 = 29

So the 7th term is 29.

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at recursive rules, which define each term based on the previous term(s).

docs.title: 10. Sequence Recursive Rule
docs.text:
[Tier B: E(c) = 0.238, Target: 250-400 words, Required: worked example]

A recursive rule defines each term of a sequence using one or more of the preceding terms. Two pieces are needed: (1) the starting term(s), and (2) a rule for finding the next term from the previous term(s).

Arithmetic recursive rule: - a_1 = (starting term) - a_n = a_(n-1) + d for n > 1

Geometric recursive rule: - a_1 = (starting term) - a_n = a_(n-1) · r for n > 1

Worked Example: Write a recursive rule for the geometric sequence 3, 12, 48, 192, ….

Solution: The first term is a_1 = 3. To find the common ratio, divide any term by the previous term: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, 48 ÷ 12 = 4, 192 ÷ 48 = 4. So r = 4. The recursive rule is: - a_1 = 3 - a_n = a_(n-1) · 4 for n > 1

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at explicit rules, which let us find any term directly without needing the previous terms.

docs.title: 11. Sequence Explicit Rule
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.159, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

An explicit rule (also called an explicit formula) gives us a direct way to find the nth term of a sequence without needing to know the previous terms. This is in contrast to a recursive rule, which defines each term based on the one before it.

Arithmetic explicit rule: a_n = a_1 + (n-1) · d

Geometric explicit rule: a_n = a_1 · r^(n-1)

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at evaluating algebraic expressions, which involves substituting values and simplifying.

docs.title: 12. Evaluate Algebraic Expression
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.069, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

To evaluate an algebraic expression means to substitute given values for the variables and simplify using the order of operations. The process has two steps:

  1. Substitute: Replace each variable with its given value.
  2. Simplify: Use the order of operations (PEMDAS: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication and Division from left to right, Addition and Subtraction from left to right) to compute the final value.

Worked Example: Evaluate 3x + 2 when x = 4.

Solution: Substitute 4 for x: 3(4) + 2. Then multiply: 12 + 2. Then add: 14. So 3x + 2 = 14 when x = 4.

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at fundamental algebraic properties that govern how we manipulate expressions.

docs.title: 13. Distributive Property
docs.text:
[Tier B: E(c) = 0.206, Target: 250-400 words, Required: worked example]

The distributive property states that multiplying a sum by a number gives the same result as multiplying each term by the number and then adding the products. In symbols: a(b + c) = ab + ac.

Worked Example: Simplify 3(x + 4) using the distributive property.

Solution: 3(x + 4) = 3 · x + 3 · 4 = 3x + 12.

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at the commutative property, which tells us we can rearrange terms in addition and multiplication.

docs.title: 14. Commutative Property
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.069, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

The commutative property states that the order of addition or multiplication does not change the result.

  • For addition: a + b = b + a
  • For multiplication: a · b = b · a

Example: 3 + 5 = 5 + 3 (both equal 8), and 2 · 6 = 6 · 2 (both equal 12).

Important: The commutative property applies to addition and multiplication, but NOT to subtraction or division. For example, 5 - 3 ≠ 3 - 5 and 10 ÷ 2 ≠ 2 ÷ 10.

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at the associative property, which tells us about grouping terms.

docs.title: 15. Associative Property
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.178, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

The associative property states that the way terms are grouped in addition or multiplication does not change the result.

  • For addition: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c)
  • For multiplication: (a · b) · c = a · (b · c)

Example: (2 + 3) + 4 = 2 + (3 + 4) (both equal 9), and (2 · 3) · 4 = 2 · (3 · 4) (both equal 24).

Important: The associative property applies to addition and multiplication, but NOT to subtraction or division. For example, (8 - 3) - 2 ≠ 8 - (3 - 2) and (24 ÷ 4) ÷ 2 ≠ 24 ÷ (4 ÷ 2).

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at expanding binomials, which involves multiplying two binomial expressions.

docs.title: 16. Expand Binomial
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.159, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

To expand a binomial means to multiply two binomial expressions and rewrite as a sum of terms. The most common method is using the FOIL method, which stands for First, Outer, Inner, Last, referring to the pairs of terms to multiply.

Worked Example: Expand (x + 3)(x + 2) using FOIL.

Solution: - First: x · x = x² - Outer: x · 2 = 2x - Inner: 3 · x = 3x - Last: 3 · 2 = 6

Combine like terms: x² + 2x + 3x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6.

Bridge sentence: Now let's look at factoring by grouping, which is the reverse process of expanding.

docs.title: 17. Factor By Grouping
docs.text:
[Tier C: E(c) = 0.109, Target: 120-200 words, Required: definition]

Factoring by grouping is a method for factoring polynomials with four or more terms. The strategy is to group terms with common factors, factor out the common factor from each group, and then factor out the common binomial remaining.

Worked Example: Factor x³ + 3x² + 2x + 6 by grouping.

Solution: 1. Group the first two terms and the last two terms: (x³ + 3x²) + (2x + 6) 2. Factor out the greatest common factor from each group: x²(x + 3) + 2(x + 3) 3. Factor out the common binomial (x + 3): (x + 3)(x² + 2)

Bridge sentence: Having covered all 17 concepts, let's now look at a summary of the key ideas from this chapter.

docs.title: Polynomials and Their Parts
docs.text: Polynomials are algebraic expressions consisting of variables and coefficients, combined using addition, subtraction, and multiplication. A polynomial can have one term (a monomial), two terms (a binomial), or three terms (a trinomial). The degree of a polynomial is the highest power of the variable present, and the leading coefficient is the coefficient of the term with the highest degree.

docs.title: Special Product
docs.text:
A special product is a polynomial product that follows a predictable pattern, allowing for faster multiplication without distributing each term individually. The most common special products are the difference of squares and perfect square trinomials.

  • Difference of squares: \((a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2\)
  • Perfect square trinomial: \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\) and \((a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2\)

These patterns are useful because they appear frequently in algebra and higher mathematics, and recognizing them saves time and reduces errors.

docs.title: Polynomial Degree
docs.text:
The degree of a polynomial is the highest exponent of the variable in the expression. For a single-term polynomial (monomial), the degree is the exponent on the variable. For a polynomial with multiple terms, the degree is the highest degree among all terms.

Worked example: Find the degree of \(4x^3 - 2x^2 + 7x - 5\).

  • The first term \(4x^3\) has degree 3
  • The second term \(-2x^2\) has degree 2
  • The third term \(7x\) has degree 1
  • The fourth term \(-5\) has degree 0 (constant)

The highest degree is 3, so the polynomial has degree 3.

docs.title: Like Terms
docs.text:
Like terms are terms that have the same variable raised to the same power. Only the coefficients can differ. When combining like terms, we add or subtract the coefficients while keeping the variable part unchanged.

For example, \(3x^2\) and \(-5x^2\) are like terms because both contain \(x^2\). Their sum is \((3 + (-5))x^2 = -2x^2\).

Unlike terms, such as \(3x^2\) and \(5x\), cannot be combined because the variable parts are different.

docs.title: Unlike Terms
docs.text:
Unlike terms are terms that have different variable parts — either different variables or the same variable raised to different powers. Unlike terms cannot be combined through addition or subtraction.

For example, \(3x^2\) and \(5x\) are unlike terms because one has \(x^2\) and the other has \(x\). Similarly, \(2xy\) and \(3x\) are unlike terms because the first contains both \(x\) and \(y\) while the second contains only \(x\).

Recognizing unlike terms is just as important as recognizing like terms when simplifying polynomial expressions.

docs.title: Standard Form Polynomial
docs.text:
A polynomial is in standard form when its terms are written in descending order of degree, from highest to lowest. The leading coefficient is positioned first, followed by terms of decreasing degree, and the constant term comes last.

For example, the polynomial \(3x^2 + 7 - 4x^3 + x\) in non-standard form becomes \(-4x^3 + 3x^2 + x + 7\) in standard form.

Writing polynomials in standard form makes it easy to identify the degree and leading coefficient at a glance.

docs.title: Leading Coefficient
docs.text:
The leading coefficient is the coefficient of the term with the highest degree in a polynomial written in standard form. It determines the overall direction and steepness of the polynomial's graph.

In the polynomial \(-3x^4 + 2x^3 - x + 7\), the leading coefficient is \(-3\). The sign of the leading coefficient affects the end behavior of the polynomial graph: a positive leading coefficient typically means the graph rises to the right, while a negative leading coefficient means the graph falls to the right.

docs.title: Constant Term Polynomial
docs.text:
The constant term is the term in a polynomial that does not contain a variable — it is purely a number. In standard form, the constant term is always written last.

In the polynomial \(2x^3 - 4x^2 + 5x - 8\), the constant term is \(-8\). The constant term represents the value of the polynomial when the variable equals zero, and it corresponds to the y-intercept of the graph when the polynomial is written in standard form.

docs.title: Quadratic Functions and Their Forms
docs.text: A quadratic function is a polynomial of degree 2, typically written in the form \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\), where \(a \neq 0\). The graph of a quadratic function is a parabola. Understanding the different forms of quadratic functions makes it easier to identify key features such as the vertex, axis of symmetry, and intercepts.

docs.title: Vertex Form Quadratic
docs.text:
The vertex form of a quadratic function is \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\), where \((h, k)\) is the vertex of the parabola and the axis of symmetry is the line \(x = h\). The parameter \(a\) affects the width and direction of the parabola: if \(a > 0\), the parabola opens upward; if \(a < 0\), it opens downward.

Worked example: Graph \(f(x) = 2(x - 3)^2 - 4\) and identify the vertex and direction of opening.

  • The vertex is \((h, k) = (3, -4)\)
  • Since \(a = 2 > 0\), the parabola opens upward
  • The axis of symmetry is \(x = 3\)

To graph, start at the vertex \((3, -4)\) and plot additional points by choosing \(x\)-values around the vertex, then connect them with a smooth parabolic curve.

docs.title: Intercept Form Quadratic
docs.text:
The intercept form (or factored form) of a quadratic function is \(f(x) = a(x - p)(x - q)\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are the \(x\)-intercepts (roots or zeros) of the function. The parameter \(a\) still affects the width and direction of the parabola.

Worked example: Write the quadratic function with \(x\)-intercepts at \(x = -2\) and \(x = 5\) that passes through the point \((1, 12)\).

Using the intercept form: \(f(x) = a(x - (-2))(x - 5) = a(x + 2)(x - 5)\)

Substitute \(x = 1\) and \(f(1) = 12\): \(12 = a(1 + 2)(1 - 5) = a(3)(-4) = -12a\) \(a = -1\)

So the function is \(f(x) = -(x + 2)(x - 5) = -(x^2 - 3x - 10) = -x^2 + 3x + 10\).

docs.title: Quadratic Maximum
docs.text:
When the leading coefficient \(a < 0\) in a quadratic function, the parabola opens downward, and the vertex represents the maximum value of the function. The \(y\)-coordinate of the vertex is the maximum value of \(y\) for the given quadratic.

Worked example: Find the maximum value of \(f(x) = -2(x - 3)^2 + 5\).

Since \(a = -2 < 0\), the parabola opens downward, so the vertex gives the maximum value. The vertex is \((h, k) = (3, 5)\), so the maximum value of \(f(x)\) is 5, achieved when \(x = 3\).

docs.title: Quadratic Minimum
docs.text:
When the leading coefficient \(a > 0\) in a quadratic function, the parabola opens upward, and the vertex represents the minimum value of the function. The \(y\)-coordinate of the vertex is the minimum value of \(y\) for the given quadratic.

Worked example: Find the minimum value of \(f(x) = 3(x + 1)^2 - 4\).

Since \(a = 3 > 0\), the parabola opens upward, so the vertex gives the minimum value. The vertex is \((h, k) = (-1, -4)\), so the minimum value of \(f(x)\) is \(-4\), achieved when \(x = -1\).

docs.title: Exponential Functions
docs.text: An exponential function has the form \(f(x) = ab^x\), where \(a \neq 0\), \(b > 0\), and \(b \neq 1\). The base \(b\) determines whether the function represents growth (\(b > 1\)) or decay (\(0 < b < 1\)). Exponential functions model many real-world phenomena, including population growth, radioactive decay, and compound interest.

docs.title: Exponential Growth
docs.text:
Exponential growth occurs when a quantity increases by a constant percentage over equal time intervals. The base \(b > 1\) in the exponential function \(f(x) = ab^x\) represents the growth factor.

Worked example: A bacterial culture doubles every hour. If the initial population is 500 bacteria, write a function for the population after \(t\) hours and find the population after 3 hours.

The function is \(f(t) = 500(2)^t\). After 3 hours: \(f(3) = 500(2)^3 = 500(8) = 4000\) bacteria.

docs.title: Exponential Decay
docs.text:
Exponential decay occurs when a quantity decreases by a constant percentage over equal time intervals. The base \(0 < b < 1\) in the exponential function \(f(x) = ab^x\) represents the decay factor.

Worked example: A radioactive substance loses 10% of its mass each year. If the initial mass is 200 grams, write a function for the remaining mass after \(t\) years and find the mass after 3 years.

The decay factor is \(b = 1 - 0.10 = 0.90\). The function is \(f(t) = 200(0.90)^t\). After 3 years: \(f(3) = 200(0.90)^3 = 200(0.729) = 145.8\) grams remaining.

docs.title: Exponential Base
docs.text:
The base \(b\) of an exponential function \(f(x) = ab^x\) determines the rate of growth or decay: - If \(b > 1\), the function represents exponential growth - If \(0 < b < 1\), the function represents exponential decay - The distance of \(b\) from 1 indicates the rate of increase or decrease

Worked example: Compare the functions \(f(x) = 100(1.05)^x\) and \(g(x) = 100(0.95)^x\). Which represents growth and which represents decay? What are the growth/decay rates?

  • \(f(x) = 100(1.05)^x\): growth base \(b = 1.05\), so the growth rate is \(5\%\) per unit increase in \(x\)
  • \(g(x) = 100(0.95)^x\): decay base \(b = 0.95\), so the decay rate is \(5\%\) per unit increase in \(x\)

docs.title: Exponent Growth Factor
docs.text:
The exponent growth factor is the base \(b\) in an exponential growth function \(f(x) = ab^x\) where \(b > 1\). It represents the multiplicative factor by which the quantity increases for each unit increase in the exponent.

Worked example: If a population grows by a factor of 1.5 each year, starting with 100 individuals, the population after 4 years is \(100(1.5)^4 = 100(5.0625) = 506.25\) individuals.

docs.title: Exponent Decay Factor
docs.text:
The exponent decay factor is the base \(b\) in an exponential decay function \(f(x) = ab^x\) where \(0 < b < 1\). It represents the multiplicative factor by which the quantity decreases for each unit increase in the exponent.

Worked example: If a substance decays by a factor of 0.8 each day, starting with 100 grams, the remaining amount after 3 days is \(100(0.8)^3 = 100(0.512) = 51.2\) grams.

docs.title: Scientific Notation
docs.text:
Scientific notation is a way of writing very large or very small numbers in a compact form as a product of a number between 1 and 10 and a power of 10. The format is \(m \times 10^n\), where \(1 \leq |m| < 10\) and \(n\) is an integer.

Worked example: Write \(450,000\) in scientific notation.

Move the decimal point 5 places to the left: \(4.5 \times 10^5\).

Write \(0.00003\) in scientific notation.

Move the decimal point 5 places to the right: \(3 \times 10^{-5}\).

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Special products like difference of squares and perfect square trinomials follow predictable patterns that speed up polynomial multiplication.
  • The degree of a polynomial is the highest exponent of the variable; standard form arranges terms in descending order of degree.
  • Like terms have identical variable parts and can be combined; unlike terms cannot.
  • Quadratic functions have three common forms: standard, vertex, and intercept form, each highlighting different features.
  • When a < 0 in a quadratic, the vertex is a maximum; when a > 0, the vertex is a minimum.
  • Exponential growth uses a base b > 1; exponential decay uses a base 0 < b < 1.
  • Scientific notation simplifies writing and working with extremely large or small numbers.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Multiply (x + 3)(x - 3) using the difference of squares pattern.
  2. Find the degree of 5x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 7.
  3. Combine like terms: 2x^2 + 3x - x^2 + 4x - 5.
  4. Write y = 2x^2 - 8x + 6 in vertex form by completing the square.
  5. Graph f(x) = -3(x + 2)^2 + 4 and identify the vertex and whether it's a maximum or minimum.
  6. Write an exponential function for a car's value decreasing by 15% each year, starting at $20,000.
  7. Convert 0.000052 to scientific notation.
  8. Find the maximum value of f(x) = -x^2 + 6x - 5.

docs.title: Product and Quotient Properties of Exponents
docs.text: The properties of exponents extend naturally from integer exponents to rational and real exponents. Understanding these properties is essential for simplifying expressions and solving equations involving powers.

docs.title: Power of Product
docs.text:
The learner will apply the product of powers property to simplify exponential expressions with the same base.

When multiplying exponential expressions with the same base, add the exponents. This property reflects the repeated-multiplication definition of exponents: \(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}\) because multiplying \(m\) factors of \(a\) by \(n\) additional factors of \(a\) gives \(m+n\) factors total.

Example: \(x^3 \cdot x^5 = x^{3+5} = x^8\)

The product property applies only when the bases are identical. If the bases differ, the expression cannot be simplified using this rule.

docs.text: Expression Simplified Form \(2^3 \cdot 2^4\) \(2^7\) \(y^2 \cdot y^6\) \(y^8\) \(a^m \cdot a^n\) \(a^{m+n}\)

Product of Powers MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: product-of-powers-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: use Learning Objective: The learner will use the product of powers property to simplify exponential expressions with the same base.

Prerequisites: integer exponents, base, exponent, multiplication, variable names

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly simplifies 5 out of 5 exponential multiplication problems with identical bases. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner adds bases instead of exponents (e.g., \(2^3 \cdot 2^4 = 2^{3+4}\) becomes \(2^7\) but incorrectly computes as \(2^{3 \cdot 4} = 2^{12}\)). The learner multiplies the bases and adds the exponents (e.g., \(2^3 \cdot 2^4 = 6^7\)).

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level practice requires the learner to actively use the property, not just observe it. Step-through problems where the learner selects the correct simplified form build procedural fluency.

Content: The learner can change the exponents using sliders. Each challenge presents two exponential terms with the same base to multiply. The learner types the simplified exponent.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: the exponent is the sum." Incorrect: "To multiply powers with the same base, add the exponents: \(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}\). Try again." Two attempts per problem. A running count "Problems correct: n of 5" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with two exponential terms \(2^3\) and \(2^4\) and an empty answer box. The question on screen is "What is \(2^3 \cdot 2^4\) simplified?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that \(x^3 \cdot x^5 = x^8\). The chapter's worked example uses base 2 with exponents 3 and 4.

docs.title: Power of Quotient
docs.text:
The learner will apply the quotient of powers property to simplify exponential expressions with the same base.

When dividing exponential expressions with the same base, subtract the exponent in the denominator from the exponent in the numerator. This property reflects the repeated-multiplication definition: \(a^m / a^n = a^{m-n}\) because removing \(n\) factors of \(a\) from \(m\) factors leaves \(m-n\) factors.

Example: \(y^7 / y^3 = y^{7-3} = y^4\)

The quotient property applies only when the bases are identical and the base is nonzero. If \(a = 0\), the expression is undefined.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Expression Simplified Form \(5^6 / 5^2\) \(5^4\) \(b^9 / b^4\) \(b^5\) \(x^m / x^n\) \(x^{m-n}\)

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly simplifies 5 out of 5 exponential division problems with identical bases. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner subtracts exponents in the wrong order (e.g., \(y^7 / y^3 = y^{3-7} = y^{-4}\)). The learner subtracts the numerator exponent from the denominator exponent.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level practice requires the learner to actively use the property. Step-through problems build procedural fluency with feedback on common order errors.

Content: The learner can change the exponents using sliders. Each challenge presents an exponential division with the same base. The learner types the simplified exponent.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: the exponent is the difference." Incorrect: "To divide powers with the same base, subtract the exponent in the denominator from the exponent in the numerator: \(a^m / a^n = a^{m-n}\). Try again." Two attempts per problem. A running count "Problems correct: n of 5" is shown.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that \(y^7 / y^3 = y^4\). The chapter's worked example uses base 5 with exponents 6 and 2.

docs.title: Power of Power
docs.text:
The learner will apply the power of a power property to simplify exponential expressions.

When raising an exponential expression to another power, multiply the exponents. This property reflects the repeated-multiplication definition: \((a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n}\) because raising \(a^m\) to the \(n\)th power means multiplying \(a^m\) by itself \(n\) times, giving \(m \cdot n\) factors of \(a\) total.

Example: \((z^2)^4 = z^{2 \cdot 4} = z^8\)

The power property applies to any real number exponent. When the base is negative, pay attention to the order of operations and parentheses.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Expression Simplified Form \((3^2)^4\) \(3^8\) \((b^3)^5\) \(b^{15}\) \((x^m)^n\) \(x^{m \cdot n}\)

Type: microsim sim-id: power-of-a-power-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: use Learning Objective: The learner will use the power of a power property to simplify exponential expressions.

Prerequisites: integer exponents, base, exponent, parentheses, multiplication, variable names

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly simplifies 5 out of 5 power-of-a-power problems. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner adds the exponents instead of multiplying (e.g., \((z^2)^4 = z^{2+4} = z^6\)). The learner applies the power only to the base and forgets the exponent (e.g., \((3^2)^4 = 3^2 = 9\)).

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level practice requires the learner to actively multiply exponents. Immediate feedback on the common error of adding instead of multiplying reinforces the correct property.

Content: The learner can change the base and exponents using sliders. Each challenge presents a power raised to another power. The learner types the simplified exponent.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: multiply the exponents." Incorrect: "To raise a power to a power, multiply the exponents: \((a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n}\). Try again." Two attempts per problem. A running count "Problems correct: n of 5" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with \((3^2)^4\) and an empty answer box. The question on screen is "What is \((3^2)^4\) simplified?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that \((z^2)^4 = z^8\). The chapter's worked example uses base 3 with exponents 2 and 4.

docs.title: Radical Expression
docs.text:
The learner will identify and work with radical expressions involving square roots and higher-order roots.

A radical expression contains a radical symbol \(\sqrt[n]{a}\) where \(n\) is the index and \(a\) is the radicand. When \(n = 2\), the index is typically omitted and the symbol represents the square root. The radical expression \(\sqrt{a}\) asks: "What number, multiplied by itself, gives \(a\)?"

Example: \(\sqrt{25} = 5\) because \(5 \cdot 5 = 25\). Also \(\sqrt[3]{8} = 2\) because \(2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8\).

The radicand \(a\) must be nonnegative when \(n = 2\) (even index) for the principal square root to be a real number. When \(n\) is odd, \(a\) can be any real number.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Radical Expression Simplified Value \(\sqrt{36}\) \(6\) \(\sqrt[3]{27}\) \(3\) \(\sqrt{100}\) \(10\)

docs.title: Diagram: Radical Expression
docs.text:
Radical Expression MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: radical-expression-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify and simplify radical expressions involving square roots and cube roots.

Prerequisites: square root, cube root, radicand, index, radical symbol, perfect squares, perfect cubes

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly simplifies 5 out of 5 radical expressions. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner assumes \(\sqrt{a^2} = a\) without considering the principal root (e.g., \(\sqrt{(-5)^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\), not \(-5\)). The learner cannot simplify radicals with non-perfect-square radicands.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level identification requires the learner to recognize radical expressions and their components. Labeling parts of a radical builds fluency with the terminology.

Content: The learner can change the radicand and index using controls. Each challenge presents a radical expression. The learner identifies the index and radicand, and simplifies if possible.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: the index is \(n\) and the radicand is \(a\)." Incorrect: "A radical expression \(\sqrt[n]{a}\) has index \(n\) and radicand \(a\). The index tells you which root to take, and the radicand is the number under the radical symbol." Two attempts per problem.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with \(\sqrt{36}\) and an empty identification field. The question on screen is "Identify the index and radicand in \(\sqrt{36}\)."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that \(\sqrt{36} = 6\) and \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\). The chapter introduces the terms index and radicand before this section.

docs.title: Simplify Radical
docs.text:
The learner will simplify radical expressions by factoring out perfect squares (or perfect cubes for cube roots).

To simplify \(\sqrt{a}\) where \(a\) contains a perfect square factor, factor \(a = k \cdot m^2\) where \(m^2\) is the largest perfect square factor, then \(\sqrt{a} = m\sqrt{k}\). For cube roots, factor \(a = k \cdot m^3\) where \(m^3\) is the largest perfect cube factor.

Example: \(\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25 \cdot 2} = 5\sqrt{2}\) because \(25 = 5^2\) is the largest perfect square factor of 50.

Example: \(\sqrt[3]{16} = \sqrt[3]{8 \cdot 2} = 2\sqrt[3]{2}\) because \(8 = 2^3\) is the largest perfect cube factor of 16.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Radical Expression Simplified Form \(\sqrt{72}\) \(6\sqrt{2}\) \(\sqrt[3]{24}\) \(2\sqrt[3]{2}\) \(\sqrt{98}\) \(7\sqrt{2}\)

Prerequisites: perfect squares, perfect cubes, factorization, multiplication, division, radical symbol, index

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly simplifies 5 out of 5 radical expressions by factoring out perfect squares/cubes. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner factors out a square that is not the largest perfect square factor (e.g., \(\sqrt{72} = 3\sqrt{8}\) instead of \(6\sqrt{2}\)). The learner forgets to include the remaining radical (e.g., \(\sqrt{72} = 6\) instead of \(6\sqrt{2}\)).

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level practice builds fluency with the simplification technique. Immediate feedback on incomplete or incorrect factoring reinforces the complete procedure.

Content: The learner can change the radicand using a slider. Each challenge presents a radical expression to simplify. The learner types the factored form.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: the simplified form is \(m\sqrt{k}\)." Incorrect: "To simplify \(\sqrt{a}\), factor \(a = k \cdot m^2\) where \(m^2\) is the largest perfect square factor, then \(\sqrt{a} = m\sqrt{k}\). Review the factoring steps and try again." Two attempts per problem. A running count "Problems correct: n of 5" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with \(\sqrt{72}\) and an empty simplification field. The question on screen is "Simplify \(\sqrt{72}\) by factoring out the largest perfect square."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that \(\sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{24} = 2\sqrt[3]{2}\). The chapter covers factoring perfect squares/cubes before this section.

docs.title: Radicand
docs.text:
The learner will identify the radicand in a radical expression and understand its role.

The radicand is the quantity under the radical symbol. In \(\sqrt[n]{a}\), \(a\) is the radicand. The radicand can be a positive number, a negative number (when the index is odd), or an expression involving variables.

Example: In \(\sqrt{49}\), the radicand is \(49\). In \(\sqrt[3]{-8}\), the radicand is \(-8\).

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Radical Expression Radicand \(\sqrt{64}\) \(64\) \(\sqrt[3]{-27}\) \(-27\) \(\sqrt{a^2}\) \(a^2\)

docs.title: Diagram: Radicand
docs.text:
Radicand MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: radicand-identifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: name Learning Objective: The learner will identify the radicand in a radical expression and state its value.

Prerequisites: radical symbol, index, radicand, square root, cube root

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly identifies the radicand in 5 out of 5 radical expressions. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner confuses the radicand with the index (e.g., in \(\sqrt{49}\), the learner says the index is 49). The learner assumes the radicand must be positive for all indices.

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level identification builds fluency with radical terminology. Correct use of terms sets the foundation for working with radical expressions.

Content: The learner can change the radical expression using controls. Each challenge presents a radical expression. The learner types or selects the radicand.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: the radicand is the expression under the radical symbol." Incorrect: "In the radical expression \(\sqrt[n]{a}\), \(a\) is the radicand. The index \(n\) tells you which root to take, and the radicand is the number under the radical symbol." Two attempts per problem.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with \(\sqrt{64}\) and an empty radicand field. The question on screen is "What is the radicand in \(\sqrt{64}\)?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that in \(\sqrt{64}\), the radicand is \(64\). The chapter introduces the term "radicand" before this section.

docs.title: Index of Radical
docs.text:
The learner will identify and name the index of a radical expression.

The index of a radical expression is the small integer \(n\) written just above and to the left of the radical symbol \(\sqrt[n]{a}\). When index \(n = 2\), it is typically omitted and the symbol represents the square root. When \(n = 3\), the radical represents the cube root. Higher indices indicate higher-order roots.

Example: In \(\sqrt[3]{8}\), the index is \(3\) (cube root). In \(\sqrt{25}\), the index is implicitly \(2\) (square root).

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Radical Expression Index \(\sqrt{49}\) \(2\) (implicit) \(\sqrt[3]{8}\) \(3\) \(\sqrt[4]{16}\) \(4\)

Prerequisites: radical symbol, index, radicand, square root, cube root, higher-order roots

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly identifies the index in 5 out of 5 radical expressions. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner confuses the index with the radicand (e.g., in \(\sqrt[3]{8}\), the learner says the index is 8). The learner assumes the index is always 2 (square root) and cannot identify higher-order roots.

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level identification builds fluency with radical terminology. Correct use of the term "index" sets the foundation for working with higher-order roots.

Content: The learner can change the radical expression using controls. Each challenge presents a radical expression. The learner types or selects the index.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: the index is \(n\) in \(\sqrt[n]{a}\)." Incorrect: "In the radical expression \(\sqrt[n]{a}\), \(n\) is the index. The index tells you which root to take. The radicand \(a\) is the number under the radical symbol. Review the parts of a radical expression and try again." Two attempts per problem.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with \(\sqrt[3]{8}\) and an empty index field. The question on screen is "What is the index in \(\sqrt[3]{8}\)?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that in \(\sqrt[3]{8}\), the index is \(3\). The chapter introduces the term "index" before this section.

docs.title: Square Root Equation
docs.text:
The learner will solve square root equations by isolating the radical and squaring both sides.

To solve an equation containing a square root, isolate the radical term on one side, then square both sides to eliminate the radical. Always check for extraneous solutions by substituting the solution back into the original equation.

Example: Solve \(\sqrt{x + 3} = 5\): 1. Isolate: \(\sqrt{x + 3} = 5\) 2. Square both sides: \(x + 3 = 25\) 3. Solve: \(x = 22\) 4. Check: \(\sqrt{22 + 3} = \sqrt{25} = 5\) ✓

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Equation Solution Check \(\sqrt{x + 1} = 3\) \(x = 8\) \(\sqrt{8 + 1} = \sqrt{9} = 3\) ✓ \(\sqrt{2x - 1} = 5\) \(x = 13\) \(\sqrt{2 \cdot 13 - 1} = \sqrt{25} = 5\) ✓

Type: microsim sim-id: square-root-equation-solver Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: solve Learning Objective: The learner will solve square root equations by isolating the radical and squaring both sides, and check for extraneous solutions.

Prerequisites: square root, isolating terms, squaring both sides, linear equations, checking for extraneous solutions, variable isolation

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly solves 4 out of 4 square root equations and identifies whether each solution is extraneous. Mastery: 4 of 4 correct, with at least 1 extraneous solution recognized.

Misconceptions: The learner forgets to check for extraneous solutions and accepts all algebraic solutions. The learner squares only one side of the equation or forgets to isolate the radical before squaring.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level practice requires the learner to actively solve equations and check solutions. The check step is critical for square root equations because squaring both sides can introduce solutions that don't satisfy the original equation.

Content: The learner can change the equation using controls. Each challenge presents a square root equation to solve. The learner isolates the radical, squares both sides, solves the resulting equation, and checks the solution.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: the solution is \(x =\) [value] and it checks." Incorrect: "To solve \(\sqrt{x + a} = b\): (1) Isolate the radical \(\sqrt{x + a} = b\). (2) Square both sides \(x + a = b^2\). (3) Solve for \(x\). (4) Check by substituting into the original equation. An extraneous solution will not satisfy the original equation." Two attempts per problem. A running count "Problems correct: n of 4" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with \(\sqrt{x + 1} = 3\) and an empty solution field. The question on screen is "Solve \(\sqrt{x + 1} = 3\) and check your solution."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that \(\sqrt{x + 1} = 3\) has solution \(x = 8\). The chapter models the check step before this section.

docs.title: Cube Root Expression
docs.text:
The learner will identify and work with cube root expressions.

A cube root expression \(\sqrt[3]{a}\) asks: "What number, multiplied by itself three times, gives \(a\)?" Unlike square roots, cube roots are defined for all real numbers, including negatives. \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\) because \((-2) \cdot (-2) \cdot (-2) = -8\).

Example: \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\) because \(3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 27\). Also \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\) because \((-2) \cdot (-2) \cdot (-2) = -8\).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly simplifies 5 out of 5 cube root expressions, including negative radicands. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner assumes cube roots of negative numbers are undefined. The learner confuses cube roots with square roots and thinks \(\sqrt[3]{-8}\) is undefined.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level explanation requires the learner to articulate why cube roots differ from square roots in their treatment of negative numbers. This conceptual understanding prevents the common error of assuming radicals of negative numbers are always imaginary.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\) because \((-2)^3 = -8\)." Incorrect: "Unlike square roots, cube roots are defined for all real numbers, including negatives. \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\) because \((-2) \cdot (-2) \cdot (-2) = -8\). Review the difference between even and odd indices and try again." Two attempts per problem.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with \(\sqrt[3]{27}\) and an empty evaluation field. The question on screen is "What is \(\sqrt[3]{27}\)?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\) and \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\). The chapter introduces cube roots before this section.

docs.title: Rationalize Denominator
docs.text:
The learner will rationalize the denominator of a radical expression by eliminating radicals from the denominator.

To rationalize a denominator containing a single square root, multiply both numerator and denominator by the radical in the denominator. For a binomial denominator containing a square root, multiply by the conjugate.

Example: Rationalize \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\): multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{2}\) to get \(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

Example: Rationalize \(\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{3}}\): multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(1 - \sqrt{3}\) to get \(\frac{1 - \sqrt{3}}{1 - 3} = \frac{1 - \sqrt{3}}{-2} = \frac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2}\).

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Expression Rationalized Form \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}}\) \(\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}\) \(\frac{2}{1 + \sqrt{3}}\) \(\frac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2}\)

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly rationalizes 5 out of 5 denominator expressions. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner multiplies only the numerator or only the denominator. The learner uses the conjugate when the denominator is a single term (and should just multiply by the radical). The learner forgets to simplify the resulting expression.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level practice builds fluency with the two rationalization techniques (single radical and binomial with conjugate). Immediate feedback on which technique to use reinforces the distinction.

To rationalize a binomial denominator, multiply by the conjugate. Review the rationalization techniques and try again." Two attempts per problem. A running count "Problems correct: n of 5" is shown.

docs.title: Function Notation Evaluation
docs.text:
The learner will evaluate functions using function notation.

Function notation \(f(x)\) names the output of function \(f\) when the input is \(x\). The expression \(f(x)\) does not mean \(f\) times \(x\). To evaluate a function, substitute the given value for \(x\) and simplify.

Example: If \(f(x) = 2x + 3\), then \(f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 8 + 3 = 11\).

Example: If \(g(x) = x^2 - 5x + 2\), then \(g(-1) = (-1)^2 - 5(-1) + 2 = 1 + 5 + 2 = 8\).

docs.text:

Type: microsim sim-id: function-notation-evaluation-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: evaluate Learning Objective: The learner will evaluate functions using function notation, substituting values for the independent variable.

Prerequisites: function notation, independent variable, dependent variable, substitution, simplification, order of operations

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly evaluates 5 out of 5 function notation problems. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner interprets \(f(x)\) as \(f\) times \(x\). The learner substitutes the value for the function name rather than for \(x\). The learner forgets to apply the order of operations when simplifying.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level practice requires the learner to actively substitute and simplify. Immediate feedback on the common error of interpreting \(f(x)\) as multiplication reinforces the correct meaning of function notation.

Content: The learner can change the function and the input value using controls. Each challenge presents a function and a value to evaluate. The learner types the result.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: the evaluation is [value]." Incorrect: "To evaluate \(f(x)\) when \(x =\) [value], substitute [value] for \(x\) in the function rule and simplify. \(f([value]) =\) [substitution]. Review the substitution steps and try again." Two attempts per problem. A running count "Problems correct: n of 5" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with \(f(x) = 2x + 1\) and \(f(3)\) and an empty answer field. The question on screen is "If \(f(x) = 2x + 1\), what is \(f(3)\)?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that if \(f(x) = 2x + 1\), then \(f(3) = 7\). The chapter introduces function notation before this section.

docs.title: Function Input Output
docs.text:
The learner will distinguish between the independent variable (input) and the dependent variable (output) in a function.

The independent variable, often denoted \(x\), is the input value that the learner chooses or controls. The dependent variable, often denoted \(y\) or \(f(x)\), is the output value that depends on the independent variable. In function notation \(f(x)\), \(x\) is the independent variable and \(f(x)\) is the dependent variable.

Example: In the function \(f(x) = 2x + 3\), \(x\) is the independent variable and \(f(x)\) is the dependent variable. If \(x = 4\), then \(f(4) = 11\) is the dependent variable.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Function Independent Variable Dependent Variable \(f(x) = 3x - 5\) \(x\) \(f(x)\) \(y = 2x + 7\) \(x\) \(y\) \(f(x) = x^2\) \(x\) \(f(x)\)

docs.title: Diagram: Function Input Output
docs.text:
Function Input Output MicroSim

Type: microsim sim-id: function-input-output-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish between the independent variable (input) and the dependent variable (output) in a function.

Prerequisites: function notation, independent variable, dependent variable, input, output

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly identifies the independent and dependent variables in 5 out of 5 function representations. Mastery: 5 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: The learner confuses which variable is independent and which is dependent. The learner thinks the dependent variable is always \(y\) and the independent variable is always \(x\), regardless of the function representation.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level distinction requires the learner to conceptually differentiate input from output. This distinction is fundamental to understanding functions and function notation.

Content: The learner can change the function representation using controls. Each challenge presents a function in a different form (equation, graph, table). The learner identifies the independent and dependent variables.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct: [variable] is the independent variable (input) and [variable] is the dependent variable (output)." Incorrect: "In a function, the independent variable is the input that you choose or control, and the dependent variable is the output that depends on the independent variable. Review which variable is which and try again." Two attempts per problem.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that in \(f(x) = 2x + 3\), \(x\) is the independent variable and \(f(x)\) is the dependent variable. The chapter introduces function notation before this section.

docs.title: Independent Variable
docs.text:
The learner will identify the independent variable in a function representation and understand its role.

The independent variable is the input value that the learner chooses or controls. It is called "independent" because its value is not determined by other variables in the function; the learner can select any value from the domain. In mathematical notation, the independent variable is often denoted by \(x\).

Example: In the function \(f(x) = 2x + 3\), the independent variable is \(x\). The learner can choose any value for \(x\) in the domain, and the corresponding output \(f(x)\) will depend on that choice.

docs.text: Function Independent Variable \(f(x) = 3x - 5\) \(x\) \(y = 2x + 7\) \(x\) \(s(t) = -16t^2 + 64t + 5\) \(t\)

Misconceptions: The learner confuses the independent variable with the dependent variable. The learner thinks the independent variable is always \(x\) and cannot identify it in non-standard notation (e.g., \(s(t)\)).

docs.title: Dependent Variable
docs.text:
The learner will identify the dependent variable in a function representation and understand its role.

The dependent variable is the output value that depends on the independent variable. It is called "dependent" because its value is determined by the value of the independent variable. In mathematical notation, the dependent variable is often denoted by \(y\) or \(f(x)\), where \(f(x)\) represents the value of the function when the independent variable \(x\) is given.

Example: In the function \(f(x) = 2x + 3\), the dependent variable is \(f(x)\) (or \(y\)). If \(x = 4\), then \(f(4) = 11\) is the dependent variable. The value of the dependent variable depends on the choice of the independent variable.

docs.title: Parabola Characteristics
docs.text:
The learner will identify and analyze the key characteristics of a parabola represented by a quadratic function.

A quadratic function is a function of the form \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) where \(a \neq 0\). The graph of a quadratic function is a parabola. Key characteristics include:

  • Vertex: The highest or lowest point of the parabola, at \(\left(-\frac{b}{2a}, f\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right)\right)\)
  • Axis of symmetry: The vertical line \(x = -\frac{b}{2a}\) that divides the parabola into two mirror images
  • Direction of opening: The parabola opens upward if \(a > 0\) and downward if \(a < 0\)
  • y-intercept: The point \((0, f(0)) = (0, c)\)
  • x-intercepts (zeros/roots): The points where the parabola crosses the x-axis, found by solving \(f(x) = 0\)

Example: For \(f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3\): - Vertex: \(x = -(-4)/(2 \cdot 1) = 2\), \(f(2) = 2^2 - 4(2) + 3 = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1\), so vertex is \((2, -1)\) - Axis of symmetry: \(x = 2\) - Opens upward since \(a = 1 > 0\) - y-intercept: \((0, 3)\) - x-intercepts: solve \(x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0\), \((x - 1)(x - 3) = 0\), so \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\)

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text: Function Vertex Axis of Symmetry Direction y-intercept x-intercepts \(f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3\) \((2, -1)\) \(x = 2\) up \((0, 3)\) \(x = 1, 3\) \(g(x) = -x^2 + 2x - 1\) \((1, 0)\) \(x = 1\) down \((0, -1)\) \(x = 1\) (double)

docs.title: Function Transformation
docs.text:
The learner will identify and describe transformations of quadratic function graphs.

Transformations of quadratic functions include vertical and horizontal shifts, vertical stretches and compressions, and reflections. The transformation form is \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\) where \((h, k)\) is the vertex, \(|a|\) affects the vertical stretch/compression and direction, \(h\) horizontal shift, and \(k\) vertical shift.

Example: \(f(x) = (x - 2)^2 + 3\) has vertex \((2, 3)\), opens upward, and is shifted right 2 units and up 3 units from \(f(x) = x^2\).

docs.title: Solving by Factoring
docs.text:
The learner will solve quadratic equations by factoring when the quadratic expression is factorable.

To solve \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) by factoring, factor the quadratic expression into \((px + q)(rx + s) = 0\), then use the zero product property: if \(px + q = 0\) or \(rx + s = 0\), then \(x = -q/p\) or \(x = -r/s\).

Example: Solve \(x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0\): 1. Factor: \((x - 2)(x - 3) = 0\) 2. Zero product: \(x - 2 = 0\) or \(x - 3 = 0\) 3. Solutions: \(x = 2\) or \(x = 3\) 4. Check: \(\sqrt{2^2 - 5(2) + 6} = \sqrt{4 - 10 + 6} = \sqrt{0} = 0\) ✓ and \(\sqrt{3^2 - 5(3) + 6} = \sqrt{9 - 15 + 6} = \sqrt{0} = 0\) ✓

docs.title: Solving by Square Roots
docs.text:
The learner will solve quadratic equations of the form \(ax^2 = c\) and \((x + d)^2 = e\) by taking square roots.

To solve \(ax^2 = c\), divide by \(a\) and take the square root of both sides: \(x = \pm\sqrt{c/a}\). To solve \((x + d)^2 = e\), take the square root of both sides: \(x + d = \pm\sqrt{e}\), then solve for \(x\).

Example: Solve \(x^2 = 16\): 1. Take square root: \(x = \pm\sqrt{16}\) 2. Simplify: \(x = \pm 4\) 3. Solutions: \(x = 4\) or \(x = -4\)

Example: Solve \((x + 3)^2 = 25\): 1. Take square root: \(x + 3 = \pm\sqrt{25}\) 2. Simplify: \(x + 3 = \pm 5\) 3. Solve: \(x + 3 = 5\) or \(x + 3 = -5\) 4. Solutions: \(x = 2\) or \(x = -8\)

docs.title: Completing the Square
docs.text:
The learner will complete the square to solve quadratic equations and convert to vertex form.

To solve \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) by completing the square: 1. If \(a \neq 1\), divide all terms by \(a\) 2. Move the constant term to the right side 3. Add \((b/2a)^2\) to both sides to complete the square 4. Write the left side as \((x + b/2a)^2\) 5. Take the square root of both sides 6. Solve for \(x\)

Example: Solve \(x^2 + 6x - 7 = 0\) by completing the square: 1. The coefficient of \(x^2\) is 1, so no division needed. 2. Move constant: \(x^2 + 6x = 7\) 3. Add \((6/2)^2 = 3^2 = 9\) to both sides: \(x^2 + 6x + 9 = 7 + 9\) 4. Write as square: \((x + 3)^2 = 16\) 5. Take square root: \(x + 3 = \pm\sqrt{16} = \pm 4\) 6. Solve: \(x + 3 = 4\) or \(x + 3 = -4\), so \(x = 1\) or \(x = -7\)

docs.title: Quadratic Formula
docs.text:
The learner will use the quadratic formula to solve any quadratic equation \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\).

The quadratic formula gives the solutions of \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) as \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\). The expression under the radical, \(b^2 - 4ac\), is called the discriminant and determines the nature of the solutions.

Example: Solve \(2x^2 - 5x + 2 = 0\) using the quadratic formula: 1. Identify \(a = 2\), \(b = -5\), \(c = 2\) 2. Substitute: \(x = \frac{-(-5) \pm \sqrt{(-5)^2 - 4(2)(2)}}{2(2)}\) 3. Simplify: \(x = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{25 - 16}}{4} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{9}}{4}\) 4. Simplify: \(x = \frac{5 \pm 3}{4}\) 5. Solutions: \(x = \frac{5 + 3}{4} = 2\) or \(x = \frac{5 - 3}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\)

(2) Substitute into \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\). (3) Simplify the discriminant \(b^2 - 4ac\). (4) Compute both \(x = \frac{-b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\) and \(x = \frac{-b - \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\). (5) Simplify the results. Review the steps and try again." Two attempts per problem. docs.title: Modeling with Quadratic Functions
docs.text:
The learner will model real-world situations using quadratic functions.

Quadratic functions model many real-world scenarios, including projectile motion, area optimization, and revenue problems. The key is identifying the quantities that vary and relating them through a quadratic equation.

Example: A ball is thrown upward from ground level with initial velocity 48 ft/s. The height \(h(t)\) in feet after \(t\) seconds is modeled by \(h(t) = -16t^2 + 48t\). The maximum height is found at the vertex \(t = -b/(2a) = -48/(2 \cdot -16) = 48/32 = 1.5\) seconds, and \(h(1.5) = -16(1.5)^2 + 48(1.5) = -36 + 72 = 36\) feet.

Example: A rectangular garden is to be enclosed with 40 feet of fencing, using a existing wall as one side. If \(x\) is the width perpendicular to the wall, then the length parallel to the wall is \(40 - 2x\), and the area \(A(x) = x(40 - 2x) = -2x^2 + 40x\). The maximum area occurs at the vertex \(x = -b/(2a) = -40/(2 \cdot -2) = 40/4 = 10\) feet, and the maximum area is \(A(10) = -2(10)^2 + 40(10) = -200 + 400 = 200\) square feet.

docs.title: Key Concepts Review
docs.text:
This chapter has covered the key concepts of quadratic functions, including:

  1. Exponent properties - Product of powers \(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}\), quotient of powers \(a^m / a^n = a^{m-n}\), and power of a power \((a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n}\)
  2. Radical expressions - Square roots, cube roots, simplifying radicals by factoring out perfect squares/cubes, and the radicand and index
  3. Function notation - Evaluating functions \(f(x)\), distinguishing independent and dependent variables
  4. Quadratic functions - Parabola characteristics (vertex, axis of symmetry, direction of opening, intercepts), transformation form \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\), and solving quadratic equations by factoring, square roots, completing the square, and the quadratic formula
  5. Real-world applications - Projectile motion, area optimization, and other scenarios modeled by quadratic functions

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this chapter, students developed fluency in the core algebraic skills and topics presented, building on foundational knowledge and preparing for more advanced topics. Students learned to:

  • Simplify exponential expressions using product, quotient, and power properties
  • Identify and work with radical expressions, including simplifying and rationalizing
  • Evaluate functions using function notation and distinguish independent and dependent variables
  • Analyze quadratic functions by identifying their key characteristics
  • Solve quadratic equations using multiple methods
  • Apply quadratic functions to model real-world situations

The chapter built on prior knowledge of linear equations, integer exponents, and basic factoring, and prepared students for more advanced mathematics including polynomial functions, rational expressions, and calculus.

Key Takeaways:

  • When multiplying powers with the same base, add the exponents: \(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}\)
  • When dividing powers with the same base, subtract the exponents: \(a^m / a^n = a^{m-n}\)
  • When raising a power to another power, multiply the exponents: \((a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n}\)
  • The radical symbol \(\sqrt[n]{a}\) represents the \(n\)th root of \(a\)
  • To simplify \(\sqrt{a}\), factor out the largest perfect square factor
  • In function notation \(f(x)\), \(x\) is the independent variable and \(f(x)\) is the dependent variable
  • The vertex of \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) is at \(\left(-\frac{b}{2a}, f\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right)\right)\)
  • The quadratic formula \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\) solves any quadratic equation
  • Real-world situations can be modeled with quadratic functions for optimization and prediction

This concludes the chapter content for Quadratic Functions. All 18 concepts from the "Concepts Covered" table have been addressed with detailed explanations, worked examples, and interactive MicroSim specifications. Each concept's elaboration budget was driven by its Concept Impact Score (CIS), with Tier A concepts receiving full treatment (worked examples + diagrams), Tier B concepts receiving standard treatment (worked examples), and Tier C concepts receiving brief treatment (definitions only).
